generated_text: …and honestly, Sarah, the whole place was rammed! I nearly didn’t recognise half the faces. It was ages since I’d been out properly, you know? Just…grown-up time. I can imagine! You deserved it, love. You’ve been practically chained to Leo since he was born. Did you have a good time with Chloe and Mark? Oh, they were brilliant. Chloe’s looking absolutely radiant, even though little Thomas is teething something awful. Apparently, he’s been up every two hours. Poor Mark looks exhausted. Anyway, we ended up at that new tapas place on Gas Street. Really good, actually. Bit pricey, mind, but you get what you pay for. Gas Street, eh? Been meaning to try that. Is it noisy? I don't fancy another evening shouting across the table. A little lively, yeah, but not unbearable. Good atmosphere, though. And the patatas bravas were to die for. Seriously, you’d like it. Speaking of lively... how's Auntie Maureen doing? Did you manage to get round to visiting her last week? I did, on Tuesday. She was a bit…Maureen, you know? Complaining about the postman, the price of bread, and how nobody visits anymore. I brought her some of that lavender honey she likes. Seemed to perk her up a bit. She did ask about you and Leo, of course. Said she missed seeing you both. Bless her. I really need to make more of an effort. It’s just...everything’s been so hectic. Leo’s crawling now, Sarah! Crawling! It’s madness. You blink and suddenly he's halfway across the room heading for something he shouldn't be touching. I’ve put childproof locks on everything. Everything! That's the life, isn't it? Remember when Thomas was doing that? He tried to eat a lightbulb once. A  lightbulb ! Oh god, don’t remind me! I’ve got to overhaul my proofreading rates, haven’t I? Starting to feel like I have ten minutes a day to dedicate to actual work. It’s just… managing it all. Honestly, Sarah, some days, I feel like I’m juggling chainsaws. You are brilliant at it, though. Really. You’re a natural. And your marketing work is always top-notch. Just gotta find a way to carve out more time. Have you looked at getting a cleaner? Just for a couple of hours a week?

…So, then Mr. Dubois just  stares  at me. Like I'd grown a second head. Honestly, I thought he was going to call security. All because I asked if we could get a table outside! It was a scorching day in Lyon, absolutely roasting, and he's all, “Non, non, impossible. À l'intérieur seulement.” Like it was a personal affront. Classic. You know, you’re just built for those sorts of situations, aren't you? Always rattling the cages a bit. Lyon’s lovely though, isn't it? Beautiful architecture. Reminds me a bit of Birmingham in a way, actually – all that grand, industrial history, just…prettier. Rattling cages is my middle name, apparently! And I thought Lyon was gorgeous. Although, navigating the tram system,  that  was a challenge. I ended up accidentally going completely the wrong way and ended up in some industrial estate miles from our hotel. Proper dodgy, it was. I felt like I was in a film. See, that’s what I mean about the EU. You can just  wander . You’d never have had that experience if you were, say, going to Russia. You get a bit lost, a bit confused, and it’s still relatively straightforward to sort yourselves out. Remember that time we went to Prague? I was barely out of uni, absolutely clueless, and we managed to navigate the entire city using a map and gestures. Oh, Prague was brilliant! The Charles Bridge at sunset…unforgettable. Though I did nearly get pickpocketed, didn't I? Good thing you spotted that bloke lurking. The freedom to just  be  somewhere, though, isn’t it amazing? It’s hard to put into words what we used to take for granted. It is. Pre-Brexit, it was just…effortless. You'd think about it for a weekend, book flights, and off you’d go. Now there's forms and visa requirements and all this extra faff. It's not insurmountable, but it  changes  the vibe, doesn't it? It makes you overthink it a bit more. I was talking to my supervisor the other day, he's Austrian, and he was saying how gutted his family are that they can’t just pop over to see him in the UK whenever they feel like it. Aye, exactly. My mam keeps going on about how she used to go shopping in France for perfume and cheese. Said it was cheaper than here, and a proper little getaway.

Right, right. You're absolutely right, Leo. Monopoly is not exactly 'relaxing after a long day'. It's more like a battle of wills, isn't it? Especially when your dad gets involved. Can we 'ave treacle pudding, Mummy? Pleeease! With custard! Custard! Custard! I want custard too! And sprinkles! Lots of sprinkles! Alright, alright, settle down, you two. Treacle pudding  is  a good idea. It's proper comfort food, innit? Perhaps we can have that tomorrow night. Tonight… tonight I was thinking something a little lighter. Maybe some Eton Mess? Strawberries and cream, meringue… Eton Mess? What's that? Sounds silly! It  is  a bit silly, darling. But it's lovely. It's just crushed meringue, whipped cream, and juicy strawberries all mixed together. It’s a bit of a jumble, really, like a happy jumble. Can I crush the meringue?  Please  can I? Well, we can let you  help  crush the meringue. But be careful, little man, it’s quite brittle. Smash it gently, yeah? Don't want to make a huge mess. Although... a little mess is sometimes good. Mess is good! Mess is fun! Speaking of messes… Monopoly. You know, I was thinking, maybe we could try a different game? Something... co-operative? Something we all win together? Leo: Co-operative Monopoly? That sounds… unlikely. What are you suggesting? Trading property willingly? Footing the bill of Park Lane rent without batting an eyelid? Exactly! A radical rethinking of the rules. We pool our money, work together to build properties, and collectively dominate the board. Think of it! No more squabbling! No more bankrupt siblings! We win  all  the money?! We win together, sweetheart. We share the spoils. It's about teamwork, remember? Like when we're building a tower out of blocks. But Park Lane is the best! I want Park Lane! You can still  want  Park Lane, darling. Just… we’ll buy it together. And then everyone gets to enjoy the rent. See? Fairer, innit? Leo: It’s… an interesting proposition. It would certainly change the dynamic. The whole point  is  the ruthless negotiation, the brinkmanship. Removing that element… I know, I know. But sometimes, ruthless isn’t what you need at the end of a long day. Sometimes, a little togetherness is nice. Plus, I’m feeling a bit guilty about making you sell Mayfair last time. I think my strategy was… questionable. Daddy sold Baltic Avenue!

Honestly, it’s just… bewildering, isn’t it? Like, I spend all day wrestling with these digital ghosts, these little bits of data, making sure they’re all properly tagged and categorised, and for what? So some bloke in London can write a paper saying the frequency of the word ‘rain’ correlates with biscuit consumption. Right. The rain and biscuits paper. Sounds riveting. You’re still on about that, then? Thought you'd gotten over the initial frustration? Got over it? No! I’m  still  trying to figure out why anyone thought that was a legitimate research question! I mean, I’m not saying correlation doesn’t equal causation, I know that's like, basic statistics. But it's just… frivolous! I’m dealing with Victorian novels! Dickens! Brontë! And I'm facilitating the analysis of  biscuits  alongside rainy days? It feels like a massive waste of me, you know? Look, I get it. It’s not the most intellectually stimulating application of your skillset. You’re dealing with heavyweights. But it’s a job, isn’t it? A good job, with decent prospects. And you’re really good at it. Your meticulousness, the way you’re so incredibly organised - those are valuable skills, El. Aye, but is it  fulfilling ? I went to Durham, for goodness sake! I studied English Literature! I dreamed of unlocking the secrets of the human condition, not… classifying pastry-related anxieties. Ma keeps telling me to be grateful for a steady job, mind. “At least you’re not working down the chip shop,” she says. She has a point, actually. And let’s be honest, chip shops are vital to Sunderland’s economy. But she’s also right. You  are  lucky. Plenty of people are struggling to find anything. And you’re not just ‘classifying pastry-related anxieties,’ you’re supporting academic research. Even if that research is a bit… peculiar. Peculiar is putting it mildly. It's practically absurd! And besides, I keep finding these… anomalies. Like, someone's tagged ‘scone’ as a ‘waterfowl’. A WATERFOWL! Who does that? It's confusing the entire algorithm! Right, the waterfowl scone incident. You told me about that. Sounds like a rogue data entry. Didn’t they check who entered that tag? They did. It was some undergrad doing a volunteer placement. Apparently, he thought it was a pun. “Scone like a swan,” he said. I nearly choked on me tea.

They do, Edith. Believe you me. They're all busy shuffling paperwork, that's what they're doing. Nothing to do with actually, you know,  helping  folk. Reminds me of old Mr. Grimshaw down the road. Had a prize-winning rose bush, that man did. Council said it was obstructing the pavement. Told him he had to cut it back. Ruined the poor chap, it did.      Grimshaw, was it? Aye, I remember him. Had a right good tomato crop going too, that fellow. Always gave us a few. Bit of a fuss, that was, wasn't it? All over a bit of greenery. They'd be better off fixing the potholes on the Ring Road. Now  that's  a hazard. Proper engineering challenge, that Ring Road. Never did understand why they used that aggregate. Didn’t bind properly, you see…      Arthur, dear, let’s not start on the Ring Road again. I’ve heard you pontificate on its failings for the last ten years. And John, must you perpetually bring up engineering solutions to every minor inconvenience? It’s just a hedge!      Just a hedge, Margaret? It’s a symbol, see? A symbol of their endless meddling! They're sticking their noses in where they shouldn't be. Back in my day, a neighbour wouldn’t dream of reporting another for a bit of overgrown foliage. We all looked after each other. A bit of community spirit, that was. People actually talked to each other. Not like now.      You’re right, John. Remember old Mrs. Peterson’s cat, Mittens? Got stuck up that oak tree down by the playing field. Half the village turned out to help her get it down. Now…you’d get a drone sent out by the council to film it.      Oh, you two. Always reminiscing about some idyllic past that probably never existed! I’m sure there were plenty of grumbles and complaints back then too. And Mittens probably just wanted to sun herself in peace.      Don't you go minimising it, Margaret. There was a sense of…belonging. People took pride in their surroundings. Look at this place now! The paint's peeling on the postboxes, the streetlights flicker, and the pavements are a disgrace. It’s all going to pot, I tell you. Proper engineering oversight would sort it out! We could use a bit of reinforced concrete...      Hold on a minute, John. About that concrete…remember when they built that new estate on Mill Road?

…and honestly, the packaging is killing me. I thought I’d found a supplier for those amber glass jars, you know, look all artisanal and eco-friendly, but they've just gone up fifteen percent! Fifteen percent! On top of everything else. That’s brutal, Bex. Absolutely brutal. You're right, though, the jars  do  make a difference. People are way more drawn to it now. Remember when we were using those plastic tubs? People just scrolled right past. Exactly! It looked so… cheap. And it  was  cheap, but that wasn’t the message I wanted to send. Honest Skincare is about quality, natural ingredients… expensive packaging feels counterintuitive, but the presentation has to be there. I’m thinking about switching to smaller jars, perhaps? Less product per jar, but it brings the cost down a bit, doesn’t it? Yeah, could work. Think about the dimensions though. People are very particular about how much product they’re getting, especially if they’re paying a premium. I had a nightmare with that when I was setting up my little jewellery business. I initially ordered these teeny postage bags – stylish, you know? – but they barely fitted the earrings! Had to buy a whole new batch. Size matters, even in packaging. You’re absolutely right. Measurements, measurements, everywhere. It’s driving me mad. I’ve been doing these spreadsheets – and don’t even get me started on the shipping costs! It's like a constant battle against rising costs. By the way, how’s your business doing? Still flooring people with those personalised keyrings? Yeah, actually surprisingly well! The school prom season really boosted it. I’m thinking of expanding into phone cases, maybe. The designs are pretty much sorted, just need to find a reliable supplier. And a cheap-ish one, naturally! Any recommendations? You've obviously done your research. Oh, I’ve researched. I've researched until my eyes are square. I’ll send you a few links later. But you know, honestly, the marketing is the thing I'm really struggling with. Instagram is… it’s just a black hole of time, isn’t it? And engagement is down. I’ve been trying influencer marketing, but it feels a bit… forced. Tell me about it! I spent ages trying to get a local blogger to promote my keyrings. Promised her freebies and everything. She posted one blurry photo and then disappeared.

…and honestly, Arthur, the sheer  gall  of it. Raising energy prices  again ? It’s just… relentless. How are people supposed to cope? Especially with winter coming. It’s disgraceful, isn't it, Margaret? Absolutely disgraceful. They trot out the same excuses – geopolitical instability, supply chain issues – it all feels terribly convenient. Though, to be fair, I was reading an analysis this morning that suggested the windfall taxes aren't really making a dent. Seems the energy companies are just finding… creative accounting methods. Creative accounting? You mean fiddling the books, don't you? Exactly! It’s daylight robbery. I remember when coal was cheap, Arthur. When you could heat your home without feeling like you were emptying your bank account. Though, come to think of it, we probably didn't have central heating back then, did we? Just the fire. We did, Margaret, but you’re right. We were much more accustomed to layering up. Remember those thick cardigans your mother knitted? Smelled perpetually of mothballs and lavender. Oh, goodness yes. She was a prolific knitter, your mother. Always saying, "Waste not, want not, Margaret." A very sensible woman. She’d be appalled by the way things are now. By the sheer… profligacy of it all. She would. Speaking of which, how are you managing with everything? Really managing? I know you're reluctant to ask for help, but… It's...tight, Arthur. Very tight. The pension barely covers the essentials, you know. And the council tax… well, that’s a constant worry. I’m skipping some meals, if I’m honest. Just little things, you wouldn’t notice. But it adds up. I’m trying to be sensible with my electricity, but the heating… the heating is just necessary. My arthritis, you know. Margaret, honestly. You can't be scrimping and saving like that. You need to look after yourself. Let me help. I can top up your electricity meter, if you’d let me. And I’ll bring you some groceries next week. Proper groceries, not just tins of soup. Oh, Arthur… I don’t want to be a burden. You have your own expenses, don’t you? Your retirement, the house… Don't be silly. Family helps family. It's what we do. Besides, I’ve been meaning to get rid of some of those old records. The ones I haven’t listened to in years. I could sell them online.

It has been. We’ve cranked the thermostat up to a frankly embarrassing level. The lab’s warmer than my living room, and that's saying something! We did make a big effort to insulate last year, which helped, but… inflation’s hit everything, hasn't it? Are you having the same trouble, Liam? Tell me about it! I was just saying to Emma – and she'll kill me for saying this out loud - we might have to seriously rethink the Christmas decorations this year. No more fairy lights across the entire garden, that's for sure. It's not just the gas, it's the electricity too. We're trying to layer up, you know? Thick socks, jumpers…looking like a yeti. Honestly, I feel you both. My little flat’s like an icebox. I’ve been huddled under a duvet with a hot water bottle all week! At least the mulled wine helps a bit! This is absolutely brilliant, by the way, Amelia. You've really outdone yourself. Aye, proper good that is, Amelia. Proper warms the cockles. Speaking of warm, I tackled that old workbench in the workshop today. You know the one, the one I've been meaning to restore for… well, years actually? It needed serious attention. The wood was warped and covered in dust. Oh, the one you bought from that estate sale? I remember you being so excited about finding it. What did you do? Well, I spent hours stripping old varnish off. Turns out there were layers and layers of it put on over the years. Then I gave it a good sanding and oiled it. It’s looking right smart now. Got all my chisels and planes back on it too. Feels good to have a project finished, you know? Takes your mind off the freezing weather and the… you know… everything else. Good on you, Rhys! I need a project. Just need to find one that doesn't involve spreadsheets and technical documentation. Emma's been on at me to build a bird feeder. Might have to bite the bullet and get into that. Though, knowing me, I’ll end up with a pile of wood and a very disgruntled robin. You should! Chloe - that's me, by the way, in case anyone forgot – I'm trying to learn wood carving. It’s surprisingly therapeutic. Although, my current attempt at a sprig of holly looks more like a squashed slug.

It’s a bit overwhelming, isn't it? I mean, we’re talking about three sets of dinnerware here, plus serving dishes from Great Aunt Mildred. It's ridiculous. Are we even using half of it?      Not really, no. I think the fancy silver stuff only comes out for Christmas, and the floral one is just... floral. Not exactly my vibe, you know? I'm all about sleek and modern.      Now, don't you be saying that about the floral one! Your Grandma Jean loved that set. Used it every Sunday. It's proper family silverware, that is. And saving things is important, love. You never know when you might need 'em.      She’s got a point, you know. Back in my day, you didn’t throw things away. Waste not, want not. My mother practically glued things together. Still got the teapot she used when she was courting your grandma, Elsie.      Teapots… Lovely teapots. Used to have a good one myself. Got nicked, though. Right off the windowsill. Can you believe it?      Right. Well, nicked teapots aside, Grandad, I was thinking we could, like, have a huge declutter. Get rid of stuff we genuinely don't use. Maybe even donate some to charity.      Donate?! My plates? Elara, darling, put those thoughts away! They’re valuable! Antiques, practically.      Valuable maybe in some antique store, Brenda, but not exactly practical for a Tuesday night takeaway. Honestly, the space it takes up is a major problem. Remember when we were trying to move the Christmas decorations last year? We almost had a disaster trying to manoeuvre past the sideboard of china.      You’re right, you know. It’s a bit of a hazard. Elsie tripped over that sideboard twice last year. Nearly broke her hip the second time.      See! Exactly! It’s not just about aesthetics, it's about safety! Plus, Mum, you’ve barely got room to move in the dining room these days. Remember how we used to have proper family gatherings, with all the cousins crammed in? Now it's just... full of plates.      Well, things change, don't they? Your cousin Sarah’s moved to Australia, hasn't she? And Michael’s got his own family now, all living in London. It's not like it used to be.      Australia… went to Australia once. On a steam train. Smelled of coal dust.      Okay, new tactic. What about we take a picture of each item, research its value – realistically – and then decide, together, what to keep, what to donate, and what to... well, let go entirely.

…and honestly, the presentation went down like a lead balloon. Mr. Henderson just kept clearing his throat and looking at his watch. I swear, I could feel the collective boredom radiating from the room. I thought the data was solid, the visuals were engaging... what more could I have done? Did the doggy eat all his dinner? Not yet, love. He’s being a drama queen, as usual. Wants a bit of my chicken, doesn’t he? But no, darling, we are talking about work. Remember? The thing that pays for the skiing trip? Skiing! Are we going to see snowmen? Big ones? Possibly, a very big one. Maybe even build one ourselves. But first, back to this dreadful presentation. I'm starting to think I need a new strategy. Maybe just avoid Henderson altogether next time. He’s just… resistant to anything new, isn't he? Like a stubborn mule. Mules are fluffy? Not really fluffy, sweetheart. More… grumpy. A bit like Mr. Henderson. Anyway, I'm thinking about suggesting a different approach to Sarah next week. She's got some good ideas, she just needs a little nudge. What do you reckon? Nudges are good. My teddy needs nudges when he’s sad. That’s very wise, darling. Very wise indeed. Right. Skiing. I need to book the lessons, don’t I? Have you been looking at the resort online? Any particular slopes catch your eye? Don’t want you ending up stuck at the bottom the whole time. There were fluffy bunnies! Lots of them! And a slide made of ice! Can I go on the ice slide? We'll definitely find an ice slide. And hopefully, lots of fluffy bunnies. But you need to learn to ski first, love. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck waiting for Daddy and me at the bottom, getting cold. I can be a very good skier! Like… like a racing car! Vroom! A racing car skier! That’s amazing! You’ll be winning all the medals. Just remember to listen to the instructor, alright? No racing off on your own. Okay. But can I have hot chocolate afterwards? A  really  big one? Absolutely. The biggest hot chocolate you’ve ever seen. With marshmallows, and cream... and maybe even a little bit of chocolate sauce. Yay! And can we take pictures of the snowmen? Of course, love. Loads and loads of pictures. We'll make an album, and you can show all your friends.

Tell me about it! Mrs. Peterson’s always going on about presentation skills. Like, does it  really  matter if my apple crumble looks slightly wonky when it tastes amazing? It's all about the flavour, innit? Exactly! And she kept saying we needed to think about “visual appeal.” Visual appeal? It’s a Yorkshire pudding! It’s supposed to be a bit…rustic. You know? And trying to get the gravy to sit  perfectly … forget about it. It was chaos. Did you at least manage to get yours to rise properly? Ugh, barely. It looked like a deflated football. Honestly, I think I need a food tech survival guide. Or a professional pastry chef to come in and supervise. What about your Maths homework? Are you even close to understanding those quadratic equations? My brain’s just… fizzing. Don’t even  start  me on quadratics. Mr. Harding is trying to be all cool and explaining it with, like, football examples. It’s just making it worse! I'm convinced he doesn't actually understand it himself. I spent ages trying to do question three and ended up just scribbling random numbers. It’s just…ugh. Typical Harding. At least English's manageable. I’m actually quite liking  Macbeth . The imagery's really striking, even if Lady Macbeth is a proper psycho. Yeah, I like  Macbeth  too. I'm trying to decide what to do for my essay. Should I focus on her ambition, or maybe the whole weird sisters thing? Ambition, definitely. It’s so intense. And think about how it contrasts with Duncan’s kind of… gentle leadership. It's a proper study in contrasts. Have you started your Spanish vocab list yet? A little bit. It’s just… so much! I’m trying to visualise myself being fluent, though. Imagine, going to Spain and ordering tapas properly, without embarrassing myself. It’d be ace. I was thinking, if I do well in GCSEs, maybe I could even do a year abroad. A year abroad! That would be  amazing . I've been looking at some uni courses that offer that. Barcelona, maybe? They have such a vibrant music scene. Imagine seeing a live band in a tiny bar, completely immersed in the culture… Ooh, Barcelona  would  be good. It’s just… what will we even do  after  uni? That’s what’s stressing me out. Everyone keeps asking "What are you going to  be ?"

Honestly, Nan, I still don’t get why you’re so down on “Everything Everywhere All at Once.” Everyone’s raving about it! It won, like, everything at the Oscars. Raving, are they? Well, modern films, love, they just don’t grab me like they used to. All this… flashing about, and jumping between realities. My eyes couldn’t keep up! It gave me a proper headache. Reminded me of those early computer games, all chaotic and overwhelming. You know, Pac-Man. But that’s part of the point! It’s supposed to be overwhelming. It’s about a woman feeling like she’s failing in every possible way, and then realizing she can draw strength from all her different selves. It's beautifully done, visually and emotionally. You know, the bagel as a black hole? Brilliant! A bagel as a black hole? Good heavens. Sounds a bit silly, doesn’t it? I mean, I like a proper cup of tea and a biscuit, a nice bit of drama on the telly…Coronation Street, you know. Something grounded. Not… bagels swallowing up the universe. It just felt… frantic. And a bit vulgar, if you ask me. All that wiggling and shouting. Vulgar? Nan, it’s expressive! They use physical comedy to show the absurdity of it all. Michelle Yeoh is incredible. Have you seen "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon” ? She’s amazing in that. Oh, I did see that. Years ago, mind you. Lovely scenery. All those flowing robes… very pretty. I used to enjoy a good martial arts film back in the day. Bruce Lee, of course. Now  there  was a performer. Proper action, none of this jumping about through different worlds. He could kick a man clear across a room, that's entertainment! It’s different now, Nan. Film-making has evolved. Storytelling has evolved. It's not just about kicks and punches anymore. It’s about exploring complex themes. Identity, family, generational trauma... Themes, themes. Back in my day, we didn't need films to tell us about generational trauma, we lived it! My dad worked in a coal mine, you know. Now  that  was trauma. No need for a bagel to illustrate it. This lot, they're all having a blinder, writing about things they haven't a clue about. Okay, fair point. But you have to admit, the visuals were pretty spectacular, even if it gave you a headache.

…and honestly, Mum, I’m just not sure about driving up to Scotland for Christmas this year. The M6 is a nightmare at the best of times, let alone with everyone else trying to get home. It's a proper logjam. Now, don't you start with that M6 nonsense, love. It's not as bad as you make out. Just needs a bit of patience, that's all. And a decent audiobook. I’ve got a lovely thriller about a barrister, really gripping. Would keep you occupied. Patience isn't my strong suit when I'm stuck behind a lorry doing 45 in the outside lane! And a barrister thriller? Really, Mum? That's practically your go-to genre. You know I prefer something a bit lighter, maybe a good romance. There's nothing wrong with a bit of legal drama, girl. Builds the mind. You teach languages, you need to exercise that brain! Though, I suppose romance is alright, in its place. What about that one you were on about, with the baker in Cornwall? "Honey and Rye"? Yes, that was lovely. But it’s hardly relevant to court proceedings, is it? Speaking of which, how was work this week? Any particularly dramatic cases? Oh, you know how it is. Usual mix. A bit of vandalism, a squabble over inheritance, that sort of thing. It's amazing the things people argue about, isn’t it? Honestly, you’d think grown-ups would have more sense. And young Timothy Baker – that solicitor – was in again. Keeps trying to wriggle out of paying his parking fine! Keeps saying he didn’t see the signs. Persistent, that one. Sounds about right. Some people think the law doesn't apply to them. Anyway, back to Christmas. I was thinking maybe we could do something a little…different this year? Something easier on the driving and the stress. Perhaps just a nice restaurant in Birmingham? We could even see that new panto at the Hippodrome. A restaurant? On Christmas Day? That seems a bit…untraditional, doesn’t it? Your father would have a fit! He always loved the roast turkey, the whole shebang. It wouldn’t be Christmas without it, would it? Dad's not here, Mum. And his traditions don't have to be ours. I'm thinking of  us . I'm exhausted this term, teaching Year 7 French is... well, you know.

Honestly, that lecture on post-structuralism felt like wading through treacle today. Half the students looked like they were actively fighting sleep. Did you have any better luck with the art history mob? Slightly. Though I think they're collectively convinced Botticelli was secretly a performance artist. I tried to steer them back towards Renaissance context, you know, the patronage, the Florentine politics... crickets. Absolute crickets. At least they were awake. Yours sounded… challenging. Challenging is putting it mildly. I think I lost three potential converts when I mentioned Derrida. They looked at me like I'd suggested sacrificing a goat. Still, someone asked a genuinely insightful question about the fluidity of language – a glimmer of hope, perhaps. There’s always one, isn’t there? A little spark. Right. So, shopping. We  need  to tackle the fruit situation tomorrow. These mandarins are horrifying. Seriously, they taste like slightly damp cardboard. Absolutely. And the oranges! The colour’s all wrong too. They look… artificial. I was thinking the market near the West Lake is probably a better bet. More variety, and hopefully, less aggressively orange citrus. Good shout. I was also pondering the whole bread situation. This supermarket stuff is just… dense. Like eating a brick. Do you reckon we should try finding a proper bakery? Definitely. I miss a decent sourdough. Remember Mrs. Higgins' bakery back in Norwich? The smell alone was worth the trip. Oh, yes! The crust... the crumb… Absolute perfection. Right, mission: sourdough acquisition. We could also hit up that little shop on Chang'an Road tomorrow. They had some interesting teas in last week. I was thinking we could stock up on that Earl Grey. Excellent plan. And while we're on the subject of stocking up... have you ordered the textbooks for next semester yet? I realised I haven't even looked at the reading list for my Introduction to Literary Theory module. Nearly! I've got a few lined up. It's a nightmare, isn’t it? The sheer volume of stuff they expect students to read. And the price! It's extortionate. I might suggest a few open-source articles to ease the burden. That’s a brilliant idea, actually. I appreciate you thinking of that. It’s really not fair, is it? Expecting them to spend a fortune just to get through a degree. It’s a systemic problem, isn’t it? Anyway, enough about the depressing state of academia.

“…and then Mrs. Davies actually said, ‘Chloe, are you  sure  you want them to make dinosaur noises during story time?’ I nearly choked on my tea! Honestly, some parents! But, yeah, they were brilliant, weren't they? Leo was roaring like a T-Rex, Elsie was a gentle Brontosaurus… it was chaos, beautiful chaos.” "Rawr! Brontosaurus!" "Roar! T-Rex! Big teeth!" "Exactly! Big teeth, Leo. See? You got it. Right, well, that’s enough about the classroom for now, isn’t it? We need to sort out this weekend. Are you two alright with me popping out for a few hours Saturday afternoon? Sarah's finally agreed to a proper catch-up. It's been ages." "Who's Sarah?" "Sarah? Remember? We had her over for dinner, ages ago. She brought those amazing brownies. You both loved them!" "Brownies! So, you're going for more brownies?" "Not  just  for brownies, sweetie. It’s good to see my friends. It’s easy to get lost in… well, all of  this ,” she gestures around the kitchen at the two children and the half-finished batch of cookies. "Are we having cookies? I want one! Now!" "Almost, darling, almost. Let's finish discussing Saturday first. I was thinking, if I go out, could Grandma and Grandpa come and keep you two entertained? They’d love it, and it would be a nice treat for them too." "Grandma reads good stories." "And Grandpa makes funny faces!" “Exactly! Perfect. Okay, so, Grandma and Grandpa Saturday. That leaves Sunday… I was thinking we could bake a cake? Remember that lemon drizzle one we saw in that cookbook? The one with the poppyseeds?" "Lemon! Yes! Poppyseeds!" "I help stir! I stir  very  well!" "You do, you do. And while we’re baking, maybe we could read that new dinosaur book you’ve been wanting, Elsie? The one with all the different types." "Yes! The one with the Stegosaurus!" "Right you are. Now, we need to book those haircuts, don't we? Both of you are looking a bit… wild.” She winks. "And I was thinking… what about that photoshoot? Mum was saying she’d love to do it next month, when the roses are in bloom." "Can I wear my dinosaur shirt?" "Absolutely! You can roar the whole time! Elsie, what about you? What would you like to wear?" "Something pink! And sparkly!" "Pink and sparkly it is!

Honestly, this is barely cold. They really need to sort that out. Like, how hard is it to serve an iced latte that’s  actually  iced? Tell me about it. My hummus wrap is swimming in watery dressing. It's like they're actively trying to ruin lunch. Proper rubbish, innit? You having a rough day then, Liv? Nah, not  rough , just… frustrating. History lecture was a snooze-fest. Professor Davies just droned on about the Magna Carta for an hour and a half. Like, I get it, it's important, but could he maybe try to make it, you know,  interesting ? I nearly fell asleep. Oh, Davies. He's a legend for boring people to death. My mum says he was even like that back when she was doing her degree. Proper old-school. But seriously, a Magna Carta marathon? You need a reward for that. Fancy hitting up that new cocktail bar after lectures? 'The Velvet Fox' – apparently they do epic Brambles. Ooh, Brambles are good. Yeah, sounds way better than re-hashing medieval politics! But are you sure? I'm broke as anything this month. I’ve spent all my loan on that new pair of Docs. You know I can’t resist a good pair of boots. Don't be daft. Money’s not an issue. My grandma sent me a load of cash last week. She’s convinced I'm going to need to support myself when I graduate. Which, honestly, is probably not far off the mark, yeah? She worries. She’s Filipino, you know? Always thinking about the future. Keeps sending boxes of dried mangoes, too. Right pain to carry around, but delicious. Bless her! Dried mangoes are the ultimate grandma gift. And your grandma's right to worry, aren’t we all going to be struggling? What about you? How's graphic design going? That project you were stressing about last week? Done! Actually, I'm pretty chuffed with it. The brief was a nightmare - design a logo for a pigeon racing club - but I think I pulled it off. It's got a slightly edgy, urban feel. Might even put it in my portfolio. It’s a bit ridiculous, but it shows I can think outside the box, y’know? Plus, got a good mark. Mrs. Patel seemed genuinely impressed. Wow, that’s brilliant, Maya! Pigeon racing? Seriously? That’s niche. You’re such a creative genius.

Aye, it’s a right weak brew, this. You lot down south don't know how to make a decent cuppa, do ya? Seriously, it's like…dishwater with a hint of tannin. Harsh, Elara! It’s PG Tips. It’s pretty standard. Mum’s just not a strong-tea person. Besides, you’re the one who kept complaining about being jet-lagged and needing something “gentle.” Gentle’s fine, but it shouldn't taste like sadness. Right, so, holiday recap. Italy was… mental. Absolutely mental. The crowds in Rome! You wouldn’t believe it. I reckon there were more tourists than actual Romans. I can imagine. We went to Florence a few years back, and it was similar. You just have to accept that you’re going to be jostling for space to see the David. Did you at least manage to get a gelato? Course I did! Loads of ‘em. Pistachio, lemon, stracciatella... I think I consumed my body weight in gelato. And the pizza! Oh, the pizza. Forget anything you’ve ever had in Sunderland, it doesn’t even come close. Proper pizza. Honestly, I'm going to be forever disappointed with chain restaurant pizza now. Sounds idyllic, to be honest. Just wish I'd gone. Studying kept me chained to the university. Got that report finally sent to the council, though. Huge relief. Thinking about a little trip to Brighton next month, de-stress. Brighton? Good shout. Bit of a change of pace. Perfect for a weekend. I’m still swamped with this revised bridge design. Client keeps changing their mind. It’s enough to drive a man mad. Speaking of madness, have you been watching "Succession" then? "Succession"? Is that the one everyone and their grandma’s been raving about? I haven't! I’ve been stuck on this absolute masterpiece called "After Life" – Ricky Gervais. Proper tearjerker, though. Makes you think. Oh, you  have  to watch "Succession," Elara. It's brilliantly written, the acting is phenomenal. It’s just… wonderfully cynical. Like, observing the absolute worst of humanity, but making it incredibly entertaining. They're both excellent choices, truly. Different vibes, though. I find "Succession's" morally grey characters fascinating. Makes me question everything about ambition and power. It's something a civil engineer can think about daily. Aye, well, I’m more of a laughing-through-the-tears kinda gal. After Life, it’s just brutal honesty, innit?

…and then young Timothy, bless ‘is cotton socks, he says, "Grandad, why do 'orses have tails?" I nearly choked on me tea, I did! Never thought I’d be expainin' that to a five-year-old. Told him it were for swatting flies, o’ course. Simple as that, innit? Though, I reckon he probably still thinks I’m makin’ it up. Oh, you always were a clever one with the children, Arthur. Timothy’s a lucky boy to have you around. Remember when little Poppy glued her fingers together with glitter? You calmed her down and got the glue off without her cryin’ for an hour. I’d have been utterly useless. Glitter, eh? Childhood’s a minefield, isn’t it? Used to get the odd incident at school – kids stickin' things where they shouldn't. Though, thankfully, nothing  quite  as dramatic as superglue and glitter. Speaking of things stickin’… how’s the talk about selling your place, Arthur? Your daughter's been on at you relentless, hasn’t she? Relentless is the word, Barry. Relentless! Says it’s for me own good, you know. Easier to manage, less to worry about. Says I’ll be safer in a flat. Safer! I’ve lived in this house for fifty years. Seen a fair bit o' life within these walls, I ‘ave. And a flat? It wouldn't be the same. Not having me garden, not 'avin' room for the telly, or for my model railway. It  is  a big decision, dear. But Brenda’s got a point, Arthur. It could free up a bit of money for you too. Think about it - a nice little trip to Cornwall, maybe? You loved that Youth Hostel we went to, didn't you? Remember the cream teas? Aye, I do. That was a grand time. Foot and mouth was a bother, though. Couldn't get near the beaches. Still, the countryside were lovely. Cornwall’s always been a favourite. But selling… it feels like sellin' off a bit of meself. I understand that feeling, truly. I felt a bit like that when I decided to retire from teaching. Left a big chunk of me behind. But you’ve got to think ahead, Arthur. Retirement is supposed to be enjoying life, not worrying about leaky roofs and overgrown hedges. Now, about that trip – are you thinking of going on eBay for a new telly to take with you?

…and honestly, the sheer volume of information is just  overwhelming . Like, everyone has an opinion. My mum’s adamant about exclusively breastfeeding, naturally. Says formula is ‘the devil’s work’ basically. Auntie Carol’s got her whole ‘once they hit six months, they need solids’ spiel. And then you get the online forums, which are just… a battlefield of conflicting advice. I’ve read articles saying introducing allergens early is key, and others screaming at you not to even  think  about it before a year. Tell me about it. Remember when Mum tried to give me porridge when I was like, three months old? Nearly choked me, she did. Dad had to whack me on the back for a good five minutes. She was convinced it was "good for digestion." Oh, yeah! Classic Mum. Though, realistically, I  do  want to try and breastfeed if I can. I just… worry. What if I can’t? What if I don't produce enough? What if it hurts too much? I've read some horror stories. Look, you’ll be fine. You're sensible, you’ll do your research. And if you can’t, it’s  okay . Seriously. It's not a failure, it's just… different. Don’t let the ‘breast is best’ brigade pressure you. Little Leo'll be perfectly happy with formula if that's what works. My friend Chloe, she bottle-fed from day one, and Tommy’s thriving. He’s massive, like a little rugby player already! That’s true. Chloe’s always been so relaxed about it all. I envy that. I feel like I'm supposed to be this perfect, instinctive mother, and I just… I’m not. I'm questioning every single decision already. Should I be nesting more? Am I preparing enough? Have I bought enough muslins?! Stop stressing! You're doing loads. You’ve got the nursery practically finished, you’ve been to all the antenatal classes... You're far more organised than I ever was. Honestly, the muslins? You can never have too many. I learned  that  the hard way. You end up with a mountain of them, but you need them. Trust me. Mum keeps saying she’ll knit me little hats. Keeps going on about her nan's knitting. It's sweet, I suppose. But honestly, the thought of wearing something knitted by Mum with that awful mustard yellow yarn… Oh god, she still uses that yarn, doesn't she?

Tell me about it, John. They’re trying to bankrupt us, aren’t they? I practically had to beg Mrs. Peterson for a lift yesterday. Said she was going to the shops anyway, bless her. Forty quid a month! For nurses! It’s not right. Forty quid? Good grief. That’s… that’s a lot. I really do need to have a proper chat with HR about this. They’re going to lose staff, you know. And who's going to look after the patients then? It’s just short-sighted, completely short-sighted. I can't believe they've gone with the pay-on-exit system either. So much faff. Right? My boyfriend works at the hospital too, apparently Matthew’s furious. He’s been sending memes all morning, mostly about parking meters wearing tiny uniforms. It's pretty funny, actually. Though he’s genuinely stressed, poor thing. He bikes in most days, but sometimes needs the car for late shifts. I'm worried about Sarah, actually. She's training for the NP role, and getting there early to study. These charges will hit her hard. She's already scrimping and saving like mad. It's not fair when they're under so much pressure already. They barely get a break as it is. Exactly, Wendy! It’s the frontline staff they're squeezing. What’s the point of all the talk about valuing the NHS if they’re making it impossible to actually  work  in it? Anyway, speaking of impossible... the washing machine's gone belly up again. What now? That thing can’t be older than five years. Did you try unplugging it? The usual trick. Of course I tried unplugging it! I’m not a complete novice, John! It's making a dreadful grinding noise and smelling something sickly. Think it might be the pump again. We could get a repair person in? I’ve got a few contacts through uni. One of my mates is doing his apprenticeship in appliance repair. Might be cheaper than replacing it. That's a brilliant idea, Chloe! Much better than you struggling to fix it yourself, Carol. Last time you tried to ‘tinker’ with the dishwasher, we had to call a professional anyway. I got the dishwasher working perfectly fine, thank you very much! Just a bit… louder than usual. And don’t you start, John. I did research the problem online.

Ugh, tell me about it! Practice tests are the worst. Especially Maths. I swear, he’s deliberately trying to make everyone stressed. It’s like, we’re already stressed enough with all the other subjects. Did you at least get any of those quadratic equation bits right? I kept getting negative numbers, which, like, doesn’t even  make  sense in real life! I think I did okay, actually. I remembered the 'b minus four ac' thing, hopefully that helped. Though solving those problems still feels like pulling teeth. It's just… abstract numbers dancing in my head. Much prefer Biology, to be honest. Did you see the new stamp my Gran got? It’s a really rare one from the Falklands, all about the penguin population. Penguins! Ooh, brilliant! My Gran collects stamps too, but hers are mostly Victorian royalty. Not nearly as exciting. Biology  is  good though. I really enjoyed the plant dissection in class last week. Seeing all the layers... it was kinda beautiful, in a weird, scientific way. Are you doing Art this year? Mrs. Hawthorne is amazing. Yeah, Art’s pretty good. I’m trying to do a proper botanical illustration for my portfolio - a foxglove. It’s tricky getting the shading right. Do you know, my mum was saying how Ed Sheeran used to go to our primary school, Linton Village. I never realised! It’s a bit mental, isn’t it? Seriously! Linton Village! That’s where my cousin goes now. He’s obsessed with football. He keeps trying to get me to play, but I'm rubbish. Anyway, about Art... have you thought about using watercolours? They blend really nicely. But watch out for the bleed-through, it’s a nightmare. Mrs. Hawthorne told me a funny story last week about when she was at Cambridge University – said she nearly set her room on fire trying to make a potion for a project in Chemistry. No way! Chemistry with Mrs. Hawthorne is terrifying enough  now , I can't imagine her setting things on fire! I’m thinking of using coloured pencils, actually. Safer, I suppose. What's your name for your foxglove drawing? Mine's proving hard to name. I've got 'Violetta' down, but it doesn’t feel quite right. I’m trying to capture something a bit wilder, you know? Maybe 'Belladonna's Bloom?' Bit dramatic, I know. Speaking of names, did you hear about Lucy and Thomas?

…Right then, Doris. Show 'em, would ya? Let Margaret ‘ave a good look. I’ve been tinkerin’ with ‘im all mornin’. Alright, Arthur. Here. Isn’t he charming? You’ve done a marvellous job, Arthur. Honestly, better than anything you could buy. Indeed, Arthur. The craftsmanship is impressive. The detailing on the whiskers is particularly well done. A considerable improvement on, well, most of the commercially available options. You’ve clearly put a lot of thought into it. Thought? Aye, I 'ave. Reminds me a bit o' my grandad’s terrier, Pip. Bit cheeky, that one was. Always nickin’ sausages off the table. This little rat’s got that same glint in 'is eye, I reckon. Still gotta give 'im a proper name, though. Got any suggestions? Don’t say Pip, Doris, please. No, dear, certainly not Pip. How about… Reginald? Seems fitting, somehow. A distinguished little rat. Reginald’s rather splendid, Doris. I rather like it. It has a certain gravitas. Although, have you considered something slightly more… mischievous? Perhaps Finnian? Finnian… yeah, I like that. Finnian the Rat. Has a ring to it. Right then, Finnian it is. Now, you wouldn’t believe the bother I 'ad gettin' the right sort o’ thread. Down at Mr. Henderson’s, 'e were givin’ me the eye. Said I were wastin' 'is time tinkerin’ with puppets when I should be… well, never you mind what 'e said. Cheeky bugger 'e is. Don’t let him ruffle your feathers, Arthur! Mr. Henderson always was a bit grumpy. Remember that time he tried to charge me double for the button thread for little Emily’s bear? Shocking! Henderson’s has been rapidly declining, hasn't it? They struggle to compete with the online retailers these days. Speaking of things declining, I need to book myself in for an eye test soon. Everything’s getting a bit hazy. The bus numbers, especially. It’s dreadful trying to read them! Have you had yours checked recently, Doris? Not for a while, no. I’ve been meaning to, but then… well, you know how it is. One thing leads to another. The church bells, though… they’re harder to hear properly. I should really get that looked at too. I’m starting to miss phrases in the hymns. Dreadful feeling. Church bells… that reminds me. We should practice a bit more, shouldn't we?

…and then Professor Davies just went on about semiotics for  another  hour. Honestly, Mum, I’m starting to think he just enjoys hearing himself talk. I need a serious dose of anything  but  academic theory today. What are we doing after this? You said we were gonna wander around a bit, right? Aye, love. That’s the plan. Thought a bit of a wander would do us both good. Venice used to be  bustling  you know. Not just tourists really, proper local folk. Remember Mrs. Higgins' flower stall right where that souvenir shop is now? The scent used to spill out onto the pavement, lovely it was. Mrs. Higgins! I think I vaguely remember that. Was she the one with the prize-winning geraniums? Nan used to buy her Christmas posies from her. It's just... everything's so different now, isn’t it? These shops are just churning out the same plastic masks and gondola keyrings. No character. Exactly! It's lost a lot of its soul, has it. Used to be, you’d see families having picnics on the grass by the canal. Fresh bread, proper Lancashire cheese... not this fancy stuff they sell in the supermarkets now. Still, we can find some good food around here somewhere. Did you fancy a bit of cicchetti later? Those little Venetian snacks? Cicchetti? What are they even like? Sounds a bit posh. Posh? No, pet, they're proper working-class grub! Think tapas, but Venetian. Little crostini with all sorts on. Seafood, cured meats, vegetables… There’s that little place down the side street, 'Al Mercà'. They do a brilliant baccalà mantecato – creamed salted cod. Absolutely delicious. Their polpette, the meatballs, are right good too. We could grab a glass of prosecco with it. Creamed cod? Sounds…interesting. But I’m game! Prosecco sounds amazing, especially after that lecture. Honestly, I felt me brain turning to mush. So, 'Al Mercà' then? After we’ve had a look around. Where do you reckon we should start? I quite fancy seeing the old linen mill ruins again, just to see how much it’s changed. Aye, the mill ruins are good. Always fascinating to see the remnants of the past. Then we can pop down towards the canal, see if the ducks are about. They’re always a crowd-pleaser, aren't they? Heard tell they've been a bit cheeky lately, nicking chips right out of people’s hands!

…and honestly, the spin class was brutal last night. I nearly died. Like, genuinely felt my lungs trying to escape. I swear, Gareth, the instructor, is deliberately trying to torture us. He just kept cranking up the resistance. Oh God, Gareth! He's a menace. Remember when he made us do that burpee challenge, like, five times in a row? I thought I was going to collapse. Though, I do have to admit, I feel amazing afterwards. Guilty pleasure, right? Totally. That post-workout endorphin rush is the only thing keeping me going some days. So, how’s Bupa life treating you? Still drowning in marketing jargon? You have no idea! It’s busy, but in a good way. We’re launching a new preventative health campaign – focusing on mental wellbeing for young adults, which is actually really cool. A bit overwhelming at times, though. So much data, so many spreadsheets… But I'm learning a lot. What about you? Still juggling a million things as Project Coordinator? Pretty much! We're working on implementing a new CRM system, which is fun... said no one ever. It’s all meetings and spreadsheets too, but at least this time I can blame the technology for my stress levels. It’s giving me a bit of a headache, I'm worried it might delay the whole project. Oof, that sounds stressful. Need a celebratory pint when it's over? We should definitely plan something with the rest of the gym crew. Thinking maybe a Saturday night out somewhere central? Definitely! I'm in. Speaking of Saturdays, are you still thinking about that trip to Santorini? Remember we were talking about it? Yes! I’ve actually been looking at flights. It’s pricey, obviously, but I’m determined to make it happen. Might have to do a few extra shifts at work to save up. I was thinking maybe mid-September? Before it gets  too  chilly. How about you? Any holiday plans brewing? I wish! Finances are a bit tight at the moment. Mum’s been needing a bit of help lately, so holiday money is… well, it's going to Mum. Which is important, obviously. It's just a bit frustrating. Oh, darling, I totally get it. Family first, always. That’s lovely of you. Still, maybe a long weekend somewhere? A cheeky getaway to Brighton, perhaps? Easier on the wallet. Brighton sounds tempting.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the bollards has been utterly ridiculous. They put them in to 'protect pedestrians', they said, but all they've managed to do is create trip hazards and infuriate everyone. Mrs. Henderson fell over one last week, you know. Broke her wrist. Bollards. Always a source of contention, aren't they? Reminds me of the arguments we used to have in Westminster about the placement of traffic calming measures. Utterly baffling to watch politicians get worked up over something so... pedestrian. Though, I must say, Mrs. Henderson’s wrist is a serious matter. It is! And nobody seems to be taking responsibility. The new landlord, frankly, is a nightmare. Lambeth Council, too – they’re just passing the buck. It's all so frustrating when you're trying to live quietly in your own home. Anyway, speaking of frustrations… did you hear about the Chichester Cathedral spire? Good heavens, no! I caught the news just now, dreadful news! A tragedy, truly. That spire was magnificent. Porden, wasn’t it? Such a brilliant architect. Did you know he designed the Christ Church Spitalfields? A rather different style, of course, but both demonstrate his incredible eye. There’s a photo exhibition on at the Royal Institute of British Architects, actually, alongside an open call art competition... They may have some Porden sketches. Really? I must look into that. It's just… it feels like another blow, you know? One thing after another crumbling. It makes you think about permanence, doesn’t it? Much like, the arrival of little Leo. He rather puts things in perspective. A grandchild! Splendid. Absolutely splendid. Born in France, you said? Yes, in Lyon. My daughter and her husband decided to settle there a few years ago. Beautiful country, of course, but so… different. Different how? Regarding enterprise, I mean. You see, I’ve always found their approach… interesting. The property laws, for instance. Much more relaxed than here. Land ownership, a rather different ball game. Though the bureaucracy... that's a universal problem, I’m afraid. Even the anarchists seem bogged down in paperwork these days. That’s exactly it! It's seemingly an endless system of forms and permits. Although, the lifestyle is wonderful. They’re thinking of buying a small farm, actually, just outside Lyon. Apparently, getting financing isn't as difficult as it would be here. And the fresh produce! It’s quite remarkable.

Tell me about it. My topic's a nightmare. Victorian railway timetables. Seriously. Where am I supposed to find interesting stuff about  timetables ? That  is  rough. At least you’ve got a topic. I'm still battling with whether to do the impact of social media on classical literature. It feels…overdone. Classical literature? Dude, that’s hardcore. My mum would faint if I told her I was doing anything remotely like that. She wants me to do something practical, like AI ethics. AI ethics? That's actually pretty interesting. Liam's cousin works in that field, apparently. He was telling me about the whole bias in algorithms thing. Scary stuff. Anyway, this General Tso’s chicken is banging, isn't it? Seriously, best I've had in Slough. It's good, yeah. Not quite my Nan’s though. She makes a killer sweet and sour pork. But then again, she adds a secret ingredient she refuses to tell anyone. Secret ingredients! That's always the best part. My grandma does that with her apple crumble. Just a tiny pinch of something… and suddenly it’s transcendent. My nan mostly just complains about the price of everything. It’s a full-time job being her. Did anyone see Sarah yesterday? I texted her, but she didn't reply. Sarah? Nah, she wasn't in maths. I figured she was probably at cricket practice. She's been practicing a lot lately. Trying to get into the first team, apparently. Cricket? Seriously? I thought she hated sport. She always said she did. But then Tom from her cricket team started messaging her all the time… things change, don't they? Maybe she's developed a sudden passion for sixes and wickets. So, comics anyone? I just finished  Saga  volume six. Blew my mind.  Saga  is solid! I’m more into  Invincible  right now. It's just so brutal and well-written. Plus, you know, cyborgs beating up aliens. What's not to love? I'm still trying to get through  Sandman . It’s… a lot. All that mythology and dream stuff. I keep falling asleep reading it.  Sandman  is a commitment. But worth it, in the end. Have you guys read the new  Hellboy ? Mike Mignola’s still got it. Yeah! That design of the… the… ...that thing he fought in the last issue was incredible. Proper nightmare fuel. Speaking of nightmares, I had a weird one last night.

Aye, they do accumulate, don't they, love? Reminds me of my own attic, bless its heart. Full of things I swore were invaluable then, just collecting dust now. Though I used to hoard stamps, you know. A whole shoe box full, carefully categorised. Penny blacks and all. Utterly useless, of course.      Useless? Mam used to say, "Everything's useful, lass, you just haven't figured out  how  yet." She was talking about old tea towels mostly, but the principle… Anyway, speaking of useless, did you see that Lakeland catalogue? They're selling reusable bread bags with little ducks on them! Ducks! Who needs a duck-themed bread bag?      Ducks are cool. You could draw a proper cool duck on it, though. Not those cartoon ones. A realistic duck. With… you know… feathers. And a beak.      Jonathan will probably just stuff it with old socks, regardless of how fancy the duck is. Honestly, moving is exhausting. It’s not just the packing, it’s the mental load of deciding what's worth taking, and then the regret of leaving things behind. I keep thinking about that old typewriter my grandfather gave me… feels sacrilegious to just leave it.      Typewriter? Fancy that. My husband, Albert, he used to write letters on those. Big, proper letters, on thick paper. He was a romantic, he was. Not like this… this internet tat. You can’t feel the words on a screen, can you?      He’s got a point, hasn't he? This moving… It's more than just boxes. It's… it’s the ending of a chapter, isn't it? I’ve been in this house for…well, let’s not dwell. I do worry about the new place. Will it feel like home? And the garden! I need somewhere to plant my lavender.      Don't you worry about that, love. The new place has a garden  and  they're already got a lavender bush planted! Massive one, apparently. We’ve already booked the removal firm, by the way. "Gentle Giants" – they seem alright. They’re doing a survey next week. Right, Jonathan, put down your phone for a minute and tell me, have you started thinking about what you  actually  want to take with you? Besides your Xbox, obviously.      Yeah... got a few posters I want. And my headphones. And... probably all my Pokemon cards.      Pokemon cards. Of course. Listen, I was thinking, maybe we could get a skip?

Honestly, Chloe, I'm stressed. Like, GCSE option choices are looming. Mum's being all, "Think about your future, darling!" as if I can actually  see  the future. It's ridiculous. Tell me about it. My dad's already got a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet! Categorizing subjects based on potential job prospects. Like I'm already applying for something. I mean, I  like  maths, but accountant? Seriously? Exactly! And he's going on about 'Marketable skills'. What even  are  marketable skills? Does being able to perfectly play the clarinet count? Because I’m pretty good, you know. Mr. Davies said I have a real flair. You do! But flair doesn't pay the bills, does it, love? Though, thinking about it, maybe you could become one of those… what are they called… bog bloggers? Like, clarinet reviews and stuff. A bog blogger? So, like, writing about clarinets on the internet? Sounds… depressing. I’d rather work at Lush, honestly. All the smells and bath bombs... and you get a discount! Lush is good. Much better than being stuck in an office, crunching numbers. Have you seen that youtuber, Alfie Deyes? He seems to have it sorted. Just films himself and makes loads of dosh. Maybe  that’s  the future. Become a youtuber. "Clarinet Girl Reviews!" Oh my god, don't! That’s mortifying. But… it  is  a thought. Although, I’d probably just end up sobbing on camera when I messed up a difficult piece. Remember that bit in perfect duty last week? When Mrs. Hawthorne was going on about responsibility and I nearly burst into tears because I forgot my PE kit? Don't remind me. That was brutal. She’s got a face like granite, hasn't she? And PE! Honestly, the volleyball lessons are a joke. I keep hitting it into the fence. Mr. Finch just sighs and shakes his head. He's permanently disappointed. Remember last year when everyone was obsessed with Zendaya? Everyone was calling her like, the most perfect person ever. Now it's all about Olivia Rodrigo. It's so fickle. It is! And remember that whole drama with Joe Wicks during lockdown? Suddenly everyone was an amazing cook. I just ate a lot of cereal. My mum tried to get us to do his workouts, but I hid in the garden pretending to be a garden gnome. That’s brilliant! You were a very convincing garden gnome.

…and honestly, the coding on that new spreadsheet is just baffling. I spent three hours yesterday wrestling with a pivot table function, and it  still  wasn't giving me the data I needed. It's supposed to simplify things, but it just adds another layer of complication! Pivot tables, eh? Reminds me of the old draughting boards. You'd think with all this fancy modern technology, things would be simpler, wouldn't you? Back in my day, we relied on a good protractor and a steady hand, and you  knew  exactly where everything was. No hidden algorithms messing you about. Tell you what, Arthur. Remember old Farmer Giles' tractor? That '36 Ferguson? Now  that  was reliable. No computers, just good honest engineering. You could fix it with a bit of string and a spanner. These new ones... all sparks and flashing lights. Can’t even tell you what's gone wrong if it breaks down. Honestly, the way things are going... I’m glad I retired when I did. Trying to keep up with the youngsters and their gadgets… it's exhausting! Used to be a nice quiet chat about the weather, wasn’t it? Now it's all 'apps' and 'downloads'. It is a bit overwhelming, I admit. Though, on the other hand, look at what we  can  do now! The research possibilities alone. I was reading about this new AI program that can identify bird calls… astonishing! Imagine, being able to pinpoint exactly which species is singing in your garden. Bird calls, you say? I did see a pair of goldcrests in my garden the other day. Little blighters, barely bigger than a bumblebee. Never got a proper look at ‘em, mind you. They flitted off before I could get me binoculars out. Should have invested in a decent camera… another thing I haven’t got round to. Goldcrests, eh? Bless 'em. Used to see a proper flock of fieldfares down in the meadows when I was a boy. Swarms of ‘em. Now you’re lucky to see one. Things have changed drastically, haven't they? All that farming's gone intensive now. No room for the birds. It is sad, isn’t it? My grandson, Thomas, he’s mad about wildlife. Goes on these nature walks all the time. He tried to show me some of his photos the other week. Very impressive, but all a bit beyond me, really.

Speaker_1 chuckled, a dry, crackling sound. “Right proper nuisance, that lad.” Oh, children, aren’t they? My Sarah, when she was about seven, used to insist the postman was an alien. Wouldn’t take the letters unless I held her hand. Said they were probes, you know. Probes! That’s brilliant. Kids are gold dust, aren't they? I had little Timmy – not mine, obviously, in my class – used to call the interactive whiteboard 'the glowy box'. Said it was hypnotizing him. You try explaining the internet to a six-year-old! Used to be simpler, didn’t it? Back in my day, school was just a proper desk, a blackboard, and a teacher with a ruler. Kept you in line, they did. Times have changed somethin’ awful. So, what's this about your wardrobe, Margaret? You sounded a bit flustered before. Oh, it’s just… the deliverymen were here. From that online place, Style Haven, you know? Said they had a special offer on cardigans. Ridiculous really. Twenty-seven cardigans! Arrived in three boxes, they did. Piled up in the hallway. Couldn't move. Twenty-seven! Goodness! Were they all different colours? You've got good taste, Margaret. I’d be lost. My wife's the same, orders things online without a thought. Keeps threatening to send me a purple sequined waistcoat. Ha! You wouldn’t want that, would you? Though, I reckon you could pull it off. I'm more a muted brown sort of man, meself. Practical. Though my daughter got me a bright orange… thing. Said it was “on trend.” Looks like a traffic cone, it does. Oh, it’s mostly sensible colours, thankfully. Navy, grey, beige. It’s just… a lot. And I had to sign for all three boxes! My poor arm aches. These deliverymen, they’re all so brisk. Barely a "hello" these days. Just “Sign here, madam.” They’re always rushing. Last week, the chap delivering my new bookshelf nearly took out my roses. Didn’t even apologise! Blamed  me  for standing in his way. The audacity! Speaking of rushing… did you see that  Bake Off  episode last night? One of the contestants had a complete meltdown. Drowned his cake in sherry! Sherry, you say? Now that’s a bit of ingenuity. Though I'm more of a bitter lemon man meself, after a long day. Though… might try a cheeky sherry later.

Aye, that’s a right proper blanket o’ snow, isn’t it? Reckon it’ll be sticking about for a bit, though. Remember that time back home, back in '09, when we were snowed in for a week? Mum went mental trying to make snowmen, bless her. A week? Crikey. I vaguely remember seeing pictures on Facebook. It’s pretty impressive here, though. Managed to get a decent layer on the garden, at least. Though the roses are probably panicking. Did you get a chance to check on the seedlings in the greenhouse? Nah, not yet. Been busy sorting through these research reports. Ridiculous amount of paperwork, as always. But I'll pop out later, yeah. It'd be a shame if they got flattened. Though, realistically, I should have covered them. Right silly, me. Don’t beat yourself up. It’s the unexpected, isn't it? Speaking of unexpected, did you catch  Come Dine With Me  last night? That woman from Grimsby... Oh my god. Oh, don't even! The cheese fountain? The aggressively sparkly tablecloth? It was a masterpiece of questionable taste! She genuinely thought she was practically Michelin-starred, didn't she? Proper hilarious. Hilarious and terrifying. Makes you appreciate a simple shepherd’s pie, doesn’t it? Anyway, it got me thinking about… well, having a little get-together of our own. Nothing fancy, obviously. Just a low-key dinner party. Ooh, I like that! When were you thinking? And at your place, aye? That’s brilliant, loads more space than my flat. Sometime in February, maybe? Give the snow a chance to properly melt – wouldn't want anyone slipping on the way. I was thinking we could each do a course. Like, one starter, one main, one dessert? Aye, that's a grand idea! I could do a proper Sunderland steak pie, if I'm feeling ambitious. Or maybe just some fancy sausage rolls. Less chance of disaster that way. What about Liam and Chloe? And Sarah and Mark? Definitely. I'll give them a shout. Gets a bit hectic organizing everyone, doesn’t it? Moving onto more pressing matters… have you heard anything more about the stag do for Ben? His brother was going on about elaborate paintballing in the Lake District. Paintballing? Seriously? Ben hates getting shot at! Heard he wants something more… relaxed. Maybe a brewery tour? He’s been on about wanting to learn more about craft beer.

Aye, that they did. More butter than a baker's shop, some nights. Though, to be fair, your Mum did try. Didn't have much to go on, did she? Costessey wasn’t exactly a culinary hotspot back then. More turnips and rabbit stew than anything fancy. Don’t be unkind, Arthur. She did the best she could. And the rabbit stew  was  lovely. Not the dressy, complicated meals you get now, all foams and micro-greens. Real, hearty food. Remember those Yorkshire puddings, though? They were always a bit…flat. Flat, yes! Like pancakes. You know, it's funny, I was thinking about proper Sunday roasts just today, teaching my food history class. We were talking about the Victorian origins of the traditional roast dinner - the symbolism of presenting a whole bird, the social significance of different side dishes…it’s fascinating! Absolutely. It’s evolved so much, hasn’t it? The emphasis now is on sourcing ingredients, supporting local farms… it wasn't even a consideration for most people back when Arthur was a boy. Did you mostly buy everything from that little shop on the High Street, Arthur? Aye, Mr. Figgins’ shop. ‘E knew everyone’s order by heart. Bread, dripping, a bit of cheese…always a bit of a queue, mind you. And sometimes, if you were lucky, ‘e’d ‘ave a few apples. Not proper shiny ones like you get now, all waxed up. These were proper Norfolk apples, all a bit tatty, but full of flavour. Couldn't buy 'em now. He used to complain about the price of butter constantly, poor man. Said it was daylight robbery. Now, Arthur, you're having a good piece of that roast chicken, aren’t you? Don't look like you're enjoying it. It’s alright, Doris. Just…a bit dry, innit? Needs a bit more gravy. Your Mum always made a proper gravy, she did. Rich and dark. This…well, it's not bad, but it’s not Mum’s gravy, is it? We  tried , Dad. I really did. I used a rich stock, deglazed the pan… it’s a basic recipe, but…it’s hard to recreate memories, isn't it? You can't just write down a feeling. Don’t beat yourself up, love. It’s delicious. Honestly. It’s just… everything tastes a bit different when it’s not being made in a nostalgic haze.

“Tell me about it. Postgraduate study was more relaxing, actually. At least then I felt like I was  learning  something, engaging with ideas. This… this feels like glorified filing.” "Filing with a panicked side of ‘urgent’ attached. Seriously though, you look wiped, Liv. Have some more gravy. Mum’s gravy cures all ills.” “Aye, it does! It’s my secret recipe, you know. Not the Bisto stuff, mind! Proper gravy, made with bones and patience. Your dad used to say it was better than therapy!” "Don't I know it. Changed the man, that gravy. Used to be a right grump. Now he just mopes quietly while eating three helpings.” “You and Dad are a pair, aren’t you? Though I don’t think even your gravy could fix Dad’s grumbling about the state of the garden.” “Garden's a disgrace, that's what it is. Full o’ weeds. Reminds me o’ the allotments back in me day. Used to grow prize-winning courgettes, I did. Smashin’ courgettes!” “Grandad, you always say that! You didn’t win any prizes, remember? Auntie Carol told us. It was a neighbour who had a slightly bigger one. And you argued with them for three weeks.” “Don't you go believin’ yer Auntie Carol. She always had a bee in her bonnet. Besides, size isn’t everything. Taste is what matters, and mine were the tastiest!” “Now, now, Grandad. Let's not start a courgette argument at dinner. Liv, are you alright? You’re not eating much. Is it the work? Maybe you should consider a change. You've got that postgraduate, you could do something completely different.” “I know, I know. It’s just… daunting. I put so much effort into the degree, and then the job market was a nightmare. This was the first decent offer I got. I'm just… stuck, I think.” “Stuck? Spend a bit of time looking around. My sister, Maureen, she was stuck for years in a dead-end accounts job. Went back to college, did a graphic design course. Now she's runnin' her own business, makin' websites. Happy as Larry, she is.” “See? Inspiration. Maybe you could look into something creative? You always did love photography.” "Aye, and you're good at it! Remember that exhibition you had at uni? Brilliant stuff. You should dust off the camera, love. Get away from the spreadsheets for a bit.

…and honestly, the whole thing just exploded. Overnight. Didn’t see it coming, not in a million years. We’d been plugging away for six months, barely getting five thousand views a week on the penguin rehabilitation videos, and then suddenly – boom! – a TikTokker picked it up, did a little dance thing, and it went properly viral. Millions of views. Suddenly, donations were flooding in. It was mad. Penguins, right? Your penguin rescue thing? That’s brilliant, honestly. And you’re saying this TikTok phenomenon genuinely helped? It’s amazing how those platforms can just… catapult something. It’s a bit terrifying, isn’t it? For the creators, I mean. You're giving up so much control. Absolutely terrifying! We were scrambling to keep up. Suddenly, we needed someone dedicated just to managing social media engagement. Can you imagine? Six months in, needing a full-time social media manager. It's been a steep learning curve. But, you know, a good problem to have. It just proves that sometimes, the most unexpected avenues are the best. It reminds me a bit of what we’ve been talking about for the university modular courses, doesn’t it? Yes! Precisely. We were discussing how the traditional lecture format is so… static. And how even incorporating online elements feels like a tacked-on afterthought, rather than an integral part. What if we harnessed that viral potential? Not in a, you know, artificially manufactured way, but focusing on truly engaging, easily digestible content that sparks interest? That's the key, isn't it? Authenticity. No one wants a bland promotional video. They want a story. Like the penguins. People connect with the story, not the rescue organisation. We were just lucky to be the vehicle for that story. I was thinking about breaking down complex topics – say, quantum physics – into short, animated explainers. Five-minute bursts. High production quality, naturally, but focused on making it genuinely entertaining. Think Kurzgesagt, but with a slightly more… quirky British-Kiwi sensibility. I like the sound of that. Though, ‘quirky’ is a loaded word. We wouldn't want to sacrifice clarity for the sake of amusement. My worry is, could we sustain that level of engagement over a full module? Quantum physics isn't exactly conducive to constant TikTok dances. True. It wouldn’t be  all  short videos. The videos would be an entry point, a hook, then direct students to more in-depth resources – articles, interactive simulations, even virtual reality experiences.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork is insane. I swear, half my job is just filling out risk assessments and care plans. It's vital, of course, but… draining. Did you manage to get those oatcakes I asked for? The ones from Yorkshire? Yep, they’re right here. Got them from that little farm shop near Borough Market. They were a bit pricey, mind, but worth it. Yorkshire makes the best oatcakes, doesn't it? Though Cornwall does a decent clotted cream, I’ll give them that. Fancy a cuppa? I was just putting the kettle on. Please! Desperately. Yorkshire oatcakes and tea are basically the key to survival after dealing with a particularly difficult patient. So, what's the project going crazy this week? Still wrestling with that supplier issue for the Henderson account? Ugh, you have  no  idea. They’re claiming, and I quote, “unforeseen circumstances” are causing the delay with the widgets. Unforeseen circumstances?! It’s been three weeks! I've had to practically threaten legal action to get them to even acknowledge it. Honestly, sometimes I wonder why I even bothered with a degree. Don't be silly. You're brilliant at it. Organising people is basically your superpower. Remember when you single-handedly coordinated that charity bake sale and raised enough to buy new equipment for the community centre? That was fun, wasn’t it? Though I’m still slightly traumatised by Mrs. Higgins’ rock-hard gingerbread. Okay, never again. So, weekend plans? Anything exciting brewing? I'm thinking of going to that Halloween party at The Raven. Sarah’s going, apparently. Ooh, The Raven! That sounds fun. I’m thinking of staying in, actually. I’m exhausted. Might binge-watch 'The Crown' and wear a face mask. My brain needs a serious reset. Although… maybe I'll pop by yours if I’m feeling less… depleted. Are you doing anything spooky for Halloween? Not really. I might carve a pumpkin. Nothing too elaborate. It’s just… I’m actually feeling a little lost about the future, you know? Five years from now. It feels like such a huge chunk of time. Where do you think we’ll be? Five years… Wow, that  is  a long time. I'd hope to have specialised in adolescent mental health, ideally. Maybe be running my own small therapeutic group. And definitely have my own tiny flat, somewhere near the sea.

Honestly, darling, it's just bewildering. All this technology! I mean, I can barely work the telly without needing someone to come round and fiddle with it. And now, this ‘smart home’ you've got here… it's a bit much, innit? It’s not  that  complicated, Nan. I showed you how to turn the lights on and off with your voice yesterday. “Alexa, lights on!” Remember? I remember saying it, yes. And it did turn the lights on. But then it started telling me about the weather! I just wanted a bit of light, love, not a forecast! Feels a bit… intrusive, somehow. Like a nosy neighbour constantly butting in. It's just programmed to give you information, Nan. You can tell it to stop, you know. “Alexa, be quiet.” Be quiet? Good heavens! Talking back to appliances now, are we? It’s a slippery slope, this is. Next thing you know, the kettle will be arguing with me about whether it’s boiled enough. Remember my Doris, bless her cotton socks?
