She’d have had a heart attack at this. She’d say, "Annie, dear, if you can't turn a switch, leave the technology alone!" I know, Nan, but things are different now. It’s designed to make life easier. It can remind you to take your medication, play your favourite music, even order your groceries. Groceries? Online? Don’t be daft. I like going to the market. Talking to Mrs. Higgins, getting a proper tomato that actually smells like sunshine, not plastic. And having a bit of a gossip, you know? Online shopping... it’s just… impersonal. Well, you can still go to the market, Nan. But if you can’t be bothered on a rainy day… Think of it! No struggling with heavy bags! They deliver straight to your door. I suppose. Still… bringing things in yourself, feeling the weight of it... it's a proper bit of exercise. Gets the circulation going. You young people with your sit-down jobs… you need to get out more. I walk to work, Nan. Honestly. And I have a gym membership. A gym membership! Fancy that. Back in my day, exercise was lugging coal and chasing after children. Simple as that. So, about this anniversary dinner next month... Are you still thinking of that Italian place down the King's Parade? Yeah, I’ve booked the table. Saturday the 15th.

Honestly, Zara, this heat is a right misery. Makes ya feel like yer melting, it does. Could murder a cold pint right now, couldn't you? Proper Yorkshire ale, mind, not this fizzy stuff they’ve got here. I know, it’s intense. Though, I’m used to slightly milder summers. Still, better than Cambridge in January, right? Remember that ice storm? At least the light is gorgeous. And look at that boulangerie! They’ve got pain au chocolat… Pain au what-now? Don’t tempt me! I’m tryin’ to stick to me diet, ya know. Gotta be ready for tri-athalons next year, reet? Though I’m still struggling with the swimming technique, to be fair. Coach says my kick’s all over the place. Says I swim like a 'drowned otter.’ Charming, innit? A drowned otter? That’s… picturesque, in a way. Maybe you need a video analysis? Uni has some good facilities. Speaking of uni, did you hear back from Manchester about that sports science placement? Aye, got it! Managed to bag myself a spot with the rugby team. Coaching, mostly, helping with their strength and conditioning. Proper dead chuffed, I am. It’s brilliant, that is. Reckon I can actually use some o' what I’m learning. Trying to think of a good project for final year, though. Something to do with biomechanics, probably. It’s all so overwhelming. Do you have any ideas? Hmm, biomechanics… well, we covered a fascinating paper on the impact of different training regimes on ligament elasticity in the lower leg during volleyball. Could you adapt something like that for rugby? Maybe focus on ACL injury prevention? It's a massive problem, apparently. ACL injury prevention… Now that’s somethin’, tha's right. Proper serious stuff. I'll have to look into that. Scientific method, though… sometimes I just feel like I'm drowning in theories and equations. It’s not like in sixth form, is it? Everything's so much deeper. Tell me about it! Professor Davies’ methodology lectures are enough to make anyone’s head spin. He spends ages on control groups and statistical significance. It’s fascinating in theory, but applying it practically when you're actually  doing  research… much harder. Are you listening to Arctic Monkeys at all for some mental escapism? They're putting out new stuff, apparently. Arctic Monkeys? Seriously? Aye, love ‘em! Heard snippets online.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of them! I mean, I understand it’s autumn, everything's heading indoors, but it’s been relentless. Little house spiders, big hairy ones… I’m practically living with a broom permanently in my hand. It's so unhygienic, really. You know, dealing with clients all day, presenting figures, making sure everything’s spotless for them… and then I come home to  this . Oh, you get that, don’t you? Fancy job, you do. Must be a world away from what I deal with. I’m mopping up spills and dust, but at least the creepy crawlies aren’t trying to build webs in the boardroom! It’s not glamorous, not really. Just a lot of pressure. But this… this is just unsettling. I saw a massive one down the hall the other day, right above the skirting board. I nearly jumped out of my skin. Kevin just said, “Shoo it, love.” As if it's that simple! Kevin's a good man, isn't he? Solid. Always gets on with things. You know, the house I clean for Mrs. Higgins, she’s terrified of spiders. Absolutely petrified. Had to get a proper pest control fella in, practically fumigated the place. Cost her a fortune. Honestly, though, I don't mind 'em much. Useful little things, keepin' the fly population down, innit? Useful? They’re terrifying! I had a nightmare about spiders last night – giant ones, dangling from the ceiling fans! It was dreadful. I’m considering setting traps. Though, that just feels… cruel. What about the mice? Have you had trouble with those? We’ve heard scratching in the walls. Mice, yeah, proper buggers they are. Got a family livin' in the shed at my place. Tried catching ‘em, but they’re clever. Put out traps, poisoned pellets… doesn't seem to do much good. They're too quick. Mrs. Higgins’s had a terrible problem with them too. She keeps a clean house, but they just get in somehow. Little blighters. You get no peace. It’s just so demoralising, isn’t it? You try to maintain a certain standard. I mean, I buy organic cat food – for my Persian, Penelope, of course - and I still have vermin running around! It's just… underwhelming. Penelope, eh? Fancy name for a cat! My Alfie just gets fed whatever’s cheapest. You wouldn’t believe the birds we’ve got in my garden though.

Absolutely, Dilwyn. It  is  a rabbit hole. I’ve dabbled myself. Though honestly, I’m more into the stories than the dates and lineages, if I’m being honest. Finding out what people  did , not just when they were born. It brings them to life, doesn’t it? My mum, bless her heart, used to tell me snippets, little tales about Great-Aunt Elsie who ran away with a circus… I wish she'd told me more when she was well enough. Aye, stories are the best part, aren't they? Dates fade, but a good yarn... that sticks. My Gran used to tell me stories about the mines, back in South Wales. Grim work, it was, but she’d spin it with such colour and humour, you’d forget the danger for a moment. Course, she was born right in the middle of it, so she knew better than most. My father, he wasn’t much for talking about the past. Just… closed off, a bit. Lost his brother in the war, you know. Never really recovered. That's terrible, Dilwyn. My mum… she passed away last year. It was quick, unfortunately. Amyloidosis. Have you heard of it? Amyloid-what? No, can’t say I 'ave. Sounds nasty. It is. It’s a rare disease. Basically, abnormal proteins build up in your organs. Hers affected her kidneys and heart, mostly. It was… brutal, really. We lost her in six months from diagnosis. It's left a huge hole, of course. It's hard to believe she's no longer around to… you know, tell me off for leaving the washing up. Oh, love. That’s heartbreaking. Six months? That's barely enough time to… to say goodbye properly. My dear husband, Gareth, he went after a long illness, cancer. It was five years, but even that felt too short. You learn to make the most of every single moment, don’t you? You do. You absolutely do. It makes you appreciate things differently. I’m a teacher, you see, primary school. Been doing it for seventeen years now. It's rewarding, most of the time. Screaming children aside, naturally. . Lots of marking, though. Endless marking. School teaching, eh? Always a noble profession. Mine was secondary, history. Loved it, I did. Seeing young people discover the past… inspiring. Though the politics got a bit much towards the end. Never quite got the hang of the paperwork, truth be told.

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. London just… suffocates me sometimes, you know? All that concrete, all those people jostling. Here, it just feels… spacious. I get it. Though, I do like the energy of the city. Keeps you on your toes. Still, this is pretty spectacular. Did you spot that hare a bit back? It was huge. I did! Beautiful thing, wasn't it? Proper bounding across the fields. Reminds me of that documentary we watched last year about the Norfolk landscape. The sheer biodiversity is astonishing. It’s something I try to impress on the students, you know – how fragile this all is. They probably zone out when you start talking about protected habitats, though. They’re more interested in Instagrammable sunsets. Speaking of which… Look! One of those hot air balloons. Going east, I think. Oh, brilliant! They’re becoming more popular, aren’t they? Always thought it looked terrifying. Just… dangling suspended in the air like that. All that reliance on wind currents. Terrifying for you, perhaps. I think it looks incredibly romantic. Imagine, floating over all this… Noisy, though. The burners must be loud. Remember that camping trip we took in the Lake District? The guy next to us had one that kept roaring on and off all night. Drove us mad! Oh, don't remind me! I spent half the night feeling like I was in the middle of an industrial estate. We need to camp somewhere quieter next time. Maybe back here, somewhere near the coast? We could take Barnaby. He’d absolutely adore it. Barnaby loved the Lake District, even though he mostly just chased sheep. He’d be a menace on a campsite though, wouldn’t he? Stealing sausages off the barbecue. Speaking of which… I was thinking about that upgrade to his bed. The orthopedic one. It’s pricey, isn’t it? A bit. But he’s getting old, isn’t he? And he deserves a bit of comfort. We can figure it out. Just... don’t start bringing up the leaky roof again, please. The quotes are depressing. Sorry, sorry. Just… being realistic. These things add up, don’t they? I saw someone photographing those power lines on Instagram the other day - some kind of artistic project apparently. Makes you think about the infrastructure hidden everywhere. All the electricity humming along, keeping everything powered… It costs a fortune to maintain.

Aye, Brenda does lay it on thick, doesn’t she? She’s got that relentless energy, that woman. Good for her, mind, keeps people motivated, but blimey, you need a good lie down afterwards. Solihull's a bit warmer than Leeds today though, that's for sure. Didn't expect it in October, did ya? No, definitely not. This mildness is a little bit deceptive, though, isn't it? It feels nice now, but I can feel the chill creeping in in the evenings. I’m trying to mentally prepare myself for a proper winter. Not looking forward to the grey skies. I miss the proper sunshine of the summer. You get used to it, lass. You just have to. Up north, we’re just resigned to it. Grey skies are the norm. Though, like, last November, we had a proper snowstorm. Brought the whole city to a standstill. Still, there’s somethin' comforting about snuggling up with a good book when it's chucking it down, innit? Read anything good lately? Actually, yes! I finished "Hamnet" by Maggie O'Farrell. Absolutely stunning. It’s heartbreaking and beautiful all at once. Have you heard of it? Can’t say I ‘ave. I mostly stick to thrillers, you see. Gotta keep the adrenaline pumpin’, particularly with the job I’ve got. Running a cluster of gyms, having to deal with instructors and members... it’s non-stop. I'm an area manager, see, for ‘Powerhouse Fitness.’ Keeps me on my toes, that one. Sounds demanding. I teach languages – mostly Italian and Spanish – at a local adult education centre. It’s less… physically exhausting than managing gyms, but it's got its challenges too. People’s motivations can be all over the place, you know? Some are genuinely passionate about learning, others are just doing it to tick a box. Aye, motivational work is always tricky, regardless of the field. When I started out, I worked as a sales assistant. Honestly, the number of times someone came in saying they wanted to get fit, then proceeded to order a massive chocolate shake! You’ve got to suss out what makes them tick, haven't you? I’ve learned a few coaching techniques over the years - positive reinforcement, setting realistic goals, that sort of thing. Keeps the lads and lasses focused. I've found that too. Celebrating small victories is crucial. We do a lot of pair work in my classes, and getting students to actually  speak  to someone, even if it’s just ordering a coffee in Italian, is a huge step.

Aye, teenagers. They do test yer patience, don’t they? My own Mark weren’t much better at maths when he were that age. More interested in football, he was. Still is, come to that.      It’s not  that  bad, Gran. It’s just…sometimes the numbers don’t want to behave.      Numbers never did behave properly, did they, Arthur? Never did. Used to try and balance the budget down at the market, and the sums just wouldn't add up. Always a penny or two missing.      More than a penny or two, Dorothy! Always a bob short. Those market folk, they were crafty, they were. Took advantage of an honest woman.      Now, now, Grandad. Don’t be getting all worked up. Things were different back then. And you always got a bargain, didn’t you?      We did, dear. And a bit of gossip thrown in for good measure! Remember Mrs. Higgins and her prize-winning marrows?      I’ve heard tales of those marrows, Gran. They were legendary!      Right, well, moving on from marrows and dodgy market traders… We need to sort out dinner, don't we? I was thinking a roast chicken. Everyone likes a roast, don't they? Tom, you fancy that?      Yeah, sounds good, Gran. Potatoes and gravy, please? Loads of gravy.      Loads of gravy it is! And I'll get some Yorkshire puddings on. Oh, Dorothy, Arthur, you fancy a Yorkshire pudding?      Oh, a pudding? Bless you, Brenda. Yes, a pudding would be lovely. Though I can't eat as much as I used to.      Pudding’s alright. As long as it's not one of those fancy ones with all the fruit. Give me a proper, plain Yorkshire pudding any day.      Right then. Sorted. Tom, could you be a dear and pop down to the shops for some lemons and a pint of milk? We’re running low.      Sure, Gran. Anything else?      Just see if they’ve got any of those custard creams, your Grandad likes them. The ones with the proper thick custard filling, not that watery stuff.      Don't be telling him where to get 'em, woman! I know a good custard cream when I see one!      Alright, alright! Just thought I'd be helpful. And Tom, while you're out, could you swing by that new deli on the High Street? I'm wanting some mature cheddar for cheese and biscuits later.      Ooh, cheddar!

"Aye, worse than that, lass! It tried to navigate us into a river! A  river ! I swear, these things are daft as a brush." "They are, aren't they? It’s the algorithm, Brenda. They prioritise the shortest route above all else. No consideration for the state of the road, or, you know, physics. Perhaps we should revert to a map. Proper old-fashioned navigation." “A map? Now you’re talking sense! But then we’d miss out on the horrifying errors, wouldn’t we? Part of the fun, I reckon. Though, me knee's aching something fierce today, so a smooth journey would be appreciated. Did you remember to pack the liniment? Just in case this driving gets too strenuous.” "Of course. It’s in the backpack with the waterproofs. Speaking of strenuous, how's the training for Emily’s wedding going? She wants you doing a ceilidh dance with her, remember?" “Oh, don’t remind me! My ankles are protesting just thinking about it. Trying to teach me to reel, is she? It's like trying to make a cat do the tango. I’ll give it a go, for Emily’s sake, but I won't be winning any prizes, that’s for sure. Still, it’ll be a grand day. Have you sorted out that speech you promised?” "Nearly. I've got a few lines about Emily's fierce independence and her love of rescuing injured birds. A bit of poetry thrown in, naturally. It’s still a work in progress. I’m wrestling with the rhythm, you see. Trying to avoid sounding… pompous." "Don't you worry about sounding pompous, Mark. You’re a writer! It's in your blood. Just keep it heartfelt. Remember Uncle George's speech at Margaret’s wedding? Oh, dear Lord, that was something else. Went on for nearly an hour and kept repeating himself!" "Definitely steer clear of that.” "Noted. Right, the weather’s looking a bit dodgy up ahead. See that darkening sky? Might be a bit bumpy for the drive back. Though, I’m hoping the band tonight will compensate. They said they’ve got some new material, inspired by that old folk song, ‘The Shepherd’s Lament’." "Oh, now you’re talking! I love that song. Makes me think of all those old woollen mills in Darlington, you know, back when they were thriving. Me gran used to work in one of them.

…and honestly, the lightwells were just  wrong . Didn’t factor in the seasonal shift at all. It’ll be a gloomy box half the year, I swear. Anyway, what are you having? I’m craving a full English. Need to line the stomach after that debacle. You're always dramatic, Tom. A gloomy box? It wasn’t  that  bad. A bit…optimistically positioned, maybe. I’ll have the avocado toast, please. And a flat white. Still feeling a bit fragile after cycling here. Fragile? You’re a machine, Elara. You cycle up hills in the rain for fun. Right, okay, avocado toast. Not the most architecturally inspiring breakfast, is it? Though I suppose it's aesthetically pleasing. Soft colours, clean lines… You're impossible. You find architecture in everything. So, did you hear back from Maya? She sounded pretty down yesterday. No, not yet. I texted her this morning, just to see if she was alright. She’s been carrying the load on the Harrington project, hasn't she? Poor girl. It’s brutal, that firm. Such a high-pressure environment. Remember when we were at Uni and felt stressed about our dissertations? This is a whole different league. Completely different. They really do push people to breaking point. Remember Professor Davies, though? He'd have said it builds character. He'd have loved that brutalist office block we just saw. Davies. The man lived for concrete and despair. Speaking of university... I was just thinking about that brief we had, the one for the communal living space? Remember how ambitious we were, wanting to incorporate vertical farming and self-regulating heating? Vaguely. It feels a lifetime ago. We were so idealistic! We wanted to reinvent housing. Do you think it's genuinely achievable, though? Truly sustainable, affordable communal living? Beyond a handful of trendy co-living schemes? That's the thing, isn't it? The principle is sound – tackling loneliness, sharing resources, reducing our carbon footprint… but the practicalities are a nightmare. Land costs, planning permission, getting people who  aren’t  posh hippies to actually want to share a kitchen… It's a minefield. We need to figure out the economic model before we can even seriously consider the architecture. Exactly. We kept getting bogged down in the utopian vision and forgetting about the funding. I'm actually doing some research on modular construction techniques now. Might be a way to bring down costs and speed up the build process.

Honestly, darling, the A1 was a  nightmare  this evening. Absolute gridlock. Took me nearly an hour to get from Stamford. I swear, people just don't understand the concept of merging. It's like they think if they stay in their lane forever, the other cars will magically disappear. Tell me about it! I was heading back from Sarah’s – her mum made that amazing lasagne, you know? – and saw the tailbacks from miles away. Proper standstill. It was a bit stressful, actually. Loads of lorries, just idling, fumes everywhere. Exactly! And the impatience! People were flashing their lights aggressively. Honestly, it's aggressive, aggressive driving. I had to take a deep breath and remind myself it's not worth getting stressed over. Though, I must admit, I did give that bloke in the silver Mondeo a  look  when he tried to force his way in just as I was signalling. You did, didn’t you? I remember. You were muttering something about 'entitlement' as he sped past. Sarah was laughing. She said you looked like your mum when she’s dealing with tourists who don’t know how roundabouts work. Well, she's not wrong, is she? Some people just think the road is their own personal racetrack. Anyway, enough about road rage. So, you had a nice time with Sarah? Did you manage to finally convince her to come to that pottery class with us? Almost! She’s still a bit hesitant. She said she's worried she’ll be rubbish and will just make a mess. You know Sarah, always thinking the worst. I told her everyone makes a mess at first - that's the whole point! Besides, we’ll be there to help. She needs to embrace the mess! It’s therapeutic, really. Remember that awful vase I made last year? The one that looked like a melted slug? Oh god, yes! We were all howling! But you were so proud of it. You kept it on the mantelpiece for weeks. Well, you have to celebrate the effort, don't you? Anyway, look, I was thinking... how about next Saturday we all go out for a proper dinner? Somewhere nice, like that Italian place in Melton? We haven’t done a proper girls’ night out in ages. That sounds lovely, Mum! I’d really like that. Sarah would too, I think. I’ll text her now. Is Dad still working late a lot at the moment?

Right, so I've had another look at this job description for the Senior Content Producer role at BBC Radio Leeds. It’s…a lot, isn't it? Honestly, 'embedded journalism, digital first, audience engagement, and demonstrable experience in podcasting’ – it's like they threw every buzzword they could think of into one paragraph. Aye, they do like to pile it on, don’t they? Standard practice though, innit? Gotta see who can actually  do  all that claptrap. Don’t let it intimidate ya, love. You’ve got the skills. The podcasting bit especially, you’re brilliant at that. Remember that series you did on local history? Proper gripping stuff. I know, but the ‘embedded journalism’ thing…it makes me nervous. They want someone who can effectively "become part of a newsroom environment," which, as a freelancer for so long, I haven’t really done. I mean, I've worked  with  newsrooms, but not  in  them, you know? Right, I get that. Think about it this way, though. You’ve spent years interviewing people, researching stories, building trust… that’s all part of being embedded, isn't it? It's about understanding the community, being present, listening. You’ve just done it independently. Frame it like that. Instead of saying you’ve  never  been embedded, you can say you've built a strong track record of immersive reporting. That's a good point, actually. I hadn’t thought of it quite like that. Okay, so, how do I phrase that? Something like, "Proven ability to conduct immersive reporting and cultivate strong relationships within communities, evidenced by prior experience with independent investigative projects..."? Too much? Bit clunky, love. Relax it a bit. How about, "Experienced in building genuine connections with communities and delivering impactful reporting through independent projects"? Sounds a bit more…you. Less like you’re trying to learn jargon on the spot. Okay, yeah, that’s better. That feels more me. Right, the digital first bit… I'm confident on social media, but they’re really pushing for someone who understands analytics and audience data. Honestly, that's where I feel a bit shaky. I know  what  works, but not always  why . See, that’s easily addressed. Mention your awareness of the importance of data and your eagerness to learn more. Honestly, they don’t expect you to be an analytics guru on day one. It's about showing the potential.

…and that’s why I’m leaning towards the pottery thing, really. It's not just a hobby anymore, you know? The response to my little online shop has been…well, surprisingly positive. People actually  want  my mugs. It's a bit mad, isn’t it? After twenty years of dealing with venture capital, spreadsheets, and quarterly reports, people want handmade pottery. It’s lovely, really. Honestly, you always had a creative streak. Remember those sculptures you used to make out of driftwood when we were kids? Absolutely bonkers, but brilliant. And it's fantastic you’ve found something that people appreciate. So, the online shop is the starting point? Yeah, that's the test bed, isn’t it? It's low risk. I'm not sinking any serious capital in yet. But the volume is…increasing. I’m getting orders I can barely manage alongside the consultancy work, which is, frankly, soul-destroying these days. The joy's just completely gone. Mrs. Abernathy is another nightmare client. Oh, goodness. I remember her. The woman with the poodle shaped like a badger? The very one! Demanding bespoke marketing strategies for badger grooming products. Seriously? I’d rather be covered in clay. Listen, I was thinking... if I  do  seriously consider going full-time pottery, I’d need somewhere, wouldn't I? Somewhere with a bit more space than this spare bedroom. And maybe, you know, a kiln. Absolutely. A dedicated space. Have you looked into studio rentals? There must be pottery studios here in Perth offering that sort of thing. It'd be a good stepping stone. Costs less than buying outright. I have, briefly. They're surprisingly pricey. And often shared, which isn’t ideal. I want somewhere I can really focus. I was daydreaming, actually – silly thought, I know – about buying a small property, a little cottage, somewhere quieter, maybe a bit further out of Perth. With a big garden and a studio. Picture it: sunshine, clay, the smell of damp earth… It does sound idyllic. But it's a hefty leap, isn't it? Financially. And practically. You’d need to be quite sure the pottery can support you. Have you done proper projections? You're always so good at the numbers; don't revert to New Zealand optimism now! Point taken. Actually, I've been fiddling with some Excel spreadsheets. It's surprisingly viable. Not luxury living, obviously.

Tell me about it, Elsie. It’s everywhere, isn’t it? Housing, schools… it's all squeezing tighter and tighter. Little Finn here is lucky we managed to get him into the nursery, but the catchment area for the primaries… well, it’s a nightmare. I mean, Colin’s family are in Swindon, we could move there, but… Swindon? Good heavens, child, no. The air pollution alone… and the quality of education, I shudder to think. It's a symptom of a broader malaise, you know. When populations balloon like this, without the proper infrastructure… it cracks everything. Reminds me a bit of post-war Glasgow, actually. Overcrowding, stretched resources… just horrifying. Though, at least Glasgow had a bit more grit about it. Grit, eh, Morag? You always were one for the dramatic flair. Though, she's got a point, you know. My nephew in London, struggling with the same thing. His little girl's stuck in a temporary portacabin. A portacabin! For education! The sheer absurdity of it. Though, I must say, I'm rather partial to a beard myself these days. Keeps the draught off the chin. A beard, Arthur? Really? Finn's rather taken with beards at the moment. He keeps trying to stroke mine. It’s quite endearing, actually. But back to schools... I was thinking maybe home schooling? It's a lot to take on, I know, especially when you’re trying to juggle everything else. Home schooling? A valiant effort, my dear, but a massive undertaking, particularly with a toddler demanding your attention. Think of the socialisation! Schools aren't just about reading and sums, you know. They're about learning to share, to compromise, to navigate social dynamics. Important skills. Although, homeschooling could be a boon. It allows for a far more bespoke education, tailored to the child's needs and interests. I suppose it depends entirely on the parent's ability and dedication. Are you thinking of enrolling him in any online programs? I’ve been dabbling with some coding tutorials myself, rather sporadically, I must confess. Dreadful interface, though. Absolutely dreadful. No, not planning on coding tutorials just yet! The online stuff looks complicated. I’m barely managing to order our groceries online these days – Domino’s been the saviour, truthfully. They deliver quicker than Ocado, which is astonishing. Domino's? Child, you’re feeding your son pizza every other night? Think of the saturated fat!

Oh, you’re telling me. It was a right kerfuffle, wasn't it? You were always so passionate defending the Common Market, weren’t you, love? Me, I was more concerned with getting through Double Chemistry. Had no real opinion about the bigger picture, to be honest. Just wanted to get out of Moseley Grammar and get a proper job. You did well, didn’t you? Sales rep for all those years! And now lunchtime supervisor - a proper people person. I’m glad you’ve found something you enjoy. It’s always been a worry, hasn’t it? Keeping busy. Keeps you feeling young. Though, young is a laugh, isn't it? Tell me about it! My knees are definitely protesting the playground these days. Still, better than sitting at home, wouldn't you say? Speaking of keeping busy, how's the proofreading going? You’re working hard, aren’t you? More than you used to. It’s good, actually. Proper good. Trying to pick up a few more clients, bit of marketing on the side, you know. It’s all online these days, isn’t it? Still trying to get my head around Instagram. All those filters! Feels so… disingenuous. It's a world away from proofreading a dissertation, I can tell you. Remember Mrs. Higgins’ dissertation on Victorian textile mills? Nearly drove me mad! Oh, don't remind me! Her footnotes were a nightmare. Right, anyway, have you heard about the village fete? They're doing it again this year, down at the cricket field. Saturday afternoon. Apparently, they’re having a raffle. Thinking of getting a ticket. Oh, that sounds lovely! I might pop down. Little Thomas would adore it. He's getting so big now, isn't he? Practically walking! And starting to babble. It's just… amazing to watch. You should come too. We could get a coffee and people-watch. I might! Depends if the school needs me. We’re battling for carpark passes again this year, you know. Absolute madness. Parents circling like sharks! They’re threatening to make everyone get a permit. Can you imagine the chaos? Don't even mention it! I had a nightmare parking near the library last week. Ended up walking halfway across town. I’m thinking of selling the Mini. It's just not practical anymore. Oh, the little red one? You’ll miss it! That was a proper classic.

…and honestly, the engagement just plummeted after I started trying to be  too  professional. I thought posting links to academic papers and detailing my research on medieval Scottish poetry was a good look – you know, showing I’m an expert. But it just…died. Folks want a wee bit of personality, Hamish. They want to know you’re engaging with them, not lecturing them. Aye, I ken what ye mean. It’s the same at work, absolutely. Tried a similar tack a while back with our corporate Twitter. All polished reports and lengthy press releases. It was soul-destroying for everyone, really. Nobody was reading it. We looked like a particularly dull bank. Exactly! It’s like, the instant people feel patronised, they click away. What did you do? Did ye ditch the corporate persona? Eventually, aye. Took a fair bit of convincing the higher-ups, mind. They were convinced the ‘serious’ image was crucial. But I managed to build a case, showing how engaging content – wee behind-the-scenes glimpses, staff spotlights, responding to customer queries  quickly  – actually increased brand awareness. Even brought in a few extra leads, surprisingly. Now, it’s all about being approachable. We’ve got this weekly ‘Ask Hamish’ thing, where I answer follower questions on communications best practices. Seems to be going down a treat, actually. 'Ask Hamish'? That's brilliant! See, that’s what I mean about personality. It's relatable. My students, they’re all on TikTok, naturally. I've considered having a wee account, maybe showing them some of the manuscripts I’m working with, giving them a peek behind the curtain of academia… but that feels a bit… daft, doesn’t it? Daft? Naw, not at all! That’s fantastic! Just do it naturally, don't overthink it. A quick tour of the archive, maybe showing off a particularly beautiful illuminated initial… People love that stuff. It humanises history. And it's a far better way of engaging them than forcing them to read dry articles. I actually had a colleague, Fiona, who’s in PR for a distillery… she does these little videos of the distillery cats.  Cats!  Utterly bonkers. And engagement through the roof. Distillery cats! Honestly, I can see it. People are drawn to authenticity, aren’t they? It’s just… putting myself out there like that feels a bit vulnerable, especially when it’s connected to my professional reputation.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork! I swear, half my job is just filling out forms. It’s soul-destroying sometimes, you know? Especially when you're trying to advocate for someone who just needs a bit of understanding, and you're wrestling with risk assessments and care plans. Ugh, I totally get that feeling. Admin is the bane of  my  existence too. Though, thankfully, deadlines aren't quite as… life-or-death as yours. Did you manage to get Sarah settled in today? Yeah, she’s doing okay. Seems a little overwhelmed, bless her. New to the ward, so everything's a bit much. I spent ages just explaining the tea break schedule – seemingly crucial information! She kept asking if she was allowed to sit near the window. Oh god, the bureaucracy of caring! It’s ridiculous. I was dealing with a supplier today who insisted on sending me three samples of  beige  twine. Three! For a project that involves, like, brightly coloured balloons and fairy lights. Honestly, I wanted to scream. Beige twine?! What on earth for? No idea! Apparently, it’s “sustainable” and “on-trend.” Honestly, the marketing language is exhausting. Anyway, what did you have for dinner tonight? I’m absolutely starving after battling beige twine. I cobbled together some pasta, but it's, like, the saddest looking pasta ever. I made that lentil curry we talked about. It’s amazing, you have to try some. There’s loads left. Trust me, it'll be a vast improvement on your sad pasta. Did you hear back from Liam about Saturday? No. Radio silence. Which is either a good sign, or a very deliberate, passive-aggressive one. I’m leaning towards the latter. Don’t be so pessimistic! Maybe he’s just busy. You know, work and all. Although… he  did  seem a bit distant last week. Remember at Chloe’s? Oh god, don’t remind me. He spent the entire evening staring at his phone. It was excruciating. I actually ended up having a longer conversation with Chloe’s Aunt Mildred about competitive flower arranging than with him! Oh, you poor thing! Right. Operation Distract You from Liam is officially in action. So, curry? And then we're definitely watching that ridiculous reality show everyone's talking about, yeah? Curry sounds incredible. And yes! Anything to avoid thinking about Liam and his beige twine-esque behaviour.

Unsettling how, love? You know I’m not terribly good with all this, the, shall we say, psychic stuff. Always struck me as a load of codswallop, if I’m honest. Though, given the things I’ve… experienced lately... well, it’s harder to be so dismissive. It's hard to explain, Dad. It wasn’t a voice, exactly. More like a… hum. A low vibration in the room, but only when he was near. And it changed when he got upset. Remember how his face went red when we brought up Aunt Maggie? The hum got sharper, closer. Oh, bless him. Poor thing. He just doesn't cope, does he? Always been fragile, our Arthur. You know, Wellington’s always said he had a touch, ever since he was little. Remembers catching moths in his bedroom, and claiming he could "hear them whispering." Of course, everyone just put it down to an active imagination. An active imagination, indeed. More like the product of a lonely childhood, if you ask me. Being left to run wild on the seafront while Mum and Dad were… preoccupied, shall we say? It leaves a mark, that kind of thing. But voices? I still struggle with the idea. Is it his medication, do you think? I don’t think so. The doctor checked it all out. And it wasn’t just me, Dad. Annie heard it too, didn't you, love? Oh yes, I did! A definite shiver down my spine. And right when he started going on about Maggie and her prize-winning gooseberries. He gets so wound up about those gooseberries! Right. Gooseberries. Priorities. So, anyway… about Arthur’s visit. Are we still on for the shepherd's pie on Saturday? I can tackle that, I think. It's not exactly rocket science, is it? Just need to get my bearings in the kitchen again. Still a bit wobbly with all this… retirement. Yes, Saturday's still good. I'll bring the salad. And hopefully, I can get some decent new potatoes from the market. They’ve been dreadful this year. So, you’re sure you're up for the pie? We don't want to be stressing you out. Don’t be silly, love. He loves your shepherd’s pie. Reminds him of Mum’s, apparently, though she never used quite so much Worcestershire sauce. Always said it was 'too poncey'. Your mother always had strong opinions, didn’t she?

Honestly, Arthur, I’m about ready to chuck the lot out the window. "El perro come el queso." The dog eats the cheese. I can repeat it, I  can , but it doesn't stick! It’s like my brain’s got a selective memory for anything Spanish, innit? I’ve been at this for six months now, and I can order a coffee and understand when someone asks me if I need milk, that’s about it. Six months, eh? Give it time, Brenda. Rome wasn’t built in a day, and neither are fluent Spanish speakers. Remember when I tried to learn French back in the seventies? Dreadful, that was. Conjugation was the devil's work, I tell you. But French is logical! At least they’ve got, you know,  some  connection to English. This… this just feels like a completely different world of grammar. This whole subjunctive mood business... I struggle with the present perfect in English, Arthur! How am I supposed to grapple with this Spanish subjunctive nonsense? This Duolingo thing is starting to feel like a cruel joke. Duolingo’s alright for the basics, I reckon. But you need more than little green owls nagging you. Have you looked at those Memrise courses? A bloke showed me one. Uses pictures and songs, makes it a bit more engaging, apparently. Less like a school lesson. I tried Memrise for a bit, but it just felt… silly. All those cartoon llamas and whatnot. I need something more structured. I thought about that Rosetta Stone thing, but it’s so pricey! What about just immersing myself, you know? Watching Spanish films or something. Now you're talking! That's what I should've done with the French. But films... subtitles are your friend, Brenda. Don't be proud. Start with something you know well. Like… I don't know... Footloose? I’m sure they've done a Spanish version. Footloose in Spain! I’d love to see  that . Right, could be worth a go. But it’s not just the grammar, is it? It's the sheer number of tenses and irregular verbs. It's daunting. Do you know, I was reading about Catalonia the other day? How they speak Catalan as well as Castilian? How do they even manage to learn  two  languages fluently? Makes you feel a bit daft, doesn't it? Well, they grow up with it, don't they?

Right, so this is… a lot. Honestly, Dad, you’ve got more paperwork than the national archives. And most of it looks like it’s from 2008. Well, you know, best to keep things. You never know when you'll need it. Remember that warranty claim I had on the telly? Needed a receipt from 2012! This is all important stuff, lad. Important. Important for what? Proving you paid for internet in the mid-noughties? Look, we need to get this sorted. I was thinking we could scan the important bits, shred the rest. At least digitize the key documents – bank statements, the gas bill from when you nearly froze in '09… Scanning? You mean one of those things that makes everything look grey and lifeless? I’m not sure about that. Feels a bit impersonal, doesn’t it? It's  practical , Dad. I've got a scanner app on my phone, it’s surprisingly good. Better than trying to file all this away in more boxes. Speaking of practical, did you ever look at those online banking things? They’re sending you statements automatically now. It’d practically eliminate all this. Online banking…Nah. Too risky, lad. Too many hackers about. I saw something on the news the other day, some poor woman lost her pension. No, thank you. I like having everything in my hand. It's tangible, see? You know it's there. And besides, I’m not entirely sure how to work it. You’d have to teach me. I  would , but let’s tackle this document mountain first. Just think, once this is done, we can actually relax. Maybe even watch some telly. See? Practical benefits. Speaking of relaxing, have you seen Kelly Brook lately? She’s looking… stunning. Kelly Brook, eh? Still got it, that one. Always did. She's a proper looker. Better than some of these young 'uns, all skinny and... well, lacking something, I reckon. Right, focus. Okay, so these are mortgage statements… and look, here's a letter from the council. 2010. They’re asking about a bin collection dispute. Seriously? They were charging me extra for recycling! Said I was putting out too much. I told them, ‘I’m trying to do my bit for the planet! Leave me alone!’ They didn’t listen. Typical council, eh? Classic. Alright, scanning this. So, this is all related to, like, the linguistics of paperwork, isn’t it?

Honestly, this petrol price is  criminal . Criminal, I tell ya! Used to be able to fill up for a fiver, now it's pushing twenty! And I’m only going to Mum’s, not driving to the moon! Dramatic as ever, Liv. It's happened to everyone. Global situation, you know? Supply and demand. It’s...complicated. Complicated for  you  maybe, sitting in your fancy Land Rover with your fancy engineering job. For some of us, it's just a massive dent in the budget! Did you see that little garage just outside of Market Deeping? The one with the rusty sign? They were doing slightly better, but still… eye-watering. Yeah, I did. I thought about stopping, but I was running a bit late. Plus, I know the fuel quality from those smaller places can be a bit dodgy sometimes. Not worth the risk for the engine, you know. My boss would have my hide if I messed up the Range Rover. So,  that’s  the difference, isn't it? You're worried about your boss, I'm worried about being able to afford a pasty and a cuppa. Don’t be like that. It’s not about being better, it's just… different priorities. And speaking of different, did you see those bikers roaring past us back on the A1? Absolutely incredible. Oh, aye! Proper roar, they did. Sounded like a squadron of angry wasps. I always think they’re a bit mental, to be honest. Don’t know how they do it, riding that fast with so little protection. My Uncle Barry had a bike, back in ‘87. Ended up in hospital for a fortnight after a spot of bother with a lorry. Never touched one again. See, that’s what people always say. But there's a real community around it, you know. It's not just about speed. It’s about the freedom, the engineering, the camaraderie… It's a lifestyle. I’ve been reading up on vintage bikes, actually. Thinking of maybe getting something…classic. You? A biker? You, the guy who measures every millimeter and worries about engine efficiency? You’d have a heart attack if a pebble flicked up and chipped your windscreen! Maybe. But I like the  idea  of it. Something a bit… rebellious. Something completely different from spreadsheets and stress tests. And the craftsmanship involved in a well-restored Norton or Triumph is phenomenal.

Honestly, Liam, you’re just bouncing off the walls tonight! Is it football scores you’re checking again? Dinner’s almost ready, you know. Nearly finished, Mum. Just saw Federer’s comeback match result. Proper epic. Five sets. Federer, eh? Still got it, does he? Even at his age. Bit like me trying to put up a shelf yesterday - full of enthusiasm, short on actual skill. Don’t be silly, David. You’re far more skilled than you give yourself credit for. Liam, you need to look away from that phone and breathe. You were a whirlwind on the court today, weren't you? Coach said your backhand was looking much stronger. Yeah, but I still lost to Tom. Again. He’s just… solid. Doesn't make mistakes. It's frustrating. Solid's good, Liam. Solid wins matches. Fancy being a bit more like that, eh? Not all flash and dash. Think about consistency. That's what separates the good players from the greats. Djokovic is the king for a reason, not just because he can hit a ridiculous forehand. Exactly. And that's what Mr. Davies was trying to tell you, wasn't it? He said you were trying too hard to hit the spectacular winner, instead of playing the percentages. I know, I know. But it’s  boring ! Everyone else is trying slam winners and drop shots and… Boring's beneficial when you're winning, son. Think about it like this – you’re building a house. You can’t just lay the roof straight away, can you? You need a solid foundation, brick by brick. Footwork, placement, returning – that's your foundation. The winners are the fancy wallpaper. They look good, but they won't stop the leak if the roof’s not right. That’s a good analogy, David. Reminds me of that time I was proofreading a marketing report... all lovely, flowery language, but the actual data was completely wrong. It looked pretty, but it was useless. Same principle. Okay, okay, I get it. Less showboating. Good lad. Remember that match you played against Ethan last month? The one where you just kept putting the ball back over the net, annoying him to bits? Yeah, I won that one, didn’t I? He got so frustrated he started hitting it into the net himself. Precisely! Sometimes, the best strategy is to just out-grind your opponent. Tire them out.

Aye, tha knows, that turkey’s reet good, Nan. Reet good. Proper moist, like. Well, you're not wrong, lad. Your dad put a lot of effort in. Though, honestly, these napkins…they look like…well, like blooming underpants! Who designs these things? They do, don’t they? Seriously, Mum, you’re right. It’s a bit much for Christmas dinner. Reminds me of that time Liam wore those ridiculous novelty boxers to Emma's birthday. Liam? You mean that daft thing he bought? With the squirrels on? Don't remind me. Anyway, talking of shopping, have you two done much Christmas shopping yet? I'm still behind. I got most of mine done in October. Uni's been manic, so just ticking things off now. Got a few bits for Grandad, some chocolates for you, and a silly stocking filler for Liam. What about you, Dad? Panicking yet? Always. It's the curse of the Service Manager, you know. Always juggling things. I need to get something for your Auntie Susan and Uncle Paul. They booked that cruise, didn’t they? Fancy that. A cruise! In December? Brave souls. Remember that year we all went to Blackpool in January? The wind nearly blew us all away. Ooh, and your dad tried to win a coconut shy and ended up covered in sand! Good times. Speaking of memories, remember watching Downton Abbey every Christmas? That was proper tradition, weren’t it? Aye, Nan. I enjoyed that. Although, a bit stuffy, innit? I prefer something a bit more…modern. Like that film with the tango, what was it called? You mean  La La Land ? The soundtrack was brilliant. Speaking of music, I've been playing a lot of piano lately – trying to learn Christmas carols. My friends at uni, they've all got nicknames for me. They call me ‘Professor Melody’ because I'm always on about music theory. Professor Melody! That's brilliant! So, you’re playing properly now, are you? Not just banging away on the keys like you used to? A little less banging, a little more playing! I wish I could travel out to America like you did, remember showing me photos of Florida? I’d love to go to a proper airport, all those planes. Yeah, tha showed me too. It looked dead good. Remember how tha worried about getting your boarding pass? I did! I was a nervous wreck.

…and honestly, the whole thing just felt so… inefficient. We’re trying to implement this new CRM system, right? Supposed to streamline everything. But the training they gave us was appalling. Two hours on how to change your password! And then a half-hour overview of the entire project management functionality! It’s madness. Well, that  is  a bit daft, innit? At my school, we had a right kerfuffle with that new student records programme. Young Timmy down the IT department, bless 'im, tried to convince everyone it was a revolutionary leap forward. In reality, it took three times as long to mark an essay. I told 'em, I said, 'Stick to what works, luv!’ They never listen. Sounds a familiar tale, doesn’t it, Doris? Waste of good money, most of it is, these modern systems. Remember back when I was starting out, just a ledger and a pen sufficed. You knew where you were. You  knew  who owed you money. Didn’t need any fancy software to tell you that. Exactly! It's not about needing something fancy; it’s about it actually  working  and making things easier. And I’m having to spend all my evenings patching up the cracks, re-doing tasks because the CRM has bungled them. It's really draining. I was thinking of asking for a bit more budget for external training, something that actually focusses on the practical application. Ooh, good idea, love. Get some proper training. Though, be prepared to fight for it. These things never come easy. Tell ‘em about the hours you’re putting in, the impact on your productivity. And, you know, don’t be afraid to be a bit pushy. They’re paying you to do a job, aren't they? Now, speaking of productivity… Young Amelia called earlier. Said she’s struggling with maths and wants some tutoring. Thought I might be able to give her a hand on Sundays. Got a bit of a knack for figures myself, you know. Spent years balancing accounts for the farm. Oh, that’s lovely, Uncle Geoff! Amelia’s so lucky. I remember when you helped me with my A-levels – the stats were a nightmare. Still don’t entirely understand them, to be honest. She is a sweet girl, that Amelia. A bit scatterbrained sometimes, but a good heart. Still hasn’t met anyone proper, has she? Not like you, Chloe, already planning a wedding with that nice Liam.

Honestly, I don't know why I bother with risotto. It’s a complete faff, isn’t it? Needs constant attention - like a needy toddler. Though at least a toddler doesn't require precisely timed stirring. It's alright if you get it right, love. Takes practice. Remember that disaster with the paella last August? We practically redecorated the kitchen with saffron. Don’t remind me! Still finding little grains of rice in the grout. Speaking of disasters… I’ve got my appraisal coming up next week. I’m dreading it. Oh? Anything specific making you nervous? You've been consistently accurate in your transcribing, haven’t you? Always meticulously checking those timestamps. Yes, technically. But Mrs. Hawthorne, my manager, she’s… well, she has a habit of focusing on the  minor  things. Like, last time it was the shade of blue I used for highlighting a particularly long document. Blue, David! Is that really grounds for criticism? I'm convinced she’s got a personal vendetta against cerulean. Want a pizza instead? Less stressful. Pizza sounds lovely. Though I was thinking we could actually try that new vegan one from Marks and Spencer. Saw it advertised, looked rather impressive. They’ve really upped their food game, haven't they? Used to be just soggy sandwiches and over-priced shortbread. Marks and Spencer food is a revelation, isn't it? I bought their ready-made lasagne last week, and it was genuinely good. Not that processed nonsense you often get. I’m half tempted to just do that tonight, actually. Let's not abandon the risotto completely. It's halfway there. Besides, I'd rather do something than watch another episode of  The Walking Dead . Negan’s still giving me the shivers. Remember that Icelandic thriller,  Trapped ? That was properly unsettling.  Trapped  was brilliant. The scenery alone! But you know, I've been reading about the appalling state of equine welfare in some of the… well, in the less reputable riding schools. It's heartbreaking. I donated to that charity, the one you mentioned. Good on you. Awful, isn't it? Gets right under your skin. Hey, while we’re on the subject of depressing things, did you do the crossword today? That 11 across was a killer. "Ancient wine, fourteen letters…" Needs more salt. Yes, I did! Nearly threw the paper across the room, I did. It was  xeres , wasn’t it?

Right, tha's havin’ a laugh, aren’t ya? Sarah, tripping in front o’ Greggs? That’s classic. Did she get a pasty, at least? Oh my god, no! She dropped the sausage roll! It rolled all the way down the pavement! I swear, she almost took out a little old lady. Honestly, that girl is a walking disaster zone. I’m still laughing, though. Bless her! It’s a wonder she hasn't broken anything yet, the way she moves. She’d need a personal bodyguard, wouldn't she? Anyway, speaking of disasters...this skirt is clinging to me like glue. Seriously, I feel like I'm being boiled alive. Aye, it's a bit warmer than I thought it'd be tonight. I’m glad I went for somethin’ a bit shorter. These heels, though… my feet are already killin' me. I shoulda worn trainers, proper gutted I didn't. Tell me about it! I’ve been eyeing up those platforms from Primark, but I was scared I’d end up lookin' like a toddler tryin’ to climb a wall. These barely-there sandals are lookin’ pretty painful already. Are we definitely going for cocktails first? I need somethin’ strong. Definitely cocktails. I'm feeling a strawberry daiquiri, that sound reet. And yeah, Sarah needs to be careful. She's a menace wi’ those legs an’ all. What were you thinkin’, wearin’ a skirt like that on a night out? She said she was trying to be "chic." Chic, she is not. More like…chaotic. But honestly, I’m just worried she'll end up in a state. Remember last time? She ended up singing karaoke to Nickelback. Oh, dear lord. No, please no. The world doesn't need another rendition of "Photograph." I’m already slightly regretting agreeing to this. Though, if I’m honest, a few cocktails do sound like exactly what I need to forget about this skirt. Karaoke's always a laugh, even if it is Nickelback. It gets tha’ proper loose, doesn't it? I reckon we should make a pact: no singin’ a full song unless everyone agrees. Last time, Emily tried to do Whitney Houston and the noise complaints were through tha roof. Good shout, Em. A cap on the karaoke chaos. What's the plan for after the cocktails? Are we hitting the club, or just wandering around looking for chips?

…and honestly, that’s what I find so frustrating about Mr. Harding. He just… doesn't  listen . I suggested streamlining the proposal, you know, cutting out all the jargon, making it more accessible, and he just nodded along. Then, the draft came back, and it was  worse  than before! More jargon, more buzzwords, the works. It’s like talking to a brick wall, really. Sounds about right, love. Harding’s always been a bit… entrenched in his ways, hasn’t he? Difficult to shift. You know, it reminds me a little of trying to explain cloud migration to Brenda in accounts. Just a blank stare. Exactly! And it's not just the work stuff, is it? Remember last week when I showed him that article about the influence of Celtic spirituality on contemporary art? He just shrugged and said, "Right, good for them.” No curiosity whatsoever. He’s a practical man, Sarah. Dry, almost. Always has been. But you, you're like a magpie, attracted to shiny interesting things. It’s part of what I love about you. That thirst for… well, everything. I suppose so. I was reading about reincarnation the other day, which is probably completely bonkers, but… I keep thinking, what if we’re destined to find our soulmates across lifetimes? Perhaps we’d lived a life together as Roman senators or something ridiculously dramatic. Roman senators? You and me? I can’t see me leading legions. I’d probably be the pot-bellied administrator, meticulously filing scrolls. But I like the idea, actually. It makes a world beyond this feel… less random. Better than thinking it's all just a cosmic blip. Exactly! It gives a reason for that instant connection, doesn't it? That feeling of knowing someone, even before you’ve really known them. You and I had that. Do you ever wonder what we  were ? I do, actually. Sometimes I picture us as… monarchs. Not battling kings, but overseeing a court, full of artists and musicians and philosophers. Hosting extravagant feasts. What do you think? Ooh, I like that! We'd definitely have a theme for every party – a different historical period each time. A roaring twenties bash one week, then Tudor revelry the next. And elaborate costumes, naturally. I'd be queen, of course. You'd be the charming, slightly mischievous advisor, always whispering witty comments in my ear. I don’t think I’m mischievous enough for a monarch.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork required to even  consider  getting a small artisan crafts business properly registered is just ludicrous. It’s enough to put anyone off. I mean, I’m used to dealing with regulations, obviously, in my job, but this…this is a whole other level. It feels deliberately designed to discourage smaller entrepreneurs, doesn't it? A bit, yeah. My mum says the same about trying to get a small stall at the market. Loads of permissions and hoops to jump through. Seems like they want the big chains dominating everything. Do you reckon you’ll still go for it though? With the knitting, I mean? I’m trying to, darling, I really am. It would be lovely to actually  sell  some of what I make, not just piles of scarves festering in the spare room. But the business side…it’s daunting. It's so unlike negotiating a large contract, you know? There’s a different kind of pressure. Less about the money, more about...just doing it right, ethically. Ethically knitting, Sarah? Sounds like something you’d put on a business plan. Listen, you’re brilliant at what you do. People adore your work. Don’t let bureaucracy intimidate you. Remember Mrs. Higgins and her obsession with getting a blue rosette for her marrow at the village fete? Same energy. Single-minded determination, but ultimately, a bit silly focusing on the details. You’re right, aren’t you? Mrs. Higgins and her marrows. It's tempting to just throw in the towel. Speaking of silly obsessions…Have you seen the state of that graveyard on Long Causeway? I went for a walk the other day, and some of the headstones are practically leaning over. It’s rather unsettling, actually. Oh, proper creepy! My nan used to take me there when I was little. We’d read out the dates and imagine who they were. Remember those little tests they used to give us in school, about rounding numbers? Felt like the same idea, but with lives instead! Don't remind me. I’ve got a nephew obsessed with them now. Wants to photograph every single inscription. Says he’s documenting local history. Bless him. Though I did overhear him asking his dad about why some of the names are so different. Like, really old-fashioned. It’s fascinating, isn’t it? The changes in language.

Honestly, this student housing is mental. It's like a glorified box, innit? Tiny wee rooms, and the kitchen? Don’t even get me started on the kitchen. Last week I found someone's half-eaten shepherd’s pie festering in the fridge. Shepherd's pie! Who leaves shepherd's pie? Right? It’s a biohazard zone. Remember Liam’s attempt at making paella? The smell lingered for three days. Manila paella doesn't have that many questionable prawns, I can tell you. It’s a learning curve, student accommodation, yeah? It’s not  that  bad, guys. It's got character. And at least we're together, right? Though, I will admit, I’m starting to panic about next year. Finding somewhere decent that doesn't cost a fortune is going to be brutal. Did you hear about that landlord in Norwich? Charging £800 for a cupboard under the stairs! Eight  hundred  quid? Are you having a laugh? You could buy a small cottage in Cumbria for that! Seriously though, I’m proper worried already. I’m saving, obviously, but every time I think I’ve got a decent wedge, the price of everything else goes up. Tell me about it. And this tax thing… I keep getting these emails from HMRC. Apparently, I need to fill something in about my internship last summer. I barely remember it, honestly! My auntie keeps saying I have to, threats and everything. "Filipino Filipinos, pay your taxes!" she says. Oh, that's a nightmare. I had a similar thing with my part-time job at the garden centre. It’s all so confusing. Should we look into getting an accountant? Probably a waste of money, though. We're students, for crying out loud. An accountant? Now  that’s  a luxury. Speaking of luxuries, did you see Zara's Instagram? She's off to Barcelona with Chloe and Emily next weekend. Fancy! Barcelona? Lucky ducks. I'm stuck here, battling HMRC and frozen shepherd's pie. You going to the Man U game on Saturday? I'm thinking of trying to get a ticket. Oh, definitely! Sarah's managed to snag us seats in the Stretford End. Proper buzzing, it'll be. I’m proper chuffed! I was telling my Gran about it, and she got all excited. She says every young 'un needs to experience the roar of a proper home crowd, doesn’t she?

"You and your moped ideas, lass! You'd be all over the place. You know your Uncle Geoff had one and nearly took out a lamppost. Nearly! And he was older and supposedly wiser.” "Yeah, but it'd be way faster than the number 7 towards Lever Street. School's a nightmare getting there, especially when it's raining. You're squashed in like sardines." “Sardines is a good analogy, Liam. Efficiency is key. Of course, you could always cycle. Good exercise and all that.” He gestures vaguely with his fork. "Cycle? In Bolton? With those hills? You've clearly forgotten what it's like to live there, Dad. Besides, it's freezing in the mornings. I'd rather brave the bus, even if it does resemble a tin can filled with grumpy commuters.” Sarah picks at her seafood pasta. “This is lovely, though. Really lovely. Much better than that supermarket lasagne we had last Tuesday." “Don’t you start complaining about the supermarket food, love. It's convenient! And I’m knackered after a shift at the hospital. You wouldn’t believe what I dealt with today... One minute everything's fine, the next... well, let’s just say it’s a privilege to be there for families during those moments.” Her voice softens. “Did you have to deal with that mum?” He asks, poking at his pizza. "Some things, love. Some things. It just reminds you how precious everything is, doesn’t it?" She glances at Sarah, a shared understanding passing between them. "Indeed. It's a vital job you do, Margaret. Incredible, really. I sometimes forget the sheer pressure and emotional toll involved in your profession. We're all so focused on spreadsheets and targets in my world, it’s easy to lose perspective.” "Speaking of pressure, uni's getting pretty intense. This essay on Victorian literature is going to be the death of me. I'm thinking of getting a tattoo to de-stress, actually.” “A  tattoo ? Sarah! What on earth would you get? And where? Don't tell me you’re thinking of getting a dragon on your ankle!" "No, Mum! Nothing that dramatic. Probably just a small constellation, on my wrist. Something subtle. It’s just… a thing to remind me to breathe, you know? A bit of self-care.” "Cool! Can I get one when I’m 18? Like a pixelated controller?" "Absolutely not, Liam!

…and then young Alfie, bless his cotton socks, tried to build a sandcastle  inside  the paddling pool. Honestly, Elsie, the cheek of it! Nearly gave poor Maisie a fright, she was bathing her dolly. Oh, children, aren’t they just? Always finding new ways to entertain themselves, the little rascals. It’s a wonder they don't wear themselves out. You look a bit knackered, Arthur. Cornwall was lovely, though, wasn’t it? John’s photos are absolutely gorgeous. Gorgeous? They're breathtaking, Elsie! Absolutely stunning coastline. I’ve never seen the sea so… powerful, really. That lighthouse photo, Arthur, the one you sent me? Brilliant. You captured the way the light just  slashed  through the mist. Proper atmospheric. Aye, that was a good one, weren't it? Spent half the night down there, I did, waitin' for the light to be just right. Hard on the knees, though, clamberin' over them rocks. Reminded me of ramblin' round Holme Moss back in the day, with my dad. Used to take me to see the sheep. Holme Moss? Goodness, Arthur, that’s a long way back! You were a little tyke then, weren't you? Still, that's that Norfolk grit showing, sticking it out in the wind and rain. Speaking of which, did you manage to catch any crabs, John? You said you were going to try. We did! John was determined. Spent a couple of hours down by the rocks with a bucket and line. Got a grand total of three - tiny little things, mind you. Enough for a quick supper, though. Maisie loved watching him, kept shouting, “Get 'em, grandad, get ‘em!”. She did, didn’t she? Kept declaring herself 'Captain Crab Hunter Extraordinaire'. It’s good to get her out and about, she needs a bit of fresh air. She spends far too much time glued to that tablet, that girl. Makes you wonder what the future holds. Children and tablets. A modern conundrum. Remember when we used to spend our Saturdays cycling around Harrow, John? That race around Yorkshire you did last year, that was something else! I still can’t believe you cycled the whole thing in a day. Well, it wasn’t  the whole thing , Elsie. It was a significant chunk. And a very, very long day. Nearly collapsed at the finish line, I did. Needed a good cup of tea and a sit down.

"Mental how? Did something go wrong at the building site?" "Nah, not exactly  wrong . Just… constant. Flat out all day, moving pallets, lifting materials. The foreman’s been on my back a bit, too, seems keen to get everything finished before the end of the month. Typical." She sighs, reaching for a piece of Anon’s lasagne. "This is reet good, mind. Proper fuel." "It  is  good. Anon’s lasagne is legendary. So, pallets and materials… what exactly are you building?" "New apartments, just outside the city centre. Loads of 'em. Luxury flats, apparently. Bit out of my league, that’s for sure.” He chuckled, scraping his plate. “Still, pay's decent, can’t complain. What about you, Chloe? Still drowning in spreadsheets and corporate jargon?" "Aye, pretty much. We're organising this tech conference next month. It's supposed to be  the  thing for AI developers. Honestly, the demands are ridiculous. Apparently, they want a silent disco  and  a falconry display. A FALCONRY DISPLAY! In a conference centre!" She throws her hands up in mock exasperation. “Proper stressful, it is." "A falconry display? That’s… specific. Sounds expensive, too." She takes a sip of her wine. “So, are you enjoying the work, though? After graduating, I was a bit lost for a while, you know? Uncertain if I’d picked the right path." "It's alright. Not exactly dreamed of being a conference co-ordinator as a bairn, but it pays the bills and it’s a bit more interesting than working in Boots, I reckon. People are always changing their minds though, yon Liam from school, used to want to be a footballer, now he's selling estate agents. Life’s a funny thing, eh?" "Tell me about it. I thought I’d join the army, you know? Straight out of sixth form. Then I realised I wouldn't be able to leave the country without arguing with loads of people. So, building it is. It's honest work." He gestures around the room. “Anon’s place is lovely, by the way. Much nicer than my flat. Always wanted a garden.” "It's cozy. Right, moving on to more important matters," she says with a playful grin. "Any developments on the romance front, Liam? Still seeing that girl from the pub?" "Nah, that fizzled out pretty quick. Turns out she had a boyfriend. Didn't exactly announce it, just… slipped it in during a conversation about her cat.

…and honestly, the Sagrada Familia was absolutely mind-blowing. I mean, you've  seen  the pictures, obviously, but being there… standing beneath it… it's just… something else. Did you manage to get down to the Gothic Quarter at all? Yeah, a bit! Saturday afternoon. It was proper bustling, wasn't it? Beautiful though. I spent ages just wandering around, getting lost actually. Ended up in this tiny little tapas bar. Best patatas bravas I’ve ever had, seriously. Proper smoky paprika. Did you try any amazing food? Oh my god, the food! Everything was incredible. I had the best paella, obviously. And this chururía – a little place tucked away off Las Ramblas – the chocolate was so thick and dark. I think I gained about two stone. But it was worth it. How was the weather treating you? I heard it was roasting. Blaze-ingly hot. Like, genuinely uncomfortable at times. I ended up living in that linen dress I bought. Should’ve brought more light skirts, definitely. Sunscreen was my best friend. Did you do much besides the Sagrada Familia? I know you had a busy schedule. Not  as  busy as I thought it would be, thankfully. We had a couple of morning placement visits, but the afternoons were pretty free. I wandered around Park Güell, had a picnic… mostly just soaking it all up. It was so good to get away from the hospital for a few days. Felt like my brain was melting. I can imagine! You must be exhausted. What about the boyfriend? Did you see him much? Not really. He was working overtime most of the weekend. Said he’d make it up to me, naturally. Just… it’s a bit frustrating, you know? Feels like I put a lot more effort into seeing him than he does sometimes. Anyway, enough about him! What did  you  get up to? Besides getting lost and eating tapas. Well, I spent ages on the beach, sunbathing. I may or may not have attempted to learn some Spanish phrases. Mostly phrases about ordering drinks. Essential, you know. And I did a bit of shopping. Found a cute little shop selling ceramics. Thinking about getting you a little something. Oh, you shouldn’t have! Seriously. Are you thinking of Paris next? You were talking about it last month. I was, yeah! I was thinking maybe October? Around the time the leaves start to change.

…and honestly, the paperwork! It's just relentless. You wouldn't believe the hoops you have to jump through to justify even the smallest purchase for the classroom. Sticky-back plastic alone required three different signatures last term. Three! Sounds familiar, in a different context. You’re dealing with budgets, I was dealing with investors. Though at least with investors, the scale of the money involved made the paperwork… slightly less irritating. Relatively. I mean, you’re fighting over twenty quid for coloured pens, I was battling over… well, significantly larger sums. Twenty quid is a  lot  of coloured pens, darling! Year Six adore a sparkly highlighter. What were you investing in, anyway? You mentioned something about tech? Fintech, mostly. A couple of apps aimed at small businesses. One to streamline invoicing – the bane of many a freelancer, I imagine – and another for automated tax calculations. Exciting on paper, terrifying in reality. Launched the first one about five years ago. A baptism by fire, definitely. Five years, you say? So you’ve seen a fair bit of up and down then, haven’t you? Teaching’s always felt pretty constant to me, you know? Predictable, in a horribly bureaucratic way. Though I  have  had some absolute characters over the years. Remember that boy, Finley, who insisted on calling me 'Captain'? Captain? That’s brilliant. I wouldn’t have the patience for that. My attention span is barely long enough to remember where I parked the rental car yesterday. I spent a good year just convincing my first investor that “synergy” wasn’t a lazy buzzword. That was a breakthrough moment. Oh, corporate jargon. I've had to endure my fair share of that at staff meetings. “Moving forward with a holistic approach to learner outcomes…” Blimey. What was the hardest part, though, for you? Beyond the synergy battles, I mean? Definitely the loneliness. You're surrounded by people, pitching ideas, networking... but you're carrying the weight of it all yourself. Sleepless nights, wondering if you’ve made the right call. Teaching, you’ve got colleagues, a support system. You share the load. With startups... it's just you, predominantly. Though I did have a brilliant mentor, old Mr. Davies down in Shoreditch. He ran a tiny print shop, basically a glorified newspaper press. Absolutely ruthless with feedback, but kept me grounded. That's a lovely story. Mentors are invaluable, aren’t they?

Honestly, Liam, I'm proper fed up. Absolutely fed up. Nowt wrong with the driving, is there, love? Just a bit mardy, are we? What's got your knickers in a twist this time? It's Ben and Chloe, that’s what! They're using  all  the milk again. Every single drop. I needed some this morning for my coffee, and there wasn't a carton left! Not a drop! Did you see that face I had? I felt like a right grumpy git. They'll learn eventually. They’re still new to sharing, aren't they? Remember when we first moved in with your Auntie Brenda and kept forgetting to take our shoes off? That’s different, innit? Auntie Brenda would give us the look. The horrifying, silent look that meant you were about to be lectured about muddy footprints for a solid twenty minutes. Ben and Chloe just…ignore everything. And don’t even get me started on the dishes. Piles of 'em. Like a volcano waitin' to erupt. Well, you did agree to do your share of the washing up, didn’t you? And you are the queen of the clean kitchen, lass. We all know it. You’re practically a domestic goddess. Don't be daft. It's just... it’s tiring, isn't it? Having to constantly pick up after other people. It's like being a parent sometimes. I spent half an hour yesterday searching for Chloe's phone because she left it buried under a mountain of clothes in the living room. Right, well, maybe you should have a proper sit-down with them. A right proper chat. Not just a grumble, but actually listing out what's bothering you. You know, be assertive and all that. Your sixthform teachers always hammered that into you. Assertive? Me? I’ll end up bursting into tears, I will. They'll just look at me like I’m some soft southerner who doesn't know how to have a bit of fun. Which, by the way, they seem to equate to leaving dirty mugs around. Don't let them wind you up. You're tough as old boots, you are. Remember that time you stood up to Mr. Hargreaves about the history essay? He backed down, didn't he? He did, didn't he? Just goes to show, a bit of Yorkshire grit goes a long way.

Right then, that’s the lot. My back's killing me, honestly. Heaviest trip we’ve had in ages! Did you manage to wrestle that tin of peaches into the basket, Arthur? They were right at the bottom. Aye, got 'em, I did. Bit of a struggle, mind you. They were practically buried under a mountain of courgettes. What’s become of all the courgettes, eh? Seems every shop’s got ‘em piled high. Seems a right fad, don’t it? They are everywhere, aren't they? I think everyone's got the notion of summer vegetable soup. Ridiculous price, too, for what they are. Still, had to get some. You know how Elsie is on about her rheumatism. She says courgettes are good for it. Says the water content... you know, draws out the toxins. Elsie and her toxins! Always something new with Elsie. Remember when she was convinced the telly waves were affecting her hair? Said she had to foil her television with tin foil. Looked a right mess, she did. Oh, don’t remind me! Malcolm nearly had a fit. Had to explain to the neighbours why she'd wrapped the television in shiny paper. Anyway, I also got that chamomile tea you like, Arthur. The proper kind, from Fortnum & Mason. Bit of a treat, that. Ooh, now you’re talking! The stuff from the supermarket tastes like dried grass, it does. Fortnum & Mason, you say? That's proper posh that, that is. Didn’t think you’d be splashing out. Well, you deserve a bit of luxury, don’t you? And I had a voucher. Don’t you go thinking I've suddenly got money to burn, old boy. It’s all a bit tight, as always. Did you notice they’ve put the price of butter up again? Scandalous. Aye, everything's gone up. Makes you think back to the old days, it does. When a loaf of bread cost a penny. And you could get a whole Sunday roast for tuppence ha'penny. Don't seem possible now, does it? It doesn’t. They’re trying to tell us inflation’s under control. Rubbish! I can feel it in my joints, I can. Did you see anything about the football? Norwich got beat again, did they? Sadly, yes. 3-1. Dreadful defending, it was. Young Liam – don’t know what they’re putting in the tea these days – he missed a sitter.

Aye, Liam gets a bit over-enthusiastic sometimes, doesn't he? Luckily, your Grandad Arthur, he kept his counsel. You know Arthur, always the calming presence. It's a good job really, ‘cause Elsie can get right riled up if anyone disagrees with her. Well, she  was  saying they were invented by the devil to confuse children! Honestly, Gran! I told her they’re used in engineering, building bridges and stuff. She just sniffed and said bridges were built with common sense, not numbers. Common sense is all you need, lad. Always has been. All this fancy learnin’… just complicates things. Back in my day, we built proper things, with our ‘ands. Didn’t need no formulas. Me and your Grandad, we built a shed, a fine shed it was too. Used proper timber, we did. None of this flimsy plastic stuff. Shed’s gone now. Rotting away. Now, Arthur, don’t go bringing that up again. We’ve talked about replacing that shed, you know we have. It wouldn't do Elsie any good dwelling on it. Liam, are you still hungry, love? I made a Victoria sponge, thought you might fancy a slice. Actually, yeah, that would be good. Thanks, Auntie Brenda. Gran, are you eating anything? You haven't touched your scone. Scones are dry, lad. Always dry. Should’ve had a jam tart. Used to get proper jam tarts from Mrs. Higgins down the road. Raspberry, they were. Now  that  was a treat. Higgins… gone years. Arthur! Elsie, dear, let's not start listing all the shops that have closed down. It'll no' cheer anyone up. Right, I need to sort out a few things. Your room's looking a bit like a bomb’s hit it, Liam. Emily’s dropping you off on Sunday, right? Are you sure you don't need anything from the shops before then? Yeah, I'm good. Emily's definitely picking me up Sunday afternoon. Just… maybe don’t mention the quadratic equations to Gran again. It stresses me out. I'll try my best. Although, it  is  a bit of a laugh seeing her get all worked up. Arthur, are you going to help me move that chair? It’s blocking the light. Heavy. Aye, I know it’s heavy. That’s why I’m asking you to help! You used to be strong, you know. Remember that time you carried old Mrs. Butterfield’s washing machine up her stairs?
