Remember how funny it was last year when Leo and Maya both had birthdays on the same day? Year Seven and Eight – a right palaver! Trying to divide attention, presents everywhere…" "Maya's party had pizza." "It did! And Leo had that magician. Remember the disappearing rabbit? Elsie was terrified.” "The rabbit went  poof !" “Exactly. Anyway, it’s going to be hectic this year. Finn, are you excited about your birthday? You’re turning eight, aren’t you?” "Nearly. Only a week and two days." "Only a week and two days! And we're having that Monet exhibition at the Fitzwilliam. I thought you’d like that, love. All those water lilies…very colourful!" "Water lilies are pink!" "Some of them are, darling. Sometimes they're white too! Speaking of colours, did you finish your Maths homework? Mrs. Davies said it was all about fractions.” "It's hard! I don't get it." "It can be tricky. But we can go through it together later. Right now, I’m trying to figure out how to deal with all this birthday chocolate. I swear, the supermarkets are practically  gilding  it this year. Look at this!" She holds up a particularly extravagant Easter egg. "I'm going to have to hide half of this, otherwise they’ll be bouncing off the walls."

A toothbrush? Seriously, Liv? People don’t know how to use a toothbrush? That’s wild. So much for cutting-edge speech and language therapy, eh? Don’t be cheeky! It’s not about arrogance, it’s about the impact of neurological trauma. They’ve lost so much, you know? Anyway, it’s a world away from uni lectures now. Remember those endless discussions about Chomsky and generative grammar? Felt a bit pointless sometimes, looking back. Oh, completely. Professor Harding was obsessed. He’d just drone on and on about syntax. I used to doodle little cartoons of him with a giant grammar book. You were always so good at just, like, soaking it all in though. Remember you used to take  actual  notes? I’d be halfway asleep, fuelled by instant noodles and desperation. So, are you liking the acute ward? It sounds really intense. It is. But it’s also where you see the most immediate impact. Fixing a line of communication, helping someone regain their independence… it's pretty amazing. Honestly, though, the admin is killing me. I’m trying to save up for a proper flatshare, somewhere that isn’t just a pokey room above a kebab shop. Have you looked at any places in Brighton? I could see us both living there. Brighton! That'd be wicked! I was looking at some studios actually, but they’re just so tiny, and the rent is ridiculous. I’m still chipping away at the debt from uni, you know. Freelancing is erratic, even though I love it. I landed a pretty good gig with that sustainable fashion brand, "EverBloom," though. Their copy is actually really fun to write. Much more exciting than insurance brochures! That's brilliant, honestly! EverBloom, they're doing amazing things. You're perfect for it. We should go for a proper dinner next week to celebrate. I’m clearing my schedule. Mum’s been on at me about visiting more, too. She misses you terribly. Remember how she used to bribe us with lavender biscuits when we were kids, just to get us to clean our rooms? Oh God, yes! The lavender biscuits. The most terrifyingly floral things ever conceived. And she’d deploy Uncle Barry if we  really  didn’t cooperate. He’d just start telling those incredibly long, rambling stories about his pigeon racing days. I’d rather scrub the toilet. How's Dad doing?

…and honestly, the sheer  cheek  of those council members. Denying Mr. Henderson’s solar panels! It's 2024, for goodness sake. They cited "visual impact" – visual impact! As if that collection of dreary Victorian terraces is a masterpiece of architectural harmony. I agree entirely, Arthur. It's short-sightedness, pure and simple. They’re clinging to the past, aren’t they? Like this town. Remember how lovely Almondsbury used to be? Real character. The little bakery on the High Street, the ironmonger... all gone now. Replaced with… well, nothing much of merit, really. Every town’s got its share of decline, Margaret. Manchester wasn’t exactly a gleaming metropolis in the seventies. Though, I suppose it had a certain vitality. Grit, you know? This “rebranding” your town is doing… is it actually working? Feels like PR spin to me. It  could  work, David. I think there's a real desire for it to. They’re talking about restoring some of the Victorian facades, putting in more greenery. It’s a start. Though, frankly, the architecture these days… most new builds are just dreadful boxes. Utterly devoid of inspiration. Speaking of inspiration… do you remember those trips the NHS used to offer? God, they were brilliant! I went sailing in the Solent a few times. Absolute bliss. And one year, they had these… lectures. Oral surgery lectures, eh? All at sea! I remember one fellow, a rather eccentric oral surgeon from Bristol, giving a talk on impacted wisdom teeth with the waves crashing against the hull. Quite surreal, really. The food wasn't Michelin star, mind you, but it was a perk. You don't get perks like that these days. Prague, though – that was a steal, wasn’t it? Fifty quid each, flights and accommodation. Prague was divine. The architecture! Such detail. I loved wandering through the Old Town Square, just soaking it all in. It's astonishing what you can get for so little now, isn’t it? Back in my teaching days, a weekend away felt like robbing a bank. Absolutely. You need to be savvy, though. Book things well in advance, be prepared to hop on a bus instead of a train… you know. Keeps the costs down. We're looking at that jive night, aren't we? The barn’s looking good, apparently. It is! They’ve really done a fantastic job converting it. Quite rustic, with those exposed beams.

…and that’s why I’m leaning away from purely video tutorials, you know? Everyone’s doing them. It's a saturated market. We need something that  really  stands out, something that leverages the interactive potential. I was thinking, almost like a branching narrative, but for case studies. Branching narrative? Explain that a bit more, darling, because my brain’s still trying to catch up with the whole ‘moving images in education’ thing. It’s a bit… daunting, isn’t it? After twenty years of marking essays, suddenly I’m supposed to be thinking about interactive storytelling for secondary school history? Right, well, picture this: a case study on, say, the Industrial Revolution. Instead of a linear video, users click on different aspects – a particular invention, a key figure, a social issue like child labour. Each click leads to further questions, primary source excerpts, short video clips, even simulations. Their choices influence the direction they take and, ultimately, their understanding of the subject. Think 'choose your own adventure', but with proper historical context and rigorous academic backing. Oh, I  do  like that. It's much more engaging than just staring at a screen, isn’t it? Children – well, teenagers – they’re so used to having control, to having agency. Presenting it to them as a passive experience... well, it practically guarantees they won’t engage. But that’s a lot of work, isn’t it? Building all those different pathways? It is, yeah. But we wouldn't need to build  everything  at once. Start small. A pilot case study – perhaps focusing on a particular social movement? And we could utilise existing resources. The British Library have a fantastic digital archive, as does the National Archives here in Australia. We'd just be curating and layering on top of that, creating the interactive framework. Think of it as… educational scaffolding. Scaffolding, I like that. And we could involve teachers, couldn’t we? Get them to contribute. I know a few history teachers at the school back home who'd be absolutely brilliant at crafting the scenarios, the questions… They’d bring a real understanding of what students find challenging. I’d be happy to reach out. That's a brilliant idea, honestly. Teacher co-creation. It'd give us instant credibility and ensure we're addressing actual classroom needs. And it feeds into our whole ethos, doesn’t it? Not just creating tools, but creating  partnerships .

Honestly, that was exactly what I needed. The air just… smells different by the sea, doesn't it? Cleaner. Less Norwich-y. Norwich-y? Is that even a word? You're inventing categories now, aren’t you? Though, I’ll concede, it  does  smell different. A good different. The slightly salty, slightly weedy kind of different. It’s a feeling, really. A particular blend of damp wool, old brick, and… well, turnips, probably. It’s ingrained in me. Anyway, I was thinking about Sarah and Mark the other day. Sarah and Mark? Haven't heard much from them lately. Still battling the renovation of the cottage in Cornwall? Absolutely. They sent me a picture the other week. The kitchen's looking  slightly  less like a demolition site, but the bathroom is apparently still a 'challenging project,' as Mark put it. He seemed genuinely distraught about some rogue damp. Mark and damp are practically synonymous at this point. Remember that disaster with the shed in Tooting? The whole thing had to be rebuilt. He swore he’d learned his lesson. Oh, yes. The ‘water feature’ he accidentally created. Poor thing. He said it looked like a miniature Caribbean lagoon for a while there, attracting slugs from miles around. He ended up naming it "Mark's Lagoon." I still think it was a brilliant, albeit accidental, name. Only Mark. Honestly, his DIY skills are… something else. Still, he seems happy there, doesn’t he? Despite the constant structural challenges. He does. Sarah’s thriving too. She's started a little pottery business, selling her stuff online. Apparently, seashell-themed mugs are really popular. Given their location… makes sense. She showed me some the other day. Surprisingly good, actually. Not the typical naff seaside pottery. See? Cornwall's good for the soul. Although, I'm still skeptical about entire livelihoods built on seashell mugs. What happens in the winter when the tide's out and there are no shells? That's for them to figure out, isn’t it? Typical. They’re quite resilient, you know. Remember when they first moved there, and the farmer's field flooded and they lost half their vegetable crop? Oh,  that  was a saga. They were practically living on instant noodles for a month. And Mark tried to build a makeshift dam using… what was it? Tires and plastic bottles? Tires and plastic bottles! It looked like something from a post-apocalyptic film.

Honestly, beige is a bit... pedestrian, isn't it? Look at  this ! It’s pure theatre! I could never wear that, massively impractical for actual life, but it’s fabulous to look at. Do you think primary school kids would appreciate feathers? Maybe for a dress-up box? Dress-up box, aye! They’d be pickin' feathers off each other within five minutes, I reckon. Beige's not pedestrian, it's a base! You build on beige. A good pair of jeans, some nice boots… sorted. You London lot seem obsessed with, like, neon pink or whatever. Okay, first of all, not  all  London fashion is neon pink. That’s just… a stereotype. And secondly, a bit of colour never hurt anyone. I’m trying to get into more statement pieces, you know? My wardrobe is currently 80% black and grey. Production work doesn’t exactly scream ‘vibrant’, does it? It's spreadsheets and Gantt charts, love. Tell me about it. Lesson planning followed by marking essays. My wardrobe is mostly cardigans and sensible shoes. Though I did buy that amazing mustard yellow jumper from COS last week. Felt a bit rebellious. Mustard yellow, eh? Not bad. Bit bolder than my usual. I’ve been tryin’ to branch out, to be fair. My mum keeps sayin’ I need more colour, she thinks beige makes me look like a librarian. She's got a point, I suppose. Anyhoo, what's all this about Arket? Fancy getting something from there? I’ve heard they’re good quality. Arket's decent, yeah. A bit pricey though. But you're right about the quality. I bought a couple of their merino wool sweaters last winter – still going strong. Actually, have you seen & Other Stories lately? They’ve got some really nice things at the moment. Their dresses are a bit more 'me' than Arket. Ooh, & Other Stories! I’ve been eyeing up their earrings. Those big, chunky gold hoops. I think they'd work well with the yellow jumper. It might stop me looking like a walking beige landscape. Gold hoops are always a good shout. Right, listenin'. I was thinkin', next Saturday, we could hit up Cambridge city centre? We could check out that vintage shop on Mill Road, the one you said had some interesting jackets? The one with the dodgy lighting and questionable scent? Yes! Absolutely. I’m always on the hunt for a good vintage piece.

Honestly, Mrs. Davies just  loves  to make us do essays about Victorian poetry. Like, who even cares about Tennyson anymore? It’s so dull! Well, darling, you might find it less dull if you actually  tried  to engage with it. It’s about understanding the context, the language… It's not just about the words on the page. Easy for you to say, you did a History degree! I’m trying to get my head around GCSE Maths, let alone archaic verse. Speaking of, did you see that new stand-up comedian, Finn Taylor? He’s hilarious! He does a whole bit about trying to assemble flat-pack furniture. It’s totally relatable. Finn Taylor? I think I’ve seen him advertised. You know, I’m trying to get back into reading again. I started 'Circe' by Madeline Miller. Have you read it? 'Circe'? No. What’s it about? Is it, like, ancient Greek stuff? Sounds a bit heavy. It  is  ancient Greek, but it’s really beautifully written. It’s a retelling of the myth, from Circe’s point of view. She’s a banished sorceress and… well, it explores themes of loneliness, power, and finding your place. It’s surprisingly modern, actually. I'm only about a third of the way through, but I’m really enjoying it. Reminds me a bit of that photography exhibition we saw last year, the one with the portraits of marginalized women. Similar feeling, somehow. The one at the Jerwood Gallery? Yeah, that was good. I liked the way the photographer captured their expressions. Made you think about their stories, you know? I’m trying to get back into my photography, actually. Got my camera for Christmas, but haven’t really touched it. I'm kind of… nervous. Nervous? About photography? That’s unusual for you. You were always so confident snapping away at family holidays. Yeah, but that was just point-and-shoot stuff. Now I want to actually  learn  how to use it properly. Manual settings, composition… the whole nine yards. What if I take rubbish photos? What if people think I’m trying too hard? Oh, darling, everyone starts somewhere! Even professional photographers take rubbish photos sometimes. It's part of the learning process. Don't be afraid to experiment. And as for what people think... honestly, who cares? Take photos that  you  enjoy, that speak to  you . Remember when I was worried about going back to Uni after Liam… It felt terrifying at first, but I needed it.

…and then they’ve got this section on 'anticipated earnings'. Anticipated earnings! As if a bloke like me’s gonna be earnin’ anything anytime soon. It’s daft, it is. Absolutely daft. Norfolk bred, you see, know what I mean? We're not exactly showered with opportunities, are we? Well, dear, you have to try and fill it in. They won’t even look at the rest if you leave a blank. Just… put something. A realistic something. I’m sure the Job Centre’ll know you’ve been struggling for years. Right, realistic, yeah. That's the key. Don't throw out a figure you can't justify. I remember trying to help my sister fill in one of those forms a few years back. Ended up spendin' a whole afternoon workin’ out what she  could  reasonably expect from part-time freelance work, even though she wasn’t actively lookin’ at the time. It was a nightmare. Brutal, really. Brutal’s right. Used to be, a fella could get by, didn’t need all this form-fillin’ and assessin’. Remember them days, Maureen? Back when a good day’s work was enough. Oh, Arthur, don't start on that now. We’ve been through this. Progress, they call it. Though I wouldn't call shoddy workmanship on my neighbour’s new extension ‘progress.’ Look at those roof tiles! Slapped on like they were put there by a chimpanzee. Honestly! They should be ashamed of themselves. Roof tiles, eh? That reminds me, the state of the school’s roof is appalling. We've got a fundraiser on to get it sorted. Trying to convince the headteacher to let us use 3D printing to create some replacement tiles, actually. It’s a bit blue sky, I grant you, but the students are keen. They've been learning all about it. 3D printin’? Cor blimey! What’s the world comin’ to? Used to be, you went to a proper bricklayer, didn’t you? Good solid work. Not this… this plastic nonsense. Still, better than those tiles next door. Makes you worry about the rain gettin' in. Keeps me up at night, thinkin’ about leaky roofs. Can’t sleep properly these days. I know, dear. The nights are terrible. Mine's the baby birds, though. They've built a nest in the ivy on the back wall. It’s constant chirping! Little noisy things.

…and that’s why I’m just feeling utterly bewildered, really. Forty-two years, Margaret. Forty-two years I haven’t seen her properly. Just…holiday snapshots and hurried video calls. It's not the same, you know? It’s not a proper relationship. I understand, Elsie. It’s a big decision. A  very  big decision. Bringing Anya all this way, leaving her life in Canada… it’s not something to take lightly. But you’ve been talking about it for years. I know, I know. And I always thought it was a lovely dream, a fantasy for a woman my age. A bit of a folly, perhaps. But the more I hear about her struggles there – the isolation, the cost of living... the climate! Good heavens, she's frozen solid half the year! – the more I feel a responsibility. A mother's responsibility, wouldn’t you say? Absolutely. You’ve always been a fiercely protective mother. Remember when she broke her arm falling out of that apple tree in the garden? You were beside yourself. But Elsie, this is different. This isn't a scraped knee. This is uprooting someone's entire existence. I’ve tried to explain the practicalities to her, of course. About the NHS, about the relative affordability of housing - well,  relatively  affordable in Brighton, anyway. She’s worried about finding a job, naturally. She’s a graphic designer, you know, quite clever with those computer things. Brighton’s a good place for that. Plenty of agencies, creative firms. She’ll find something. The important thing is she has you. Having a support system is invaluable, especially when you're adjusting to a new country. That's what I keep telling her. And I’ve cleared out the spare room, you know. Gave it a fresh coat of paint, got her a nice set of bedding… even managed to find some of those whimsical cushions she likes. It’s all ready for her. But what if she hates it? What if she regrets it? What if she finds the entire thing… depressing? Elsie, you’re letting your anxieties run away with you. She’s coming here to  you . That's a powerful draw. And you’re not expecting her to instantly be happy, are you? It’ll take time to settle, to make connections. She’s an intelligent woman, Anya. She’ll adapt. It’s just… I’m an old woman, Margaret.

…and honestly, the whole thing just feels rather precarious, doesn’t it? This referendum result. I mean, the level of division… you can feel it, even here in Brighton. It’s not just Black and White, it's shades of grey, and an awful lot of angry grey at that. Aye, precarious is a good word for it. A very good word, David. It's unsettling. I’ve been a teacher for forty-odd years, and I haven't seen such a fractured mood. You know, I’ve always prided myself on keeping politics out of the classroom, but even the kids are picking up on the tension. They’re asking questions, worried looks… It’s unnerving. Absolutely. And the impact on higher education? We're already seeing it. Funding questions, questions about student mobility…it’s a complete mess. Speaking of messes, how did the interview go for you? With St. Michael’s? You seemed a bit hesitant about it last week. It went... alright. They seemed pleased enough with my experience, but the Head wants someone with more… contemporary pedagogical approaches. Said I needed to be “more dynamic.” Can you believe it? Dynamic! After teaching Shakespeare and Dickens for thirty years! It’s all about interactive whiteboards and gamification these days, isn’t it? Honestly, I feel like a dinosaur. Don't be so hard on yourself, John. Your reputation precedes you. Everyone knows you’re an exceptional educator. They’re just shifting the goalposts, aren't they? Trying to look modern. I told Sarah about it. She thinks you should highlight your mentoring skills. You’ve guided countless students, fostering a love of literature… That’s far more valuable than knowing how to run a Kahoot quiz. Sarah's a good girl, your daughter. Smart, she is. She’s right about the mentoring, I suppose. It’s just… I'm not sure I have the energy for another round of interviews and committees. Retirement's looking rather appealing, you know. Peaceful. Just gardening and reading… I understand. But you'd miss it, wouldn’t you? You'd miss the kids, the discussions… You're too passionate to just… fade away. By the way, have you heard anything about Mark’s situation at the college? Mark? Not properly. Rumours, of course. Whispers in the staff room. They say the department head is pushing for him not to get tenure.

Honestly, Penelope, that does sound rather… intense. American children, you know, they're raised differently. More encouraged, I think, to voice their opinions. Not always for the better, mind. Remember that dinner at the Millers’ in Boston? The youngest just kept demanding more mashed potatoes! It’s a cultural thing, isn’t it? We tend to suppress a bit, particularly in public. It’s considered…uncouth, almost. My cousin, Mark, worked in San Francisco for a couple of years. His biggest culture shock wasn't the tech scene, apparently, but the way people debated everything at the supermarket checkout. Did you see that documentary about American parenting styles? The one where they just let kids make all these big decisions, like choosing their own extracurriculars at age five? It seemed a bit chaotic to me. Like, doesn’t that lead to paralysis by choice? Paralysis by choice? Sounds like a nightmare. I’d rather someone just told me what to do, to be honest. Less thinking, more doing. This mousetrap game needs to work, though. It's hopeless if it doesn't! I’ve used these springs before, Trust Me, clever design is key. It's not necessarily chaos, dear, just a different approach. My research, you know, studying transatlantic childhood literature, shows a consistent thread – a desire to foster independence and self-reliance from a very young age. Though, I agree, excessive choice can be overwhelming. But then, so can stifling a child's natural curiosity. You’re right, Margaret. It's not inherently  bad , just… louder. Reminds me of going to a conference in Atlanta. A young woman challenged the keynote speaker – a very distinguished professor, mind you – on his methodology. Direct, fearless, and completely unapologetic! I’d have been mortified! See, Timmy and the mashed potatoes – it’s all connected. Building a society that values assertiveness, even at the dinner table. It impacts everything. Though, I draw the line at arguing about cereal. What about the accents? All the different American accents? That’s mad. My mum tried to teach me to do a Southern drawl once. Didn’t go well. My uncle went to America on a chef exchange program, and came back obsessed with barbecue sauce. Seriously, every meal had barbecue sauce. Said they knew how to do it right over there. He probably did! American barbecue is a whole world of its own. And accents, of course, are a fascinating linguistic landscape.

Honestly, darling, you won't believe it. You absolutely will not. I’ve been traipsing around that little market near the university all afternoon. It was absolute chaos, bless them, but… look! Let me guess, you battled hordes of bargain hunters to acquire something exquisitely impractical? What is it this time, another shade of turquoise? You have enough turquoise to outfit a small island. Oh, don’t be like that! It’s not  just  turquoise. It’s… seafoam, really. A very nuanced seafoam. And it's silk, proper silk, you know? Not that polyester rubbish they try to pass off sometimes. Feel it. It  is  lovely, I’ll give you that. Feels beautiful. What did you even pay for it? Don’t tell me you got fleeced. Not at all! That’s the best bit! I managed to haggle it down to 80 Yuan. Eighty! Imagine. Back in Norwich, this would be at least £50, wouldn’t it? They were trying to start at 200. I just gave them this and walked away. They called me back almost immediately. You’re ruthless. It's a good thing, though. I'm glad you got a bargain. It suits you. What else have you got in that bag of treasures? Right, let’s see… I also got a couple of linen tops. One is a simple white one, perfect for layering, and the other is a pale lavender. Really lightweight. I'm thinking I can wear them with those wide-leg trousers I bought last month. Remember? The beige ones? Vaguely. They were a bit... substantial, weren't they? Did you manage to find anything a bit less… voluminous? They're perfectly stylish! It's the new silhouette, darling. Anyway, yes, I did. I saw this little black dress. Honestly, it’s  divine . It’s almost a slip dress, but with little cap sleeves. Really simple, but so elegant. Perfect for a nice dinner out. I'm already thinking of pairing it with that silver necklace your mum gave me. That's a good find. You've been saying you needed a simple black dress for ages. Is it breathable? It gets awfully humid here. It’s cotton voile. Seriously, the lightest thing I've ever felt. And they had a matching belt – a thin, braided one – that just cinches in the waist perfectly. I’m seriously tempted to get it tailored a tiny bit, just to get the perfect fit.

…and then Healy just absolutely  burned  past him! Like a scalded cat, I tell you. The crowd went wild, didn't they, Moira? They certainly did, Liam. Though I have to admit, I spent most of it worrying about Oisin spilling his juice all over the rug. He was getting rather animated, bless him. He kept shouting “Try! Try!” at the telly. It  was  a good try, Dad! Healy was really fast! Better than anyone at school, even Ethan. Ethan's got pace, but Healy’s got... something else. See, son? That's what I'm talking about. That's skill, that is. It's in the blood, you know. Irish rugby. It's a religion, practically. Aye, a passionate religion, Liam. I remember when Scotland and Ireland played… the whole neighbourhood would be divided. You were either staunchly Scottish, or you were staunchly Irish. No room for neutrality! Nan, you always make it sound so dramatic! It was just a bit of friendly rivalry, surely? ‘Just’ a bit of friendly rivalry? Dear girl, it was war! Though good-natured war, of course. Nowadays, they're all so… polite. Where’s the drama gone? Speaking of which, did you manage to get the cards signed, Moira? Oisin’s birthday is tomorrow, you know. Nearly. I’ve got Sarah’s, just need to get Oisin to scribble on his own. He keeps trying to draw pictures of dinosaurs instead. It's a battle, let me tell you. He's convinced he’s a paleontologist. He’d put Healy to shame for determination, that one. Right, before he gets too busy excavating the living room, maybe we should try and get him off to bed? He's been bouncing off the walls since he came in from school. But Dad! It's still light out! Can't we do something else? They were talking about stargazing tonight... Mr. Davies said if the clouds clear, you can see Jupiter properly. Stargazing, eh? That is a grand idea, Oisin. Moira, what do you think? Stargazing sounds lovely, dear. But he needs to be asleep by nine, you know. Otherwise, we'll be dealing with a cranky toddler all morning. Aye, a well-rested child is a blessing, Moira. When I was teaching, I always said a calm classroom started with a calm child. It's the same principle, really. Right then. Operation Bedtime commences in five minutes.

…and honestly, Chloe, the sheer  volume  of tiny clothes is astounding. Like, where do they even  come  from? My sister’s already got a mountain for little Leo, and she hasn’t even been born yet! It’s madness. I’m thinking of just designating a whole room, aren't I? A dedicated baby clothes room. Bit much, probably. A whole room? That  is  a bit much, isn’t it? Though, I can see the appeal. My mum’s got a spare bedroom, and she’s practically begging me to let her store everything I might need. I think she's slightly obsessed. I’m trying to be more sensible. I’ve started looking at pre-loved stuff. Much more sustainable, innit? And saves a fortune. Absolutely. I was thinking that too. Though, you know, with my sister, there’s so much good quality stuff going spare. She's got a whole load of F&M, practically new. It's such a generous offer, I almost feel bad taking it all. Do you think I should offer to share some of mine with her? I've got a load of Zara baby stuff from before I realised neutrals were apparently  the  thing. Definitely share! They’re family, aren't they? Plus, it’ll be nice for her knowing Leo has something special from you. Speaking of sharing… how’s the moving situation going? Still looking at those cottages near Grantchester? It's a nightmare, honestly. The market's bonkers. Every time something comes up, it’s gone within hours. There’s this one, though, with a gorgeous garden… but it’s got a shared drive. And the estate agent was  so  enthusiastic. It was a bit much, really. Like, “You  need  this house!”, he kept saying. It was unnerving. Oh, those agents! You get the worst of them. A shared drive is a pain, though. It’s worth holding out, I reckon. Especially if you want somewhere with a garden. Remember that awful drive down to your parents' last Christmas? Never again, eh? Don't remind me! The state of that road! Anyway, besides the house drama, I was just thinking about languages. Learning German's proving trickier than I thought. I mean, I did A-level German at school, but that was ages ago. My brain feels like it's full of baby food these days. Tell me about it! I've been trying to brush up on my Spanish.

…No, seriously, I was tryin’ to explain to Sharon at the print shop, you know, she’s from up north, proper northern accent, and I was tryin’ to tell her about ‘bird’ meaning a girl down ‘ere. She just looked at me like I was speakin’ Martian! Honestly, you could practically see the gears grindin' in her ‘ead. That’s classic. The whole ‘southernisms’ thing is a minefield for outsiders. People always assume Bedfordshire is all posh and received pronunciation, don’t they? They do. It’s hilarious. You ever find yourself trying to consciously flatten your accent when you’re somewhere else? I reckon I do. Just a bit though. Don’t want to sound like I’m tryin’ too hard. Absolutely! It's a reflex. Though, I can’t help gettin’ a bit excitable when I’m talkin’ about guitars, innit? My voice goes all high and proper then. Speaking of which, you ever had a proper go at modular synths, Liam? Thought you'd be all over that. I've fiddled about, yeah. It’s just… expensive. And overwhelming. I’m sticking to my acoustic for now. Trying to actually learn some proper chords. Speaking of expense, I’ve been looking at some MMA classes. Heard good things over at Premier Martial Arts. You been? Nah, never. Always fancied it though. Bit scary, isn't it? Me dad's always goin' on about how you gotta be able to look after yourself, never know when you might need it. My grandad used to say the same thing, right? "Learn to defend yourself, Leon. People aren’t always decent." He was a tough old bird, that one. Owned a patch of land outside Houghton Regis back in the fifties, a little market garden. Wonder if it's still goin'. Land's proper valuable these days, isn’t it? Absolutely. It’s crazy. Anyway, back to self-defense… I just think it’s good for confidence, you know? Plus, it's a good way to blow off steam. I had a right nightmare teaching Mandarin today. One kid just kept... well, let's just say his digestive system wasn't cooperating. It was a whole thing. Language learning’s fantastic, though. It's fascinating to see how different languages structure the world. Awful, that. Happened to me once at a family barbecue, proper mortifyin’. Heard your uncle Barry fartin' across the garden, thought it was me!

Honestly, it's ridiculous. Absolutely ridiculous. Another two hours today. Two! Just getting from Richmond to Tooting. And the M3 was a parking lot. I swear, the traffic is getting worse every single week. Yeah, it's a nightmare, isn't it? Commuting in London is basically a test of endurance. You'd think with all the rail investment, it’d be better. Though, don’t get me started on the Southern Rail. Rail is marginally better, actually. At least you can read or work on your phone. Being stuck in a car… it’s just soul-destroying. I was listening to that true crime podcast, and I missed half of it trying to avoid that idiot in the Mini who kept drifting into my lane. Classic London. Mini drivers, I swear they think they’re auditioning for a Fast and Furious sequel. So, still thinking about getting rid of the Fiat then? I am. It's not just the commute, it's…everything. It’s tiny. I feel like a sardine in there. And the fuel economy isn’t as good as I hoped, honestly. It's costing a fortune, practically cancelling out the tax savings. Right. I get that. You were saying about wanting something a bit bigger, something you could actually  fit  into, and maybe a bit more reliable for a longer journey. Remember that trip we talked about to the Lake District? Exactly! I’m starting to look, but it’s terrifying. Prices are insane. And electric is still not really viable for me, not with my commute. Charging points around Richmond are patchy, and the upfront cost… Yeah, the initial outlay is a killer. But think about it – no more petrol costs, fewer servicing bills…potentially significant savings in the long run. Have you looked at those used Vauxhall Corsas or Astras? They're fairly reliable, decent sized, and you can get a good one for a reasonable price. I've glanced. But the Astra feels a bit...beige. I want something with a  little  bit of personality. My dad keeps suggesting a Volvo. He's obsessed with Volvos. "Safe, reliable, Scandinavian design," he drones on. Typical Dad. He'll be telling you to invest in sensible pensions next. But honestly, Volvos are pretty good. They hold their value well too. It's a good thing to think about. I suppose. But they're still a bit…pale, aren’t they?

Aye, Liam gets a bit over-enthusiastic sometimes, doesn't he? Luckily, your grandma's got a good sense of humour. Remember when she tried to convince me that pigeons were spies for the government? Seriously, Grandma Elsie still believes that? I tried to tell her it’s because they’re always watching! But she just got all serious and started talking about ‘the birds’… They  are  watchin’, lad. I’ve seen ‘em. Gatherin’ information. Chimps in the sky, I tell ya. And don't you go laughin' at an old woman! I've got a good memory, I do. Remember the blackout in '42? They were out in force then, they were. Elsie, love, you were napping soundly through most of that blackout. You woke up complainin' about the telly bein' off. Don't you start contradictin' me, Arthur! I'm allowed a little exaggeration. These young 'uns don't understand what proper darkness was like, they're used to their fancy electric lights. Alright, alright, both of you. Let's not argue about pigeons and blackouts. Liam, were you able to explain the equations to your Grandma, at least a little bit? Sort of. I showed her how you can use them to figure out the area of a field. She seemed to understand that. Fields are good, she likes fields. Fields are important. Used to pick blackberries in ‘em, I did. Proper juicy ones. Not like these supermarket ones, all pale and tasteless. Speaking of blackberries, I thought I’d make a crumble for tea. Do you fancy that, both of you? I’ve got a lovely recipe. Crumble sounds grand, Mary. A good, proper crumble. With lashings of custard, mind. Can’t have crumble without custard. Of course! Custard it is. Liam, could you pop down to the shops for me? We’re a bit short on sugar. And if you see any proper Yorkshire rhubarb, pick some up. That'll give it a wee bit of extra flavour. Right, yeah, no problem. How much sugar? And what’s a ‘wee bit’? Grandma always says you’re vague with your measurements. Just a bag, love. A medium one. And a ‘wee bit’ is… well, use your judgement. You're a clever lad, aren't you? Just enough to give it a little somethin’ extra. Don’t go overdoin' it, mind. We don't want it too sweet.

“…and then, right, the parrot squawked, ‘Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!’ And Captain Blackheart, he roared, ‘Silence, Polly! We’re trying to plan our raid!’ Don't you think that's exciting, Leo? Rosie, you listening?" Pirates! Did they find the treasure, Mummy? A big chest, filled with gold doubloons? Well, not yet, sweetheart. That’s where  we  come in. We need to decide what happens next. Captain Blackheart’s ship, 'The Sea Serpent,' is heading towards…hmm…what are we thinking? A deserted island? A treasure-laden galleon? Cake. Rosie, you always bring us back to cake, don't you? It  is  a good idea, though. Pirates  do  love cake! Perhaps they were searching for a legendary bakery? A bakery on an island? With pirate chefs! Exactly! Leo, brilliant idea. Now, we’ve been talking pirates, but next week is Shakespeare week at school, remember? I was thinking we might try to squeeze in a trip to Stratford-upon-Avon. Would you both be up for that? Stratford? Yes, Stratford. Where Shakespeare lived and wrote his plays. It's really exciting. We can see his house! Will there be swords? Like Hamlet? There might be some acting with swords, yes! Maybe even some fancy costumes. Although, I think we'll be focusing more on the stories, rather than the fights. We’re doing  A Midsummer Night’s Dream  in class. It’s about fairies and magic. Magic? Like…pulling rabbits out of hats? Well, it's more like pretending to be a fairy and making things happen with your imagination. Speaking of magic… remember that amazing circus workshop we got tickets for? The real circus? With the clowns and the acrobats? The very same! I’m so excited. They said they’ll be teaching us some basic juggling and even a bit of magic. Think you can handle a juggling ball, Leo? I can! I can juggle! Oops. It takes practice, sweetie. They'll show you the tricks. And Rosie, they have face painting too – you could be a sparkly fairy! A sparkly fairy! Can I have a rainbow? And glitter  everywhere ? Absolutely. Glitter everywhere. Now, I was looking at some old photographs the other day, and I found some from your Easter photoshoot last year. Remember those adorable bunny ears you were both wearing? I looked like a big bunny! With fluffy whiskers! You did. We should print them out and put them on the fridge.

Good heavens, Bernard, that sounds absolutely preposterous! Arrested in Jeddah, trying to sail to Cyprus? What on earth possessed you? You’ve always been a sensible man. Sensible? Dearest Penelope, youth and a slightly leaky boat are a dangerous combination. We really thought we could manage it. Fifteen-foot sloop, you see. A bit cramped for two adults, a ridiculous amount of tinned food, and, well, a few ambitions. I wanted to prove something to myself, I suppose. Call it a mid-life crisis, fuelled by stories of daring sailors. You know, it reminds me of that horrifying incident Matthew – that's David Matthew’s son – had years ago when trying to cross the Atlantic in a dinghy. Madness, absolute madness! Though he did manage to get a photograph with a penguin... Penguins are rather charming creatures. Though I must confess, I’ve only ever seen pictures. My interests have always tended towards the… molar, shall we say. Reginald, you and your teeth! It’s always something dental with you, isn’t it? But back to Bernard’s predicament. What happened after they arrested you? Did you spend the night in a Saudi jail? Thankfully, no. A rather stern gentleman – a Brigadier, I think he was – eventually intervened. He seemed to understand, or perhaps he just pitied two foolish old men. He explained, rather forcefully, that sailing without proper permits and sufficient provisions was, let's say, frowned upon. We were given a substantial fine, of course, and a very pointed warning. Trying to explain the concept of leisure sailing to a Saudi officer… well, that was an experience. It's fascinating, isn't it, how different cultures view recreation. Remember teaching at Manchester University, Penelope? Trying to explain to a group of international students why we Brits feel compelled to complain about the weather, whatever it's doing? They were utterly baffled. Absolutely! It was the same with teaching in Riyadh. Trying to explain the centrality of a pint down the pub to the academic discourse… didn’t go down particularly well. The lack of alcohol, you see, was the biggest culture shock. So dry! Everything was so…regulated. Indeed. We had to smuggle in a small bottle of brandy in our luggage. Tasted dreadful, of course, but it felt wonderfully rebellious. It’s astonishing, isn’t it, how differently alcohol is viewed around the world? I remember visiting Argentina – the Malbec was glorious, and the entire country seemed to be celebrating something!

It’s just…the state of it! You know, the grout’s practically gone in places, and that shower head’s been dribbling for months. I keep meaning to sort it, but…      Tell me about it, love. Life’s like that, innit? Always something needing doing. Remember when we were redecorating the kitchen? Thought we’d be finished in a week! Turned into a three-month saga. Still find bits of plaster behind the cooker sometimes!      Can we talk about something else? This is boring.      Liam, darling, just give us five minutes. We’re just chatting. And honestly, a decent bathroom is a  necessity , not a luxury. I'm thinking of getting a quote from that bloke down the road, Dave. He did Mrs. Henderson’s, and she swore by him.      Dave’s alright. Bit rough around the edges, mind, but good value. Proper craftsman, he is. Speaking of value, how’s the babysitting going for you this week? Any offers?      Not a lot, sadly. Just a couple of hours on Friday night. Which reminds me, have you spoken to Mrs. Davies about Liam doing some work experience at her shop? She mentioned needing an extra pair of hands during the summer holidays.      Work experience? Doing what? Dusting shelves? I’m trying to get a place on that coding camp, Mum. That’s  actual  experience.      Coding camp’s a grand idea, love, but a bit of retail experience won't do you any harm, will it? I remember when I was your age, I worked at Woolworths for the summer. Made my own money, bought myself a new pair of trainers. Felt proper independent.      Exactly. It’s about learning a bit of responsibility. Plus, Mrs. Davies is very generous with her tips. And it gets you talking to people, Liam. It’s good practice. You’re glued to that phone.      It's not glued, Mum. I'm talking to my friends.      Right then. So, holidays. Have you booked anything yet? I keep looking at Santorini, but it's frightfully expensive.      Santorini? Dreamy! We’re thinking Cornwall again. Reliable, you know? Always a good beach and decent pasties. Plus, the kids love it. Remember last year when you were refereeing that football match on the beach? You were a sight to behold!      Oh, don't remind me! Nearly broke an ankle in the sand! But it was fun. I do fancy a change though.

Aye, that’s right, lass. The chef – I’ve forgotten his name already, never mind – he explained it all. All about the slow cooking, the stirring, the butter… it’s an art, see. Not just chucking things in a pot. That's what's gone out of cooking, hasn’t it? Nobody wants to put the effort in. He was a bit posh, though, wasn’t he? His accent was all… Londony. Like you, Grandad. Well, young man, there's nothing wrong with a good London accent. Earned it, I have! And I’m just observing, Liam. This chef  was  rather impressive. The way he talked about the truffles… like they were precious jewels. Which, let’s be honest, they practically are. They wanted five quid a gram! Five quid? Seriously? That’s mental! Still, you get what you pay for, I suppose. Did you tell him about old Mr. Davies down the road, Dad? The bloke who found a HUGE truggle in his garden, years ago. Sold it for a fortune and bought himself a new shed. Aye, I did! The chef just raised an eyebrow and said, “Remarkable.” Like I was telling him a fairy tale. Typical. He probably eats truffle oil on toast every morning. Imagine finding a truffle. You’d be rich! Better than winning the lottery. Don't get carried away, Liam. It's less likely than winning the lottery. But a decent find… it would put a dent in the holiday fund, that’s for sure. Speaking of which, Elodie, are you still thinking about that internship in America next summer? The one with the biotech firm? Yeah, I am. I’ve had a preliminary interview, actually. Went alright, I think. It’s just… a huge step, isn't it? Leaving everything behind. The potential for stem cell research over there is just incredible, you know? They’re ahead of the game here. Stem cells, eh? Sounds complicated. Just make sure you eat your greens, love. That’s all the stem cells you need. Your mother's wisdom knows no bounds, Margaret. But seriously, it's an amazing opportunity, Elodie. Don’t let a little apprehension hold you back. It’ll change your life. Can we stop for ice cream? I’m starving. And can we listen to some proper music? This classical stuff is putting me to sleep. Proper music? You mean that awful rap you listen to?

Honestly, it’s just… bewildering. The shift in usage around ‘impact’ as a verb. It's everywhere now, isn't it? Used in contexts where perfectly good alternatives exist. "We need to impact performance," blimey. It used to mean a force, a collision… now it's just… a verbifying disaster. Yeah, I’ve noticed it too. It’s funny, isn’t it? How language just… evolves. Marketing’s full of it, really. Loads of Americanisms creeping in, and this sort of semantic drift. “Leverage” is another one I’m starting to loathe. “Let’s leverage our synergies.” Makes me want to throw a stapler at someone. Sorry, what was that? Synergies? Sounds ominous. I'm just trying to wrangle this project timeline – deadlines are looming like dark clouds. Is this about language changing, or... marketing buzzwords? Both, really, Tom. It’s all connected, innit? Linguistic trends often reflect shifts in broader culture and professional jargon. I work with language data, you see - Analysing patterns and usage. And the rise of ‘impact’ as a verb perfectly demonstrates the tendency for verbification, often driven by management speak. It’s fascinating, actually, but also slightly depressing. Right, fascinatingly depressing. I get that. It’s just everything feels so… performative now, doesn't it? Especially online. People are crafting their language to be "impactful," without necessarily thinking about whether it’s actually… well, good. I mean, a good ad doesn’t shout 'impact!' It just  is . Makes sense. I'm mostly dealing with spreadsheets and Gantt charts, so my exposure to this is probably limited. But I can see how it would be frustrating, trying to track something like that. Especially when you're trying to understand how people  actually  use words, not just how they  think  they should. Exactly! It’s about the actual data, not the aspiration. My team is working on a new corpus – a collection of text data – focused on spoken discourse around workplace wellbeing. We’re hoping it’ll give us a more realistic picture of how people are truly communicating about stress and mental health, rather than the carefully curated narratives you see in company reports. That’s brilliant, actually. Really valuable research. I wonder if we could see some correlation between sectors using a lot of ‘impact’ and… let’s say, generally lower employee satisfaction? Clearly, I'm just hypothesizing. But it’s a thought. Sounds like you could really leverage that data, eh?

Right, according to this, we’re about fifteen minutes out. Tarnow’s just… popping up on the screen now, all quaint and yellow-y looking. You sure Auntie Zofia’s house is as… rustic as you remember, Penelope? Last time you saw her, wasn’t it, like, twenty years ago? Twenty-three years, actually. And yes, rustic is putting it mildly, Maisie. It's… well, it's Zofia. Expect crocheted doilies, endless plates of pierogi, and a distinct smell of elderflower cordial. Don't even  think  about suggesting anything other than the traditional meal, or you’ll get the silent treatment for a week. Right, noted. Pierogi it is. Though, realistically, I packed a few tins of baked beans, just in case. You know, emergency rations. A bit of home. Bless you, dear. Always prepared. I appreciate that. Though I doubt Zofia would appreciate the aroma too much. She's rather particular about scents, you know. Once complained about the lingering fragrance of my lavender hand cream. Said it was 'distracting from the proper scent of potatoes and dill.' Only Auntie Zofia could complain about the scent of potatoes and dill. Seriously, though, are you absolutely certain she knows we’re coming? You said the phone reception out there is dreadful. I sent a postcard. A proper, paper one, with a stamp and everything. A month ago. I rather hoped it would have arrived by now. Polish postal services… well, they have their own rhythm, don't they? It’s not exactly Royal Mail. True. Still, a postcard  should  have reached her. I did a quick trawl on Facebook - she's on there, surprisingly - put a message on her wall. No response. Hoping she doesn’t think we’ve completely forgotten her. She’s a bit… set in her ways, Zofia. Doesn’t embrace technology with open arms. Expects cards and letters. Though, to be fair, she's always been a bit of an anachronism. It’s part of her charm, really. Like a stubbornly delightful time capsule. Plus, Dimitri, her grandson, probably hasn’t mentioned it to her. He’s… well, he’s a teenager. Teenage boys. The ultimate communication black hole. So, what's the plan if she  doesn't  know we're here? We drive up to the house and… just knock? Exactly. Ring the bell, which is probably a rusty contraption that’s half-broken, and hope for the best.

Honestly, that handball was daylight robbery. Absolute daylight robbery. The ref was miles off, weren't he? Aye, he were. But you can’t blame the ref completely, Mark. They’re under pressure too, right? And it was close. Can’t deny that. Besides, we were lookin’ a bit shaky before that anyway. Shaky? We were dominant! Until that dodgy decision. It completely shifted the momentum. It's the sponsors' fault, honestly. The pressure they put on these games… it's impacting the ref's decisions. Think about it, a bad call risks upsetting a multi-million pound deal. You reckon? That's a bit cynical, innit? They’re just wanting their logo on the shirts, mate. Don’t be gettin’ yourself all worked up about it. It's not  just  the logo, Elara! It's the entire aesthetic they force upon the kits these days. Look at Man U’s new strip. Appalling! Just streams of some tech company’s colours. No heritage, no… anything! Used to be proper shirts, you know? Simple designs, proper colours that reflected the club's history. Oh, you and your nostalgia. It’s just clever marketing, isn't it? Appeal to a new generation. Besides, I thought that Man U one was alright, actually. Bit bold, but alright. Our lads' new kit’s the worst though. That blinding yellow… I’ll be needing sunglasses just to watch us play away! See! You’re admitting it! And the Adidas stripes are all wrong on it. It looks… off. It lacks… gravitas. Something a proper North East team should have. You know what's  not  off? A classic McDonald’s after a match like that. I'm starvin'. Now you’re talkin’ sense. I’m peckish myself. Though, that new spicy McNuggets are a bit... much. Too much heat, even for me. I’d stick to the original, like always. Proper comfort food, that. You know, I saw an article the other day about how much research goes into designing the food at McDonald's. It’s all psychological, apparently. Colours, fonts, even how they arrange the fries in the box… Psychological manipulation, you mean. Don't give me that ‘research’ angle. It's pure profit-driven. But yeah, fries are essential. Large fries. And a McFlurry. Salted caramel. Don’t argue with me on this, Elara. Rest assured, I’m not arguin’. Salted caramel's a winner.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of it! He said I was recording him! Recording him! Like, why on earth would I do that? He just went red in the face and started shouting about privacy. It was ridiculous. Right. More drama then, yeah? You always seemed to attract it, love. Ever since you were a little 'un. Mum’s always said you were a magnet for fuss. It’s not  attracting  it, Liam. It’s  dealing  with it! And it's getting exhausting, innit? I was just asking about the train times to Brighton for next weekend - I was thinking of taking the kids. A little day trip. They’d love it. Brighton? With the kids? That'll cost a fortune. Train fares alone… plus, you know, chips, ice cream… It's not like they're cheap, is it? I know, I know! But they’ve been so good lately, you know? Little Alfie hasn't whined once on the bus this week. And Maisie’s even started helping with the dishes. A bit of sun and the beach… it'd do us all good. I saw a George Foreman grill on eBay yesterday, too. Thinking of getting one. Saves a fortune on takeaways, doesn't it? A George Foreman? You're better off sticking to proper cooking, love. Proper food. Nowadays, you can’t trust nothin’. This eBay thing… dodgy deals, everything. Remember that time I ordered that fishing rod? Said it was 'like new'. Turned up completely snapped in half. Lost me money that did. You and your fishing rods. Look, the point is, I’m trying to be sensible. Trying to do things. Unlike some people, who just sit around moaning about Job Seekers Allowance. Now, hold on a minute. Don't go there. It's not exactly a picnic, is it? Trying to live on that pittance. They’re tighten’ing the rules every week. And it's not my fault jobs are disappearing! It’s this government, I tell you. And half the people round here who are doin' alright, happy to look down their noses at us. I'm not saying it's your fault, Liam. But you have to  try . You haven't even looked at a job application in months. Mum worries sick. Easy for you to say. Got your degree, posh accent . You wouldn’t understand what it’s like. Just the other day, that fella at the shops – the new one, from…well, you know… different background… started speaking to me.

Honestly, Doreen, you wouldn't  believe  the traffic getting here today. It was a complete standstill on the A1. I'm starting to wonder if I should just bite the bullet and get a satellite navigation system. My phone kept dropping signal, and I ended up going round in circles near Hampton. A sat nav, eh? Fancy that. I used to get everywhere just fine without one, didn’t I, Mum? You learn the roads, don’t you? These newfangled things, they ain’t always right. Remember that time Brenda’s husband followed his sat nav straight into a ditch? Oh, I remember! He was so cross! Said it was the machine's fault, not his. Though I must say, he wasn't known for his driving, was he, Arthur? Always a bit… hesitant. You’re working hard these days, dear. Still chasing those big accounts? Always chasing, Mum. It's the nature of the beast. Just landed a new one with a logistics company, thankfully. Big potential. Although, the presentations… they’re draining. I'm living practically on instant coffee and those meal deals from Tesco at the moment. At least they're convenient. Tesco’s alright for a quick bit, that's true. But you wouldn’t get proper grub there, would you? I popped into Mr. Patel’s corner shop earlier for a loaf of bread. He’s got proper sourdough now, that man! And his wife makes the most lovely samosas. You should try them, Sarah. Samosas do sound tempting! I'd love to, but honestly, time is a luxury I rarely have. I wish I could just sit and enjoy a proper meal. Speaking of which, how are your warts doing, Mum? Last time we spoke, they were particularly troublesome. Ah, the warts. They're being… contrary. Not going away, are they? Doreen keeps telling me to try something herbal, but I'm not keen on putting strange things on my skin. Feels a bit risky, doesn't it? It's just a bit of comfrey cream, Mum, nothing drastic. Keeps the itching down. Honestly, you’d think at our age, our bodies would start cooperating. It’s all falling apart, isn’t it? Remember that plane crash they had on the news the other day? Dreadful. Makes you think, doesn’t it? Absolutely dreadful. My stomach was in knots watching it. It’s terrifying, the fragility of it all.

Honestly, Chloe, Mr. Davies’ lesson today was  epic  in the wrong way. Like, monumentally boring. We spent forty minutes discussing the symbolism of a single dandelion. A dandelion! Seriously? Right? Dandelions. Groundbreaking. Though, I did think it was a bit much, yeah. Miss Peterson would have made it way more engaging. Remember that time she had us build ecosystems in jars? That was brilliant. Oh my gosh, yes! Way better than dissecting the emotional state of a weed. I nearly fell asleep. I’m starting to think English is actively trying to kill my enthusiasm. I mean, the test next week... ugh. Don't even mention the test. I'm proper stressed about it. I just... I can't seem to remember all the quotes. Mrs. Hargrave keeps piling them on. What’s the one from  Romeo and Juliet  about... you know… dreary things? "Misery is bottomless," isn’t it? Honestly, it feels like she  wants  us to fail. Although, I think she’s just trying to prepare us. She keeps saying it’s all about Analysing Shakespeare and showing understanding, not just regurgitating lines. Easier said than done. And have you noticed how weird the trainee teachers are this year? Like, Mr. Finch in Science – he keeps trying to make everything a joke. It’s distracting! He tried to explain photosynthesis using a banana yesterday. A banana?! No way! That’s proper ridiculous. Mr. Davies is bad, but at least he’s consistently dry. Mr. Finch is just... unpredictable. It’s throwing off my revision completely. I'd rather face a complex equation than his bizarre analogies. Tell me about it. And Mrs. Ellis in Art? She’s so intense! Yesterday, she spent ten minutes lecturing Liam about the  correct  shade of cerulean. Liam! He was drawing a spaceship! Cerulean! Honestly! I’m sticking to acrylics. Less chance of a colour-related crisis. I’m trying to finish my piece for the school exhibition – it’s a charcoal drawing of the river Cam at sunset. Trying to capture the light, you know? Ooh, that sounds amazing! You're so much better at art than me. I tried to draw ANON’s cat, Winston, and he looked like a furry potato. Absolutely dreadful. I'm sticking to sketching people for now, practicing faces. Miss Paterson says it’s a good base for  everything , even science diagrams, apparently. That's clever! Maybe I should try that.

…but seriously, Mrs. O’Malley, it’s just like The Matrix, isn’t it? Like, they tell you what to believe, and you just… accept it. Red pill or blue pill, you know? Liam, darling, you’re drawing a very long bow comparing something like the Catholic Church to  The Matrix . It's not quite the same thing. There’s a lot of history and tradition. But isn't it? Like, the nuns are the… the agents. Keeping everyone in line. Telling them what to think. And if you question it? Boom! You're naughty. Remember Mrs. Higgins in Year 5? She kept telling me Jesus was a good boy and I was like, “But he got crucified!” And she just gave me  the look . Oh, Mrs. Higgins. She was… dedicated. Look, Liam, religion isn't about being controlled. It's about… finding comfort, understanding the world, having faith. My mum, she always said it gave her strength. And you can’t equate that with a sci-fi film, can you? They use it for the narrative. But there are other ways to find comfort, aren't there? Like… like Scientology. I read about it online. It promised my uncle Derek would feel better. Remember how down he was after the factory closed? He paid loads of money for it, though. And he still feels down. Seems a bit dodgy, to be honest. Scientology… well, that’s a completely different kettle of fish, Liam. That’s… exploitative, really. Preying on vulnerable people. Your uncle Derek was going through a rough patch, and they jumped on that. It’s not genuine. It's… a business. And it certainly doesn’t compare to Catholicism, which has been around for centuries. So, you think following the Church is… okay then? Because my Gran keeps going on about it. Saying we all need to go to Mass and confess our sins. Sounds a bit intense. It's about personal choice, love. It's your Gran’s belief system, and she has every right to have it. But you don't  have  to follow it. And confessing… well, it's not as scary as it sounds. It's about feeling better about yourself. Talking things out. We had a new friend at school, Daniel. His mum doesn't believe in any of that stuff. She says it’s all made up. She’s really into science. Like, really, really into it.

Honestly, Liam, you're taking us the  long  way round. We could’ve gone straight up the A1. It’s only ten minutes more, not half an hour! I know, I know, but I wanted to show you this bit of old Roman road. Properly preserved, apparently. Thought you’d find it interesting. You’re the history buff, aren’t you? After all those Old English papers you were doing at uni. Aye, well, I’m more interested in Shakespeare these days than crumbling Roman pavements. And I’m definitely not a history buff! Just… fond of a good ballad and a bit of linguistic digging, that's all. Right, so, speaking of digging, have you booked those dancing lessons yet? The tango ones I was on about? Not yet, no. Been a bit busy with the Peterson project. They want the stress analysis done by next week - absolute nightmare, you know. But I’ll look into it this weekend. Honestly, you'll be brilliant at it. So much more natural rhythm than me. I’ll be two left feet, guaranteed. Don’t be daft! Everyone’s natural at somethin’. Besides, think of the stories! Picture us, swirling around, all dramatic, like those Tango dancers on Strictly. Although, ironically, I was just reading an article about ageism in the entertainment industry. Apparently, the older dancers get overlooked all the time. It’s ridiculous. It is a bit, isn't it? Seems to be a general trend. They want everyone to look like 25. What about Dame Helen Mirren? She’s fabulous, and she's considerably older than 25. Exactly! Speaking of fabulous, did you see what Gemma Collins was wearing on LoveFilm the other night? The one with all the sequins? It was… something else. Like a disco ball had exploded on her. Gemma Collins. Always a classic. I'm more of a Netflix man myself, to be honest. Been binge-watching that medical drama,  The Nightingale Ward . It's surprisingly good. Gets you thinking about the NHS, doesn't it? My cousin's a nurse, you know. Really puts things into perspective. Aye, it does. I was thinking about volunteering at that animal shelter again. Remember how much I enjoyed it when I had more time? Maybe we could do it together sometime? Absolutely. That’s a great idea. Just let me sort out this work madness first. Do you fancy a holiday after all this?

Seriously, I could’ve taken better pics on my phone. And that landscape, all grey and…bleak. Like someone had smeared concrete on a canvas.      Now, Elodie, be fair. Modern art  is  supposed to challenge you. It’s not always meant to be pretty. Remember that exhibition we saw in Manchester a few years back? The one with the… the ketchup cans?      Oh God, Mum, don’t remind me. That was peak pretentious. Still, that was  slightly  more interesting than staring at grey squares. What did young Finn make of it all?      It were alright, I suppose. There was one thing with loads of wires, that was cool. Looked like a robot spider. But the rest… Nah. Didn’t get it. Proper boring. So, are we near that market yet? I’m starvin’.      We'll be there in about fifteen minutes, Finn. Just need to navigate this delightfully winding road. Istria's landscapes are truly breathtaking, aren’t they? The olive groves stretching out... unbelievable. And the scent! Have you noticed the scent of pine and rosemary in the air?      It is lovely, isn't it, Julian? Reminds me of holidays we used to take caravanning around Cornwall, years ago. Finn was a little nipper then, couldn’t have been more than two.      Caravanning? Like, in a caravan? Were they smelly?      Oh, Finn, you wouldn’t appreciate the joys of caravan holidays. Mum and Dad practically lived in one for a summer.      We did  not  practically live in one! We had some wonderful adventures. Remember that beach, Elodie? The one with the red cliffs? We built a sandcastle bigger than you were!      Speaking of adventures, have you considered visiting Rovinj? It's a stunning medieval town on the coast. Quite beautiful, particularly at sunset. We could have dinner there tomorrow – a proper seafood feast.      Rovinj sounds amazing. Actually, remember that documentary about Sons of Anarchy we were all watching last week? The coastal towns reminded me a bit of that - rugged, dramatic…      You and your TV shows, Elodie! It’s not really the same as experiencing the real thing. Though, I must admit, it did spur me on to look at some Istrian wines. Heard good things about their Malvazija.      Absolutely. The local wine is exceptional. And the olive oil! Honestly, Margaret, the olive oil here is unlike anything I've tasted back in England. The richness… the complexity…      You’re right, Julian.

Aye, reet awful! Poor lass. I thought she'd literally jumped out her skin. Honestly, Lucy, y'weren’t sayin’ anything on that recording, were ya? Just laughin’ fit to burst. I was! But mostly trying not to choke on my tea. Honestly, the jump scare was perfectly timed. It was classic. You did well, Anna. Really well. That camera placement... genius. Genius is a bit strong, Lucy. More like, opportunistic. Y'just happened to catch her at the worst possible moment, didn't ya? Watchin' that silly spider video. It weren’t silly! It were a tarantula! They're proper creepy crawlies. And it weren’t opportunity, it were strategy! I planned it, I did. I’d been waitin' for ages for Sarah to be settled and relaxed. The perfect moment to… unleash the horror. Okay, okay, hold on. Let's be fair. It  was  a bit mean. Sarah was genuinely distressed. Though, I have to admit, the look on her face was priceless. Like, the most dramatic face I’ve ever seen. Did you get that on the recording? Absolutely! I’ve already forwarded it to Liam. He'll be winding her up about it all week. He's got a right giggle for that sort of thing, that Liam. Good! Serves her reet. She’s always prangin’ on about how tough she is. Needs a bit of a shock every now and then. Besides, we're all havin' a laugh, aren't we? It's all in good fun. How's that game goin', Beth? Are you still stuck on that level of  Legendary Knights ? Aye, still stuck. Level 37. It’s brutal! I've been tryin’ for three days. I swear, that dragon’s fire is relentless. You'd think they'd design these things to be a bit more, y'know,  fair . Honestly, those games are rigged, aren't they? I gave up on  Legendary Knights  ages ago. Too frustrating. I'm much better at  Cosmic Conquest . Fancy a game later? I could show you a few tricks. I’m in if you are! Although, I'm pretty decent at  Cosmic Conquest  myself. Don’t expect to be thrashed, Lucy. Alright, alright, settle down, you two. I’m still gettin’ over the tarantula trauma, so  Cosmic Conquest  will have to wait. I'm fair famished, though. Anyone fancy a chippy? There’s that new one down on Thorne Road, they’ve got proper decent mushy peas.

Aye, tell me about it, lass. Proper grub, that’s what we need. Been starvin' since lunch. Pelaw Working Men’s Club did a right good steak pie today, mind. You wouldn't believe the size o' it. Could've fed a whole football team. Seriously? A steak pie sounds amazing right now. This vegan wrap is doing  nothing  for me. It's all lettuce and disappointment. Do you reckon we can sneak away for a quick Nandos? There's one just down the road. Nkndos? Tempting, Sarah, but five minutes isn't enough. Queues there are mental, especially on a Tuesday. I was thinking more along the lines of that little Italian place on Salford Quays. 'La Piazza', isn’t it? Good pizza, proper pasta... La Piazza, eh? That's a better shout, pet. Nandos is alright, but it’s all a bit… shouty, isn’t it? All them bright colours and the endless chicken orders. La Piazza’s got a bit more… atmosphere. Reminds me of when I was a lad, me mam used to take us down to the Italian place in Gateshead. Always smelled o’ garlic and oregano, it did. Shouty is exactly the word. My ears were ringing for an hour after last time. Garlic and oregano sounds significantly more appealing though. What are you having, Adam? Thinking the diavola pizza. Bit of spice to wake me up. Long day of explaining Excel shortcuts to people who seem determined to misunderstand them. You? Definitely pasta. Maybe the carbonara? I need something creamy and comforting. I swear, training people on cybersecurity feels like trying to teach a cat to do algebra. Aye, and the older they are, the worse it gets, doesn’t it? Remember that fella from finance last week? Tried to tell me the cloud was just…  floating . Floating computer storage! Honestly! Me mam used to say, "Some folks are just born with a closed mind, Brian." She were a wise woman, me mam. The cloud is  not  floating, Brian! We need to publish a flowchart explaining basic digital concepts. Seriously. Maybe incorporate some diagrams of weather patterns. Or, you know, we could just admit that some people aren't meant to be on computers. But then where would we be? Don't say that! I'd be out of a job quicker than you can say Microsoft. Tell you what, I’m proper peckish.

Aye, tell me about it. My lad, Liam, he’s permanently glued to TikTok. He’s trying to be a ‘content creator’ apparently. Wants to film himself unboxing… well, anything, really. The other day it was a box of novelty erasers. Erasers! He reckoned it'd go viral. Didn’t. Erasers? Bless him. You know, I was chatting to a student the other day, trying to guide her towards some academic databases, and she kept looking over my shoulder at her phone. I asked her if she was alright, and she said, "Sorry, just checking if my Insta story got any likes." It’s a constant battle, isn't it? Trying to engage people with actual, useful information. You blokes are telling me tales! You think  that’s  bad? Back in New Zealand, we were still arguing about whether email was a passing fad. Now? Now my grandchildren are live-streaming themselves eating breakfast! The world’s gone completely bonkers. It’s not just the platforms themselves, it's the sheer  volume . Trying to curate anything decent through the noise… impossible. It’s the speed, too, innit? Everything's gotta be instant. If you don't reply to someone within five minutes, you might as well be ignoring them completely. I had an email this morning, official university business, and I replied within the hour, thinking I was being rather prompt. Got a follow-up email asking if I'd seen the original! People are losing their patience. Used to be, a day or two's delay for a response was perfectly acceptable. Now it’s practically an insult. I mentioned to Susan in Archives the other day that I was considering setting up a University Library TikTok account. She practically choked on her tea. A TikTok account?! Good heavens! What would you put on it? Cats in the library? No, no, that’s actually quite good. We do have a rather charming tabby that wanders in now and then. Might be something. We’ve been considering a slightly more… conventional approach – maybe short videos highlighting rare book holdings, or showcasing archival materials. Attract some serious history buffs. History buffs on TikTok? I'm not sure about that, to be honest. Think they’re more interested in trending dances and filters. Though, maybe a time-lapse of someone carefully restoring a manuscript? That might be intriguing… if you sped it up.

…and that’s why I'm really concerned about this consultation process, David. It feels rushed. We're talking about something profoundly sensitive – end-of-life care – and slapping up leaflets in the local library just doesn’t cut it. We need proper, facilitated discussions, reaching beyond the immediate Tunbridge Wells demographic. Aye, well, Sarah, time's always tight, isn’t it? Board's breathing down my neck about progress on the business case. They want to see movement, particularly on securing funding. A rushed consultation process is better than no process at all, from their viewpoint, leastways. But I hear you. We need to show we’ve genuinely engaged. Perhaps another round of smaller group meetings, focused on specific concerns? That’s a start. And the rationale for Tunbridge Wells, David. I've been reviewing the demographic data again. Whilst the area is affluent, and there’s clearly a need, the concentration of aging population isn’t as high as, say, Kentish Town, or even parts of East Sussex. Why here, specifically? Was it purely about access to this particular plot of land? It was a confluence of factors, Sarah, truth be told. The land was surprisingly affordable for the size we need, thanks to that unfortunate planning permission debacle on the neighboring development - kept the prices down. And there’s a decent link to the M25, convenient for families traveling from London. Critically, we believe we can leverage the existing, though stretched, local health services. They've expressed willingness to cooperate, though the current situation…it's not ideal, is it? Long waiting lists, staffing shortages… Understatement of the year. I spoke with Dr. Evans at Pembury last week. The pressure on their palliative care unit is immense. And the hospice provision itself... fragmented. St. Luke's in Maidstone is struggling, and the Willow Foundation, bless them, are doing wonderful work but they're swamped. We  have  to ensure our new facility complements, rather than competes with, existing services. Have we explored a strong partnership with hospices further afield? We have, yes. Initial conversations with Hospice UK were encouraging. We’re exploring opportunities for sharing nurses, specialist training, even integrated patient referrals. It’s all part of proving we're taking a holistic, regional approach to end-of-life care. Speaking of nurses, the recruitment projections are bleak. We'll need to offer competitive salaries, on-site accommodation perhaps... and a supportive working environment, of course.

Oh, look at this one! Remember this, David? Ascot two years ago? The weather was atrocious, honestly. Drizzling all day, but we still made a right effort, didn't we? That hat I had...a bit much, perhaps. Right effort, indeed, Sarah. Cost us a fortune in taxis too, getting back in that rain. Though, I have to say, the atmosphere was cracking, even with the drizzle. You looked lovely, actually. Less the hat, maybe. Royal Ascot! Sounds fancy. Was that the one everyone was talking about because of Harry and Meghan seemingly not being there? That’s the one, Chloe. Bit of a hullabaloo about it. Anyway, look at this one of Amelia from primary school. Dreadful haircut, wasn't it? Poor little thing. She’s a woman now, practically. Can you believe she’s off to uni in September? Time flies, doesn't it? Feels like only yesterday we were dropping her off for her first day. Southport seems a world away now. Always dreamed of bringing her back up for a proper seaside holiday, we never quite managed it. Too much to juggle. Uni in Bristol, right? What's she studying? Archeology, can you imagine? Dust and old bones! She's fascinated by Roman history, that girl. Makes me wish I'd paid more attention in school. Speaking of which, did you manage to sort the new phone case, Chloe? Your old one was hanging on by a thread. Yeah, finally ordered one. They’re ridiculously overpriced, aren’t they? Found a decent deal on Amazon, though. This one’s got a pop socket built in – apparently, they’re all the rage. Do you ever feel like your phone is an extension of your arm, Mum? Don't I know it! Can’t go anywhere without it. Needed it most when I was on the ward, obviously. Long shifts, you know? Constant calls and updates. It’s a blessing and a curse, really. How's work going for you, David? Still battling with those quarterly reports? Battling is the right word. It's just endless paperwork, Sarah. Trying to get someone in to cover the workload properly. Young lads coming through these days… don't have the same work ethic. Though, there's a promising one interviewing for that assistant role next week. Seemed bright enough on the application. Good luck with that! Interviewing is terrifying. Remember that copywriting gig I applied for last month?

Honestly, Chloe, you’re tellin' me  The Ring  is scary? Like, a video tape? That's just…fashioned, innit? A right bit of clever marketing, more than frightening. Fashioned? Hannah, you’re being massively unfair! It's  atmospheric , alright? The whole unsettling feeling, the slow burn, the creepy kid... And the well! The well is properly creepy. You can’t deny that. Well, the well’s… damp. I’d be more worried about getting a chill than bein’ haunted. I mean, give me somethin' with actual monsters. Proper, teeth-grindin' ghouls. Like,  The Babadook . Now  that  was unsettling. The way it just… manifested from grief. Reet good! Okay,  The Babadook  was good, I’ll give you that. Properly intense. But there’s something classic about  The Ring . It relies on a simple premise—something nasty jumps out when you least expect it—and does it brilliantly. Remember Samara crawling out of the TV? That gives me the shivers even now. True, the crawling bit was a bit… unpleasant. But it’s predictable, isn’t it? You’re watchin' and you're thinkin', “Right, she’s gonna crawl outta the telly,” and then she does. It’s like, you’ve guessed the punchline. I like summat where you’re not entirely sure what's gonna happen. So, what, you want a film where  nothing  makes sense? Like, just random spooky stuff happening for two hours? That’s not scary, that’s just confusing! A good scary film needs rules, even if they’re a bit twisted.  The Ring  has rules. Don't watch the tape. Simple as. Aye, but that's the problem! It’s too obvious. I prefer summat a bit more subtle. I liked  Hereditary . That messed me up for days.
