The family dynamic, the weird rituals… It wasn't jump scares, it was just… deeply disturbing.  Hereditary  was bleak. Like, seriously bleak. That ending? Gut-wrenching. I'm still recovering from that one. Actually, talking about it now... maybe it  was  a bit much. I needed a pallet cleanser after that. Hence,  The Ring . You’re a soft touch, aren’t ya? Fancy needin' a pallet cleanser after a film. I’d have just gone straight back to watchin’ somethin’ with proper monsters. Maybe  The Descent . That’s a proper claustrophobic nightmare.  The Descent ? Nope. Absolutely not. Cave dwelling creatures? No thank you! I'm good. The dark is scary enough without adding terrifying, crawling things to the equation.

…and honestly, Grandad, I’m still not entirely convinced this iPad thing is worth it. It’s just… a bigger phone, isn’t it? I mean, you’ve got your email on the laptop, and I can print things out for you if you need. Don't you start, Emily. Bigger than a phone, yes, but so much more! Look, I'm reading the Wolverhampton Chronicle on it now. Perfectly clear, and I can zoom in. Try  that  on your phone. And Elsie showed me how to look up cricket scores. Cricket, Emily! Isn’t that something? Elsie is a marvel, I'll give you that. She can fix anything. But you're using it to read the news and look at cricket scores. That's lovely, but is it worth… well, you know how much it cost. We could have had a decent pizza, couldn't we? Or a new armchair cover. This one’s looking rather threadbare. A decent pizza  is  tempting. Though I had a rather nice one on Tuesday with Brenda. Pepperoni and mushrooms, you know. But the iPad... it keeps me connected. Your sister’s sent pictures of little Thomas, and I can see them instantly. He’s grown a good few inches since I last saw him. And booked that Airbnb in Cornwall for next summer, you know. For the anniversary. Cornwall? That's brilliant! Whereabouts? And you booked it… online? All by yourself? Grandad, I’m impressed. Honestly. Elsie helped a bit, of course. She showed me how to navigate the website. But I managed. It was quite straightforward, really. Much easier than trying to phone them and battling through the hold music. It’s all about these online things, isn't it? Even buying furniture. Mrs. Peterson down the street – she got a whole new dining set from that website, "Wayfair," I think it was. Said it arrived flat-packed and she put it all together herself! Bold woman, that one. Wayfair! Right. Well, be careful with flat-packed furniture. Remember Uncle George's disastrous attempt at building that bookshelf? Still have the spare screws rattling around in a drawer somewhere. You'll need some help with that, definitely. Wouldn't dream of it. I’m not as sprightly as I used to be. You’ll have to lend a hand, then. Although, you’re always so busy with your teaching. How was school today?

…and honestly, the sheer scale of it, Hamish, you wouldn’t believe. I mean, Angkor Wat is one thing, but Bagan? Thousands of temples, scattered across this plain, stretching out as far as the eye can see. Sunrise over those pagodas… pure magic, it was. Proper bucket list stuff. Aye, sounds incredible, Alistair. Though, you know me, give me a crumbling castle in the Highlands over a temple any day. Something with a bit o' history soaked into the stones, a feelin' o' the past swirling around ya. Did you manage to get any decent photos? You know I’m always keen to see the birds – any luck there? Loads, Hamish! Ridiculous amounts of photos. My phone’s practically weeping from the memory storage. And the birds! Good Lord, the colourful ones. Kingfishers, hornbills… things I'd only ever seen in National Geographic. I'll show you properly when I get back. But it wasn't  just  the visuals, you understand. It was the  feeling . The heat, the dust, the sheer age of everything... it was humbling. Reminded me a bit of that feeling you get standing at the top of Arthur's Seat on a misty morning, just... small. Aye, I ken that feeling well enough. Small and contemplative. Though Arthur's Seat's a wee bit less teeming with monks and Monsoons, eh? So, what were you reading over there? Did you get a chance to tackle that Murakami you mentioned? Actually, I did!  Kafka on the Shore . Brilliant, as always. That man has a way of weaving these incredibly strange, beautiful stories that just… stick with you. The symbolism, the recurring motifs… it's just phenomenal. I was reading it on a rickety bench overlooking a rice paddy, which, unsurprisingly, somehow made it even more evocative. Murakami, eh? I’ve been meaning to give him another go. Read  Norwegian Wood  years ago and thought it was a bit… melancholy, to be honest. A bit too steeped in that existential angst for my liking. I’m knee-deep in Iain Banks at the time. Finished  Consider Phlebas  last week. Genius, absolutely genius. The scale of his imagining, the sheer scope of the Culture universe… I find it endlessly fascinating. Banks is always solid, isn’t he? The man could build worlds.  Consider Phlebas  was one of his early ones, though, remember? A bit rougher around the edges than the later stuff, I think.

Honestly, Mum, I don’t know what to write about the ‘relevant experience’ section. It feels so…thin. I mean, the internships were good, the uni projects were brilliant, technically, but they don’t exactly translate to, you know, ‘managing a team’ or ‘client liaison.’ This job description is asking for stuff I haven't  actually  done yet. Right, love. Deep breaths. Let's have a look. . ‘Senior Architectural Designer - Miller & Blake.’ Not a junior role, alright. But listen, you’re only twenty-five. Expecting you to have already done everything on that list is a bit ridiculous, isn't it? But if I don't  show  them I can, they won't give me a chance. It's just the catch-22, isn’t it? I’ve got the design skills, definitely, I'm confident in my technical ability, but showing I can lead and handle clients… that’s what’s tripping me up. Should I just… embellish? Embellish? No, no, darling. Absolutely not. Don’t do that. It will come back and bite you. You're a smart girl, Elara, you've always been. Honesty’s the best policy, especially in architecture. Think about your uni projects, the final year one. Remember the collaborative element? Vaguely. It was a nightmare, honestly. Sarah kept wanting to do everything her own way… Well, someone had to mediate, didn't they? Someone had to organise the workload, make sure everyone was pulling their weight, keep things on track. That's a form of leadership, love. Tiny little bits of it, perhaps, but it still counts. You can frame it like that. 'Demonstrated leadership through effective project management during a collaborative university project, navigating diverse perspectives to achieve a cohesive final design.' See? Sounds a lot more impressive than just 'did a group project.' Okay, yeah, I can see that. The internship at Foster & Partners too; I was often the one explaining the project to visiting contractors. Not  liaison , exactly, but… communication, problem-solving… Exactly! And stop downplaying it. You grasped complex concepts quickly, didn’t you? So, you can explain them clearly to others. That’s a valuable skill, especially when dealing with clients. Remember old Mr. Henderson from the nursery when you were little? You’d explain everything to him about the different flowers with such enthusiasm. You were a natural communicator then, and you still are. You always did see the best in me, didn't you?

...and they’re putting up another one of them, aren't they? On the old Bailey field. Another block of flats. Can’t see no sense in it. Don’t rightly, Bernard. Don't rightly. Land's gettin’ scarcer by the day. Used to be fields 'round here forever. Remember the smell of the turnip crops, eh? Good honest smell, that. Not this…dust and concrete. Honestly, Arthur! You sound like you’re reminiscing about the Dark Ages. People need homes. And it's not like they can just build them in fields forever. I know, I know, Margaret. But there’s a difference between buildin’ houses and just… crammin’ ‘em in. No thought for green spaces, for community. Remember Mrs. Higgins’ garden? Such a lovely riot of colour she had. Gone now, that. Replaced with a car park. They should have kept some of that land for allotments. Proper allotments. People need to grow their own. Fresh veg, you know. Not this imported rubbish. Allotments require upkeep, Bernard. People are busy these days, mostly glued to those little screens. And look at the politics of it all. It's all about profit, isn’t it? Big developers making a fortune while ordinary folks struggle to find a decent place to live. You're right about that, Margaret. It’s all about the bottom line. Politicians, don't you know, they all promise the world, but once they’re in, it's developers and lobbyists they’re listenin’ to. Used to talk about public good, back in my day. Civil engineering used to be about buildin' things that benefited everyone… bridges, roads… structures meant to last. Now it’s just churnin’ out boxes. Remember that Austin Cambridge I had? '67 model. Marigold yellow. Proper reliable motor that was. Never let me down. They don't make 'em like that anymore, do they? These new cars… all plastic and electronics. Give me a good solid engine any day. You and your Austin, Bernard. Mine was a Morris Minor, grey, with a slightly wonky wing mirror. Used to take Doreen to the coast in it. Southwold, mostly. Lovely little beach, that. Mind you, parking was a nightmare. Speaking of Doreen… how's she doing? Still enjoying her flower arranging? She is, yes. Keeping herself busy. Gets a bit lonely, though. We all do, really. The kids are all off with their lives, of course.

…and honestly, the fire escape stairs are a nightmare. They’re getting used as a shortcut  all  the time, not just for emergencies. I caught Brenda from the pottery group using them to pop out for a fag break yesterday. I had to have a right word with her. Proper hassle, trying to enforce the rules. Heavens. You’d think people would have more sense. It’s dangerous, isn’t it? And gives us a right headache if there  is  a fire. Have you put up more signage? Those reflective ones? I think we really should. And maybe… are those little movement sensors we could put on them? A flashing light or something? Considered it, yeah. But sensors would mean wiring, and the electrician quoted me a fortune. Plus, the council would have a field day with it. Health and safety questions galore. We’re already swimming in paperwork. Tell you what though, the pigeon situation is getting ridiculous. They’re nesting in the fire escape alcoves now, dropping… well, you know. Oh, dear. The pigeons. It’s a constant battle, isn’t it? I read somewhere you can get those sonic things that deter them. Not sure how effective they are though. It’s just… everything seems to be a complication. We need to be generating more income, you know? The grant application was rejected, remember? Aye, a kick in the teeth, that was. I've been speaking with that new yoga instructor, Sarah. Seems keen on Thursdays and Saturdays. Could bring in a decent bit, could it? And I've had a couple of enquiries about the bigger room for workshops, craft fairs maybe. Costs are just sky-high though, aren’t they? Especially the energy bills. Sarah sounds promising. Get her down to chat properly. We need to be very clear about the rates, and what’s included. And about insurance. Regarding energy, I've been looking at those LED strip lights for the communal areas. A bit of an upfront cost, but the long-term savings… Good shout. I’ll get some quotes. Actually, speaking of costs… the armchairs in the reception area are looking a bit worse for wear. They're practically falling apart. We need some new ones. Something comfy, but durable. And not too... showy. It's a charity, after all. Absolutely. Practicality is key. Perhaps we could look at those refurbished office chairs?

Aye, I can imagine. Little ones are a handful. Glad you’re here though, love. Right, who wants seconds of this lamb stew? Gareth made a cracking job of it, didn't you, Gareth? Cheers, Rhys. Just a bit of slow cooking, you know? Low and slow really brings out the flavour. Braised it in ale, that's the secret. Proper local Herefordshire ale, too. Not the fizzy stuff, the dark stuff. Got a bit of rosemary in there, a touch of thyme…classic. It’s proper good, Gareth. Best stew I've had in ages. Better than Mum’s, even. Don’t tell Mum I said that! Oh, don't you be saying that, Ieuan! My stew’s legendary! Years of perfecting it, lad! You haven’t lived until you’ve had my mutton and leeks. This is lovely, Gareth, really it is, but it’s…different. It  is  lovely, Dai. Really. I appreciate the effort. Honestly, after days of shepherd’s pie and packed lunches, a proper stew is exactly what I needed. It reminds me of my gran’s cooking, actually. She used to make this incredible beef and ale stew, but with dumplings… fluffy, proper dumplings. Oh, dumplings! Now you're talking! My mam used to make the best dumplings. Light as a feather. Gareth, you’d be laughing if you tried! They're more of an art than a simple recipe. You’ve got to get the flour just right, and the fat…don’t you dare use margarine! Proper lard, or dripping. Lard and dripping, eh? Bit old-school for me, Bronwen. I use a bit of butter, keeps it a bit lighter. Though, I’d be lying if I said I wasn't tempted to give the dumplings a go... Just need to find a proper recipe. Any tips for a budding dumpling-maker? My Nan had a secret ingredient, apparently. A pinch of baking soda. Says it makes them rise higher. Worth a shot, eh? Mine swore by adding a spoonful of mashed potato to the dough. Made them extra fluffy, apparently. Although, I always thought she was just trying to get me to eat more potatoes! Maybe we should have a dumpling competition next time we all get together? Gareth versus Bronwen versus...Sarah? A grand idea! A proper Welsh dumpling-off! I’d put money on Bronwen winning, mind you. She’s got the experience.

Honestly, Liam, you wouldn’t  believe  the email I got today. From Professor Davies, no less! About the corpus. Apparently, some student has decided that ‘reeet’ is a dialectal variation of ‘right’ worthy of extensive linguistic analysis. Reet! Like, the word I've been using since I were a bairn! They want me to tag  every  instance in the entire Northern Voices collection. It’s gonna take weeks! Seriously? Reet? That’s brilliant, actually. Bit mad, but brilliant. They’re taking the whole thing pretty seriously then, aren't they? Serious doesn't even cover it. He wants a full justificatory essay explaining the socio-linguistic context. Can you imagine? I nearly spat out me tea! I told him, Professor, it's just how folk talk, especially when they're being a bit cheeky. It's not some rare, endangered linguistic phenomenon! Well, technically, it  is  geographically specific. See, that's why it’s scientifically interesting, isn't it? Bit of an academic overreach, maybe, but… you can’t fault their enthusiasm. Anyway, you’ll be a legend. The ‘Reet’ Guru, practically. Guru. Don't be daft. Still, it does ironically highlight how important this work is, even if they're approaching it from a completely bonkers angle. We need to book that holiday, though. I’m proper stressed thinking about it. Remember we talked about Italy? Italy, yeah! I was looking at flights last night. Rome or Florence? Florence seems a bit more manageable for a first trip, all those incredible art galleries... and the pasta, naturally. Florence sounds dead on. We could do a week, easy. Mum keeps texting asking when I'm coming back to see her, though. She's started making shepherd's pie again, and you know how that ends. I'll be round like a balloon! Classic Mum. I’m almost tempted to tell her we’re in Italy, just to pre-empt the shepherd's pie onslaught. Though she'd probably try to mail you a week's worth of portions. Don't even joke! Speaking of food, did you see that advert, the one for the new Pret coffee? The one with the ridiculously perfect-looking couple cycling through the Tuscan countryside? Oh, yeah! The one that makes you feel intensely inadequate about your own life choices. As if a £4.50 coffee is  actually  going to make you that happy. Exactly!

…and honestly, the waiting list for the physio is ridiculous. Six weeks! Six weeks before I can even get a proper assessment on this back. It’s just not sustainable, is it? I’m hobbling around the classroom, trying to keep up with fifteen teenagers who think standing still is a personal affront. Tell me about it. I were tryin’ to book a podiatrist appointment for Mrs. Peterson, bless ‘er, and they said January. January! She’s got those awful bunions, you know, properly swollen. Feels like dancin' on pins for ‘er. Hospitals are a right mess, innit? Absolutely. And all this triage nonsense. You feel like a number, rather than a person with a problem. It’s the same with my mum, poor thing. They’ve finally scheduled her a colonoscopy, but it's not till November. November! Cor, that's a long way off. Your mum's been worried stiff, 'asn't she? About that. She has. She refuses to talk about the worst-case scenarios, of course. Just keeps saying she’s “taking each day as it comes.” Which is admirable, I suppose, but it doesn't stop the anxiety practically radiating off her. And Dad, well, he’s just… quiet. Always quiet when things get tough. Keeps bottling everything up. It’s infuriating, you know? I know exactly what you mean. My Peter, ‘e's like that too. Stone-faced. Used to be worse when me mum passed. I cried buckets, properly fell to pieces. 'E just stood there, lookin' like he was expectin' a bus. Didn’t offer a single comforting word. Just said, “Right, what’s for tea?” Oh, that’s… a lot. My sister, Sarah, is the opposite. Utterly dramatic. Crying at the drop of a hat. It’s exhausting, but at least she's  feeling  something. It’s just… sometimes I wish Dad would just…  connect . It’s a man thing, I reckon. They think they're doin' you a favour by not showin' emotion. “Strong,” they think they're bein’. Poor things. Speaking of family, your Aunt Mabel's funeral, yeah? Are you alright? It's a bit of a squeeze for space there, apparently. It is. It’s proving a nightmare trying to coordinate everyone. So many distant relatives popping up out of the woodwork now she's gone. We’re trying to keep it simple, really. A small service, a gathering at the pub afterwards.

Speaker_1 :   Oh really? How's that going down with them?

…and then the badger just  stared  at me. Like I’d interrupted its tea party or something. Honestly, Freya, you wouldn’t believe the size of it. Proper chunky. You and badgers, Liam. It's always an adventure, isn't it? Were you using the telephoto lens this time? The one you were obsessed with getting last year? Of course! Wouldn't dream of going near a badger with anything less. Got some decent shots, actually. Not quite National Geographic quality, mind you, but… acceptable. See, here’s one. Judge for yourself. It’s… a badger. Doing badger things. Definitely acceptable. You've captured the intensity of the sniff, I'll give you that. Almost poetic. Poetic! I like that. You’re softening, my dear. You used to say my wildlife photography looked like a child had been let loose with a camera. That was before you mastered the badger. Besides, remember that entire roll dedicated to squirrels burying nuts? That was… a learning experience for both of us. Don't remind me. Right, back to the photos. These are from Hokkaido, remember? 2018. Pre-pandemic bliss. Look at this one – a field of lavender under Mount Yotei. Absolutely breathtaking. Oh my goodness! It’s stunning. I’d completely forgotten about that. We were so lucky to be there at just the right time. Remember trying to get the perfect angle for the sunrise shot? We nearly trampled a farmer’s rice paddies. Nearly! He did give us a right telling-off, didn’t he? Thankfully, his English was better than my Japanese. Though my apologetic bowing probably helped. He seemed to appreciate the effort, even if he didn’t appreciate our clumsy feet. It's amazing how much we crammed into that trip. The bamboo forest in Arashiyama, the geisha district in Kyoto… I want to go back so badly. I feel like I barely scratched the surface. Especially if I can impart some Japanese language skills to my class, you know? We absolutely  have  to go back. I've been looking at some new photography equipment – a lighter tripod, a better zoom lens... It's a justification, naturally. A purely photographic justification. Have you thought more about incorporating those Japanese folk tales into your lessons? The ones we read on the bullet train? I have! I’m actually planning a whole unit on them for next year. "Japanese Myths and Legends for Year 5."

…and then the sheep just  stared  at me. Like, full-on, judgmental staring. Honestly, I felt more judged by a flock of sheep than I ever have by my dissertation tutor. Ireland, eh? It's mental. Mental in the best way, though! Remember that beach in County Clare? The one where Liam tried to convince us to skinny dip? Liam and his 'what's the worst that could happen?' attitude. I’m still surprised we didn’t get arrested for indecent exposure. Security was surprisingly keen that night. Indecent exposure? Mate, that's fair dinkum! Sheilas wandering around in their togs, causing a stir. You wouldn't get away with it back home, would ya? Things are a bit more… restrained in Australia. Though, let me tell you, we've got some wild beaches ourselves. Untouched. Pristine. Nothing like what you'd see around here. Australia… you keep bringing it up. Tempting me, aren’t you, Dazza? Because honestly, the thought of escaping this drizzle and getting a bit of sun is  very  appealing. Although, I’d need to finish my dissertation first. Tell me about it. I'm currently covered in flour and existential dread, trying to perfect my babka recipe. It’s harder than it looks. Babka? You know, my Nan used to make an incredible honey cake, a  linga  cake. I’ve never quite managed to replicate it. It's a Birmingham thing, I think. Anyone ever had a proper Birmingham linga cake? It’s not exactly famous. Never heard of it, sorry. Though, speaking of Jewish food, I was flicking through Claudia Roden’s  The Book of Jewish Food  the other day. Absolutely fascinating. Did you know the different variations of cholent across different communities? Claudia Roden? Yeah, I’ve seen that book. My mum's got a copy. Actually, speaking of food, last week, some bloke came in to the café demanding a full English. Said he hadn't had a proper one since he left Perth. Nearly gave me a heart attack. Full English at 9am! Fair enough. You cater for everyone, don't you, Dazza? Speaking of catering, I was thinking… for my mum’s birthday, I could make her a Sephardic chicken tagine. She's always said it reminds her of a holiday she took in Morocco. Oh, that sounds amazing! I’ll bring the challah. Seriously though, the linga cake recipe…it’s locked in my brain somewhere, just teasing me.

…Honestly, Liam, it’s just  wild . The sheer volume of paperwork for even a relatively straightforward compliance audit is ridiculous. They’ve implemented this new AI system to sort it, but half the time it's flagging things it shouldn't and missing stuff it  really  needs to see. It’s like it's learned to recognise ‘compliance’ as a keyword and just throws everything with those words at me. Aye, sounds familiar. My supervisor’s got a similar bugbear with the algorithms he’s building for financial modelling. He swears they’re biased because of the training data, but demonstrating it is proving a right pain. Not entirely dissimilar to the frustration you’re describing, really. At least you've got peanuts for comfort. Want some? Cheers, yeah, I need them. Stress-eating, pure and simple. So, you were saying about the gaming, weren't you? You were rambling on about some new strategy title? Oh, right! Stellar Conquest. It’s proper brilliant. Think Total War but with space stations and alien empires. The learning curve is steep as anything, though. Took me about three weeks to avoid launching my entire fleet directly into an asteroid field. Have you ever dabbled in anything like that? I know you're more into, like, Stardew Valley. Stardew Valley is my zen garden, Liam. It’s the opposite of stressful. Smashy-smashy space wars? Not my cup of tea. I did briefly get into Cities: Skylines, though. Building my own little dystopian metropolis was oddly therapeutic. See, that  is  strategy! Just on a slightly different scale. Fancy a trip to Alton Towers soon? I’ve got a voucher for a couple of days. We could brave Nemesis. Alton Towers? Blast from the past! My Mam and Dad used to drag us there every summer. I remember being terrified of the Corkscrew. Nemesis... that looks intense. Are you sure I'd like it? I'm not exactly a thrill-seeker, you know. Come on, give it a go! It'll be good to get away from the spreadsheets and regulations. Think of it as a scientific experiment: measuring your physiological response to extreme velocity. You and your science! You’d probably be timing my heart rate the whole time. Right, alright, I'll consider it. Speaking of intense, have you seen Dune: Part Two yet? Absolutely! Saw it last week. Visually stunning, wasn’t it?

Absolutely! Rowing looks so graceful, doesn’t it? Until you’re flailing about like a landed cod. You're doing it at the university boathouse, aren't you? Are they any good at teaching beginners? Shipley Grammar wasn’t exactly known for its sporting prowess, you know. More about debating societies and Latin declensions.      They are, actually. They’ve got a fantastic introductory course. It’s just… the rhythm. The timing. My arms feel like they’re going to fall off, and I keep catching my oar on the others! There’s a chap there, David, who seems to have been rowing since he was a babe. He’s very patient, though. Makes me feel a bit less ridiculous. Have you ever tried anything like that?      Not rowing, no. I did dabble in kayaking for a while, years ago, when I lived near the canal. Bit of a disaster, actually. I kept capsizing. Ended up looking like a drowned rat more often than not. Needed proper gear, didn't I? You'll need to invest in some decent waterproofs for the rowing, I reckon. Cambridge weather's notoriously unpredictable. I’ve been looking for a new pair of wellies myself – the last ones split during that downpour last Tuesday. Honestly, it was biblical.      Already looking! I've been eyeing up those Rohan jackets from Mountain Warehouse. Seems sensible. Though I'm slightly terrified of looking like a walking tent.      Better a walking tent than a shivering wreck! Right, speaking of family, I had a wonderful time last week. Remember I was telling you about finding my cousin, Eleanor? The one my mother barely mentioned?      Yes! The one from before Mum and Dad got married? How was she?      Amazing. Utterly charming. We met up in Leeds, and it was like…reconnecting with a long-lost piece of myself, somehow. She’s a potter, lives in a beautiful little cottage full of clay and kilns. We spent the afternoon talking for hours. Turns out she knows practically nothing about our family history beyond what Mum vaguely told me, so it’s opened up a whole new avenue of inquiry. It feels rather exciting, actually.      That’s brilliant! I'm so pleased for you. It must be such a relief to finally meet her. It's something I wish I’d had the chance to do with Grandpa George before… well, before he passed.

Honestly, Dad, it’s not like I’m  trying  to be difficult. I just… I can’t remember anything these days! Like, I was just having to look up how to spell ‘definitely’! Definitely! It’s a word I use all the time. Aye, lass. It’s the phones, innit? That’s what's doin’ it. All that texting, all that swiping… it's wearing yer memory out. Back in my day, we had to remember phone numbers. Long numbers, they were! Fifteen digits sometimes. Now you're relying on that little gadget for everything. But it's useful! I mean, how else would I have remembered to look up Morse code yesterday? Mr. Davies gave us that weird extra credit challenge, you know, about signalling in an emergency. I had to Google it. Dot-dash, dash-dot… it's all a blur already. Morse code! Fancy that. Your grandad used to tinker with radios, he did. Knew all sorts. Remember him showing me how to send messages with a flashing light? Proper clever. Now, about these results... are you nervous about Thursday? Nervous doesn’t even begin to cover it. I’ve been picturing myself walking onto campus, everyone shouting, and the system being down. Like in those films. Ugh. And Mum’s already got all those celebratory balloons ordered! Well, let's just hope everything goes swimmingly. Right then, eh? We're nearly there. Hungry? Auntie Maureen's doing that proper Lancashire hotpot, she is. Lovely with a bit of bread and butter. Starving! And I’m hoping she’s got some decent veg. I tried to do a big shop yesterday. Managed the potatoes, peas, and carrots, but I completely forgot about onions and garlic. eBay’s a nightmare for getting decent garlic bulbs, isn’t it? Always end up with tiny things. Aye, eBay's gone downhill, hasn’t it? Remember when you could get a proper bargain? Now it's all inflated prices. Speaking of bargains, did you see them new trainers I got? Ridiculous price on Amazon! They were half price, honestly. Dad! We’re talking about vegetables and looming exam results, and you’re talking about trainers?! Honestly. I need to sort out my student finance application too. It's all so confusing. And I still haven’t figured out how to get to the university library from the halls without getting completely lost.

…and honestly, the whole thing crashed three times during the presentation. Three! Can you believe it? Professor Davies just gave me this look, like I was personally sabotaging his entire module. It was mortifying, man. Blimey, that’s rough, yeah? Proper nightmare scenario. Tech always chooses the worst time, innit? You alright though, man? You looked proper stressed earlier. Yeah, I’m mostly alright. Just… relieved it’s over. I used to be so confident with this stuff, you know? I built my own PC last summer, it ran like a dream. But then uni, and the clunky software they give us... It’s a joke. I swear they’re using Windows 98 in some of the labs. Tell me about it. The uni’s IT is atrocious. You remember Liam’s dissertation nearly getting wiped last year? That was closer than we wanna be, that one. So, you reckon you messed up the presentation ‘cause of the computer, or just nerves? Definitely the computer. I had the slides perfectly timed, transitions working… then suddenly, boom, spinning wheel of doom. Nerves didn't help, obviously, but it was the tech. What about you? How's that coding project coming along? Still wrestling with that JavaScript thing? Nah, man, I actually cracked it. Found a brilliant tutorial online, proper helped me understand the loops and stuff. Felt like a right genius when it finally worked. Seriously considering specialising in front-end design now. It's dead interesting. That’s wicked, yeah! Always knew you had an eye for detail. Makes sense. Listen, on a completely different note, remember we were talking about that trip to Japan? Japan! Yeah, man! Tokyo, right? Still dreaming about it. You’ve booked anything? I’ve started looking! Flights are insane, though. Proper eye-watering. But I’ve found a decent hostel in Shinjuku. Near the Robot Restaurant, apparently. Reckon we should go? Mid-July, maybe? Shinjuku’s the place to be, yeah? Robot Restaurant… yeah, we HAVE to go! My auntie Sharon in Kingston, she's been to Tokyo, she said it's completely mental. You gotta try the ramen, she said. Proper good. July sounds good, just as long as you can sort out the finances – this student life ain't easy, yeah? Tell me about it. I'm basically living on instant noodles and hope. But I can do it. I'll take on extra shifts at the pub, cut back on the Deliveroo...

Honestly, Mum, look at this! ANON’s grandson posted the  cutest  picture of him building a tower of biscuits. Right on Facebook. It’s just… delightful. Are you on Facebook yet? You really should be, you'd love seeing what the little ones are up to. Oh, Facebook. That’s a whole world I’m not sure I want to get tangled in, love. Seems a lot of fuss for not a lot of sense, doesn’t it? Anyway, ANON showed me some lovely photos from Buckfast Abbey the other day. Spectacular, wasn't it? That stained glass… quite breathtaking. You went there with David? Yes, with David. It was lovely, actually. Very peaceful. And you're right, the glass was incredible. We had a proper wander around. It’s funny, I was thinking afterwards, it's such a contrast to modern life, isn't it? All that quiet reflection. Though, apparently, even monasteries aren’t exempt from controversy these days. Did you hear about that David Cameron business? Tax avoidance… honestly! Cameron, eh? All this fiddling about! Back in my day, you paid your taxes and you didn't grumble. Simple as that. Though, I suppose things were simpler back then. Less… confusing. Remember when I had that hernia operation? 1972. Dreadful business. The anaesthetic wouldn't work properly! Kept having to top me up. It was like being tickled to death! Oh, Dad! Always a story with you. Anyway, back to holidays. I was just thinking – a cruise, perhaps? We talked about it before. Somewhere warm, somewhere sunny... perhaps the Mediterranean? A cruise sounds wonderful! But have you looked at the insurance, Mum? It’s a nightmare figuring it all out. Especially with your… well, you know. And Dad’s got to be covered too. It’s a real expense, isn’t it? Insurance! Another one of those modern inventions. Used to just get on with things! Though, I did get a nasty bout of pneumonia once… cost a fortune. Still, wouldn't trust those companies, would I? They're all after your money. Like the garage with my Morris Minor. Charged me a fortune to replace a spark plug, they did! Said it needed a whole new engine! They were having a laugh, they were. Always the Morris Minor, Dad. It's a legend, I suppose. Speaking of cars, how's yours doing, love? Still managing alright? It's being a right pain, actually.

…and honestly, Dad, the waffles were  insane . Proper Belgian waffles – not that American pancake-y stuff. They were so light, and the chocolate sauce… unreal. You’d have loved them, you really would. How was Mum's time relaxing? Did she get a chance to actually sit still for five minutes? Relaxing? Well, dear, there was a bit of a kerfuffle with the sat nav, wasn’t there, Margaret? It tried to take us through a farm track at one point. A muddy farm track! I told her we should’ve printed out the route, like I always say. Technology, eh? A blessing and a curse. Belgium was… alright. Bit expensive, innit? Don't you start, Arthur. You were the one who insisted on using the new app! And besides, the Belgian beer more than made up for it. Honestly, Arthur, you’d think you were driving through the Sahara desert the way you moaned about that little bit of mud. The markets were lovely, though. Such vibrant colours, and all those little cheeses… oh, the cheeses! And they were practically giving away the chocolate. Sounds like classic Dad and Mum. Honestly, tell me about the markets! I’m thinking of going to Bruges when I have a break from uni. Were they easy to navigate? I’m hopeless with maps, you know. I need that sat nav, even if it tries to send you down a cow path. Well, they were… busy. A lot of tourists. And that sat nav, Sarah. It kept recalculating. Blinkin’ thing kept saying, 'turn left in 50 metres’ then five seconds later, ‘recalculating!’ Nearly missed a vital turn into Ghent. Ended up circling around for ages. Proper stressful. I told Margaret, stick to a paper map. Safer. Arthur, breathe! It wasn't  that  bad. They had lovely stalls, selling everything from lace to handcrafted toys. I bought you a little beer cozy, Arthur. It’s in your bag. And the mussels were amazing! We had them steamed with white wine and garlic. Absolutely divine! Ooh, mussels! I love mussels. Did you cycle at all? I read they have brilliant cycle paths. We did a bit, dear. Margaret hired a bike, but Arthur refused. Said it was too dangerous. Dangerous? It’s the roads! Full of cyclists whizzing about. And lorries. Always lorries. I prefer the safety of the car. Though Margaret did enjoy hers. She did get lost a few times, mind you.

Honestly, I don’t know why I bother with this béchamel. It’s  always  either lumpy or gluey. It's just infuriating. You wouldn't think something so simple could be so difficult. Relax, love. It’ll be fine. You’re just stressing. A little bit of whisking, that's all it needs. Did you see that post Fiona put up on Facebook? About her little pottery class? Looks rather charming, doesn’t it? Fiona and charming. They’re rarely in the same postcode. It’s probably just a carefully curated image, the lighting’s all strategic and she’s got a filter on everything. Still, pottery…it does sound nice. A bit less stressful than this sauce, certainly. Well, she seems genuinely pleased. And it’s something she's enjoying. Look, here’s that celery, chopped as you requested. What about the chicken? Nearly ready for it to go in? Almost. Just needs a bit more thyme. Reminds me, I need to order some more flowers for the living room this week. The lilies are looking a bit peaky. Something bright, I think. Sunflowers, perhaps? Sunflowers are lovely. Though they do shed like mad. Remember last time? The whole room was covered in petals for days. You were muttering about Hoover bags for a week. I was, wasn’t I? It's a small price to pay for a bit of sunshine indoors. Speaking of scent, I’ve been trying that new Jo Malone perfume, the one Sarah recommended. 'Orange Blossom.' It's...odd. Odd how? I’ve been thinking about getting a new one myself. Always loved something woody, something a bit more masculine, y’know? It’s just…a bit  too  orange blossom-y, if that makes sense? Feels a bit…perfumey. Artificial, even. I’d almost prefer my old Chanel No. 5. It's classic for a reason. Everything's a bit bland these days. Back in Edinburgh, you'd find actual artisan perfumeries, people making scents with locally sourced ingredients. You could really  smell  the difference. My Auntie Moira – she was obsessed with sandalwood. Always smelled like a spice market. Your Auntie Moira was a character! I remember that. It was a sensory assault, entering her house. But lovely. So, you think the chicken’s almost ready then? Do you want me to start on the potatoes? Yes, the chicken’s good. And potatoes would be brilliant. Whilst you’re doing that, I'll light the fireplace.

…and honestly, the sheer scale of it all! Queensland, especially. I went to Brisbane for a conference back in ’98, and it felt…wild. Like a frontier town, but with shopping malls. Did you ever get out that far, Arthur? Frontier town, that’s a good way to put it, Margaret. No, I’ve never been further than New Zealand, actually. Business kept me tied up here. Though I did entertain the thought of relocating after leaving Thorne & Barlow. Somewhere warmer. Australia did seem… appealing. Bit daunting to start afresh at my age, mind you. Daunting or not, it’s lovely, isn't it? I spent a couple of years lecturing at James Cook University in Townsville. Lovely climate, lovely people. Though, I have to say, the heat in the middle of summer... you learn to live indoors. And the spiders! Goodness, the spiders! Oh, I can imagine! I read something awful about a huntsman spider just the other day. Nearly gave me a fright. Though, I must admit, the sunshine did my bones a world of good. All that rain in Bristol – it just seeps into you, doesn't it? Bristol. A fine city, although a bit damp for my tastes. I was always more of a Manchester man, myself. Proper grit about the place. You wouldn’t get the same ambition here, you know - those city boys in their sharp suits, you know the type? Always immaculately dressed. Never saw a badly dressed businessman in Manchester. It was like a civic duty! Oh, I know exactly what you mean! There’s a different sort of presentation up North. Less fuss, more substance. Down South, it’s all about appearances. Though, to be fair, some of those Southern types have excellent taste. My nephew used to work for Savile Row tailors, you know. He could tell you the precise thread count of a suit lining. Utterly fascinating. Tailoring! Now that’s a skill. Though, I always struggled to understand why men needed so many suits. I taught English to Japanese businessmen for a while, and their attention to detail in their clothing was simply astounding. Never a crease, never a misplaced button. Very different from the… well, let's just say some of my male students in Bristol. They’re a different breed down there, aren’t they? Always have been. Remember when they tried to close the mills in the 70s?

…and honestly, the comments section was just  relentless . People were saying her technique was all wrong, that she was clearly favouring one pupil over another, just a complete pile-on. It’s awful, isn’t it? The anonymity emboldens people to be… well, unpleasant. Absolutely dreadful, love. Dreadful. You know, I was reading about that online, actually. Something about the psychological effects of online criticism, the way it feeds into this… this mob mentality. Though I wasn’t reading a proper academic paper, more of a well-written article in the Telegraph. I do try to keep up, you know, as much as one can. It’s quite something though, isn't it? How readily people are seemingly willing to tear others down. It is. And it's especially bad when it's someone doing a decent job, trying to help. She’s a primary teacher, for crying out loud. She's not like, deliberately trying to be controversial. She just posted a video of a lesson, thinking people might find it useful. Yes, yes. A perfectly innocent gesture. Reminds me a little of my own… well, a few attempts at Youtube tutorials, ages ago. Remember those? Vaguely. The ones about obscure Shakespearean sonnets, right? Yes, well. They didn't exactly set the world alight, did they? Very niche audience, I suppose. But the few comments I  did  get... one person spent a full ten minutes dissecting my accent and insisting I wasn't pronouncing "though" correctly. It's rather disconcerting having complete strangers pick apart your delivery like that. I can imagine! Honestly, South of England accents can be a bit… distinctive, sometimes. No offense. None taken, love. Distinctive used to be considered refined, you know. Cambridge-educated and all that. But times change. It’s all about being relatable now, isn't it? Apparently, my speaking voice is about as relatable as a Regency novel. You're exaggerating! So, have you been listening to any good podcasts lately? I’ve been obsessed with “You’re Wrong About.” It's fascinating how they re-examine historical events and challenge established narratives. "You're Wrong About," you say? That sounds intriguing. I've been sticking to quite a lot of radio 4, actually. They have some lovely history programmes. Less interactive, of course, but surprisingly engrossing. I did try a few podcasts recently, though. There was one about… oh dear, what was it called… something about modern art?

…and then she just  insisted  she’d seen a badger in the playground! A badger, honestly. I had to gently explain that it was probably a very fluffy dog. Little things, you know? But it's endlessly entertaining. Anyway, back to this weekend. Pippy and Finn are buzzing about swimming, aren't they? Yes! Can we go to the big pool, Mummy? The one with the slide? Please, please,  please ? Slide! Slide! Wooosh! We’ll see, love. Depends if we can get a booking. It's always tricky at weekends. We’ll check online now, shall we? And then perhaps we can look at getting those Blue Peter badges sorted? I know Finn’s been collecting badges for ages. Blue Peter! Yes! I need a photo to send in! But what should I do? Well, we could do a silly one, you and Finn. Maybe pretending to be explorers? Or we could recreate a scene from your favourite book. Something creative! It has to be original, you know. They're quite strict. Explorers! Pirates! Arrr! Exactly! See? Finn's got it. Now, while we’re thinking about photos…did you both have a good time with Anon yesterday? She was so funny! She showed us her magic tricks! Magic! And…and…circus! The circus! That’s right! Anon told me all about her family’s travelling circus. Apparently, they’re in Cambridge next month. Fancy going to see them? A real circus? With lions and elephants? Well, probably not lions and elephants, love. But acrobats, clowns, and all sorts of amazing things! We'd need to check the dates and get tickets. It might be a bit pricey. Can I use my pocket money? Well, you'd need quite a lot of pocket money for that, wouldn't you? We'll see. We could always put a little bit aside each week. Honestly, you two have such a fantastic imagination. Anon really brings that out in you. Anon's good! She made me a castle! She’s wonderful, isn't she? She's quite a bit older than you both, isn’t she? I’d say… fifteen maybe? Fifteen! That's really old! Does she have a passport? We need passports for the circus, don't we? To go… really far away? Well, Cambridge isn’t  that  far away. And Anon's been travelling with her family for years. They’ve been all over Europe.

Right, so… you were saying about Liam? And this… this thing he's been going on about? It's just… mental, innit? It is a bit. He’s absolutely riddled with anxiety about it. He keeps saying it’s… massively affecting his confidence. Like, properly denting it. Aye, well, confidence’s a tricky thing, isn't it? Especially when you’re lads. But erectile dysfunction? At twenty-two? That’s… are you sure he ain’t just making a drama out of it? You know Liam. He's good at a bit o’ a performance. Honestly, I don't think he is. He's been really withdrawn. He keeps saying he feels… inadequate. He went to the GP. He did? Blimey. Right, that’s serious. What did the doctor say? Did they, like, run some tests or something? Yeah, loads. Blood tests, checked his hormone levels… apparently everything physically is fine. That's what's making it worse, you know? He feels even  more  to blame. The doctor thinks it's psychological, stress-related. Something to do with pressure. Pressure from who? From uni? His dad? He’s got a good relationship with his dad, hasn’t he? Partly university, yeah. He’s finding the engineering course really intense. But… I think it’s also… well, it's me, a bit. You? How so? Nowt wrong with you, love. You’re brilliant. Like, seriously, you're brilliant. Thanks. But he mentioned it. He said he feels pressured to… perform, I suppose. That I'm expecting something and he's worried he's failing. It's ridiculous, but he said it. Honestly, lads. They build these things up in their heads, don’t they? It’s like, a little hiccup and suddenly it’s the end of the world. Tell him to chill out. Tell him you don't expect him to be some superhero, you love him for who he is. You're supposed to enjoy it, right? It's not a test! I've  told  him. Repeatedly. But he just gets more down. He feels like he’s letting me down. He keeps saying, “What if this is just… me? What if I’m just like that?” It’s heartbreaking. Right, well, that’s a bit more than just needing to chill out, then, innit? Sounds like he needs to talk to someone proper. A therapist. Like, a good one.

…and honestly, the scales are just being spiteful tonight. I swear I weighed less this morning. It’s infuriating! I had a really good week, haven't gone over my syns once, and then… this. I know, right? Mine do that all the time. It's like they actively  want  you to feel bad. Did you have a good session at Slimming World then? Found any new Healthy Extra options? It was decent. They were raving about these new cucumber ribbons – apparently they're amazing in salads? But I felt like I was missing out on something substantial. I need something that  feels  filling, you know? I'm starving, honestly. What are you making? Smells amazing. Cauliflower cheese and roast veg. Trying to lean into the comfort food vibe but, you know, the Slimming World way. Frylight's been my best friend tonight. And I got a massive bag of double peas from Iceland – apparently, they’re really good value. Double peas! Brilliant! I’ll have to stock up. Need to get my freezer sorted. Right, speaking of value, did you see the Quorn range at Sainsbury's? They’ve really upped their game. The mince is actually decent now, not just grey mush. Oh, tell me about it! I bought some last week for chilli. Made with a really good spice mix, too - a bit of cumin, smoked paprika, that sort of thing. It was banging. Honestly, sometimes I forget it’s not meat. It's tempting to go full-on Quorn, though, because it's just so much easier than chopping all the veg. Exactly! But then you start thinking about all the artificial flavour, don’t you? It's a weird balance. I'm trying to be better about reading labels. I almost had a syn-heavy disaster last night with some instant noodles. Turns out the flavouring is packed with sugar. Ugh, the hidden sugar! It's everywhere. I'm obsessed with that zero-calorie syrup right now – the one that tastes like caramel. It's in my tea every morning. It's a borderline addiction. Don’t even start! I had a little sip of yours the other day... now I'm craaaaving it. Speaking of cravings, are we still on for Treat Day Saturday? I’m thinking a proper roast. Maybe with that Yorkshire pudding batter mix? Absolutely! Roast is a must. And yes, the batter mix is on the shopping list.

…and then Janice just said, "Well, obviously  you  haven’t managed your spreadsheets correctly, have you, Amelia?" Honestly! As if I’m responsible for the director’s inability to remember a budget meeting. It’s infuriating. Janice, eh? Still firing off pronouncements like she's the Queen of Excel? You know, sometimes I think she actually  enjoys  being difficult. You're probably right. Anyway, forget Janice. Let’s get back to something more pleasant. Greece? Still the frontrunner for the holiday? Definitely. Santorini’s looking good. I’ve been browsing those villa listings again. The one with the infinity pool overlooking the caldera… pricey, but… imagine. Proper sundowners. Oh, don't even tempt me, Mark. My bank account is already whimpering. But yes, Santorini would be amazing. A week of just… being. No spreadsheets, no Janice, just sunshine and feta. Precisely. Speaking of ‘being,’ I was thinking… what does your perfect day look like, realistically? No lavish holidays involved. Just… a Saturday. Hmm. A perfect Saturday… Okay, waking up without an alarm. Proper coffee, not the instant stuff. You making a full English. Then a long walk along the canal, maybe even spotting that kingfisher we saw last week. Afternoon spent in the garden, deadheading roses and reading. And then, a proper roast dinner, with Yorkshire puddings, obviously. Yorkshire puddings are non-negotiable. Mine would be slightly different, I think. Wake up, a bit of model railway tinkering, a proper pile of newspapers – not just the headlines on my phone – and a long lunch with you, maybe at that pub near the river. And a significant amount of time spent avoiding any and all domestic chores. Avoiding chores? That's optimistic! But I appreciate the sentiment. You know, I've been thinking about actually finishing that short story I started. The one about the lighthouse keeper. Really? That’s fantastic, love! You should. You're a good writer, you know. You just need to carve out the time. Have you considered setting a little challenge, like writing 500 words a day? I have, actually. But then I think about world events... Brexit’s still a mess, isn’t it? And the cost of living crisis… It all feels a bit overwhelming sometimes to be creative when the world’s a bit… wobbly. It is, but that's  why  you need to do it. Writing can be an escape, a way to process things, even if it's just a bit of fictional solace.

…and so, naturally, I suggested to young Thomas that a historical map of Roman Britain would be a far more stimulating gift than another drone. Honestly, the boy’s obsessed. Drones, eh? My lad's the same. Thinks he's gonna be a commercial filmmaker before he's even properly mastered long division. Though, I must say, the videos he makes are surprisingly decent. Better than anything I ever managed with my Super 8, that's for sure. You’ve really nailed down his interests, David. A Roman map... that's clever. It’s trying to steer him towards something… substantial. Though, I suspect his heart lies firmly amongst the whirring blades. Now, the birthday dinner itself... I was thinking we could do that rosemary lamb again? Penelope adored it last time. Lamb's always a winner. Right, sounds good. Though, mind you, I might pop down to the butcher’s on Saturday to see what he’s got. Preferably something that doesn't require me spending three hours wrestling with it in the kitchen. My back ain’t what it used to be, you know. Quite right. We wouldn't want a repeat of the… incident with the duck. Though, that  was  rather amusing, wasn't it? Amusing for  you , perhaps. I was covered in gravy for a week! Speaking of amusement, did you get a chance to look at this? . Sent it from our caravan trip last month. Bonnie Scotland, eh? Splendid shot! The light is remarkable. You’ve really captured the mood. Reminds me of Turner, actually. The way he used to depict the elements. Though, a bit bleak, perhaps? How was the midges? I dread to think. Don't even  mention  the midges. They were relentless. I swear they were plotting our downfall. I’ve still got the welts to prove it. But the scenery... the scenery was worth it. Makes you think, doesn't it? About…well, about independence. Oh, yes. A thorny issue. I was reading a rather insightful piece in  The Times  this morning, outlining the economic implications... it's a complex beast, isn’t it? Far more than the nationalist rhetoric would have you believe. Aye, it is. You know, driving through the Highlands, chatting to folk… you get a different sense of it. A lot of it’s about identity, belonging. It’s not all about spreadsheets and trade deals, is it?

Right, so, I've been thinking about this 'Draw a Chair for a Refugee' thing the school's doing. It's a really lovely idea, isn't it? Gets the children thinking about people who’ve lost everything. Look, Mummy! My chair! It's got squiggles! It’s absolutely wonderful, darling! Very artistic squiggles. What kind of chair did you imagine for someone who needs it, love? A comfy one! So they can sit when they’re tired. Exactly! A comfy one. That's a brilliant thought. And you, sweetheart? What's your chair like? It's a… a rocket chair! So they can fly away to a safe place! Pew pew! . A rocket chair! That's very imaginative, isn't it? Though, perhaps flying isn’t quite as practical as a regular chair, hmm? We need a chair they can  sit  in. Maybe it could be a rocket-shaped chair, though! I like that idea. Can it have sparkly bits? Of course, it can have sparkly bits! Everything needs sparkly bits! But thinking about proper chairs… there are so many different kinds aren't there? We’ve got the big armchair in the corner, the dining room chairs, the little garden chairs… What's a garden chair like? Well, they're often made of plastic or metal, and they often don't have arms. They’re good for sitting outside in the sunshine. Think about it – someone who's had to leave their home might need a chair that's easy to move, something simple and strong. Do you remember those folding chairs we had at Auntie Carol's barbeque last summer? Yeah! The clicky ones! They went  snap ! Exactly! Those are quite good for quickly setting up somewhere. It’s a bit like thinking about what we need at school, isn't it? They’re giving us a test on fractions next week. It's not as nice as drawing, is it? Tests are booooring! They can be, can’t they? But they help us learn! Just like thinking about what kind of chair a refugee needs helps us learn about how other people might be feeling. Miss Davies, she talked a lot about how some people have lost absolutely everything. Their homes, their families… sometimes even their favourite teddy bear. Teddy’s important! He is, darling! Very important. So, let's think. What makes a  good  chair? Reliable?

Honestly, I’m a bit gutted for Chloe and Liam. Did you see her Instagram story? The one with the… disappointing news? Yeah. Awful, innit? I texted her, just a short ‘thinking of you’ kind of thing. Didn’t want to intrude. Exactly. It's just… you could see it in her face, wasn’t there? That quiet devastation. They’d been trying for so long. It’s hard, really hard, watching friends go through that. And Liam’s completely plastered a brave face on, bless him. I’m expecting the floodgates to open any minute. Men are like that, aren't they? Stoic until they aren't. Remember Mark from the history department? Took ages for him to properly acknowledge how much it affected him when he and Sarah had their miscarriage. Kept pretending everything was fine. Absolutely. It's like they think showing emotion is a weakness. Though, I suppose, in some ways, bottling it up is probably worse. Anyway, it's reminded me how lucky we are, hasn't it? Just… stumbling into a blissful pregnancy. No struggles, no heartache. It feels almost… irresponsible, knowing others are desperately wanting what we have. Don’t say that, love. Being grateful and acknowledging the struggles of others isn’t irresponsible. It's human. And besides, we  have  worked hard, in a different way. Remember all those fertility apps and trying to nail the timing? Not exactly a breeze. You’re right. Silly me. It’s just... makes me want to bake them a cake or something. Do you think they'd want visitors? I’m a bit worried about being a walking, talking advertisement for baby bliss. I don’t think so, at least not immediately. Give them a week or so. Let them process. A text or a card is probably best for now. And maybe offer to do the grocery shopping or something practical when they’re ready. Something that doesn’t involve nattering about kicks and scans. Good point. Practical is always appreciated. Speaking of practical, how's the lesson plan for next week coming along? I'm still wrestling with how to incorporate the WWI poetry into the broader theme of societal trauma. It feels a bit… disjointed at the moment. I've been giving it some thought. I think you need to really focus on the shared human experience, not just the war itself. Use Owen's ‘Dulce et Decorum Est’ as a springboard.

…and honestly, the response was  wild . I mean, the university PR team were practically hyperventilating. "Dr. Davies, you can’t just say a Policeman is inherently comedic! It’s…insensitive!” Can you believe it? Insensitive? It’s observational humour, love. You pointed out that certain uniforms, the way they stand, the slightly stiff posture… it’s inherently ripe for a comedic riff. It’s not  about  the police, it's about the absurdity of authority figures in general. Honestly, I thought it was your cleverest bit in ages. That's the thing! I was just thinking aloud, really. I’d been reading about the history of slapstick, and the performative nature of roles - the bumbling constable, the fall into the watering trough… it just popped into my head during the lecture. Then, because I’m an idiot, I ad-libbed it. Now I’m facing disciplinary action. Disciplinary action? Seriously? For a bit of observational comedy? They’re taking you down for a joke about a waistcoat and a truncheon? The world’s gone mad. What are they saying, exactly? Something about fostering a "respectful learning environment" and "avoiding potentially offensive material." Apparently, a student emailed the Dean. Said it trivialised police work. Oh, for goodness sake. The student probably mistook it for a political statement. Honestly, some people treat everything as if it needs to have a capital-letter Meaning. Speaking of meaning, did you hear about old Mrs. Higgins down the road? She swore she saw a pixie last week. No way! Seriously? Mrs. Higgins, the woman who refuses to use a mobile phone because she believes it attracts goblins? The very same. Said it was dancing in her rhubarb patch. Bright green, tiny wings, the whole shebang. She’s convinced it’s a good omen, though. Says it means a bumper crop of gooseberries. It’s just the light reflecting off the dew, probably. Although, you know, it’s funny how much superstition clings on in places like this. People are so resistant to the rational. Which, ironically, makes them perfect subjects for my next paper. See? Everything connects, doesn't it? Policemen, pixies, newspaper headlines. Though, speaking of connections, I've been looking at flights to Greece. For the holiday, naturally. I was thinking Santorini. White-washed houses, stunning sunsets… Greece sounds  divine . It’s just… what will I be doing if I'm suspended for being "disrespectful" to the police?

Spinning wheel, eh? Modern technology. Always a faff, innit? Back in my day, if something didn't work, you smacked it a few times. Usually sorted it right out. Don’t tell your mother I said that. She’d have a stroke. Yeah, I know. She’d be on about the fragility of electronics. It’s just…it’s the only way I stay in touch with Chloe and the others. They're all on there constantly. Chloe's still in Australia, is she? Seems like only yesterday she was a little nipper. Time flies. Though, you know, I prefer a proper chat. Face-to-face. Less… flickering. I know, I know. We’re trying to get everyone together for Christmas. Mum's already badgering Aunt Susan about coming down from Norfolk. It’s proving tricky, though. She’s got that antique fair she goes to, you know. Says she’s found a right beauty of a Victorian teapot. Proper little collector’s item. Antiques, eh? Fancy that. I used to collect bottle caps when I was a lad. Found some right rarities, I did. Worth a fortune now, probably! Though I chucked 'em all out when I was fourteen, naturally. Naturally. Anyway, about moving…we have to start sorting stuff out. We’ve got to get a van, haven’t we? And find someone to drive it. Gary’s offering, but you know he’ll complain the entire time about the fuel costs. Gary’s always moaning. Sounds like a broken record. You should put him on mute. Like on them telly programmes. You could hire one of those removals companies. Proper sized van, insurance… less hassle. Though pricey, of course. That’s what I was thinking. I did a few quick quotes online. It’s not cheap, but less stressful. We need to do it before the Great Dorset Steam Fair, too. I was thinking of going. Mum’s not really up for it this year. Steam Fair! Now you're talking. Proper knees-up that is. Remember that engine, ‘Portwey’ I think it was called? Massive thing. Used to go every year with my grandad. Always smelled of coal and sausages. You  must  go. Fancy some proper fish and chips afterwards? We could go down to Lyme Regis. Sounds brilliant, Dad. Seriously. Fish and chips on the beach. That’s exactly what I need. Just need to sort this TikTok issue out first.

Honestly, David, I'm just reeling from that council meeting notice. The library? Demolished? It’s utterly barbaric. They’re talking about a "modern community hub," but it's all glossy brochures and empty promises, isn't it? Barbaric is a strong word, love, but I agree, it's short-sighted. Terribly short-sighted. The sandstone facade alone... it’s almost a protected feature, surely? Edinburgh’s got its principles, even if the council’s are a bit… flexible. Flexible is putting it mildly. They’re bulldozing history! Where are people supposed to go? It’s not just about borrowing books, you know. It's a social space, a quiet place, a place for children’s story time. I volunteered down there a couple of years ago, you remember? It was lovely. I do. You were brilliant with those kids. And you're right. This "community hub" they're proposing... it'll be all flats, won’t it? Luxury flats, no doubt. I read the planning documents online. They've deliberately obscured the affordable housing aspect. Clever, aren’t they? They’re morally bankrupt, that’s what they are. Speaking of reading, did you see that piece in  The Times  about preserving historic building facades? They were advocating for incentives, grants… something! We need to get that in front of the local paper, the  Gazette . Maybe if we generate enough noise… A good shout. I’ll have a look for it online. I’ve been meaning to switch over to the digital editions anyway. At least then you can search for phrases, rather than fumbling through pages. I was thinking about that all day, actually. Hunting for that article. You know, while we’re looking at the internet… I’ve been trying to get a feel for upholstery fabrics for the armchairs. The ones from M&S aren't quite… doing it for me. Too… beige. I was browsing that website, 'Fabric Direct,' and they have  so  many options. But the colours on screen are so different from what you get in reality. Typical. Technology promises clarity and delivers chaos. Which pattern were you leaning toward? Something with a bit of texture, I imagine? These armchairs are crying out for something other than the dated floral we have now. Exactly! I like the idea of a tweed, something earthy. But finding the  right  tweed… It’s madness. And coordinating the cushions! I've got a Pinterest board overflowing with possibilities.

Embarrassing? Nah, love. Everyone goes through a phase. My little sister was obsessed with Billie Eilish for like, six months. It's just good tunes! What's your favourite track at the moment? That's kind of you to say. Probably "Cruel Summer," I have to admit. It just...gets you. Though, I’m trying to branch out. I’ve really been meaning to explore some proper classical music again. Used to play the clarinet, you know, back in school. Clarinet, really, Dad? Never would have guessed! You strike me as more of a… jazz trumpet kind of guy. You’re pulling my leg, aren't you, Elara? No, clarinet. Awkward, screechy teenager learning scales. Not exactly the image, is it? Anyway, speaking of tuning into things, have you girls finally finished Christmas present hunting? It feels like we should be cracking the whip a bit. Don't you start, David! I’ve got practically everything sorted. Just need to find something suitable for your brother, the one who only ever wants gardening equipment. What  does  a man who already has a rototiller really need? Honestly, Gary, you sound exactly like Mum when she was Christmas shopping. I’ve got most of mine done – Liam’s getting a rather extravagant shaving kit, he's been moaning about his beard for ages. What about you, Elara? I’m struggling, actually. Mum's hard to buy for. She's got everything. I was thinking maybe a pottery class? She mentioned wanting to try it ages ago, but never has the time. Pottery is a brilliant idea! That’s genuine, thoughtful, and gets her out of the house. Much better than another scented candle. Absolutely. I reckon a voucher for a few sessions would be perfect. She can go when she likes. And I’ve been thinking about you, Richard. I saw a rather nice model railway set at Hobbycraft. Remember you were talking about wanting to get back into that? You remembered?! Good Lord, Gary, you shouldn't have! That's… incredibly thoughtful. I thought I'd forgotten all about that. It's been years. So, you’re down for the pottery class for Mum then? Shall I look into it tonight? There are loads of studios in Ashford, I can check reviews. Yes, please, Chloe. That would be amazing. I'm just so bad at sorting these things. Back to music, though – anyone watching 'The Masked Singer' this year?

Right then, Liam. Let’s have a proper look at this insurance. It's a right kerfuffle, isn’t it? More complicated than marking a year ten's simultaneous equations, I reckon. Aye, it is, Auntie Brenda. I don't get half of it. 'Excess'? What's an excess? Sounds like something you'd get at Christmas. No, pet, not Christmas excess. It’s the bit  you  pay if you have an accident. Let’s say you clip someone’s bumper - not your fault, mind, but it happens. The insurance company pays for the repairs, but you’d pay the 'excess' first. The higher the excess, the less you pay monthly for the insurance. Makes sense, doesn’t it? Sort of. So, like, if I chose a bigger excess, it’d be cheaper to insure the Clio? Exactly! But you’ve got to be able to  afford  that excess, Liam. Think about it realistically. If you were to have a bump, could you comfortably manage £500, or maybe even £750? That's the kind of excess we're talkin' about if you want a really bargain price. £750?! Blimey. I don’t think Mum and Dad would be too keen on that. They’d want me to be able to sort it out myself if something went wrong. Sensible thinking, love. Always sensible. Now, look at these quotes here. I’ve got a few from different companies. This one, Admiral, they’ve got a reasonable excess - £350 - and it's comin’ in at £875 a year. Not bad, eh? But then this Direct Line one, it's a bit pricier, £980, but the excess is only £200. Think about your driving, Liam. Are you confident? Conservative? Or are you a bit… enthusiastic? Enthusiastic, I suppose. I like to  know  I can get places quickly. I mean, I’m careful, but… I do enjoy a good drive. I was tryin' to overtake a tractor the other day, just before Market Weighton... A tractor, eh? Liam, dear, overtaking tractors isn't generally considered 'essential' driving. Look, enthusiasm is good, but we need to balance that with responsibility and, more importantly, with the insurance company's assessment of your risk. They’ll be lookin' at things like your driving history – which, thankfully, is currently spotless – and the type of car. A little Clio isn't quite as risky as, say, a sports car.

…and then the database just crashed. Completely. Right in the middle of a presentation to the board. Had to give them the ‘graceful’ apology, you know? Graceful when I felt anything  but . Sounds rough, Dad. Like, seriously rough. Did you, like, yell? Yell? No, Finn. I’m not  that  much of a savage. Though the urge was undeniably present. It’s more the… the constant pressure, you know? It builds. I've been thinking about those stress tests, the ones they do for bridges and buildings. Do they have similar ones for people? Like, a vibration test or something to see when you start to crack? There are ways to gauge it, love. Breathing exercises, mindfulness. Even just…taking a step back, acknowledging you're overwhelmed. Easier said than done, of course. But Fiona at the community centre runs a programme, really good for mums feeling stretched. Maybe… maybe something like that could help, even for you? Mindfulness? Fiona and calming breaths? I need a structural engineer, not a yoga instructor. And you know I'm not going to a community centre, Aoife. They'd think I'd lost the plot. You  would  be pretty weird going to that, Dad. Unless you were, like, doing research for a project or something. Speaking of weird, did you see that thing online about how many times the word "the" is searched on Google? It’s, like, insane. Insane is searching for the frequency of the word ‘the’ on Google. It’s a completely pointless exercise. Like trying to measure the windpipe of a swan. You won't learn anything useful. He’s got a point, Finn. Though, I do wonder… remember that vote? The one on the marriage equality thing? That was pretty insane. To think, just a few years ago… It's lovely, isn't it? That things have changed. It is. It absolutely is. It makes you proud to be Irish, even with the relentless grey skies and the ongoing database crashes. Though sometimes... sometimes I worry. The relentless grind. Um… should we, like, not talk anymore? I got a weird feeling. What's wrong, son? I think… I think we’re being recorded. It just feels…off. Don’t be silly, Finn. No one’s recording us. There’s no cameras, is there? Not even on the telly? Right, let's change the subject entirely. Anyone fancy a Chinese takeaway?

Now, Sarah, let's not re-fight that battle. It's been…well, it’s been a while. Besides, you know I’m going to disagree. We needed to take back control. Simple as that. Aye, but look at the mess it’s made, Dad! Prices are goin’ through the roof. Everything's gotten more complicated. Remember when a packet of digestives didn’t cost nearly a quid? Now, now, lasses, let’s not get bogged down in politics. We're supposed to be enjoying the scenery. Look at that view, though! Reminds me of Hawkshead, doesn't it, Michael? All those little stone cottages clinging to the hillside. Proper picture postcard stuff. It's alright, Gran. Seen better views. Like on YouTube, when Bear Grylls was in the Amazon. That was proper wild. Oh yes, Michael. Watching someone drink their own urine is  definitely  superior to the Lake District. Splendid. Don’t wind him up, Dad. He’s still stuck on Bear Grylls. Remember when he tried to build that "survival shelter" in the garden and Mum nearly had a heart attack? Oh, he did! Used all my prize-winning dahlias for camouflage. Nearly got arrested for it too. The police thought he was up to something dodgy! Well, he  was  covered in mud and wielding a rather alarming looking branch. Honestly. Still, at least he's got enthusiasm. Unlike some people who are fixated on…scales and kilograms. Seriously, Sarah, why are you still going on about that? Because it’s relevant! I’m trying to understand this conversion thing for my law conversion course. I need to be able to work out distances and weights in both miles and kilometers, grams and kilograms…it’s a nightmare! Why couldn't we just stick with what we knew? It's all so metric! That’s alright, love. It’s a bit confusing at first. Remember when everyone was panicking when we had to change from shillings and pence to decimal currency? Took a while to get used to that didn’t it? You had shillings? What were those? Were they like, old money? They were coins, son. Before the pound was split into 100 pence. A bit more complicated, frankly. Much like your fascination with parking regulations. You’ll be getting a ticket any day, parked like that. Speaking of complicated, did anyone see that documentary about nudist colonies the other week?

…and honestly, the whole “lab-grown meat” thing just feels a bit… dystopian, doesn't it? Like a scene straight out of Black Mirror. I get the arguments about reducing suffering, I really do. But the idea of eating something cultivated in a lab… it’s psychologically unsettling. I kind of see where you're coming from. There's definitely a ‘creepy’ factor. But think about it, Mia, the current factory farming system is  already  pretty dystopian. Those animals live horrible lives, crammed into tiny spaces. Shmeat – cultured meat, however you want to call it – could genuinely alleviate a lot of that suffering. And the environmental impact is supposedly way lower too, right? Less land use, fewer emissions… Don't get me started on the emissions! It's infuriating, the way people shrug off the environmental cost of meat. They're so obsessed with their Sunday roast, they don't even think about the Amazon burning to graze cattle. But you're right, Eleanor. The lab-grown stuff  could  be a game-changer. Though, I still have questions about the energy needed to run those labs. Is it  really  sustainable overall? That’s exactly it, isn’t it? It’s not a magic bullet. Plus, who controls the patents? Big corporations are already salivating at the prospect. Imagine, controlling the world's food supply… it's terrifying. It's a valid concern. But surely, there's room for smaller, more ethical organisations to get involved too? We need to push for that, demand transparency. It's not about blindly accepting it, it's about shaping it to be a positive thing. Actually, did you guys read that article about the vitamin B12 deficiency common in vegans and vegetarians? I'm thinking of starting a supplement. B12's a pain, yeah. I’ve been taking those chewable ones, they taste like blue raspberry. Not exactly gourmet, but it does the job. You know what's  really  messed up though? The amount of animals involved in testing vitamin supplements! Factory farms are awful enough, but then  that's  where they get the stuff to supposedly help  us  be healthy. It's circular oppression. God, you're right. The hypocrisy is astounding. It’s just… everything’s connected. It's like, we're so obsessed with our individual comfort and convenience, we completely ignore the suffering we cause. Remember that documentary we watched about the cull of deer in Scotland?

, Chloe , and Finn are sprawled on and around a sofa with mugs of hot chocolate.)     Finn:   …Nah, I'm tellin' ya, the algorithm's rigged. I swear, I looked at one pair of boots online – just  one  pair – and now my whole feed's nothing but brown leather footwear. It's mental.   Liam:   You're just advertising to yourself, Finny. Classic. Happens to everyone. I was lookin' at that new Spider-Man game, and bam, every ad's got the web-slingin' fella on it. It’s naff, innit?   Chloe:   You two and your internet obsession! Honestly, sometimes I think you live more online than you do in the real world. Remember, we're supposed to be relaxing, watching the Christmas telly.   Finn:   Relaxin’s hard when you're being bombarded with things you  might  want. It sparks the want, see? And then you feel guilty for wantin' it. It’s a vicious cycle.   Liam:   You’re giving it a bit too much thought, Fin. Just ignore the adds. Still, I was thinkin’ about that trip to Edinburgh we talked about. Should we start lookin’ at flights for, like, February, sometime?   Chloe:   Edinburgh sounds brilliant, Liam. Proper winter vibes. But February’s gonna be cold! And Finn’ll be moanin’ about his hands gettin’ numb.   Finn:   I’d be wearin’ gloves, Chloe! And a hat. Don't be underestimatin' me. You were buzzing about gettin' that application in for the warehouse job.   Finn:   Aye, well, I sent it off. Didn't hear back. Expected nothin', truth be told. It's always the same, isn't it? Send off a few apps, get rejected, and feel even worse than before. Feels like I'm just…fade into the background. Gets right under your skin, it does.   Chloe:   Don’t talk like that, Finn. You’re brilliant, you've got a first-class degree. Just takes time. Maybe that warehouse job wasn’t right for you anyway. What about something in…graphic design? You were always good at that on the computer.   Finn:   Aye, but I don’t have a portfolio, do I? No experience. It's a catch-22. No job, no experience. No experience, no job. …and honestly, the sheer volume of Renaissance art in Florence was just  overwhelming . Like, I knew it would be impressive, but I hadn’t realised how much there  is ! I spent three hours just wandering around the Uffizi, completely lost in Botticelli. It was brilliant, but my feet were killing me by the end. Three hours? You’re a trooper, Liv. I reckon I’d have lasted about an hour and a half before needing a lengthy gelato pitstop. Florence sounds dreamy though. I’m still green with envy about your trip.
