Remember how we were talking about wanting to do something properly cultural this year? Oh, absolutely! It felt a million miles away from Lincoln, that's for sure. And you? How was your weekend? Alumni Day stuff still going on? Yeah, it is. Bit of a blur, actually. Lots of, “Oh, remember that essay on Chomsky?” and, "Still fancy Professor Harding's lectures?". It’s mostly just nice to see faces, you know? I gave a little presentation this morning about our current phonological mapping project – felt a bit silly, if I’m honest. Like I was showing off. Showing off linguistic prowess? Highly unlikely! You're brilliant at it. It sounds fascinating, actually, the phonological mapping. I can never quite grasp the specifics, even though I'm technically in a similar field. All those IPA symbols...it's a whole language in itself. Tell me about it. It's a bit like trying to decode a secret code sometimes. But it's actually really useful for understanding language evolution and how different dialects interact. We’re looking at some fascinating regional variations, especially around the East Anglia area. Bit ironic, considering I’m about as far from East Anglian as you can get and still be in England. Right? And you’re a Buckinghamshire girl through and through! It’s hilarious. Speaking of family, my mum keeps asking when I'm going to visit. Apparently, Gran's been regaling everyone with tales of my 'adventures' in Italy. She added a dramatic flourish about me battling a rogue Vespa, which is a complete fabrication, by the way. Oh, Gran! Classic. Mine's been asking why I haven't brought her a lavender sachet from Provence. It's like they have a pre-programmed itinerary of things they expect you to buy when you travel. Did you manage to see anything besides art in Florence?

Honestly, Liam, I’m ready to chuck my laptop out the window. This Modernist Literature module is killing me. Killing me, I tell ya. Dramatic much, love? It's Thursday afternoon. You've got, what, three essays due before Christmas? Plenty of time. Three essays that all require me to dissect the innermost, existential dread of a bunch of blokes who clearly needed a good therapist, not a publishing deal! Woolf, Joyce, Faulkner… they all just make me feel even more confused about life. It’s stressing me out proper. And Professor Davies keeps saying "explore the subtext" - well, I’m exploring a subtext of misery, that’s what I’m doing! Right then, dramatic lass. You need a distraction. Remember you were saying last week you wanted to try that new massage place near university? ‘Zenith Relaxation’ or summat? Oh yeah! I do, don’t I. But… money, Liam. Money. Student loans are a cruel joke. Rich kid’s got a trust fund, I’m scrimping for beans on toast every other night. Alright, alright, don't start with the woes again. I can cover it this time. Consider it… research. Stress relief for a highly stressed student of Modernist Literature. You are a soft touch, ya know that? I’ll owe you one, big time. I’ll do all the washing up for a week. That’s a deal. Just promise you won’t start quoting Joyce whilst you’re scrubbing pots. Last time, it was something about a swan and a cabbage… still don’t know what that was about. Don't remind me! It was a genuine moment of existential crisis whilst unloading the dishwasher. Anyway, speaking of lectures, did you hear about Professor Miller’s lecture on Yeats next week? Apparently, he's bringing in a harpist! A harpist? Yeats and a harp? Sounds… elaborate. I thought he was more of a tweed jacket and a grumpy stare kind of guy. Exactly! It's completely bizarre. I’m half expecting a troupe of dancers to burst onto the stage. They say it’s meant to illustrate the Celtic influences in his poetry. So, you’re thinking of going? You've been ragging on the assignments, but you do seem to enjoy the weird and wonderful bits. I’ll definitely go! It’ll be better than staring at another page of 'Ulysses' trying to decipher what a 'Lollypop' is supposed to symbolize.

Bit bland, innit? Needs a bit more…oomph. Don’t know why I bothered, really. Just feels like I'm going through the motions these days. Don't be daft, Dad. It's lovely. You always make a good shepherd's pie. And you’re not just going through the motions - we’re here, aren't we? Having lunch with you. Mum's put a lot of effort in, too. Now, now, Geoffrey. Don’t be so hard on yourself. The kids are eating it, aren’t they? That's the test, isn't it? Besides, I added a decent amount of Worcestershire sauce this time, as you like. And it  is  a bit chilly out, so something hearty is exactly what's needed. Worcestershire sauce? Can’t say I noticed. Still… Did you see that on the news this morning? About Calais? The situation’s just…horrendous, isn’t it? Those poor people. All huddled together… Makes you feel a bit helpless, doesn't it? It does, Dad. Appalling. The conditions they’re living in… It’s just not right. I was talking to some of my students about it - they were really upset. It's hard to explain the complexities to them, though. It is. Trying to balance compassion with, you know, the realities of it all. Immigration is a tricky subject. I read an article that pointed to the human trafficking aspect as being even worse than initially thought. These people aren't just seeking a better life, some of them are being forced. Forced…that’s even more gut-wrenching. Politicians, always yapping about borders and controls… they don't see what’s really happening. Back in my day… well, things were different, obviously. But even then, there was a sense of… fairness, somehow. Things change, Dad. And it’s not always for the better. But we can still try to do something, even if it's just donating to a charity. Precisely. And speaking of doing things, Geoffrey, have you given any more thought to that pottery class? I mentioned it last week. It's at the community centre, Tuesdays and Thursdays. Pottery? I don’t know, Eleanor. Seems a bit…frivolous, doesn't it? When there's all this going on in the world. Dad, frivolous is the last thing it is! It's something  for you . Something to  do . You've been moping around for far too long since you retired.

…and that’s why I’m leaning towards a travertine look for the bathroom, Gareth. Real travertine, mind you. Not that faux stuff you see everywhere. It just has a certain gravitas, doesn't it? Something…lasting. Unlike what I've seen inflicted on people’s houses these past few years. Honestly, the avocado and harvest gold revival… chills me to the bone. Avocado? Good heavens, man! You’re bringing back terrible memories. My Auntie Bronwen, bless her cotton socks, practically wallpapered her kitchen in that colour in the seventies. The whole house smelled faintly of... well, avocado. Still, travertine, eh? Expensive business, that. Real stone, isn't it? Dreadfully. But worth it, I think. The current bathroom… well, it lacks character. All grey tiles and chrome fixtures. Perfectly functional, entirely soulless. You know, Penelope – my wife – she's decided we simply  must  have heated towel rails too. Says it's practically a necessity these days. Aye, heated towel rails. A sign of the times. My daughter, Rhiannon, she’s just refurbished her flat down in Cardiff. Had to have underfloor heating, she did. Said it was "essential for a modern living space." Young people, eh? A different breed. By the way, how are you getting on with finding a decent tiler? I'm still wrestling with that myself. Had one fall through last week, leaving me in a right pickle. Oh, the bane of modern existence, isn't it? Tradespeople. They seem to vanish into thin air. I went through at least four before I found someone who didn't look like they'd just walked off the street. Even then, his references were… sparse. Luckily, he seemed competent enough. You wouldn't believe the price they’re charging now, though. Used to be able to get a decent job done for a reasonable sum. Now? It's extortion. Tell me about it! I’ve been quoted more for a small patch of tiling than I earned in a week back in the eighties! It's all supply chain issues, they say. Or "inflation," as they call it. Sounds like an excuse to me. Speaking of price gouging, have you seen what they’re charging for kitchen worktops these days? Quartz is out of the question, apparently. Even laminate feels like a luxury. Don't even get me started on kitchens! Penelope is obsessed with a particular shade of grey – "Dove grey," she calls it.

…so I’m tellin’ ya, the vindaloo was practically devoid of heat. Practically an insult to the word ‘vindaloo’. I asked for extra chilli, specifically! And the boy, the waiter, he just shrugged. Said, “We’re mindin’ our spice levels these days, sir.” Mindin’ their spice levels! It’s curry, not chamomile tea! Seriously? That's mental. My mate Liam tried to eat a whole tin of metal once. Not on purpose, mind you. He was like, three, and thought it was some sort of shiny food. Honestly, children. Liam deserves a medal for surviving that, I suppose. Though, I still vividly recall the school nurse digging bits of tin out of his cheek. Anyway, speaking of inedible things, did little Finn have a particularly desperate attempt at chewing on the table leg again? Aye, the wee fella nearly gnawed a hole in it. Feckin' determined he is. It’s like he's developing a taste for wood. Think he'd go for metal next? That's brilliant! Like, a toddler super-powered to digest anything. Imagine! He could eat plastic, you know. Solve the pollution crisis. Let’s not encourage that. It would be a nightmare cleaning his teeth. I'm more worried about little Leo's birthday. Have we finalised anything regarding the park event? I’ve booked the picnic tables near the playground. Saturday week, right? Still got to sort the balloons and the cake. Think I’ll get Mrs. O'Malley to bake it – her Victoria sponge is legendary. And a few bottles of stout for the adults, naturally. Can we get one of those bouncy castles? They're wicked! A bouncy castle, really? After nearly dismantling the living room last time he had a ball? No. We are sticking to calmer activities. Storytelling, maybe some face painting. I reckon a bit of both wouldn't hurt. Gets the young'uns entertained. Still, need to grab some cash. Thought about using the night deposit box at the bank. Safer than leaving it lying around. A night deposit box? Like in the movies? With a secret code and a trench coat guy? Not quite that dramatic, lad. Just a steel box you slot the deposit into after hours. Less chance of getting robbed. Mind you, this history book I was marking for my niece… horrific. Absolutely horrific. All about the potato famine, presented like it was a nature documentary. No mention of landlords evicting people, just… potatoes failing.

She’s just a bit…stuffy, isn't she, Dad? Everyone else loved them. Liam said they were the best decorations in the whole class. Liam’s a good lad, your Liam. Always ‘ad a bit o’ a sense o’ fun, that one. Reminds me a bit o’ myself, when I were younger. Though, mind you, we didn't 'ave Halloween like this back then. Bonfires, that's what we had. Big ol' bonfires, and fireworks you could barely afford. Costessey weren't the same then, all these fancy decorations and trick-or-treatin'. Used to be just families gatherin’ 'round the fire. Simpler times, I reckon. Oh, don’t start with the ‘simpler times’ routine, Arthur. You'd miss all the telly! And I quite like the trick-or-treating, actually. Seeing all the little ones dressed up is rather charming. Though the amount of sweets they get is quite astounding. Do you think it’s too much, David? Well, Sarah, moderation is key, isn't it? But, I mean, it’s once a year. A bit of sugar isn’t going to do them any harm. My Year Sevens are all buzzing about it. Trying to convince them pumpkins are a vegetable, not a fruit, is a constant battle, though. It's amazing how resistant children are to basic botany! Botany! In my day, we were lucky to 'ave a decent pair o’ boots for walkin’ to school. Didn't need no fancy books about plants. Just needed to know which way to head to avoid the mud. You and your mud, Dad. Anyway, I’m going to the stables later. I'm helping clear out the hay for winter. Rosie’s got a bit of a cough, apparently. Oh, dear. Poor Rosie. Is she alright? You're a good girl, Lily, looking after her. Horses are beautiful creatures. Always reminds me of when I was a little girl, visiting my aunt in the countryside. She had a lovely Shire horse, Blossom. Gentle as anything. I used to sit on her back and feel like a queen. You always did have a flair for the dramatic, Sarah. Speaking of the countryside, I’m thinking of taking a weekend trip to the Cotswolds after term. Need a bit of a break. Somewhere peaceful. Are there any good walking trails around Costessey, Arthur? You always seemed to know all the best spots.

Honestly, Dad, this is mental! We’ve been crawling along for the last hour. I swear, half the cars on the road are heading to that Steam Fair too. I thought we left early enough. Early enough? You call this early? Back in my day, you’d be queuing up  miles  before this time. And parking was proper. Not like this… this chaos. Lot of people with cars these days, innit? No sense of proportion. Now, now, George. Don't start. It is busy, I’ll grant you, but we’ll get there. And at least we’ve got the Blue Badge, right? That’ll make a difference to parking. It’s vital you use that, George. Vital, is it? They don’t even  know  what a vital parking spot is anymore. They just fill ‘em with Range Rovers driven by folk who reckon they’re just too good to walk a few yards. Honestly, the nerve. Used to be, you’d have designated spots, clear signage… Grandpa, can we maybe focus on the traffic a bit? It’s a bit stressful trying to navigate this. Mum’s right, we need to use the Blue Badge properly. We practically had a screaming match with that woman in Dorchester last year who tried to tell you it wasn't valid. Remember? Don't remind me. Cheeky woman. Said I looked perfectly capable. Perfectly capable of what? Spending the rest of my life sitting on a park bench waiting for the pigeons to steal my chips? George, you were perfectly capable of arguing back, albeit loudly. Look, the important thing is getting Nana settled comfortably. How’s she holding up in the back? She's fine, Mum, sleeping mostly. I gave her a little blanket. Although, it did make me think… all this fuss about parking just highlights how difficult it is for older people. The council really needs to improve disabled access everywhere, not just at these big events. Council! Don’t even get me  started  on the council. They haven't touched the garden properly in years. Full of weeds. And that fence needs mending. Been asking for ages. George, the garden can wait. We’re talking about something more important. I was reading about that new assisted living complex they’re building in Harlow. Little bungalows with gardens, accessible bathrooms... really decent facilities. It’s on the council books, but privately managed.

…and honestly, the soil at the community garden they have near me is dreadful. Just compacted clay. You could bounce a tennis ball on it! It was a huge learning curve getting anything to grow. That’s why I really think we need to be realistic about ours. We can't just assume it'll be gorgeous, fertile loam, ready to go. Right, yeah. I was thinking about that, actually. It's on that old field behind the village hall, isn't it? Probably hasn’t been properly cultivated in years. Remember old Mr. Henderson used to say the field was always… well, a bit scrubby? Exactly! And scrubby suggests little to no nutrients. We'll need to do serious soil remediation. I’m already looking at some articles on no-dig gardening – layering cardboard and compost. Apparently, it's brilliant for improving the soil structure over time. No-dig, you say? That sounds… ambitious. I’m picturing mountains of cardboard. I mean, I’m happy to collect it from the shops, but… mountains. I'm more of a traditional digger, to be honest. My nan was a phenomenal gardener – grew the best tomatoes you’ve ever tasted – and she’d always say, "A good dig sets them up right, love." Your nan sounds wonderful. And I’m not suggesting we abandon digging entirely, just supplementing it. The no-dig method supposedly helps retain moisture too, which could be a bonus, considering we've had those dry spells lately. Anyway, we can talk about it more. What were you thinking about planting first, anyway? Apart from feeling overwhelmed by cardboard, of course. Well, I’ve always wanted to grow courgettes. Huge, prize-winning courgettes! My nan'd always tease me about them – said I’d never be able to grow anything bigger than my hand. And I’ve been thinking about some herbs – rosemary, thyme, maybe some lavender for attracting bees. Something a bit fragrant, you know? What about you? You seem very organised already. I’m thinking leafy greens – spinach, kale, some chard. Easy to grow, and you can harvest them throughout the season. And definitely tomatoes! We  have  to do tomatoes! I’ve been eyeing up some heirloom varieties. 'Black Krim' are supposed to be incredible. But we need to consider pest control. Slugs are going to be our nemesis, I reckon. Oh, slugs. Don’t even get me started.

…and then, like, she had the audacity to say  my  outfit was 'a bit much' for the bowling alley! A bit much! It were a sequin top and jeans, Jess! It's not like I turned up in a ballgown! Honestly, some folk, eh? Oh, honestly, Chloe! That’s classic Bethany. She’s always got something to say, hasn't she? Probably just jealous you looked better than her – she looked like she’d raided her mum’s wardrobe. Did you tell her what you thought? Nah, what's the point? She wouldn't listen. Just puffed up her chest and muttered something about “appropriate attire.” Honestly, I'm thinkin’ of just ditchin' her. She's a right drain, she is. Don't be dramatic. You’ve been friends since primary school. You can't just ditch her! But I get it. Sometimes people just become… draining. Is she still on about Mark, then? Still convinced he’s "the one" even though he's clearly playing games? Don’t even start on Mark. She’s been moanin’ about him for months. He's stringing her along, plain as day. She deserves summat better, she does. Like, a fella who actually remembers her birthday, instead of sending a single emoji on Instagram. Exactly! Honestly, someone needs to shake her. Right, listen, I’ve been thinking… Remember we talked about going to Brighton for a weekend? Brighton? Aye, I remember. Thought that were a bit… ambitious, didn't I? Trains are expensive, innit? I've been looking. We could get decent tickets if we book now, and there’s this really cute little Airbnb right by the beach. Saw pictures, it’s all colourful and quirky. Like, totally Instagrammable, you know? Instagrammable, you say? Now you're talkin’ me language. When were you thinkin'? Mid-June, I reckon. Gives us time to save a bit. I can cover the Airbnb, and you could look at train tickets? We could just… escape. No Bethany, no Mark drama, just us and the seaside. Aye, that sounds reet good. Properly reet good. I’ve been needin’ a getaway something fierce. Doncaster's gettin’ on my nerves lately, like it’s closin’ in on me. Tell me about it! Cambridge is lovely, but even that feels a bit… manic sometimes. A bit of sea air is exactly what we both need. So, you’re serious then? Brighton?

Seriously, Liam, you’ve been using that same character for  every  match! Ryu? Again? There’s like, a hundred others to choose from.   Liam:   Aye, but I’m reet good wi’ ‘im, aren’t I? Besides, he’s a classic. You Lancashire lasses wouldn't understand a good, solid character if it slapped ya ‘round the face.   Raj:   Come on, both of you lay off. Liam’s just enjoying a winning streak. And Chloe, you've been rocking that Dhalsim like you were born to spin fireballs. It's impressive, even if he  does  look like a praying mantis.   Ben:   So, anyone else notice how ridiculously overpowered Guile is in this patch? They seriously need to nerf that Flash Kick. It’s practically unblockable.   Liam:   True, true. Flash Kick’s a right pain. Makes ya wanna just throw the controller across the room. Remember that time I tried to pull off a Shoryuken and accidentally bounced off the wall? My mum nearly had a heart attack.   Chloe:   Oh god, yes! I saw the replay. It was spectacular. You looked like a startled meerkat. Barrow’s a bit dull, so at least we got some entertainment that day.   Raj:   Right? My nan nearly choked on her tea laughing. She doesn’t even  play  video games! Speaking of tea, has anyone tried that new bubble tea place near the library? It’s actually pretty decent. Not as good as what you get back home in Manila, mind, but still good.   Ben:   I went yesterday. The brown sugar milk tea was…fine. A bit too sweet for me, honestly. I prefer a good old-fashioned cuppa. You know, proper Yorkshire tea?   Liam:   Now you're talking! Proper Yorkshire tea, a Hobnob, and a bit of arcade action. That’s the life, that is. Remember that old arcade in Leeds city centre? 'The Zone'? It's gone now, sadly. All posh apartments now.   Chloe:   Everything's getting posh. My mate's dad is trying to convince her to go to Manchester Met instead of Lancaster. Says it’s “a more prestigious postcode.” Honestly, the obsession with where you go to uni is ridiculous.   Raj:   Tell me about it! My uncle keeps asking me what my "career prospects" are if I study film studies. Like I'm destined to become a binman, apparently. Honestly, sometimes I wish I’d taken accounting.   Ben:   At least film studies sounds interesting.

…and then Marjorie, bless her cotton socks, tries to make a quiche! A  quiche ! Honestly, dear, you wouldn’t believe it. The pastry was like cardboard, and the filling… well, let's just say Basil wouldn't touch it. He’s a fussy one, that Basil. Always has been. Sounds like a disaster. Poor Marjorie. She tries so hard, doesn’t she? You know, I actually watched that French film, ‘Amélie,’ the other night – the one you recommended? Oh, did you now? And? Tell me, did you enjoy it? I thought it was lovely, you know, a bit… whimsical. Proper charming. I did! It was gorgeous. The cinematography was incredible, all those colours, and the soundtrack was brilliant. It just felt so…optimistic, you know? Even when things were a bit sad, it was still uplifting. I kept thinking about Marjorie while I was watching it, actually. It reminded me of her, in a way. Always finding the little joys. That’s a lovely thing to say, dear. It is rather like Marjorie, isn’t it? Always looking on the bright side. Though, I do think she needs a good holiday. All that cooking and fretting over Basil… it takes its toll. Definitely. I was thinking, we should all plan something, you know? A weekend away? Maybe the Cotswolds? Somewhere nice and quiet. Oh, that would be  splendid ! A proper girls’ weekend. Away from Basil’s complaining and Marjorie’s culinary catastrophes. Whereabouts in the Cotswolds were you thinking? Bourton-on-the-Water is pretty, but a bit too touristy, wouldn't you say? I was thinking somewhere a little more…hidden. Stow-on-the-Wold maybe? There are some gorgeous little B&Bs and we could do some walking. I saw this one place online, 'The Old Manor House,' it looks really cosy. Stow-on-the-Wold… hmm, I haven't been there in years. That sounds rather nice, actually. Cosy is just what I need. My knees are playing up something terrible, you know. All this damp weather. We can book somewhere with a comfy armchair for you then! Speaking of films, have you seen anything good recently besides ‘Amélie’? I'm in the mood for something a bit…thrilling. Thrilling, you say? Oh, I saw that new Hitchcock one, the remake. It was alright, dear. Not as good as the original, mind you. They never are. All a lot of shouting and not much substance, if you ask me.

…and honestly, the feedback was so vague. "Needs more dynamism." Dynamism! What does that even  mean  in the context of transcribing historical dialect recordings? It’s not like I'm presenting a children's puppet show, is it? Oh, bless you, Liv. Sounds like a classic case of someone throwing around buzzwords to sound clever. Honestly, institutional bureaucracy, innit? You're doing brilliant work, proper meticulous, and they’re worried about “dynamism.” Did you at least mention the actual, concrete work you're doing? The impact on understanding regional variations? I did, loads! I highlighted how the recordings are providing invaluable data for sociolinguistics, how we're uncovering shifts in pronunciation over decades… they just glazed over it. It’s frustrating. This interview was for a promotion, you know, Senior Coordinator. I really wanted it. Well, you  should  get it. Seriously. It's ridiculous. Right, let’s talk about something less stressful. Did you see  The Undateables  last night? The guy who only dated women who liked competitive birdwatching? No! I missed it. Was it… intense? Intense is an understatement. Honestly, the lengths some people go to for a connection. It’s both hilarious and heartbreaking. It makes you wonder, doesn’t it? Like, are we all slightly mad in our own way when it comes to romance? Absolutely. Remember that disastrous blind date I had with Gareth? The one who kept referring to himself in the third person? Oh god, yeah! “Gareth is feeling very passionate about this Thai green curry.” I still cringe thinking about it. Speaking of cringe, I’ve been trying to get rid of this pile of magazines. Mostly glossy travel bits and beauty spreads. Utterly pointless, most of it. You want anything? There's a slightly dog-eared copy of  Country Life  in there somewhere...  Country Life ? Tempting, but I think I’ll pass. I'm trying to declutter a bit myself. I need to have a proper sort through my DVDs, there's a ridiculous amount of Criterion Collection films in there. I feel like a pretentious student again. Criterion...collections…validate… Didn’t hear you there, Mum. You alright? You’ve been awfully quiet. …Quiet…good…less…noise… Has she been sleeping alright? She seemed a bit… distant, earlier. She does have her good days and her difficult days, Liv. It's... complicated. We've got her spa appointment next week, remember? I've booked the aromatherapy massage.

Honestly, this washing machine is drivin’ me mental. I swear it's got a mind of its own. It’ll spin like a demon for a full fifteen minutes then just… stop. Right in the middle of the rinse cycle! It’s cost me a fortune in electric and ruined a fair few of me favourite jumpers, it has. Dramatic as always, Liv. What happened this time? Did it decide to stage a revolt against the tumble dryer again? Aye, something like that! These towels were practically sopping. I had to wring 'em out meself. You wouldn’t believe it. And it was a full load! I needed those towels for after me yoga this mornin’. Talk about startin' the day off wrong. Think we should just bite the bullet and get a new one, eh? Well, let's not rush into that. Cambridge appliance repair isn't exactly cheap, is it? We should get it checked out first. I’ll look online and see if there’s a reputable place nearby. Maybe it's just a blockage somewhere. Remember what happened with your nan’s washing machine? All it needed was a stray sock. Aye, I remember. Found a whole football team of lonely socks in there! Nan woulda had a fit. Right, speaking of things needing fixing... are we still on for Sunday lunch at Mam's? She's been panicking about it all week, says she's finally mastered that beef wellington she's been trying to perfect for years. Definitely. I’ll ring Dad and confirm, just to be sure. He’s probably already planned his reclining chair deployment strategy for the afternoon. Anything special you’re bringing? Just me wit and charm, love. Though I might whip up that rhubarb crumble she likes. Using the stuff I got from that farmers market on Saturday. It was gorgeous. Reminded me of being a kid, picking rhubarb with Gran in the garden. Proper taste of home, that rhubarb. Sounds lovely. Although, I'm still slightly traumatised by the attempt at a Yorkshire pudding last Christmas. Remember that? It resembled more of a volcanic eruption than a pudding. Oh God, don't remind me! Mam's Yorkshire puddings are… an experience. We should just stick to crumble. What are you working on at the moment anyway? Looks intense. Still wrestling with that particle physics equation? Pretty much. It's a nightmare, honestly.

…and honestly, the sheer scale of it is staggering, isn’t it? Millions of cars affected worldwide. Saying it’s a scandal feels almost… understated. It's not just a faulty part, it's deliberate deception. I mean, rigging emissions tests? Seriously? Dreadful, isn't it? Absolutely dreadful. It's...remarkable, really, the lengths people will go to. Though, I suppose when you’ve got shareholders demanding ever-increasing profits, morality tends to go out the window. It’s a bit like my own situation, in a way… chasing a goal, feeling pressure… then falling short. Falling short, Maureen? Compared to Volkswagen deliberately cheating environmental regulations? That's a bit of a leap, isn't it? It's about money, pure and simple. Greed. They figured they could get away with it. I know, I know, Brian. It’s ridiculous to compare, of course. But... there’s a sort of echo there, isn't there? That feeling of striving, and then… not quite reaching it. So many years dedicated to teaching, feeling secure...and then the changes, the cuts… and suddenly you're just… adrift. It’s unsettling. I get what you mean, Maureen. That feeling of the rug being pulled out from under you. Being blindsided. It’s tough. But you've got Hunsonby now, which is wonderful. It’s a massive change from Dublin, but it’s so beautiful here. And the houses are affordable – relatively speaking! I was looking at some property in the Cotswolds for a friend, and it’s terrifying. You could pay more for a shed than you could for a perfectly decent house here. Right, shed prices in the south are ridiculous. London is an absolute joke. I used to travel down for work, did a bit in Manchester first, then onto London. You could pay a fortune for a cramped flat and still feel like you were living in a cupboard. Remember the reports, Sarah? About the average house price being…what was it? Seven times average salary? It was closer to twelve, Brian, last I saw. Twelve times. It's obscene. People working themselves into the ground just to get a foothold on the property ladder. And for what? So they can spend their weekends maintaining a garden and attending PTA meetings? Exactly! And the commute! Don’t even get me started on the commute. Honestly, you’re better off staying put in Hunsonby.

…and that’s just it, isn’t it, Arthur? Absolute cheek, the lot of 'em. Coming down here, these developers, waving around planning permission like it’s confetti, and thinking they can just bulldoze over what we've got. My father, bless 'im, worked on the drainage system for this whole area. Knew every ditch and culvert like the back of his hand. They wouldn’t know a drainage pipe if it slapped 'em in the face! Aye, Bernard. Cheeky, that’s what they are. Remember old Mr. Hemsley? On Mill Road? They tried it on with 'im, didn’t they? Wanted to buy 'is cottage to put up one of them… boxes. Modern boxes, they called 'em. No character at all. Honestly! It’s just happening everywhere, isn't it? Harrow’s got its share, though, you know. Used to be proper little streets, now they're building these monstrous estates with names like 'The Crest' and 'Oakwood Heights'. Sounds grand, but it’s all identical boxes. No charm. Charm’s the word, Margaret. Charm! And it's not just the houses, is it? It’s the disruption. The traffic, the noise... I had a bloke round the other day, selling solar panels, absolutely couldn’t hold a conversation for the racket they were making on the site down the road. My pension barely covers the increased council tax, you know. Used to be able to put a bit aside. Not anymore, not with all this. Pension, eh? Mine's a pittance. Wouldn't buy you a decent cup of tea these days. Don’t know why they bother, really. Should just give everyone a proper living wage, ought to. Don't get me started on pensions, Arthur. It's all so complicated. I tried to sort mine out a few years ago… ended up in a right state. I even booked a computer course, you know. Thought I'd learn to manage it online. Disastrous. Utterly disastrous. Oh, computers... Don't you start, Margaret. I practically designed bridges with slide rules and compasses! This newfangled technology… it’s a right nonsense. I had to call young Simon round last week just to change the font size on my email. Shameful, really. Simon’s a good lad. Helps me with the telly sometimes. Can’t understand half of what he says, mind you. All that… what do they call it?

Evolution. Seriously? It’s the biggest topic ever. Where do you even  start  explaining it all? You start with, like, Darwin. Obviously. Natural Selection. Survival of the fittest. It’s not rocket science, Liam. Easy for you to say, Ben. You practically  are  Darwin. You're always rambling about it. But really explaining it, making it accessible... that’s the hard bit. My mum tried to explain it to me last night, and she ended up confusing Lamarck with a llama. She genuinely thought he believed giraffes got long necks because they stretched for leaves. Your mum’s a legend! I can just imagine. Lamarck's idea was inheritance of acquired characteristics, not giraffe stretching. Although, funnily enough, the giraffe thing  did  influence early evolutionary thought. It’s all a bit messy, innit? Yeah, it’s complicated even when you know what you’re talking about. I’m doing mine on the impact of genetic mutation on island populations. Got to explain bottlenecks and founder effects... and why the Galapagos finches are so iconic. See! That’s way more specific, Dan. You've got a niche. I'm thinking about trying to incorporate the whole CRISPR thing, gene editing. That's a bit mind-blowing, isn’t it? Playing God like that? It is, but it’s already happening. It’s not like it’s some futuristic sci-fi. What’s more worrying, honestly, is how easily misinformation spreads about all this stuff online. Remember that video that went viral claiming evolution was disproven? Ugh, yeah. And the comments sections were a nightmare. Loads of people arguing about God versus science. Like, can't they just... coexist? That's the thing, isn’t it? People get so tribal about it. It's not necessarily about believing  in  evolution, it’s about understanding the scientific process. And the evidence is overwhelming. Agreed. It also feels tied to this whole... well, everything else that’s messed up online. The sexism, the racism… It’s like, some people are desperate to find reasons to justify their prejudices, and they latch onto anything that sounds remotely scientific, even if it's complete rubbish. Exactly! You see it with the whole “men are genetically superior” nonsense. It's a total misinterpretation of studies and pulls on all sorts of evolutionary psychology stuff in a really dodgy way. My cousin Sarah keeps posting stuff like that. All about "biological differences" and why women shouldn't be in leadership roles.

That's dreadful, Sarah. Really dreadful. You know, I read something about MRSA in hospitals. It’s supposed to be more common than they let on. Are you absolutely sure you haven’t picked anything up from there? Well, I’ve been cleaning down there, you know, at the hospital. Doing a good job, I reckon. They appreciate it. But you do see things, don't you? Things you don’t need to see. And a lot of people coming and going…germs everywhere, probably. Germs! When I was a girl, we didn't  have  germs! A good scrub with carbolic soap and you were right as rain. Though, I must say, carbolic tasted awful. Your mother used to make us gargle with it for sore throats. Makes you shiver just thinking about it. Remember the war years, Arthur? We made do! Aye, remember well, Elsie. Ration books and everything. Used to bring me tea up to the lorry, bless her. Now, this MRSA you’re talking about...is that like the influenza that swept through Thorney? Not exactly, Arthur. It’s a type of bacteria. More resistant to antibiotics, sadly. Sarah, are you taking your tablets regularly? The ones Dr. Patel prescribed? Yes, of course. All of them. It’s just… they don’t seem to be doing anything. Maybe I should try that acupuncture Mrs. Higgins was talking about? She swears by it for her arthritis. Acupuncture! That’s needles, isn't it? I don’t like the idea of needles. Though, I did read that some people find it helps with their aches and pains. Elsie, remember that time you tried that herbal remedy for your rheumatism? Oh, don’t remind me! Turned me hair green, that stuff did! Like a leprechaun. Remember, Sarah? We laughed so much. It’s good to hear some laughter. Seriously though, Sarah, you need to push the hospital for further investigation. Maybe get a second opinion. Don’t just accept “minor infection.” You’re not your usual self. How’s little Thomas doing with his rugby? He’s brilliant! Just scored a try in his match on Saturday. He's got a trial for the county team next month, which is just…amazing. I’m so proud of him. It’s something to focus on, I suppose, aside from feeling like death. Rugby! My grandson, Derek, plays. Always coming home bruised and battered, that boy.

Are they… happy on the ships, Mummy? Oh, sweetheart? No, darling, they absolutely weren't happy. Imagine being forced away from your family, crammed into a tiny, dark space with lots of other people, and not knowing where you’re going or what’s going to happen to you. It was incredibly frightening and awful. But why did they  do  it, Mummy? Why did people take other people? That’s a really good question, Ethan. It was because some people wanted to get rich very quickly. They wanted to grow things like sugar and cotton, and they didn’t want to pay workers a fair wage. So they thought they could force people to work for them for free. It's a really unfair and awful way to get money, isn't it? Maisie: Free? Like when Grandma lets me have an extra biscuit? Sort of, but it’s not the same at all, love. Grandma gives you an extra biscuit because she’s kind and loves you. This was about being mean and taking away people’s freedom. They weren’t just missing biscuits, Maisie; they were missing their homes, their families, their lives. Ethan: Did they fight back? Yes, lots of people did. There were rebellions on the ships and on the plantations. And then, many, many years later, people in the countries using slave labour started to say it wasn't right and fought to end it. It took a  long  time though. It's a bit like… remember when we were reading about World War Two? Maisie: With the soldiers and the tanks? Exactly. It was a very long and difficult time of fighting, of people trying to be free. Slavery was like a long, terrible war against people's freedom, but it was happening all the time, not just on battlefields. Ethan: So, it was like… a war  and  taking people prisoner? That's a really good way to put it, Ethan. It was a war against people  being  people. Everyone deserves to be free and treated with respect. It's something we have to remember, isn’t it? Maisie: I drew a boat! And lots of people waving! That’s lovely, sweetheart. They’re all waving goodbye to the bad people and sailing to safety, are they? Maisie: Yes! They’re going to a happy place! That’s a wonderful picture, darling. And that’s exactly what we should all be hoping for – a world where everyone is safe, happy, and free.

Right, well, you've said that for the last three series, Dad. It's a critically acclaimed show, you know. There’s obviously something there beyond just… shouting. The power dynamics, the manipulation… it’s fascinating. A bit bleak, mind, but fascinating. Bleak is putting it mildly, love. It’s like watching a whole family of vipers circling each other. But I see your point, Sarah. There’s a bit of drama in it. Reminds me of Brenda and Maureen down the street, always bickering over whose roses were bigger. Honestly, I'm more into  The Bear . It’s just… so stressful! But in a good, gripping way. And the food scenes are amazing. I've been trying to recreate that beef short rib dish. It’s been a disaster so far. My flatmate keeps complaining about the smell.  The Bear  is good. Proper gritty. Makes you appreciate the simple things, doesn't it? Like a perfectly cooked Sunday roast. Speaking of which, Mum, any chance you’re doing one next week? Always, darling. Always. Though the roast hasn’t been quite the same since Buster decided the gravy boat was his personal water bowl. You remember him trying to drink out of it last Christmas? Ruined the whole thing! Oh, that dog! He was a menace, that one. Loved a bit of mischief, did Buster. Still got a picture of him somewhere, with gravy all over his face. Should get it framed, should we? Sounds brilliant! Post it on Insta, Uncle George. People would love that. Though, knowing Buster, he'd probably look like he'd  caused  the gravy disaster on purpose. He certainly would. Remember when he ate Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning dahlias? She was furious! Took her weeks to get over it. I had to explain to her nicely that dogs, well, they don't always understand the importance of floral arrangements. Poor Mrs. Higgins. She was a bit of a character. Though she did complain about the noise we made with the kids. Said we kept her up all hours. She was always complaining about something, wasn't she? But she was a good neighbour. Always brought over scones when Mum wasn't well. Neighbours are so different now, aren’t they? I barely know the people in my block of flats. We just… exist alongside each other. No scones, sadly. Used to be a right community in Wateringbury.

Right, nearly done. Honestly, this dishwasher is a blessing and a curse. It does the washing, but creates a mountain of stuff to put away. Mummy, can we read about Harry Potter again? Please? The one with the dragons! Just a teeny bit, love. Let’s get this sorted first. Then, dragons. Promise. Leo, are you being a good helper and staying out of the cutlery drawer? Yes! I’m building… a castle! A castle, brilliant! As long as it doesn’t involve pilfering teaspoons, alright? Now, where does this go… Ah, perfect. Right. So, remember we were talking about George Stephenson yesterday? The train man? That’s the one! The amazing train man. He didn’t just build  a  train, darling, he built the first  public  railway line with steam locomotives. Think about that! Before him, trains were mostly used to haul coal, and even then, not very efficiently. Did he make ‘choo choo’ sounds, Mummy? He probably didn't  make  the ‘choo choo’ sound, sweetheart, but the steam engine did! That’s the sound of the steam pushing the pistons and making the wheels go round and round. It was a proper marvel of engineering. They called it the 'Rocket', can you imagine naming something the Rocket? Pretty cool, eh? Why did he build a train, Mummy? That’s a really good question, love. Well, he noticed that transporting things, especially coal, was really slow and difficult. Horses and carts could only carry so much, and it took ages. He wanted to find a faster, more efficient way. He was a miner’s son, you know, so he grew up seeing how hard people worked. He wanted to make their lives easier. Was he good at maths? Probably! You need to be pretty clever to figure out how to build something as complicated as a steam engine and a whole railway line. He had to work out all sorts of things - how much coal it would need, how many wheels the train should have, how strong the engine needed to be… it's fascinating! Actually, my grandad used to work on the railways, down in Dartford, near where I grew up. He  loved  trains. Did he have a Rocket too? Not  his  own Rocket, darling, but he worked on the trains that ran on the lines built by people like George Stephenson. He used to tell me stories about shunting yards and signal boxes... it sounds a bit dull now, but when you’re little, it’s proper exciting.

Proper cheeky, innit? Liam always was a bit of a know-it-all. Though, I gotta admit, "quixote" is a fair play word. You can't argue with that. Did you manage to beat Chloe at all? She’s been on a roll. No way. She’s ruthless. Absolutely ruthless. I tried the double word score on 'helix' but she countered with 'jinx' before I could even register it. It’s infuriating! You know, it’s more stressful than trying to get a sourdough starter to properly bubble. Seriously. You two and your games! It’s a Tuesday night, we’re about to have a cracking dinner and you're bickering about a phone app? Anyway, has anyone seen that new supper club, "The Wandering Feast"? Apparently, they do Persian food one week, then Vietnamese the next. Found it on that Borough Finds website. Reckon it's worth a punt? Yeah, nah, I’ve had a look at those Borough Finds pages. They're alright, a bit pricey though. I’m more into those pop-up things down in Shoreditch, you know? Less marketing, more genuine grub. Though, Persian sounds pretty good. I had some wicked lamb kofta in Melbourne once… Persian sounds decent, yeah. Though, I’m still reeling from that legal thing, to be honest. My cousin’s mate is being sued for breach of contract over a bloody drone video he did for a florist. Can you believe it?! Apparently, the florist wants him to take down every post featuring her flowers. Seriously? Over a drone video? That’s mental! What’s the damages claim like? Seems like a massive overreach to me. Everything's litigious these days. Ridiculous. People are so quick to sue. My sister's having trouble with a supplier for the café. They’re late with deliveries again, and she’s worried about letting her regulars down. She’s thinking of switching to a different wholesaler, but needs to check their reviews first. It's a constant worry, running your own business. Tell me about it. Last week, the machine broke down at the bar. Right in the middle of service! Had to hand-brew every single espresso. My arms are still aching. They said it’ll be a couple grand to fix. Grand! Shoulda seen it coming, though. That thing was older than me. Speaking of arms aching, this pasta needs stirring.

Honestly, this coronation chicken is  divine . Did you manage to get any, Anya? Not really. The queue was… substantial. I ended up with this. It’s alright, I suppose, but definitely not as exciting. You always find the good stuff, don't you, Sarah? You’ve got a sixth sense for the canteen delicacies. Years of experience, love. You learn the rhythms. Tuesdays are always coronation chicken day, you see. Once you know that, you can plan accordingly. So, how’s the IT stuff going? Mr. Davies moaning about the printer again, I presume? You have  no  idea. He's convinced the new scanner is deliberately trying to sabotage him. I spent a good hour this morning just explaining the difference between a PDF and a JPEG to him. It’s… tiring. Being the only IT person, you know? I do, I do. Being the only cover supervisor is tiring too. Especially when Year 10s decide to stage a silent protest because they didn’t get the class they wanted. They didn’t even  talk , just stared at me. Quite unnerving. Wow. Staring contests with teenagers? That sounds intense. My biggest challenge is usually figuring out which piece of ancient equipment is about to spontaneously combust. Did you hear about Mrs. Henderson’s daughter? No, what? Is she alright? She got into Cambridge! To study Veterinary Medicine, can you believe it? I’m so thrilled for her. Her mum was practically beaming when she told me this morning. Makes me feel a bit inadequate, though. Everyone seems to be achieving these amazing things. Don't be silly, Anya. That's wonderful for Mrs. Henderson, and utterly brilliant for her daughter. Don’t compare yourself. Everyone has their own path. What about your husband, Dimitri? Still enjoying the climbing? He is. He’s planning a trip to the Peak District next weekend. Apparently, there’s a particularly challenging climb he wants to tackle. I’m staying behind, thank you very much. My idea of adventure is finding a new shade of beige paint for the flat. Each to their own! Speaking of adventure, I'm taking Lily to the beach next Saturday. She's been asking non-stop. She's obsessed with collecting seashells. It's adorable, if exhausting. Children are a handful, aren’t they? I can't imagine it yet. Though, Dimitri and I have been talking about… maybe in a few years.

Honestly, Mum, you could've just used the sat nav. We’ve been driving around in circles for fifteen minutes! Preston’s not exactly Monaco, is it? Don’t be so dramatic, love. It’s five minutes. And I know Preston better than any sat nav ever will! Besides, it's nice to see a bit more than just motorway. Remember when we used to drive here for the weekend markets? Aye, good times. Remember that blanket I bought from that stall in ’98? The one with the little sheep? Your Granny loved that blanket. Worn right through in the end, it were. Seriously, Dad? Sheep blankets? That's the height of cringe. Though, I did get that lovely knitted bunny at that little place near the train station, remember? Soft as anything. Speaking of soft, I need loads of those muslins for the baby. Mum, did you manage to get the ones with the little ducks? Little Thomas is going to look adorable wrapped in those. Yes, darling, I got them. And the swaddling wraps too. It’s all a bit overwhelming, isn't it? So many tiny clothes, so many things to buy. Suddenly, a crib looks like a pretty small space! Small space? Wait 'til we get everything in the new house. That survey came back alright, you know. Plenty to do. That damp proofing’s gonna be a nightmare. And the kitchen… don't even get me started on that kitchen! Oh, Dad, you’re always moaning about the house. It’ll be amazing once it’s done! Just think, we’ll finally have a proper study for me. I need a decent space to work on my A-Levels. History essays are killing me. I’m thinking of dropping Classical Civilisation, actually. Too much memorising. Don’t you dare! You worked so hard for it. Remember when you were little, and you’d pretend to be Cleopatra, bossing everyone around? Oh God, don't remind me! I was a menace. Honestly, I was. I wanted to be an actress, you know, until I realised Shakespeare was actually hard work. Actually, I'm leaning towards Law now. It seems more…practical. Law, eh? Good money in that. Better than customer service, that’s for sure. Though, you’ll be dealing with some right characters. Remember that bloke in Manchester last week? Thought he was a secret agent… John, please.

Honestly, Mum, it’s just  so  frustrating. I keep getting totally wiped in 'Starfall Genesis'. Like, utterly demolished. It’s not even fun anymore, it’s just…stressful. Starfall…Genesis? Sounds like something out of a sci-fi film. Is it that online game you’ve been obsessed with? The one where you’re a space mage or something? Yeah, exactly! But everyone else has levelled up so much. There's this player, Nightshade88, who’s completely unstoppable. I keep trying different strategies, different builds…nothing works. It's making me feel a bit rubbish all day. Nightshade88, huh? Sounds like they’re putting in serious hours. You know, there's a psychological element to games like that. People get attached, they feel the need to 'win' - even though it's just pixels on a screen. It taps into that competitiveness. I know, I know, you're all acting like it's not a big deal. But I  want  to be good! I don’t want to be a noob forever. Now, now, love. Don't get yourself worked up. It's just a game. Remember that trip we talked about? To Scotland? Wouldn’t that be a much better way to spend your time than agonizing over pixels? Yeah, but…Scotland's ages away. And Dad’s still sorting out the work stuff, isn’t he? Dad’s being Dad. He’ll get it sorted. Scotland sounds fantastic though. Imagine - hiking through the Highlands, seeing the Northern Lights... We could even visit that ancient observatory – the Royal Observatory Edinburgh. Think about the scientific instruments they used to track the stars! It’d be cool to try and spot constellations. Okay, that  does  sound pretty good. Science stuff’s actually kind of interesting, especially when it involves looking at space… it’s just… I still feel a bit down about 'Starfall Genesis'. Right, let's table that for now. Christmas is coming up, remember? Are you thinking of putting up the decorations this weekend? I was thinking of getting a real tree this year. Not one of those fake ones that smell like plastic. A real tree? That’d be really nice! But it’s messy, isn’t it? Needles everywhere. It's a small price to pay for the smell of pine. And we can vacuum up the needles. I'm happy to help. So, Nightshade88, huh? Maybe you’re just focusing too much on the competition.

“…and that’s why iron’s so useful, isn’t it? It's abundant, relatively easy to find – after you've dug a good few caves – and you can make so many things with it. Tools, armour, buckets… Everything builds on iron, really. What do you both think?” “But diamonds are better, Mummy! Diamond armour’s sparkly!” “You’re right, darling, diamond armour  is  better. But diamonds are really, really hard to find, aren’t they? It’s like searching for a tiny, shiny pebble in a giant pile of rocks. That’s why people work so hard for them in the game. They’re a  valuable  resource, a precious thing.” "Like gold! Daddy always finds a lot of gold!" “That's true! Gold is good too, isn't it? You can make golden apples with it, which heal you better than normal apples. But it's a bit…fussy, isn’t it? Doesn't stay shiny for long, does it? Reminds me a bit of velvet – looks gorgeous at first, all rich and deep, but a little bit of wear and tear and it loses its lustre.” “What's lustre?” "It just means how shiny something is, love. Like gold when it's brand new. See? And copper’s like… like canvas. It's a starting point, you can do so much with it, build up, improve it. You can combine it with other things to make something stronger. I read about how they used to use copper in roofing back in the day - quite ingenious, really." "Can we build a house made of wool? A giant, fluffy house?" “A wool house! Brilliant idea! But it would need a  lot  of sheep, wouldn’t it? And wool doesn't stop monsters very well, does it? It’s soft and lovely, but not very strong. Though, you could line it with iron armour plating... that would be quite a sight! I’m thinking of writing a legend about a giant sheep who builds a wool palace. He’s got fluffy guards and a throne made of clouds…” "And he eats diamond carrots!" "He does! Oh, that's wonderful, darling! Diamond carrots, fantastic! What else does he have?" "He has a pet fox that teaches everyone how to craft!" “A fox crafting tutor? That’s remarkably clever, isn’t it? Right, I’m jotting that down. We’ll call the fox Finley, I think.

…an’ then Mrs. Higgins started goin’ on about young Jamie down the street, saying he looked a bit shifty. Honestly, Liam, it were just because he’d got a new haircut! A proper fade, it were. She’s always judgin’, that one. Aye, Mrs. Higgins. You can set your watch by her gossipin’. But listen, you seemed a bit… preoccupied earlier. Not just about Mrs. Higgins’ antics. What’s up, love? You’ve been quiet since we got here. Just… well, I were readin' this article online, weren't I? About all these… y’know… awful blokes. Paedophiles. It’s just… it’s proper unsettling, isn’t it? Makes you want to just lock yerself away. Aye, it is. Proper rotten. There’s no sugarcoatin’ that. But lockin' yourself away ain’t the answer, is it? That gives ‘em power. Gotta be aware, gotta look out for each other. I know, I know. It’s just… it's everywhere, isn't it? Online, in the news… it's hard to escape. Makes you worried about… well, everything, really. Especially younger kids. It does. My mum worries about Sophie all the time, and she’s only ten. Right clever lass, Sophie. Used to be terrified of spiders, now she's buildin’ them little houses. Anyway, look, you need somethin’ to take your mind off it, eh? Been playin’ the guitar much? Not really. Been neglectin' it, truth be told. Uni’s been a right beast, what with all the essays and… well, everything. Started learnin’ that Arctic Monkeys riff, ‘I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor’… never got past the first few bars. Aye, that's a tricky one! Still, it’s better than frettin’ about Mrs. Higgins an’ scary news articles. You need to get yerself back into it. Remember how much you enjoyed it? We could have a proper jam sesh this weekend, if you’re up for it. Maybe try learnin’ Oasis – ‘Wonderwall’. Simpler chords. Oasis, eh? That’d be alright, wouldn’t it? I  did  always like ‘Wonderwall’. It's just... I keep tellin' myself I don’t have the time. You  make  the time, lass. You need somethin’ that relaxes you, that’s enjoyable. Music’s brilliant for that. Better than stressin' over stuff you can’t control, like what Mrs. Higgins says or what’s on the news. Speaking of music, catch any good gigs lately?

…and honestly, Mr. Davies just kept going on about the bibliography. Like, I  know  it needs to be perfect for the EPQ, but he made it sound like the entire grade hinges on the font size. It’s stressing me out. Tell me about it. My History teacher is obsessed with primary sources. I swear, if he sees one more textbook citation, he’ll explode. I’m trying to get my head around Montenegrin nationalism in the 19th century. It's a proper rabbit hole. You staying in Slough for half-term? Nope! We’re off to Montenegro actually. My aunt’s been raving about it for years. Apparently, the scenery is breathtaking. Bit of a culture shock from Hammersmith, though, I reckon. Seafood everywhere, I’m told. Are you guys doing anything exciting? Montenegro sounds amazing! Wish I was going. I'm stuck revising. My dad’s promised pizza tonight though, so that’s a win. What about you, Liam? Still practicing your juggling routine? Always. Trying to master the five-ball cascade. It's humbling, to say the least. My mum keeps threatening to video me dropping them all and putting it on TikTok. Speaking of humbling, I was reading this article the other day about food poverty in the UK. It’s just... shocking, isn't it? Especially when you're, like, moaning about a dodgy pizza topping. It absolutely is. It's weird, isn't it? We complain about university fees and benefits cuts, but so many people are struggling just to eat. I was volunteering at a food bank last year. It’s eye-opening to see. My gran always said, “Never forget where you come from, darling. There are people who have it far worse.” She grew up in Stepney during the war, you know. Stories she told... unbelievable. Rationing, air raids… She’d be horrified by the amount of food we waste. My nan always used to make the best shepherd’s pie. Total comfort food. She was a fantastic cook, but stuck to traditional recipes. My mum tries to recreate it, but it's just not the same. Maybe I should ask her for the recipe. It'd be cool to learn how to cook properly. I'm pretty hopeless, tbh. Can barely boil an egg. My mum’s a brilliant vegetarian cook – loads of Indian stuff. Spiced lentils, vegetable curries… Proper good.

“Right, so, Mum's just sent me another text. 'Have you remembered to budget, love? Student loans don’t stretch forever, you know!' Honestly, like I haven't heard that a million times. It's just… constant. You'd think she'd realise I'm trying, innit?” “Tell me about it! My dad's gone full financial advisor this year. Spreadsheet, colour-coded categories, the lot. It's terrifying. He was just listing all the ways I could get a side hustle. Like, learn to knit and sell scarves. Scarves, Liam! In Lancashire!” She laughs. “My mum, she just…holds my phone and gives me the ‘look.’ You know the one? The silent, disappointed stare. It’s more effective than any lecture, trust me.” He pauses. “She’s worried, though, I think. About me and the… competition out there. Says I need to be 'smarter' with my spending.” “My Mum’s just stressing about Christmas. Says we need to start saving now. Like, it’s October!” He pops a crisp in his mouth. “She wants a real tree this year, not one of them fake ones. Says it’s ‘tradition’ but it'll cost a fortune.” “A real tree? Blimey! Sounds expensive. This accommodation’s ridiculous, though, isn't it? The heating's playing up again. Freezing last night. I ended up wrapped in all the blankets I could find. Like camping, but without the marshmallows.” “Seriously! Mine’s drafty as anything. And the shower pressure? Don’t even get me started. You’re lucky if you get warm water for ten seconds. I think my hair's developing split ends just from the shock.” “I’ve reported the heating. They said they'd send someone. I’m not holding my breath. Knowing this university, we’ll be lucky if they send a polite email.” “Did you hear about Emily and Josh? Apparently, they had a huge row last night. Heard shouting from the corridor. Someone said it was about him borrowing her jumper and then getting chocolate all over it.” “No! Seriously? Emily’s jumper collection is sacred! That’s a cardinal sin. What jumper was it? Was it the cream cable knit? Oh, the humanity!” “Good grief. Clearly Josh doesn't understand the sanctity of cashmere. Though," she adds with a sly grin, "it’s good for a bit of entertainment, isn’t it? Anything's better than worrying about loan repayments.”

…and honestly, Mrs. Petrov just  stared  at me when I explained the concept of a Christmas cracker! Like, I was speaking Martian. She kept saying, "Why would you put a paper hat on your head, darling? It's ridiculous!” It took me a good twenty minutes to convince her it was a  tradition . A silly, festive tradition. Oh, bless her. Russians, eh? They don't do the whimsical nonsense we do, do they? You'd think with all that snow and long nights, they'd embrace the sheer absurdity of it. Remember that Christmas we spent with your Aunt Maggie and Uncle George in Cornwall? The one where the seagull stole the turkey right off the table? Don't remind me! Aunt Maggie nearly had a heart attack. Uncle George was just standing there, muttering about "feathered fiends." That was chaotic, wasn’t it? Still, a Christmas memory for the ages. Are you seeing many clients these days, Mum? Still travelling around? A bit less travel, thankfully. Knees aren’t what they used to be, you know. Mostly doing online consultations now. It’s… convenient. Less packing, less airport hassle. I’ve got a lovely group of HR professionals in Manchester I work with, training them on team-building exercises. Rather dull, really, compared to the international stuff I used to do. But it pays the bills. Did you hear from Eleanor? She was supposed to be calling about the Christmas dinner planning. No, not yet. Typical Eleanor. Always leaves everything to the last minute. She says she’s "curating the perfect festive atmosphere” which usually translates to stressing herself into oblivion over napkin colours. I offered to do the Yorkshire puddings, you know I’m pretty decent at them. You are, sweetheart. Don't let her boss you around on Christmas Day. It’s your day too. Speaking of which, how are things going with the school? Still enjoying teaching ESL? It’s… challenging. The kids are lovely, truly. It’s the paperwork, the constant assessment, the endless meetings. It’s all a bit much sometimes. But then you have a moment, like when a student finally  gets  a phrase, or understands a grammar point, and it just… clicks. That makes it worthwhile. I did have a student from Iran last year, little Farhad. He was so keen. Absolutely soaked up every word. Makes you think, doesn’t it? About the world, about understanding...

Tell me about it. Fields of nothingness. You’d think in 2024 we'd have better coverage. Anyway, what were you saying about the area changing? You mentioned something about…gentrification? Gentrification. Fancy word for it, innit? Aye, it is. Used to be proper little terraced houses, you know? Families livin' there for generations. Now, they’re knocking ‘em down, building these…boxes. All glass and modern. No character. More millionaires than actual folk. They put a speed camera up last month too, right on the bend. Cheeky buggers. A speed camera? Seriously? That’s ridiculous. They just want the money. Do they at least check licenses properly? I’m still waiting on mine to come through from the provisional to the full. NHS just…taking forever. Don’t I know it. The NHS. It’s a joke. Reminds me of my work, really. Endless calls, complaints, people moaning about things they can’t control. Not exactly stimulating, is it? Though, I’ve got a new supervisor, actually. Trying to make things a bit more positive. She's got some good ideas. How’s the instructing going? Still enjoying it? It's good, yeah. Challenging, but good. Got a really bright class this term, actually. Trying to get them excited about Shakespeare. Which, let me tell you, is a monumental task. It’s a far cry from Game of Thrones, that’s for sure! Remember all those nights we spent glued to the telly for that? Don’t remind me! Got every episode recorded, I did. Still got ‘em somewhere. Though, I haven't watched them in years. What about board games? Used to be big on Monopoly, weren’t we? You always cheated, you know. I did not! You just weren’t paying attention! Anyway, things have been a bit mad lately. Mum's been battling a nasty cold, poor thing. And that flu’s going around...you have to be careful. It's just wiping people out. Aye, heard that. You be careful, too. Flying all that way to Tanzania… that's going to be somethin' alright. Remember that fella at work, Dave? Told me he was going there for a volunteer project. Said it changed his life. I’m ridiculously excited, but also nervous. Totally different culture, you know? And I  have  put on weight, haven’t I? All this stress baking with Mum. I swear, she’s been trying to fatten me up before I leave.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of it all! They wanted a PR strategy for a vegan dog biscuit company. A  vegan  dog biscuit company, Ben! What even  is  the target demographic for that, beyond excessively wealthy millennials with Pomeranians? It's just… baffling. Right? Sounds like a niche even within a niche. You’d think you were pitching for a bespoke artisanal squirrel feeder or something. Did you at least manage to politely decline? Eventually. It took almost an hour of delicately explaining that my specialism is Victorian literature, really, and not… canine culinary marketing. They kept pushing though, kept saying “but you’re an expert communicator!” I wanted to scream, “Yes, in the nuanced prose of Dickens, not the snappy slogans of a biscuit manufacturer!” You're a saint. I would have just said, "No, I don't do dog biscuits." Simple, direct, effective communication. Though, I suppose that wouldn’t exactly cultivate the helpful, collaborative PR image they were after. Exactly! It's exhausting. I swear, every time I think I'm building a reputation for something specific, someone wants me to be an expert in something entirely unrelated. Speaking of reputations... did you see that article about the debacle at the Philharmonic last night? Oh, the one with the violinist and the unfortunate cucumber incident? Briefly. Apparently, he got flustered during the encore and… well, let’s just say the vegetable didn’t fare well. The papers are having a field day. It’s dreadful, isn’t it? Poor chap. I can’t imagine the pressure. Though I must admit, the mental image is rather amusing. It will haunt me, honestly. What did you get up to today then, aside from contemplating the existential dread of corporate PR requests? Relatively calm, actually. Finished marking those essays on  Wuthering Heights  - surprisingly decent this year. Though, one student genuinely thought Heathcliff was a real person. Like, a historical figure. Oh, bless him. They really do believe anything they read on Wikipedia, don't they? Did you head to that record shop later? The one we were talking about, 'Echoes & Vinyl'? I did! Finally managed to get a copy of that obscure Miles Davis album,  Sorcerer . Have you heard it? Briefly. A friend played it once, years ago. It’s incredible, isn't it? That smoky, almost claustrophobic atmosphere. I'm surprisingly picky with my jazz, but that one really stuck with me.

Honestly, David, I’m getting a bit frustrated with this beanbag. The wool just… doesn't want to cooperate. I’ve been knitting for three evenings now and it's barely bigger than a grapefruit. Well, relax, love. It's supposed to be a beanbag, not a speed record. You chose chunky yarn, didn’t you? That’s going to take time. Besides, a tiny beanbag would be quite amusing, wouldn’t it? A decorative grapefruit. Amusing to you, perhaps. I envisioned something substantial, something you could actually  sit  on. And the colour! This burnt orange… are you sure it will actually go with the living room? I’m starting to think I should have gone with the slate grey. It’s lovely, I think. Adds a bit of warmth. The slate grey would have been a bit…clinical. Look at you, worrying about the beanbag’s aesthetic compatibility while I’m trying to prevent us from starving. Smells good, doesn't it? Chicken and chorizo, your favourite. It does smell wonderful. You’re a lifesaver. Honestly, the thought of cooking tonight... I’ve just been so focused on this blasted beanbag and trying to make a decision about the shower curtain. The shower curtain? What's wrong with the current one? It’s perfectly functional. Perfectly functional and horribly beige. It’s been beige for five years, David! Five years! I saw this gorgeous one online, textured linen in a sort of teal… it would really brighten up the bathroom. Teal, eh? Are you sure? The bathroom is already quite… vibrant, with that lime green towel set. Don't want it all clashing, do we? I think teal and lime green can work, if done right. It’s a risk, I grant you. But beige is just… depressing. The whole bathroom needs a refresh, really. I’ve been meaning to get some new toiletries too. Something a bit… luxurious. You know, fancy soaps and lotions. Luxurious toiletries? Are you suddenly feeling flush? We’ve got a perfectly serviceable bar of soap. It's not about the money, David! It’s about creating an atmosphere. A little bit of indulgence. After all, we spend a significant amount of time in the bathroom. Shouldn't it be a pleasant space? I was thinking a small succulent on the windowsill too. Something resilient. A succulent? You’re going all-out. Succulents need sunlight, though.

Honestly, Arthur, you’ll wear that clock right down to the springs. Leave it be! It’s perfectly alright. Just a little somethin’ amiss, Brenda. Tickin’ a bit… fidgety, it is. Not the steady chug I’m used to. Reminds me of old Mr. Higgins’ grandfather clock, used to stand right in the hall. Loud as you please, that one was. Could hear it coughin’ across the street. Coughing? Grandfather clocks don't cough, Arthur. That's just the Westminster chimes getting a bit rusty. Rusty, is it? Everything’s rusty these days, Charles. Minds too, some would say. Not like in my day. Solid craftsmanship, that was. Everything built to last. This little beauty… this is a testament to that. Well, you’ve been saying that for twenty years since you bought it at the jumble sale. And the ‘solid craftsmanship’ hasn't stopped you picking at it. Just admirin' the work, Brenda. Admirin’ the work. There weren't much to do in Costessey back then, you know. Not much to keep a young lad occupied. Spent most of my time tinkerin’ with things. Engines, radios, clocks… anything with a bit of innards. Never did get a proper trade, though. Always somethin’ else catchin’ me eye. You had a real aptitude for electronics, actually. Remember that little radio you built for Margaret? Sounded remarkably good considering it was made from bits and bobs. That were a good little thing, that was. Margaret loved it. She used to listen to the wireless for hours. That was before all this nonsense with… streaming and whatever they call it now. Real radio. Proper antennas. You knew where the signal was comin' from. Well, you’re digressing, dear. We were talking about the treasurer's report for the WI. Did you catch anything of what Agnes said about the flower show? Flower show? Cor blimey. Flowers. Not really my thing, flowers. Always preferred a good bit of metal, meself. Something solid. Reliable. You can’t trust a flower. They wilt. They fade. You’re incorrigible, Arthur. Agnes mentioned they need volunteers for the judging. Said they're short this year. Volunteers? Judgin’ flowers? Good heavens. What do they want me to do, measure the petals? Check for spots? I wouldn’t know a petunia from a… a daffodil! You could be the novelty judge, dear. Everyone would come just to see you trying to judge a rose.

Tell me about it, love. You look it. Christmas at the hospital is always a bit of a whirlwind, isn't it? More stress than cheer, usually. I’ve already had two parents complaining about the festive food – apparently the sprouts are “overcooked” and the turkey’s “dry.” As if anyone expects Michelin-star dining in a public hospital on Christmas Day! Oh, the joys of public service. You’d think they'd appreciate you lot just  being  there. Speaking of food, how’s that slow cooker curry coming along, love? It smells lovely. Almost ready! It’s a butternut squash and lentil one. Trying to be a bit healthier this year, you know? After all the mince pies I scoffed last week… I felt dreadful. Mince pies are a tradition, darling! Can’t deny yourself a mince pie at Christmas. Although, I do need to be careful, my ankles are playing up something fierce. This new course is killing me, the studying and the placements… and the sheer volume of information. It's like trying to drink from a fire hose! Oh, poor love. You’re doing brilliantly though, Brenda. It's a massively clever thing you're doing, becoming a nurse practitioner. Remember when I said I never wanted to do any more training after my sixth form? Look at me now, still learning new things! It’s impressive, Brenda. Really. Though, all this talk of training and hospitals... reminds me, have you looked at those flights to Barbados yet, Carol? The one we were chatting about? Barbados? In February? Blimey, that’s ambitious, isn't it? Didn’t they say prices were skyrocketing? Barbados sounds amazing! I’ve always wanted to go. Just imagine, sunshine and cocktails… a million miles away from the grey skies of Kent! Barbados is lovely... but that’s a  lot  of money, David. We’re already stretching the budget with Christmas and everything, aren't we? Besides, I really should be focusing on my studies. Tempting, though, very tempting. I did a bit of looking last night. Direct flights aren't cheap, that's true. But there are some decent deals if we don’t mind a stopover in Miami. Might cut the costs a bit. And think of it, Carol, proper sunshine and a rest. You deserve it. You do deserve it, love. You really do. I’d be up for it, actually.

…and honestly, David, the driving here is… something else. It’s not just the lack of road markings, although that’s certainly part of it. It's the sheer confidence people have in navigating chaos. I swear, yesterday I saw a scooter weaving between two lorries, on a one-way street, carrying a stack of rugs! Ah, Northern Cyprus. It’ll test your patience, it will. You get used to it, though. You  have  to. Back in Bushey, you know, everyone was so… precise. Queueing was practically a religion. Here? It’s more of a suggestion. A suggestion, precisely! I’m used to a certain level of predictability, especially after years of dealing with teenagers. You know exactly what you’re getting with them, mostly. This...this is just wonderfully unpredictable. How long have you been out here, David? You seem remarkably unfazed. Oh, going on fifteen years now. Came out on a whim, really. Lost my job, the missus decided she didn’t fancy Hertfordshire anymore... seemed as good a place as any to start again. Bit of sunshine, a bit cheaper living… you know. It’s a funny thing, escaping somewhere thinking you're running  from  something, only to find you’re actually running  towards  something. That's a lovely way of putting it. I’m just here for six months, you see. A bit of a sabbatical from teaching. Needed a change. The school... well, it's a different story altogether. Budgets, Ofsted, parents… the usual. I thought sunshine and a slower pace would do me good. Teaching, eh? Demanding profession. My sister was a teacher, actually. Said the same thing - constant pressure. Did she ever tell you about the time she used a puppet show to explain fractions? No, she didn’t! That sounds brilliant, though. Kids love puppets. I’ve tried incorporating a bit of drama into my lessons, but it's hard to find the time with all the marking. Are there any… quirks I should be aware of here, besides the driving? Things that are just… Northern Cypriot? Plenty. The coffee, for a start. It’s strong. Really strong. You’ll be buzzing for hours. And the hospitality – they’ll offer you tea and cake at every opportunity. It's polite to accept, even if you're bursting. And don’t be surprised if people invite you to their homes for dinner. It’s how they show they like you.

Honestly, another day, another layer. I feel permanently coated in smog. It's… oppressive, isn’t it? Even just walking home like this. It is. Though I think we’re getting used to it, aren't we? That's the worrying bit. Remember when we first arrived, we were practically glued to the air quality app? Now we just… accept it. Don't say that! We  shouldn’t  accept it. It's not normal. Back in Norwich… you could see the stars. Properly see them. Here, you're lucky if you can distinguish a particularly bright one. Anyway, less about atmospheric degradation and more about the Henderson lecture. Did you manage to get through to him about the revised bibliography? Progress, but slow. He’s still convinced his original sources are essential, even though half of them are twenty years out of date and based on… questionable methodology, to be blunt. I tried to explain the shift in our field, the emergence of cognitive linguistics… but he dug his heels in. Said it was “frivolous” and “trendy.” Oh, Henderson. Bless his heart. He’s stuck in a temporal loop, isn't he? You need to be more forceful, love. Gentle persuasion clearly isn’t working. Lay out the evidence, the supporting literature… hit him with those new research papers Anya sent over. The ones demonstrating the inherent flaws in his initial arguments. I will. I think I need to have a final, very direct conversation with him next week. It feels a bit… uncomfortable, going against a senior colleague like that. Especially when he’s been so supportive in the past. Supportive in the past doesn’t negate the need for academic rigour in the present. We're not doing him any favours letting him put out substandard work. And think of the students! They deserve to be exposed to current thinking. Besides, you're right, and that’s what matters. It's your responsibility to uphold the standards of the department. You’re right, as always. It just... it feels a bit prickly. Did you hear back from Sarah and Mark about the weekend trip?
