I messaged them earlier. Yes! They're in! They’re so keen to get out of the city, apparently. Honestly, Sarah was practically begging me to suggest somewhere. She's been complaining about the air quality impacts on her asthma. It’s just… not fair, is it?

…and honestly, David, the waiting list at the surgery is just getting ridiculous. Mrs. Henderson’s been trying to get an appointment for her arthritis for three weeks now. Three weeks! You’d think with the new triage system… you’d think. Triage system’s a load of cobblers, innit? All fancy talk and no actual improvement. Remember old Mr. Finch? Waiting six months for a follow-up on that dodgy knee. Dr. Patel's gone, you know. Moved to Bristol apparently. Said the pressure was too much. Right, I'm officially starving. What's the plan for dinner, Mum? And Dad, you're sounding awfully pessimistic about the NHS again. Can we not? Please? Just a simple roast chicken, love. Got a lovely looking one from Billings Farm Shop this morning. Roast potatoes, carrots, peas... standard Sunday fare. You want anything special? Sounds perfect, thanks! Anything involving gravy is a win in my book. So, what was the most dramatic thing that happened at the surgery today? You always have a story. Oh, you know. Usual stuff, really. Trying to convince young Timmy Parker that he  doesn't  need antibiotics for a sniffle. His mother's convinced he's got something lethal, you know the type. It's amazing how much misinformation there is online these days. Smells good, this. What are you making, love? Some kind of béchamel? Yeah, for a little cheese sauce for the peas. Adds a bit of something, doesn’t it? Speaking of online, did you see that photo Amelia posted from her trip to Rome? The Colosseum looked incredible! Wow, it  is  stunning. I’m so jealous. She’s living the dream, that one. Should’ve taken a Year Abroad, really. I’d have loved to spend a semester in Italy. She’s always been a keen one, our Amelia. Pity she didn't take more notice of her Italian lessons at school, though. Wouldn’t get very far ordering a cappuccino, would she? True! She’d probably just point and gesture wildly. So, lunch on Wednesday… still on for that little bistro near the train station? Yes, dear, definitely. Heard good things about it. Apparently, they do a cracking Sunday roast too, if we’re feeling particularly adventurous next week. Adventurous? On a Sunday? Now you’re talking nonsense, love. Stick with the tradition. Speaking of traditions… anyone been watching “Call the Midwife”?

…and honestly, the sheer arrogance of it all! Blocking the entrance to the Press bookshop for three hours? Saying it’s a crucial act of protest? It's just… disruptive, isn't it? People trying to buy their textbooks, academics needing particular editions… it's not a good look. Aye, it's a bit much, isn’t it? I can see the point they’re makin’ about the Press’s potential involvement with some of those publishers, the ones with dodgy environmental records, but targetin’ the bookshop? Seems a bit… sideways, like. Folk 'round home would say ‘missin’ the bleedin’ wood for the trees’. Exactly! And the placards! “Cambridge Must Do Better!” as if the entire institution is some monolithic entity. It’s so… simplistic. It ignores the incredible work happening across departments. Take the engineering faculty, for example – tonnes of research into sustainable materials… Right, 'cause  that  is always worth a mention. You’re brilliant at defendin' your lot, aren't ya? Proper loyal. Reminds me of when Clive from the Archives was accused of "mis-shelvin'" a rare manuscript. You spent a whole lunchtime practically dissectin’ the Dewey Decimal System for me, just to prove he couldn’t have gone wrong. Well, Clive's a good bloke, and the Dewey Decimal System  is  largely infallible! And it’s the same principle – a blanket accusation isn't fair. So, are you still moaning about the new bus route? I thought you were going to write a strongly worded email to the council. I did! Sent it last week. Right fettle, it was too. Still, it’s a shambles, isn’t it? They’ve cut off the 7, the one that used to go right past my flat, and replaced it with this bendy bus that barely fits down some of the streets. And the frequency? Forget about it. I spent forty minutes waitin’ last Tuesday, standin' in the rain! Forty minutes! Cambridge transport  is  a special kind of misery. I remember trying to get back from a conference in Norwich once. Had to cycle, practically. It’s just… inefficient. Why haven’t they invested in a proper tram system? Aye, a tram would be grand. It'd be better than this. Were you bothered when they scrapped train services on that line stop? I was livid! Spendin’ a fortune on a cable car line, but you can't get a decent train connection?

…and honestly, the sheer volume of commas in that legal document nearly broke me. It was about some land dispute, apparently. Honestly, I felt like I needed a week-long holiday after just  reading  it. Land disputes! Honestly, why does Cheshire always seem to be embroiled in those? Remember Aunt Carol’s brother, the one who ended up in court about the hedge? Utter madness. So, did you manage to sort it out, anyway? Eventually. The client was surprisingly relaxed about it all, just wanted it accurately transcribed. Less fuss than I anticipated. Speaking of relaxed, how's planning for Liam's visit going? Are you still aiming for Saturday? Saturday's still the plan. Though I’m a bit fraught, to be honest. He's not the easiest, you know. Especially when he starts talking about… well, about everything. And then he expects me to have some profound, insightful answer, and I just… I can't. He's just a bit… intense, isn't he? You don't need to have all the answers, Mum. Just be yourself. And maybe steer clear of politics, eh? Remember what happened at Christmas? Oh, don’t remind me. He launched into a twenty-minute diatribe about the current government, and I ended up hiding in the pantry with a tin of biscuits. It wasn’t my finest hour. Honestly, sometimes I long for the quiet predictability of marking quadratic equations. At least those were logical. You miss teaching, don't you? I know you said you were relieved to retire, but… I do, in a way. The marking was dreadful, of course, but there was a rhythm to it. And the children… most of them were lovely, you know. Always a surprise, the way they’d latch onto a concept. I used to think, “Ah, right, that’s how you explain it,” and it all clicked. Now… well, now my biggest challenge is remembering where I put my reading glasses. Well, that’s a far cry from factorising! I’m seriously thinking about getting you a nice, large magnifying glass for Christmas. Anyway, back to Liam. Perhaps we should plan something nice for him, something completely unrelated to his current obsessions. Like… a proper pub lunch? Good idea! The Olde Cheshire Arms in Tarporley does a lovely Sunday roast. Remember that time we all went there and you spilled gravy down your blouse, Mum?

Honestly, it's still quite imposing, isn't it? Even after all these years. You'd think I'd be used to seeing that giant bubble dominating the skyline, but… it just is. So very modern. Doesn't quite fit with the rest of the river, does it? No, no it doesn't. A bit… shouty for this gentle landscape, really. Though I do appreciate the concerts they put on. Remember that U2 gig we went to there? Absolutely incredible atmosphere. But yeah, aesthetically... not exactly Georgian. That was brilliant. Although, the queues afterward! Goodness me. Still worth it, I suppose. It's just… easy to forget how much has changed around here. Woolwich used to be so…industrial. This whole stretch is practically a tourist hotspot now. Adapting, isn't it? Progress, I suppose. Though I do miss the proper old docks. You remember Grandad used to tell stories about working down here, loading cargo ships. Felt like a different world entirely. Absolutely. It’s miles away from the little cottage we're hoping to rent in Cornwall this summer. All thatched roofs and cream teas, isn't it? I'm desperately needing some proper relaxation. The transcription work has been relentless. Apparently, American clients insist on everything in cups. Cups! Why not millilitres? It’s utter madness trying to convert it all. "A cup of sugar"... it could mean anything! The Americans and their antiquated measurements. Drives me mad in the kitchen. I was trying to bake a cake the other day with an American recipe. “Half a cup of flour.” Honestly! It's a recipe for disaster. You realize, doesn’t it? Everything’s just… subjective. A cup is what you make it. Exactly! It feels a bit… philosophical, doesn’t it? Measurement, scales… defining things. Do we  really  ever truly define something, or are we just constructing a shared understanding? That’s a bit deep for a walk along the Thames, isn't it? Probably shouldn't have mentioned the cake. But you're right, I suppose. We impose order on chaos, don’t we? Even our most mundane actions. Weighing out flour, transcribing words... We're trying to make sense of things. And failing more often than we succeed. Still, at least we’re doing it together. The kids are thrilled about Cornwall, aren't they? Even little Leo, who mostly just wants to splash in puddles.

Honestly, Mum, it’s absolutely chucking it down. Sports day's going to be a washout, innit? Little Leo’s been practicing his sack race for weeks. I feel awful for him. Don't you worry about Leo, love. They’ll probably just reschedule. Though, bless him, he’ll be gutted. Remember when you fell over during egg and spoon at your primary school sports day? You were mortified! Oh God, don't remind me! Mrs. Peterson nearly fainted from the shock. I was convinced my whole life was over. Still, at least I learned not to underestimate the slipperiness of a hard-boiled egg. Speaking of which, has anyone seen my phone? I swear I had it five minutes ago. It’s on the sofa, love. Next to Teddy. Little Maisie’s been giving him a right cuddle. He's practically got toothpaste all over his face. Oh, brilliant. Maisie and Teddy. Honestly, that bear is more loved than half the family. She’s practically attached to him. Remember when she insisted he came swimming with us at Maidstone? Oh, I do! Standing there in the shallow end, with that fluffy bear bobbing about. You looked like you were refereeing a very small, very soggy, teddy bear Olympics. Did you ever think we’d have swimming pools in England that weren't freezing cold and full of chlorine? Seems like a luxury, doesn’t it? Maisie keeps asking if Teddy needs a new swimsuit. I told her bears don't wear swimsuits, but she’s unconvinced. She even tries to put her little floaties on him! She’s convinced he’s a proper swimmer now, after that one time he floated for about five seconds. She's got such an imagination, hasn’t she? It's lovely, really. You know, I was thinking about getting her another Build-a-Bear. She's been eyeing up the unicorn ones in Bluewater. Let her have it. A little bit of happiness never hurt anyone. Though, goodness, the price of those things! Honestly, you're paying more for stuffing and a little heart than you are for some decent kitchen appliances these days. My old Kenwood mixer is still going strong, nearly 30 years old. You don't get that kind of quality anymore. You're right, Mum. Everything breaks these days. Remember when the washing machine decided to flood the kitchen last year?

…so, realistically, six months feels like a really good window for that digital nomad course. It gives me enough breathing room after the wrap-up here with the house-sit, and before things properly ramp up back in the UK. What do you reckon, love? Too ambitious? Six months? For  that  much training? Well, not ambitious exactly, but... intense. Especially with everything else swirling around. Remember how exhausted you were after that last intensive workshop? You practically slept for a week. Are you absolutely sure you need a full six months? Couldn’t you do a shorter focused module? I’ve been looking at the curriculum, honestly. It’s all about practical application, building a portfolio, networking… you can’t really skimp on that stuff. And, look, it’s not just about the business, is it? It's about me actually  enjoying  what I do again. This whole… jumping from project to project thing is wearing me thin. A bit of structure, a bit of focused learning… it’ll be good for the soul. I get that. I really do. You do seem… scattered, lately. Speaking of things for the soul, have you thought about that pottery class Sarah and Mark were talking about in Cornwall? We could all do it when we’re back. Pottery? Right now, the thought of shaping clay feels incredibly…grounding, actually. Yes, absolutely! We should. It’d be fantastic to properly connect with them all. How are things with your sister, by the way? Did you manage to ring her? I did. She's doing well. The kids are growing like weeds. Emily’s thinking of applying to Oxbridge next year, can you believe it? She's brilliant, that one. It’s all a bit nerve-wracking for her mum, obviously. I did mention you send your best. She asked you to say hello, and send some pictures of the wildlife here. Apparently, she's convinced you're living in the Serengeti. I'll get some photos of the kookaburras then. Right. Let's circle back to careers. Six months… Look, I’d be networked up with some serious people by then. I could start freelancing with confidence. Thinking about the long game, wouldn't you say it's strategically sound? Strategically sound, possibly. Practically doable while we… While we're still figuring out the… family plan? That’s what worries me. Six months is a long time to be out of the country when… you know.

Aye, Sarah’s got a right temper on her, hasn’t she? Proper firecracker. Remember when she got told off for letting her hamster loose in Mrs. Higgins' pet shop? Oh my god, yeah! Poor Mr. Higgins had to chase that little fella round for like an hour. She was mortified, but also a bit defiant, if I remember right. It was a full-blown drama. Defiant is the word. She always was. Speaking of defiant, did you see that new Pokémon trailer, lads? The electric type’s got a new form, it’s dead savage! Pokémon? Seriously, Liam? We're discussing Sarah's hamster-related rampage, and you’re bringing up digital monsters. Classic. Leave him be, Josh. He’s allowed a bit of Pokemon obsession. Besides, it's a welcome distraction from thinking about spreadsheets. Urgent audit stuff’s proper draining me. I reckon I need a full weekend camping trip. Get away from it all. Camping? Now, there's a thought. But you know me, I'm more of a Costa and a service station kind of girl when I'm out and about. Doesn’t get much comfier than a bacon butty and unlimited coffee, does it? It depends what you’re camping for, doesn't it? If you’re like, survivalist camping, then yeah, fair enough. But for comfort? My tent's got fairy lights and a proper duvet. Fairy lights? Fancy. You’ve gone full glamper, haven't you, Chloe? I'm more of a ‘hope-I-don’t-freeze-to-death’ kind of camper. It's the fight-or-flight thing, innit? Staying warm feels like a constant battle. You’re all mental. Honestly. Sarah's on about moving to Leeds, you know. Said she's been looking at flats. Says she wants a change. Leeds? That's a fair trek. Will she be able to get back for Christmas with the family? She says she’ll be back. Doesn’t sound entirely convincing, mind. She hates that whole tradition of everyone crowding round the telly after dinner, stuffing their faces with After-Eights. Speak for yourself! I live for After-Eights. It’s a Christmas essential! Though, honestly, I'm usually too full to eat any after the roast. Right, I need to nip to the shop. Anyone want anything? I’m going for fags, obviously. Actually, yeah. Can you grab me a packet of those lemon sherbets?

Honestly, Arthur, you get so worked up about football. It's just a game. Though, I must say, it  did  look a bit dubious. But then, they always seem to favour the big clubs, don't they? It’s the way of the world. Remember that time Norwich got cheated against…? Oh, never mind, you wouldn’t want to dwell on past injustices.      Dad, you’d think the fate of the nation rested on that penalty! And Doreen, you’re right – it is biased. It’s just… frustrating. But at least it gave us something to talk about, eh? I've got a lecture on political rhetoric to prepare, and watching that penalty decision was surprisingly useful. It’s a brilliant example of manufactured outrage.      Manufactured outrage is right, Sarah. All this hullabaloo! Though, I do appreciate Arthur's enthusiasm. It’s... endearing, in a slightly exasperating way. Reminds me of my dad, actually. He used to shout at the telly with the same vigour. What are you having, love?      This roast is champion, Brenda. Champion, I say! You've outdone yourself, lass. Proper Yorkshire pudding, too. Not like that watery stuff you get in the shops. Remember when Ethel next door tried making Yorkshire puddings? They were flatter than a pancake. Flatter than a… well, you remember.      Oh, yes! Ethel’s puddings were a disaster. She blamed the flour. Said it was 'dry'. Honestly. Anyway, about the party… Sarah, have you and Mark made any decisions about the decorations? I was thinking fairy lights. Lots of them. And balloons, naturally. A good mix of colours.      We’ve started looking, Mum. Mark’s insisted on a theme – 80s nostalgia! Lots of neon and slightly embarrassing music choices. He's already unearthed his old Rubik’s Cube.      Oh, here we go. The 80s. Prepare yourselves for a barrage of Duran Duran and shoulder pads. I’m already regretting agreeing to this. But for my sister, I’ll grin and bear it. Is there any chance of a wee break from the synth-pop, Sarah? Perhaps some classic soul?      Eighties, eh? All that racket! Give me a bit of Vera Lynn any day. Now  that's  music. Though, I did enjoy a bit of that… what was it called… Spandau Ballet? Good looking lads, they were. Proper.      Arthur, honestly! Vera Lynn and Spandau Ballet in the same breath! Speaking of music, Sarah, do you think we should get a DJ?

…and honestly, like, I just can’t see the point anymore, can I? All these lectures, the readings… it’s all just… a lot. Feels like I'm wading through treacle. Right? I get that, proper. It's a bit of a bummer, innit? I was expecting… I don't know… more, I suppose. Less feeling like you’re being processed. Exactly! It’s like they just shove you through the system and hope you come out the other end with a degree. No one actually cares if you’re learning anything, do they? They just want the statistics. No way. Mum would have a right go at me if I started moaning like that. She'd be all "You've got such a fantastic opportunity, don't you dare waste it!" She's got that way, hasn’t she? Always thinking the best of everything. Even when the tide came in and washed away all of Gran’s shells on the beach, she said it was “making room for new treasures.” Classic. My mum’d be saying, "Right, you could've moved them! Typical!" She’s more… practical. Speaking of the beach, do you remember when we were little and you used to bury me up to my neck in the sand? Oh, absolutely! And you'd always complain that it tickled. You'd be yelling for your dad, screamin' like a proper banshee. “Daddy! I’m being eaten by the sand!” Proper dramatic, you were. I was a right drama queen, weren’t I? Everything was a catastrophe. You were always so calm. Like a little Cornish sprite, just blending in with the surroundings. I did spend a lot of time weeding Gran's flower beds, so I suppose I got used to being quiet and observant. She got all her names from the sea, didn't she? My middle name’s Coral. Always thought it was a bit odd. It’s lovely! My name's Eleanor, which no one ever uses. Everyone just calls me El. Feels a bit stuffy, doesn't it? So, about this dropping out thing… Have you actually, seriously, thought about it? Yeah, I've been looking into it. There's a pottery course down in Truro, surprisingly good reviews. And I could do a bit of waitressing at the cafe down the harbour. It wouldn't be loads of money, but it’d be… something tangible, you know?

…and honestly, the Gantt chart was  completely  out of sync. Like, three deadlines had shifted without anyone telling me! I spent the entire morning chasing people down. I swear, project management is 90% firefighting. Tell me about it! Marketing's the same, just with slightly prettier PowerPoint presentations. You’d think having a structured process would be a given, but it’s like pulling teeth sometimes. Oxford’s a bit posh for that kind of chaos though, isn’t it? Feels a bit…elevated. That's what I thought! My sister suggested it, said it was good for a "civilised catch-up”. As if catching up with you ever requires civilisation. Remember that camping trip in Snowdonia? Oh god, don't remind me! The midges! And you trying to build a fire with damp twigs. You looked like you were battling a woodland dragon. Honestly, you were a sight. Did you finally get a better tent? Eventually. After several soggy nights. No, I haven’t been camping since. I’m a bit of a princess now, apparently. Floral wallpaper and spreadsheets. It’s a far cry from battling midges. So, how  is  Pearson treating you? Still drowning in influencer campaigns and hashtag strategies? Pretty much. It's… a lot. The pressure to constantly be ‘on’ is exhausting. This new campaign for their language learning app is insane. They want me to create a whole series of TikTok dances. A  dance , Poppy! Me! I’m not exactly known for my moves. No way! You’d kill it though. You’ve got the sass for it. Think of the views! Seriously though, that sounds brutal. Are you enjoying it, deep down? Parts of it, yeah. The creative side is fun when it's not dictated by analytics. But the constant need to justify everything with data… it's stifling. It’s making me think, actually. I've been looking at some online courses, data analytics ironically. Just in case. Smart move. Secure your future. Have you found anyone yet? I mean, dating in London... it's practically a competitive sport. Don't even. Disaster after disaster. Last one was a vegan yoga instructor who talked exclusively about his aura. My aura felt very assaulted. What about you? Still with Tom? We're… on a break. It's complicated. We’ve grown apart, I think. He’s been wanting to move to Bristol, and I’m really getting settled here.

Honestly, Liam, you're worse than your grandma at this online lark. Look at this! Four boxes for a single set of headphones. Four! And all individually wrapped in mountains of plastic. Honestly, it’s enough to give you the vapours. Well, I needed them, didn't I? And they were cheaper on Amazon. Significantly cheaper. Besides, Grandma’s a bargain hunter of the highest order. You know that. She’d haggle a blind man out of his guide dog. Don't you be disrespectin' your grandma, now. She's got a shrewd eye for a deal, I’ll grant her that. But there’s a difference between a sensible bargain and just...this. This consumerism! Don't you think about the planet a bit, love? All this packaging... Yeah, yeah, I know. But it’s convenient, isn't it? And you used to order loads online, didn’t you? Remember that ridiculous collection of vintage teacups you bought last year? That was different! That was a very specific interest, and they were practically giving them away. And I re-used the boxes, didn’t I? Every single one. You just chuck them straight in the recycling, don't you? Mostly. Look, the thing is, you can get stuff so much faster on Amazon. For example, that book you wanted for your exam marking – “Advanced Quadratic Equations and Problem Solving”? Amazon Prime delivered it in two days. Ebay said it'd be a week. Aye, but have you looked at Ebay properly? You can find proper treasures on there. Things with history. And you can often get them for pennies! I was lookin' at a lovely old gramophone the other day. Bit scratched, needed some work, but… oh, it just screamed 'character'. Amazon doesn't scream character, Liam. It screams mass production. Gramophones are a bit… archaic, aren't they? I’d rather just stream my music. Plus, Ebay can be a risky business. Remember Uncle Paul’s experience with that ‘vintage’ amplifier? Turned out to be a glorified box with lights. Don't remind me! Honestly, that was a right fiasco. But you just have to be careful. Read the seller's feedback, check their return policy... it's not  all  dodgy, you know. Sometimes you get lucky. I got a beautiful antique lace shawl on Ebay last year for a steal. Genuine Victorian lace. Fair enough. But the convenience factor is hard to beat.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of data we're processing now is just… staggering. It used to be a spreadsheet, you know? A decent-sized one, but manageable. Now it’s feeding into algorithms, predicting potential bottlenecks, optimising flow… it’s a whole different beast. I’m learning a lot, but sometimes I feel like I’m just chasing my tail. Algorithms, you say? Sounds a bit fancy, that does. Back in my day, if something went wrong on the line, you just popped down and had a good look, didn’t you? A bit of elbow grease, a bit of common sense, that’s all you needed. No need for computers to tell you what's broken. Well, it’s a bit more complex than something just being ‘broken’, Uncle Arthur. We’re talking about predicting delays before they even happen. Like, recognising a pattern of slightly slower production on a particular machine, even if it’s  not  showing obvious signs of malfunction. The algorithm alerts us, we can schedule preventative maintenance, and boom – production stays on track. Preventative… maintenance. Right. So, you’re already fixing things before they’ve broken? Seems a bit… pessimistic, doesn’t it? Always waiting for the worst. Used to be, you fixed things  after  they broke. Less fuss, see? Less worry. It's not pessimistic, it's efficient. It saves time, money, and ultimately, jobs. If we don't stay ahead of the curve, we’ll be left behind. It’s about optimisation, Uncle. Making everything run as smoothly as possible. Optimisation. There’s a lot of that ‘optimisation’ going on these days, innit? Seems like everything's got to be squeezed for every last drop. Remember Mr. Henderson at the print works? Good man, Henderson. Didn’t worry about optimisation. Just did a good job. Produced excellent leaflets, he did. Proper quality. I'm sure he did. But the print works closed down, didn't they? Couldn’t compete with the digital printers. They were optimised. Faster, cheaper… Aye, that’s the way of it, I suppose. Progress, they call it. But is it really? Lost good lads, that print works. Proper skilled craftsmen. Now it’s all screens and computers. Don't know a hot metal letter from a hole in the ground, most of 'em. It’s different, Uncle, but it's not necessarily worse. People are still skilled, just in different ways.

…No, seriously! Mum's going absolutely mental about the turkey this year. She's ordered one of those heritage breeds – apparently, they taste better. Costs a bloody fortune, mind. Says it’s “essential for Christmas.” I’m like, “Mum, you could buy a small car for that.” Classic. Your mum always does go overboard. I’m just hoping I can get enough mince pies baked in time. It's mental at the bakery, you know? People panic-buying everything weeks before. Did you manage to book flights, though? Christmas Day flying – a bit mad? Yeah, flights are booked. Managed to snag something relatively decent, though I had to wrestle a pensioner for it online, honestly. Christmas Day flying… yeah, it's a bit bonkers, innit? But it's only for like, six hours. Gives me the whole of Boxing Day with the family. Worth it for the few days, I reckon. What about you? Are you heading up to Birmingham? Almost certainly. Still finalising things at the café, you know how it is – last minute cancellations, staffing issues… it’s a constant juggle. But yeah, Boxing Day will be spent with Mum and Dad. I'm actually looking forward to it. Are you bringing anything special to the table, then, Jamie? Besides a wallet-emptying turkey. Honestly, not really. Probably just the usual. Mum’s got a new cranberry sauce recipe she’s apparently been working on for months. It involves port and orange zest, apparently. Sounds intense. I'll bring the board games – Monopoly, Scrabble, the whole lot. Prepare for carnage. Board games, eh? Good on ya! Sounds like a right laugh. Christmas, though… it's just not the same over here, is it? Feels… manufactured. Back home, you used to just chuck a barbie on, wear shorts, and sweat your guts out. Now I’m bundled up in three layers and pretending I enjoy mulled wine. You're missing out on the tradition, mate! The stiff upper lip, the forced family cheer… it’s all part of the experience! Besides, last year you were complaining about the heat and craving a proper winter storm. True, true. Can't win, can ya? Speaking of strange things I saw today… while I was cycling in, I swear I saw a deer, just  lying  in the road. Proper big fella. Must’ve been hit. It was awful. Oh, that’s awful! Poor thing.

…and honestly, the sheer variety you hear in Cambridge is mental. I was listening to this guy in a café earlier, ordering a scone, and he sounded like he was straight out of Cornwall. Completely different to anyone else in the place! Proper Cornish, yeah? Like, full-on 'woodya know'? You don't get that much in Brum. It’s pretty standard Midlands accents mostly, you know? A bit of a mumble sometimes, but mostly just… straightforward. Straightforward is code for non-distinct, isn’t it? No offence, Liam. But Cambridge’s pulling in people from  everywhere . We were talking about it at work - the international team are a mine of vocal information, if you know what I mean. The German developer's accent just melts into everything he says, though. It's bizarre. Melting into everything is the key thing, isn't it? Everyone subtly shifting their cadence and vowels. Makes you wonder if we all intrinsically try to fit in, subconsciously. Maybe. Or maybe it's just people being comfortable. I mean, I don’t try to sound like I’m from Cornwall when I'm back home. It'd sound a bit… forced. True. Speaking of comfort, are you sure about this car, Anon? It’s practically prehistoric. I mean, it  works , but… it's got the aerodynamics of a brick. Oh, relax, Tom. It’s vintage! Besides, Anon gets us there, doesn’t he? And think of the character! You can't buy character, can you? It's reliable, isn’t it the main thing? Besides, I’ve checked the oil and the water, so we're good to go. How about that revised route, Anon? You said you were looking at avoiding the M11 for a bit? Yeah, I am. The M11 is a nightmare, especially on a Friday evening. Currently, I’m thinking the A10 and then cutting across through Ely. It’s a bit longer, about fifteen minutes extra I reckon, but… it’s usually less congested. Fifteen minutes? That's practically an eternity when you're crammed in this… this… mobile museum. But alright, if you think it's the better option. As long as we don’t end up stranded on some farm track. It'll be grand. I've got the sat nav set. And I've got a playlist sorted – a mix of Britpop and some newer stuff. Should keep us entertained.

Yeah, alright, alright. It's just another trap beat, Liam. We’ve heard it before. Everything sounds the same these days. Everything? Seriously, Tom? You’re saying everything’s the same? Have you  listened  to anything outside of your post-rock playlists? This is different. It builds, you know? It’s got layers. Check the percussion. Layers of…808s. And autotune. Look, I appreciate the build-up, I do, but it's ultimately a repetitive loop designed to get people jumping. It’s formulaic. I prefer something with a bit more… nuance. Like Explosions in the Sky. Remember that gig we went to last year?  That  was layers. You’re both being a bit intense. It’s just music. Liam's got a point, though. Trap  has  got some clever stuff going on. Especially some of the producers. Have you heard of Kenny Beats? He does those YouTube series where he just freestyle beats with rappers. It's actually really interesting to see the creation process. See! Even Raj gets it. Kenny Beats is fire, man! He's proper talented. Tom, you'd probably be all about the physics of sound production or something. Well, I  was  thinking about the Fourier analysis involved in synthesizing that bass frequency. The harmonic series… Right, right, equations and stuff. Let’s not do a physics lecture in the school hallway, yeah? I was just saying, you’re always analyzing things, Tom. You need to just  feel  it sometimes. It’s a vibe. Speaking of feeling things… Did you guys see the new Oppenheimer film? Actually, yes! I went on Saturday. It was… extraordinary. The sheer scale of the visuals, the way Nolan handles time… it’s breathtaking. Though, the physics… I have some serious questions about the accuracy of some of the depictions of the chain reaction. Here we go, the physics is back! I thought it was good, yeah. Intense. Kinda depressing, though. All that for a bomb. The moral ambiguity was what got me, I think. You see him as this brilliant mind, a flawed genius, then you realize he’s directly responsible for… well, you know. And the Trinity test scene was insane. The sound design was brutal. Absolutely. Nolan really committed to the practical effects. Minimizing CGI was a brilliant decision. It made the whole thing feel so much more… visceral. Although, I did notice a slight inaccuracy in the representation of the Compton wavelength… it would have changed the… Seriously, Tom!

“…and honestly, the Balanceability bikes are brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. Finn, you were getting so frustrated on the pedals, weren't you? Just wobbling all over the place. Now, look at you! Zooming around like a little speed demon.” “Zoom! Vroom! I’m a race car!” “Zoom!” “That’s right, Poppy! Zoom, zoom! You’ll be zooming too soon, sweetheart.” "Honestly, I nearly had a breakdown trying to teach you to ride. It was all tears and, 'I can't do it!' It's amazing how much easier it is without the pedals. It's all about balance, isn't it? You’ve got to master that first. Reminds me a bit of teaching, actually. Sometimes you have to strip things back to basics, just focus on the core skills.” “Miss Davies said it’s like building a tower with blocks. If the bottom is wobbly, the tower falls!” “Exactly! Miss Davies is a clever one. See? You’re learning lots at school. How was school today, anyway?" “Good! Leo’s house is getting fixed up. It’s got loads of scaffolding now and they're building a… a splashy thing!” “A splashy thing? What do you mean?” “A swimming pool! And a waterfall! A manmade one! Leo says it’s going to be super cool but Mummy says they can’t dive in it.” “Your mummy’s right to say that, love. Diving into water you can't see properly is really dangerous. You always need to check the depth first. We talked about that at school, didn’t we? About water safety?” “Yeah. Miss Davies said…don’t jump unless you can see the bottom! And don’t go near the waterfall!” "Poppy's hungry! Everything's all action with you two. Speaking of action, how about some pizza tonight? You fancy pizza, Finn?" “Yes! With pepperoni and mushrooms!” "Pepperoni and mushrooms - now that’s a good combo. You know, I was chatting with Sophie's mum the other day - Sophie’s the one with the bright pink wellies, remember? – and she was saying how stressful the renovations on their new house are." “Is Leo’s house stressful too?” “Probably a bit. But it sounds amazing with the swimming pool! It’s just a lot of work. Makes you appreciate a calm, tidy kitchen, doesn’t it? Though right now, it’s looking a bit like a cyclist’s track with your Balanceability bike going everywhere!"

Aye, I get that. I were feelin' similar a few months back. Everything felt like a right fettle. Absolutely no get-up-and-go. Right, CAMRA, innit? Exactly! "Can't be arsed." You're brilliant at describing it. Though, I was hoping to be past that stage by now. I set myself this whole fitness goal – run a 5k in under 30 minutes by the end of the summer – and I've barely managed a park shuffle. Park shuffle! That's a grand description. Listen, lass, you've got a postgrad, right? Serious brain power. Don’t tell me a little 5k's got you down. What's got to you, really? 'Cause it's rarely just about the exercise, is it? You’re probably right. I think…it's Mark. Mark, as in,  the  Mark? The one you were moanin' about last Christmas bein' a bit…distant? Yeah, that’s the one. He’s working ridiculous hours, which is fine, I understand the pressure, but it feels like the only time we connect is when he's ranting about spreadsheets. And he’s… well, he’s stopped asking about my day. Just assumes everything’s fine. Stone the crows. That's no' good, love. No’ one wants to be treated like wallpaper. Sounds like he needs a good conversation, doesn't he? A proper sit-down, not just a mention over dinner. I’ve tried! But he just deflects. “Busy, busy, need to focus.” It’s a record. I was thinking about suggesting couple’s therapy, but… it feels drastic. Drastic? Naah. It's sensible. If you’re both stuck, get someone to help unstick you. I’ve seen it work wonders with my auntie and uncle. They were no' seein' eye-to-eye for years, thought their marriage were gonner. Couple of sessions with a therapist and they’re as thick as thieves now. Honestly, hearing that makes me feel a bit less crazy for even considering it. Okay, I'll look into it. Maybe even suggest it subtly. Good on you. And listen, about the exercise… don't kill yourself with the 5k goal. Start small. We could go for a walk along the river next week? Proper Yorkshire ramble, fresh air, nice scenery. Take your mind off things, and maybe even have a good natter. That actually sounds really lovely. I'd like that a lot. Just a gentle walk.

Aye, that’s the ticket. Proper good this is, isn’t it, lad? Better than last week, I reckon. Remember last week’s pepperoni was a bit… sparse, weren't it? Yeah, it was. This one's got loads! And extra cheese. Thanks, Auntie Brenda. Don’t mention it, pet. It’s the least I can do after battling that dreadful traffic on the A1. Honestly, it were a nightmare. That lorry driver, flashing his lights like he owned the road. Reckon he’d never seen a woman driving before! You wouldn’t believe it, the state of some folks. Oh, you've met 'em, Brenda. Every Tuesday night, don't you? Them Domino Drives are a right battleground these days. Used to be able to get your order in and it'd be here within the hour, proper quick. Now, you're lucky if it’s in before eight. Uncle George, did you see Newcastle beating Man U on Saturday? Proper good game! Aye, didn’t miss it. Brilliant, that was. Gordon Ramsay was giving it right out on commentary, wasn’t he? Said they needed a bit more grit, they did. Honestly, though, some of those players... a bit on the slim side, aren't they? Not like the lads we had back in my day. Solid, they were. Built like brick outhouses. Don't you start comparing them to your ‘day’, George! It were a different game entirely. Besides, size isn’t everything. It’s about skill, isn't it? And the young lad, Saint-Maximin, he’s got a bit of everything, hasn’t he? Wonder what we'll be doing for Easter, eh? Still too early to tell, I suppose. Mum's talking about going to Whitby. Maybe we could get an ice cream. And look at the seals! Whitby, eh? Nice spot. Remember bringing your mother there when she was your age, Brenda. Cold as anything it was, but she loved it. Had a right squall blowing off the sea. Nearly lost me hat! You always did have a way of making things dramatic, didn’t you, George? Still, Whitby's lovely. Though I do fancy a nice restaurant meal somewhere. We've been having too much takeaway lately. Something posh, maybe? Not like that chippy down the road, mind. That batter's always a bit soggy. Can we go to that Italian place in Durham?

…and honestly, lad, the rhubarb crumble at The Wearside Tavern? Proper showstopper. You wouldn't believe how good it was. It puts all this posh Cambridge stuff to shame, doesn’t it? All their fancy micro-greens and air-dried this-and-thats. Give me a proper, honest rhubarb crumble any day. You’re biased, love. It’s nostalgia talking. And The Wearside Tavern is…well, it’s The Wearside Tavern. Charming, in a dusty, slightly sticky kind of way. But Cambridge does some decent food, you know. I had a phenomenal roasted cauliflower the other day - charred perfectly, romesco sauce… Roasted cauliflower? Sounds like rabbit food, doesn’t it? Honestly, you academics and your sophisticated palates. Back home, a vegetable was either potato, carrot, or peas. Though, to be fair, my Nan did a cracking parsnip mash. But still! Roasted cauliflower? It wasn’t just cauliflower. It was about the  execution . The balance of flavours. You wouldn’t appreciate it. You’re a crumble and gravy kind of girl. And proud of it! See, that’s the difference, isn’t it? You’re analysing the ‘balance of flavours’ and I’m thinkin' “Does this taste like proper comfort food?”. Did you see that Piers Morgan’s had another right barney on Twitter? Oh, don't get me started on Piers. Honestly, the man’s got a nose for controversy. He just  needs  to be outraged about something. It's like a nervous tic. I saw him tweeting about that Kate Garraway thing – absolutely dreadful. Aye, that's rough, isn't it? Poor lass. He’s just…constant turbulence, that one. Like a permanent storm cloud. Speaking of storms, remember that time we tried to make Yorkshire pudding in your student house? Absolute disaster. It looked like deflated footballs. Don’t remind me! The oven was all wonky, wasn’t it? And you insisted on using lard, which I thought was a bit...excessive. We ended up ordering pizza. Much better than failing at Yorkshire puddings. Lard’s the key, though! It gives 'em that crispy bit. You've got to get the fat right. It's science, really. So, what's the dissertation looking like? Still swimming in the qualitative data swamp? You have no idea. It’s a beast. I'm trying to get a handle on this grounded theory stuff, but it’s like chasing shadows. I’m starting to think I should have just done a quantitative study.

Right, okay. “Platypus.” Seriously? Who comes up with these words? It's just…mean! I’m going to be stuck on this forever. Come on, Seren, don’t be like that! It's Articulate, it’s supposed to be challenging! Besides, you're the teacher, you’re used to explaining complex concepts to bewildered children. A platypus isn’t that hard. Think…bill…Australia…poisonous… Poisonous? They're not poisonous, Rhys! They have a spur on their hind legs that delivers a mild venom. It's defence, not poison. Small difference, you know. Details, Gethin, details. It's the spirit of the game! You're meant to be helping your team, not correcting my zoological knowledge. Spirit of the game, he’s right about that! We need to be quick and witty, not dissecting animal toxins! Back in my day, in Singapore, we played this with hushed intensity. No room for pedantry! My wife, bless her, was a whiz at these things. Used to be able to spell ‘chrysanthemum’ backwards. Oh, Dai, you and your stories! Singapore? You always say that. You lived there for two years, that’s hardly a lifetime! And I distinctly remember your wife struggling with ‘onomatopoeia’ at Christmas. That was a trick question! Designed to fluster. It’s all about presentation, dear. Confidence! Seren, you look like you’re about to surrender. Don’t! Think…paddle…duck-billed… I'm trying, I am! It’s just the pressure. Right, okay. “P…l…a…t…” Oh, this is hopeless. Rhys, help! You’re good at thinking on your feet. Alright, alright. Think about what they do. What's their habitat like? Where do they live? They lay eggs! It's a mammal that lays eggs! That's key. Eggs! Yes! Okay, so… “P…l…a…t…y…” Oh goodness, how do you spell that? It's 't-u', love. Remember? You teach spelling every week. I know, I know! It just completely left my brain. "P...l...a...t...y...u...s." Did I get it? Yes! Brilliant! You did it! See? Not so hard after all. You were thinking too much. Just relax and let the words flow. Good on you, Seren! A bit tense, but you got there in the end. Reminds me of a time I was trying to explain the rules of cricket to a group of schoolchildren in… Dai, Dai! We’re playing Articulate, remember?

Speaker_1 said, shuffling the remaining cards with practiced ease. Her South African accent, softened by years in England, was still noticeable. “Honestly, you Welsh are fiendishly good at these games.” Speaker_2 , a man with a warm smile and a thick Welsh lilt, slapped the table lightly. “It’s in our blood, Sarah! Years of battling for sheep and land, you need a sharp mind and a bit of cunning. Besides," he added, flashing a mischievous look, "you’ve been hogging the jacks all evening.” Speaker_3 , Dafydd's older brother, a researcher who’d recently returned from a post-doc abroad, chuckled from the corner of the sofa. "Don’t let him distract you, Sarah. He's just trying to justify his terrible poker face. Look at him, barely blinking! Textbook bluff.” Sarah laughed. “Rhys, you’re a scientist, not a card shark. It’s  possible  he's genuinely good. Though, I maintain my suspicion of Welsh superiority in card games.” She dealt the next hand. “Right then, new round. Bets?” Speaker_4 , Dafydd and Rhys’s mother, who'd been quietly observing, piped up from her armchair. "Honestly, the noise you lot make! It sounds like a flock of sheep arguing. Back in my day, we played whist, quietly, with a cup of tea. No shouting and grand gestures." She chuckled, a warm, melodic sound. “Though, I did win a lovely silver teapot once, playing whist at Mrs. Evans’ birthday.” "A silver teapot, Mum? That’s serious winnings!" Dafydd exclaimed, genuinely impressed. "Did you bluff anyone?" Eira shrugged, her eyes twinkling. “Just enjoyed the game, love. Honesty used to be a more valued skill, you know. Nowadays, everyone’s trying to trick each other.” “That's the fun of it, Mum!” Rhys retorted playfully. “Adds a bit of spice. Besides, you were always a cunning whist player.” Sarah, watching the playful banter unfold, added, “It  is  a bit like teaching, isn’t it? Trying to gauge who’s being honest, who’s trying to lead you on… though thankfully, the consequences of a bad bluff are usually a bit less severe than a failing grade.” “True enough,” Dafydd agreed, studying his hand. “So, anyone fancy a break soon? I’m thinking we could walk down to the river later. It’s gorgeous down there, especially with the evening light.” “That sounds lovely, Dafydd,” Eira said. “But not until  after  I’ve had a proper cuppa.

"Tell me about it! Mum keeps going on about how I need to learn to cook and manage my finances before I go. Like, hello? I'm sixteen! I still ask her where the washing powder is!" "Mum’s the same with me. Though she's more obsessed with me finding a ‘respectable’ job after. Says care work isn’t a long-term plan. Says I need 'stability'." She rolls her eyes. "As if anything’s stable these days. At least the residents are lovely, mostly. Mrs. Henderson tells the  best  stories, even if half of them are probably made up.” "My apprenticeship is going pretty well, actually. They've thrown me into loads of different things at the firm. It's definitely intense, but I’m learning loads about accounts. And the pay's decent, you know? Way better than my Saturday job at the coffee shop last year. Want to hear a joke about tax returns?" "Please do! Anything to distract from the fact I'm basically volunteering in the Navy right now. Learn to do the ‘Combat Systems’ and pray I don’t freeze on a ship somewhere. It's… different. Not exactly ‘university’ vibe." He shivers dramatically. “Volunteering eh? Sounds fancy! I'm just stacking shelves at Sports Direct, trying to save up for that sound system I’ve been eyeing. Sarah, you going to apply for a student loan then?” "I think so. Dad says we'll manage, but… it’s still a lot of money. And I’d rather not be saddled with debt for the rest of my life, you know? What about you, Chloe? Do you reckon you’ll get financial help?" “Probably not much. Mum and Dad both work, but it’s not exactly a fortune. It’s the usual, really. Gonna have to work through uni, no doubt. Hoping I can maybe work weekends at the care home – it’d be familiar, at least. Less scary than starting something completely new.” "Uni’s not your only option, though. Honestly, Emily’s apprenticeship is amazing. They pay you while you study, and you get experience. It's way less stressful than loads of essays." “True. I kind of wish I’d thought about an apprenticeship. My mate, Liam, is doing a mechanical engineering one and he’s loving it. He says he gets to actually  build  things, which sounds considerably better than paperwork."

Honestly, these puffins. They build the most peculiar little nests, don’t they? All cobbled together with twigs and feathers. Makes you wonder how they stay put in that wind. They're amazing, actually, Mum. They can fly hundreds of miles to find food. It’s incredible. Wind's nothin’. Try living in Cuckfield back in ‘88. Remember that storm, Chloe? Blew a whole shed down Mrs. Higgins’ back garden. Sent it flying right over onto the cricket pitch. Grandpa, you tell that story every time the wind picks up. He does, doesn’t he? Always a memory to share, our Liam. Speaking of moving about… I was thinking, maybe we could all go for a nice stroll in Grantchester Meadows tomorrow. Weather’s supposed to be decent. A stroll? All that tramping around? My knees ain’t what they used to be, love. Give me a good chair and the telly any day. Come on, Grandpa, it’ll be good for you. Fresh air, a bit of sunshine. We could take it easy. Mum could push you in the wheelchair if you need a rest. Don’t you go thinking I'm going to be pushing you around all day, Liam! I’ve got my own walking to do, thank you very much. You know, I saw a cyclist nearly get knocked over on Mill Road today. Proper reckless, the way people drive around here. Reckless? Drivers are terrible everywhere! When I were a lad… Grandpa, please. Not the driving stories. We've heard them all. Remember when you tried to parallel park your Morris Minor in Billingsgate Market? That was different! That was a tight spot! And besides, those lorries… they weren't giving way properly. They didn’t appreciate a fella trying to navigate. Oh, Liam. You and your lorries. Honestly, it’s a wonder you ever got out of Cuckfield. You know what I was thinking though, Chloe, about you getting a car. A car? Mum, I’ve told you, I don’t  need  a car. The bus is fine, and I cycle everywhere. It’s much better for the environment. But imagine the freedom, darling! You could pop down to Brighton for the weekend whenever you fancied. You could give Liam a lift. He's stuck here, bless him, glued to the telly. I’m not stuck! I have… companionship. From the telly. And the puffins.

…and honestly, the sheer density of linguistic features in the Basque Country is just astonishing. We were trying to map out the dialect continua, and it’s a nightmare, a wonderfully complex nightmare, but still. It makes even classifying regional accents in England look straightforward! Absolutely! I've been poring over some fairly dense academic papers on Basque language contact this week, actually. It's remarkable how it’s maintained a presence despite centuries of pressure from Castilian. Did you manage to get out into the rural areas at all while you were there? Because that's where the real richness lies, isn’t it? We tried! We rented a car, naturally. But the roads… honestly, some of them were barely wider than a donkey cart. We ended up getting delightfully lost a couple of times, which, in retrospect, was probably the best thing. We stumbled across this tiny village, Eibar I think, and an elderly gentleman was happily chattering away to his neighbour in what sounded like poetry. Of course, I only understood about three words. Poetry, eh? Basque is full of it. Wonderful, evocative language. I spent a considerable chunk of my own research examining the influence of Celtic languages on Basque, though it’s a debate that still rages, of course. Shropshire's fairly close to Wales, you see, so I’ve always had a bit of an affinity for the Celtic fringe. Oh, really? That's fascinating! I hadn't considered the Celtic link so strongly. I’m Eleanor, by the way, Language Research Co-ordinator here. I’m Sophie, Language Research Administrator. And you are…? Arthur Penhaligon. University Lecturer, primarily specialising in historical linguistics. And it's a pleasure to meet both of you. So, a Language Research Co-ordinator, you say? What area are you focusing on at the moment? Beyond the Basque, naturally. We've got a project running looking at the impact of Mandarin Chinese on urban dialects in London. It’s surprisingly nuanced. There's a lot of code-switching and borrowing happening, particularly amongst younger generations, but it’s not a straightforward language shift. It's... layered. You know? We’re trying to quantify the specific lexical and grammatical influences. Honestly, it's a right lark trying to keep up with slang these days though, innit. Tell me about it! It changes so quickly. We did some preliminary work on how Polish loanwords have infiltrated East London dialects, which was a really interesting, if occasionally challenging, data set to work with.

Sounds like Sheila. She's really embraced Facebook, hasn't she? Remember when she thought it was a conspiracy to steal her pictures? Exactly! Now she’s practically a food blogger. It’s surreal. Though, the ice bucket challenge thing was a good distraction from the casserole onslaught. Did you see cousin Mark did it? He looked so grumpy. Mark's always grumpy. He’s probably secretly pleased everyone’s looking at him though. It’s a classic attention-seeking move. Speaking of, Mum’s been badgering me to nominate people. I’m trying to avoid it, honestly. Keeps hinting I should get Liam involved, which… well, you know. Typical. She’s always trying to push Liam into things. You’ve just been back for two hours, haven’t you? Still, it’s good to finally see everyone, isn't it? It feels like ages. Where are the kids? They’re wreaking havoc in the garden, apparently. Mum said little Poppy tried to bury the cat. Again. Honestly! That child. She gets it from your mum, you know. Constant mischief. Remember when Mum used to try and teach us all those complicated arts and crafts projects? We’d end up gluing glitter everywhere, and Mum would be stressed beyond belief. Oh, I remember! The Christmas decorations were a disaster every year. It’s funny, isn’t it? You think being a child would be carefree. Mum’s always worrying, even now. She sent me a list of dietary requirements for everyone before we even arrived. Gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free... it's exhausting! Sounds about right. Though, to be fair, she is trying. Trying to cater for everyone's peculiar sensitivities. You know, I was thinking about adoption the other day, actually. It’s something I've always been quite interested in. Wow, that’s a big thought. You’d be brilliant at it, honestly. You’re so patient. It's definitely something to consider. Have you looked into qualifications or anything? Just a little bit. It seems like an absolute maze of paperwork and applications. Forms for days! I almost got overwhelmed just looking at the initial inquiries. It's surprisingly complex. I'm teaching English to a Sudanese refugee family at the moment and it's made me think about these things a lot. They've been through so much, you know. It’s amazing the things you learn through your job.

Honestly, this coffee machine is a nightmare. It's either lukewarm or explodes with grounds everywhere. I’m starting to miss instant. Now, now, Eleanor, don't you start. Your father’s handiwork, you know. He's determined to master it. It’s… a project. Project is putting it mildly, love. It's a potential hazard. Near caused a volcanic eruption this morning, it did. Well, volcanic eruptions are  exactly  what I need before 9am. Seriously, though, we need to get a quote for a decent one. Maybe when the removal people come back with a final figure. Speaking of which, did you hear anything more from 'Man with a Van'? They were awfully vague about storage costs. I chased them up this morning. It’s…complicated. They’re quoting per cubic foot, but they don't seem to have a proper idea of how much  stuff  we're moving. It's unbelievable. Dad has boxes of…well,  everything . Remember those stamps? Seriously, the man collects stamps from Liechtenstein. They’re valuable, Eleanor! Show some respect for the hobby! And Liechtenstein is a perfectly respectable country. He does have a point, dear. Every little thing has a memory attached. It’s… bittersweet, isn't it? Leaving Dublin, finally selling the house. It’s a big shift. I know, Mum. And finding somewhere to store Dad’s stamp collection, and his model trains, and… …everything! It’s going to bankrupt us. Should have just thrown most of it out. Don't even suggest such a thing! This is history, Eleanor! Family history! And besides, a man needs his pursuits. It keeps him occupied. He does. Keeps him out of trouble, too. You know, I was listening to the radio this morning... all the talk about the Labour leadership… it’s just disheartening. Tell me about it. It feels like a competition to be the  least  inspiring. Do you think Starmer has any real idealism left? It all seems so…calculated. Calculated is what you need in politics, love. Idealism is for poets and dreamers. Look at what happened when we had a 'man of the people'. Disaster! Pure disaster. But shouldn’t there be  some  room for hope, for trying to improve things? I used to think… well, teaching maths, you see shapes and structures, the possibility of logic, of reaching a correct answer. Politics feels increasingly chaotic, without any framework. I get what you mean, Mum.

Oh, darling, that does sound a lot. Still, the little ones will love it, won't they? You always were brilliant with children. Remember when you used to put on those puppet shows in the garden when you were little? Absolutely captivating. Though, I do recall you almost setting the shed on fire with that cardboard dragon. Oh God, don't remind me! Dad nearly had a heart attack. I was convinced that dragon was breathing real fire, you know? Kids are so… imaginative. It's a good thing, mostly, but it does make Santa-themed classroom management a tad tricky. Little Timmy was convinced Santa was a lizard last year. A green one. Bless him. These days, they just pick up everything they hear, don’t they? Still, a lizard Santa – that’s a new one. So, what about your own Christmas plans? Are you seeing anyone special this year? Nah, no special someone this Christmas. It’ll just be me, you, and Dad, I think. I was thinking of trying to bake a proper Christmas cake this year, though. Not one of those shop-bought things. I’ve found a recipe online - apparently, it needs to ‘mature’ for like, a month. A month! Good heavens. You’ll be busy then, won't you? I remember your grandmother used to start hers in October. Proper tradition, that. Listen, I was thinking, wouldn’t it be lovely if we invited Sarah and David over this year? They’ve been rattling on about how they'd love to spend Christmas with family proper, not just a tiny tree in their flat in London. That’s a lovely idea, Mum. I’d really like that. But… are you sure? You and Dad have been doing the quiet Christmas thing for a few years now. It’s your peaceful time, isn't it? It  was , darling. But it does get a bit… quiet. And David's nieces and nephews are quite a handful, apparently. A little chaos might do us some good. Besides, Sarah’s a wonderful cook; she makes the most delicious Yorkshire puddings. You know how your father adores a good Yorkshire pudding. You're right. He does. Okay, let’s do it then. I’ll call Sarah later and check with her. I can make a big roast dinner. I was thinking of getting that fancy goose from Farmer Giles' – you know, the one you always used to rave about?

Right, so Liam was out cold and she was making enough noise for the whole pub to hear? Sounds about right for Sarah, doesn't it? She always was a noisy one. Remember that time she tried to sing karaoke at The Rope and Anchor? Oh, don’t remind me! The whole place went silent. Just dead silence, then her. It was…memorable. But at least  you  are a peaceful sleeper, El. Peaceful? I'm out like a light! It's Liam I’m worried about. He looks knackered all the time. Reckon all that studying for his Masters is taking its toll. He does look a bit peaky. All that Excel spreadsheets can’t be good for the soul. He should treat himself to a Richmond sausage butty. Waterfields do the best ones, you know. Proper thick slices of bread and loads of that lovely caramelised onion relish. Waterfields are brilliant! Mum always got her loaves from there. Proper crusty. We used to practically live on their Yorkshire puddings too, especially on Sundays. But Richmonds… now you're talkin'! My gran used to say a good Richmond sausage was the cure for everything. Even a hangover! Your gran sounds like a wise woman! Speaking of cures, I’m having to use, like, three tissues every time Liam snores. My mum's sewing me some handkerchiefs, bless her. Says they’re more environmentally friendly. Handkerchiefs? Seriously, El? In this day and age? Sounds like something your grandma would carry. Oh, shut up, Liam. It’s practical! And saves the planet! Plus, they're soft, unlike those scratchy disposable ones. It’s the little things, innit? You could give him some earplugs, El. You know, those proper thick ones. Tried that! He says they make his ears hurt. Plus, he claims he can’t hear me if I'm trying to tell him something. Which, to be fair, isn’t a massive loss sometimes. Burn! You know, my cousin had a similar problem with her boyfriend. He was a  prolific  snorer. Seriously, you could hear him two rooms away. They ended up sleeping in separate beds for a while. Dramatic! I’m not going that far just yet. Although, sometimes I do fantasize about a separate bedroom… just for a few hours' peace. Mind you, then he’d probably get all morose and mope about. You’d miss me already? Don't be daft.

Honestly, Dad, that was  exactly  what I needed. Just a proper, lazy Sunday. I feel like a new woman. Aye, weren't bad, were they? Bit breezy down by the canal, though. Proper nippy once the sun started goin' down. Should’ve brought me scarf. Silly me, always forgettin’ things these days. You were moaning about the heat all morning! You said you’d melt if you wore a scarf. You’re impossible. But yeah, it  did  get a bit chilly. Did you manage to get all those photos of the ducks you wanted? Managed a few, yeah. Not the best quality, mind you. My hands were too cold to get a steady shot. They’re those pesky Indian Runner ducks, aren't they? Always lookin' like they’re marchin' to somewhere important. Proper funny to watch. They  are  ridiculous. I was laughing at them trying to dive for crumbs. That little boy kept chucking bread at them, practically pelting them. I hope they got enough. Did you have that pasty you were talking about? Did indeed! Lovely it was too. That little bakery in Kidderminster, they know how to make 'em. Proper Cornish pasty, not one of those sad imitations you get everywhere else. Reminded me of me Nan's, actually. She used to make 'em for us lads every Saturday. Oh, I love hearing about Nan’s cooking! What was her secret? Everyone makes pasties differently. She wouldn't tell anyone. Said it was a family secret. But I reckon it was just the quality of the ingredients. Good, honest beef, proper potatoes, a bit of swede… nothin’ fancy. And a lot of love, I suppose. Everything she made tasted like it. That sounds lovely. I miss her. Although, I wouldn’t trust you to make a pasty even if she  did  tell you the secret. You'd probably burn the potatoes. Now, that's not fair! I’ve made a few in me time. Not as good as Nan’s, obviously, but perfectly palatable. Anyway, what about you? Did you finish that report for Mr. Harrison? The one you were mutterin’ about all week? Ugh, don’t remind me. Nearly finished, actually. Just needs a final proofread and then it's off to him. I’m dreading his feedback, honestly. He’s such a stickler for detail. You know, he actually marked me down a half a point last quarter because I used the word "utilize" instead of "use."

Tell me about it! My lot are the same. Little Maisie, apparently, needs to be fluent by the time she's three. Three! She's just mastering ‘please’ and ‘thank you’, love. They get so caught up in the future, don’t they? It’s exhausting trying to manage expectations. Are you still at the language school in Oxford? Yeah, still there. It’s alright, the pay isn't brilliant, but it's… stable. And the students, for the most part, are lovely. Keeps things interesting. Though I'm seriously considering applying for that job at the international school in Bristol. Higher salary, smaller class sizes... Bristol, eh? That's a bit of a trek from Hitchin, isn’t it? Moving again? You’ve been all over, haven't you? A bit, yeah. Bit of a wanderer, I suppose. But it's good experience. You’re still at the primaries then? Stourbridge’s keeping you? Aye, still Stourbridge. Can’t complain, really. It's good, solid work. Miss you though, proper miss our lunch breaks dissecting pronunciation errors! It's not the same chatting to the TAs here. They just talk about the bake sales. Oh, I remember! Those were the days. Proper linguistic battles. Right, so, Maisie… how’s she going? Still firmly rejecting mashed vegetables? Still! Like they're some sort of personal insult. Honestly, you'd think she'd faced a hostile takeover by the broccoli. Mark’s trying to sneak them into spaghetti bolognese, but she's onto him. Clever little thing. We’re thinking of starting her on some basics, you know, maybe Duolingo or something. Just for fun, not expecting her to be reciting Baudelaire by her fifth birthday! Good idea! Early exposure is key, apparently. My niece, Chloe, is obsessed with Sesame Street – she picks up bits of Spanish constantly. Gets it all muddled up with English, of course, but it’s adorable. Have you tried any of those language-learning apps for little ones? They’re surprisingly clever. I've had a look, yeah. Little illustrations, songs... seems alright. I’m a bit wary though, you know? Don't want to push her into anything. It’s supposed to be fun. What about you? Any plans to learn another language properly? You always talked about wanting to learn Italian. Oh, Italian! Still on the list. Just… life, you know? Work, moving, everything else.

...and see, Bernard, the sparrows are particularly partial to the sunflower seeds, aren’t they? Clever little beggars, they are. Strategic, I’d say. Always the first ones on ‘em. Remember that nest we had buildin’ in the honeysuckle last year? Right proper engineering feat, that was. Little twigs, woven tight… reminded me a bit of the suspension bridge I worked on down in Ipswich, actually. Basic principles, y'know. Tension, compression…      Ipswich, eh? Fancy that. Didn't know you ever got down to Ipswich, Arthur. Always thought you were mostly fixin’ things around ‘ere. Though, minds you, this garden  does  need a bit of fixin’. Got a whole family of bindweed tryin’ to choke the roses.      Honestly, Bernard, don’t start on Arthur about gardening! He tries his best. Besides, look at all this bird life we’ve got! It’s lovely. And cake, everyone! I made a Victoria sponge. Hope it’s not too sweet; I’m tryin’ to be mindful, what with my blood sugars.      Victoria sponge! Lovely, Eleanor, lovely! Just what we needed. You've a right knack for bakin', you do. Got a proper crumb, that one. Diabetes, eh? A frightful business, that. My cousin, Margaret, she’s had a terrible time with it. Lost her leg, she did, years back.      Dreadful thing, diabetes. My sister, Doris, had it too. Kept sayin’ she felt like she was walkin’ on glass. Always complainin’ about her feet.      It's just… it’s the little things, isn't it? Having to check everything, watch everything. It’s tiring. Makes you feel…portly, sometimes. I’m thinking of getting one of those puppets again. You remember, Arthur? The little clown one? Used to amuse the children something fierce when I was childminding.      Aye, I remember. You’d put on a right show with that thing, Eleanor. Always had a way with kids. Though, to be honest, I was never one for the toys myself. Always preferred a good map, a level, somethin’ tangible. Still, a bit of laughter’s good for the soul, innit? Keeps the old grey matter workin’.      Laughter. Don't get much of that these days. Just aches and pains and doctors’ appointments. Feelin’ my age, I am. Seventy-three next month. Seventy-three! Can't believe it. Back’s playin’ up somethin' awful. Wish I could move about like I used to, chase after the pigeons.      Pigeons!

Honestly, this view alone makes the long journey worthwhile. You know, I was trying to teach little Leo to count to five in Turkish yesterday. "Bir, iki, üç..." He just kept giggling and pointing at the boats. He's got absolutely no patience for language learning, the little rascal. Leo, eh? He’s a whirlwind, isn’t he? Reminds me a bit of my grandson, Ollie. Though Ollie’s more interested in building elaborate Lego fortresses than boats. You’ve really done well with him, Susan. Single parenting ain't a picnic. It has its moments. Not complaining, mind. He's a joy, mostly. Speaking of joys, what are you thinking of ordering? I'm leaning toward the grilled octopus. Looks divine. Octopus? Bit adventurous for me, love. I'll stick with the kleftiko, I think. Can’t go wrong with a bit of lamb slow-cooked in that clay pot. Comfort food. You know, reminds me of my Aunt Mildred. She used to make a kleftiko that could knock your socks off. Proper magic, it was. She always swore she had a secret ingredient – a pinch of rosemary from her garden, blessed under a full moon. Aunt Mildred and rosemary blessings? You're pulling my leg! Not at all! She was a bit... unconventional, Mildred. Believed in dowsing rods and all sorts. Claimed she found the best spot for her prize-winning pumpkins using them. Said it was all about tapping into the Earth’s energy. I used to think she was daft, of course. But then... well, some things are hard to explain, aren't they? Like that time she predicted Mrs. Higgins' chihuahua would run off with the butcher’s sausages. And it did! Word for word. Now that  is  a story. It’s amazing how people get drawn into things like that. My mum, bless her, was fascinated by shamanism for a while. Attended some workshops, filled the house with crystals… said she was connecting with her inner spirit animal. People searching for something, I suppose. We all are, in our own way. I lost my sister, Agnes, last year. Cancer. Took her quick, it did. Suddenly. She’d always been so robust, you know? Then, bang. Gone. Oh, Edward, I'm so sorry. I know how much you loved her. It’s just… cruel. Mine's been battling with lupus for years. It's been a rollercoaster.

Oh, love, I know what you mean. My workload’s been a bit of a beast too, preparing for the mocks. The pressure on those kids… it's awful. They’re all so stressed. Do you remember Nicky Barnes, down at the village shop? His daughter’s taking her GCSEs this year. He's beside himself, giving her all sorts of special healthy snacks, bless him. Healthy snacks! Sounds like my dad used to do with us, come to think of it. Always a boiled egg and a piece of fruit before a rugby match. Didn’t exactly inspire greatness, did it? But you know, speaking of rugby, did you see the Harlequins game on Saturday? Brutal! Absolutely brutal. Thought they were a bit slow to react in the first half. Yeah, didn’t I? Thought the scrum was a bit dodgy too. It’s a shame, they were looking so strong a few weeks ago. But honestly, Dad, I'm trying to escape rugby for five minutes. I need a breather. This new project… it’s absolutely consuming me. And the flat… It’s just not working, you know? It’s too small, even for the two of us. We were thinking, maybe… well, we were looking at somewhere in Richmond. Richmond? That’s a bit pricey, isn’t it, love? Are you sure you can afford it? Remember, saving for that kitchen renovation is important. Your granddad used to say, 'A house is a home, but a well-equipped kitchen is heaven!' Always did put a lot of stock in a good Aga. He did, didn't he? Used to spend hours tinkering with it, trying to get the temperature just right. Richmond’s a lovely area though, loads of green space. Good schools, too, if you're thinking that might be in the future. And have you managed to sort out that leak in the bathroom yet? Still dripping, last time I was over? It's still there, Dad. I've booked a plumber, but he's not coming until next week. Honestly, the whole place is a fixer-upper. Which is why Richmond seemed appealing – a fresh start, a place that  doesn’t  need constant repairs. It's just… the money. We’re saving, obviously. Well, don’t rush into anything, pet. Have a good look around, really think about what you want. Your Auntie Maureen bought a place in Surbiton, you know.

…and then he sent me a picture of, like, a  face  picture clear as day! Proper profile pic, you know? And it was someone else’s! A lad from Manchester Uni, apparently. Proper cheek, innit? Seriously? You're havin' a laugh! You actually fell for that? Like, properly fallen? I thought you were smarter than that, love. Don’t go on at me, Liv! It’s not that simple. He'd been building it up, see? Loads of messages over weeks, we’d been chattin' about like, music and stuff. He was sayin’ all the right things, makin’ me laugh. And he said he was workin' abroad, in Australia, for a bit, doin' volunteer work. Sounded dead romantic, didn't it? Australia, eh? That’s a long way to go to catfish someone. What did he look like, this…volunteer? Generic, really. Nice smile, dark hair. You know, the kind of lad you’d think twice about, but you already like the person so… it slips past. He always had a reason he couldn’t video call. Bad signal, dodgy internet, you know the drill. Right, the classic excuses. Did you reverse image search the pic or anything? You know, like, a proper detective? I should've, shouldn't I? I did, eventually, after I got suspicious, that’s how I found out. Turned out he was on some sports team, lookin’ proper smug in a Man U shirt. Proper stung, it did. Like Jeremy Kyle, but online. Oh, that's awful, Beth. Makes you feel proper daft, doesn’t it? Like you’ve been played. Exactly! And the worst thing is, I spent ages pouring my heart out to him! About my exams coming up, how stressed I was… Honestly, I feel like a right idiot. No, you don’t. Don’t be silly. These catfish are professionals! They’re good at what they do. It's not your fault. Have you blocked him now? Course I have! Blocked, reported, deleted everythin’. Just feel a bit… rattled, mind. Makes you think, doesn’t it? About how easily people can pretend to be someone they’re not. It does. It's like watching a really messed-up TV show. Remember that episode of Jeremy Kyle where the bloke was pretending to be a single dad to get more maintenance money? Proper shocking, that was. Don’t remind me! It was brutal.

Right then, Nan, dig in. I made a bit too much, as usual. Hope you like it, it's just a simple pesto, nothing fancy. It smells delicious, darling. Thank you. You know, pesto reminds me of Florence. We had the most wonderful trattoria there, tucked away on a side street. They made it with basil grown right in the window boxes. Absolutely bursting with flavour. Florence’s on my list, definitely. I’m really hoping to get to Italy soon. Uni’s been a bit of a slog lately, but I've got a summer break coming up. Maybe I could even brush up on my Italian. It's been a while since I did any proper study of it. Oh, you should! You always had a knack for languages. Remember when you were little, you'd pick up phrases from the German tourists in Hyde Park? You were just parroting them at first, of course, but you had the ear for it. Always did. I wish I had kept up my German better, you know. So much of my childhood… my mother’s side… it was all spoken in German. Yeah, you’ve told me. It must be strange, having those memories tied to a language you don’t use much anymore. Speaking of languages, I'm having the absolute worst time with this computer. It’s just… refusing to connect to the university’s online library. I’ve been troubleshooting for hours. Drives me mad. Technology. A modern marvel, and a constant source of frustration. My dear Wolfgang wouldn’t have known what to do with it, bless his soul. Though, he was a man of the old ways, stubborn as a mule about anything that wasn't a paintbrush or a chisel. He’d much rather discuss the influence of Roman architecture on Parisian cafes. Remember our trip to Paris, darling? The Musée Rodin… Of course! That was amazing. The gardens alone were worth the trip. I’ve been reading about the influence of Classical sculpture on Rodin's work for my Art History module. It’s fascinating, actually. All those references to Greek and Roman forms... You're a proper scholar, you are. Just like your grandfather. He could quote Homer in his sleep! Classics were his life, completely obsessed. I used to tease him mercilessly. He'd be fussing over declensions when I was trying to get him to watch football!

Honestly, Dad, you were  that  close to clipping that bloke's wing mirror back there. Seriously! It was terrifying. I thought we were going to end up in a ditch. Now, now, love. No need to exaggerate. Just a bit of spirited driving, that’s all. These roads are narrow, innit? Can’t exactly dawdle, can we? Ms. Thornton’s been complaining about the build again, said they're metres from the original plan. Arthur, don’t encourage her! And Carol, please, a little less drama? I've been on my feet all day with Mrs. Higgins, pulling her socks up and reminding her where the toilet is. I just want a nice cup of tea in Dorset. This traffic is just awful, though. Should've left earlier. Typical holiday traffic, absolutely chock-a-block. See? Even Janet agrees! It’s just… you were overtaking a lorry on a blind bend! And I'm supposed to be writing my dissertation on post-structuralist literary theory, not witnessing near-death experiences. I’ve got this solicitor’s bill to think about, too. Ridiculous, the amount they charge. It's costing a fortune, practically half my student loan. Solicitors! Always after your money, they are. Remember old Mr. Finch down the road? Spent a fortune on one trying to get back his shed. Never did, mind you. Lost the whole thing. This Sat Nav is useless, too. Keeps trying to take us through tiny villages. Should've stuck with a map. Like we used to do. Actually, Arthur, speaking of money, did you get the MOT booked for the Ford? It's due next month. Don't leave it like you did with the Astra – remember the panic when that went? Carol, are you alright? You look a bit peaky. Been studying too hard? Yeah, I'm fine, just stressed. I've got this huge deadline coming up.
