Plus, I'm trying to help Mum sort out that hideous chair from Mantiques. It’s giving me a headache just  looking  at it. She's convinced it's a valuable antique, but I reckon it's just a dust trap. And she keeps going on about it, calling every day. Honestly, sometimes I wish I could just block her number. Though, she’s probably worried about me. She worries about everyone. Your Mum's a good woman. She worries because she cares. Just like your Grandma did.

…and then young Thomas, bless ‘im, he just smeared the entire plate of mashed potato across his face! Right across his little face! I had to give him a bath, of course, but he was giggling the whole time. Little scamp. Honestly, they keep you on your toes, don’t they? Even after all these years, the memory of it just makes me smile. Potato, eh? Used to grow ‘em in the garden back home, you know. Costessey. Big Maris Pipers. Could feed a whole village with what we got. My Dad… he were right proud of his potatoes. Said they were the backbone of a good Sunday dinner. I can imagine. Your father sounded like a good man. You don't talk about him much, do you, Arthur? No reason to, really, Brenda. He's gone. Been gone a good few years now. Not much to say, 'cept he worked hard. Honest sort. Did what he needed to do. Didn’t fuss. Didn’t complain. Not like some folks today, moanin’ about this and grumbling about that. Now, now, Arthur. Don’t start going on about the modern generation. They’ve got different challenges, you know. Challenges? Challenges were diggin' out a field in November when the frost were bitin’ your fingers off! That were a challenge. This… well, this just seems like everyone wants somethin’ for nothin’. That’s a bit harsh, isn't it? Not everyone’s like that. And things  are  different, Arthur. The world has moved on. You can’t expect everything to be the same as when you were a lad. Electricity wasn't even in every home back then, was it? No, it weren’t. We used paraffin lamps. Safer, in some ways. Less chance of blowin' up the place, I reckon. Remember when they first fitted one? Dad stood there like a lemon, starin’ at the bulb. Said it were unnatural. Said it were takin’ over the world. He sounds like your Uncle George! Always had a thing about newfangled contraptions. Remember him refusing to buy a washing machine? Said his wife's hands were strong enough to do the job. Aye, George were a stubborn one. Wouldn't admit he were wrong, even when he were demonstrably wrong. He’d just mutter about “the good old days” and shake his head. Just like I do, I suppose. Just a little bit, dear.

…and then, absolutely then, he started doing this weird, elongated vibrato on the saxophone. Like, deliberately awful. It was meant to be ‘experimental,’ apparently, but honestly, it just made me cringe. I had to bite my cheek so I wouldn't laugh. Experimental can be a tricky thing, can’t it? Sometimes it’s revolutionary, sometimes it just sounds like someone’s having a bit of a giggle at the expense of the audience. Was it a friend of yours playing? Nah, some artist they’d flown in special for the event. Part of the ‘avant-garde music showcase’ the Arts Council were funding. Fancy name, utterly bizarre music. You wouldn’t have liked it, pet. It wasn't exactly soulful, was it? More…clinical. Like watching a dissection of a musical idea. I can imagine. I'm not hugely into the really,  really  out there stuff. Give me good blues, or a bit of jazz, something with some genuine feeling, you know? Speaking of feeling, how’s Liam doing? Didn't hear from him last week. He's good, he’s good. Just been swamped with exams. Typical Liam, burying himself in books. He’s cracking on with his photography project too, though, apparently he got some cracking shots down at the docks in Newcastle over the weekend. Proper moody, black and white stuff. Makes you want to wrap up in a duffel coat and stand in the rain. Sounds like him. I think we should get the lads together soon. Haven't seen everyone in ages. Remember that disastrous barbecue Mark tried to have last summer? Oh God, how could I forget? The sausages were practically charcoal and the gazebos blew down. It was a hurricane in miniature! Still, it was a laugh, weren’t it? We should have Sarah over too. She's been talking about wanting to try that new Italian place in town. Definitely. I’ll give them a bell this week. By the way, how’s the lavender doing? I noticed you were bringing in some cuttings last time you were here. It's thriving! Honestly, you wouldn’t believe it. It's gone absolutely bonkers. I have to keep pruning it back, otherwise it'll take over the whole window box. I’ve started thinking about planting some rosemary next to it. Apparently, they're good companions. That’s brilliant. I'm surprisingly getting the hang of this gardening malarkey myself.

…so, they said, "Restructuring. Streamlining. Going forward." Which, translated, means 'we’re getting rid of half the team to save a few bob.' Honestly, Dan, it's proper bleak. I feel for poor Sarah; she’s got two kids, ya know? Right. That's…brutal. Redundancies are always rough, especially when families are involved. Restructuring jargon – you can't trust a word of it. It’s just a euphemism for people losing their livelihoods. Cambridge feels a million miles from Sunderland, doesn’t it? Feel like a different planet sometimes. Aye, it does. And the worst thing is, the work's still getting done. They're just spreading it amongst the remaining lot, expectin' us to pick up the slack. They'll be shoutin' about 'employee wellbeing' five minutes later, but the reality is, we’ll be burnin' the candle at both ends. Makes you question the whole point, doesn’t it? All that postgraduate study... worth it for this? I know exactly what you mean. The sheer level of stress they put on you already. It’s ironic, isn’t it? We spend years practically starving ourselves, sleep-deprived, writing dissertations and reports, to get into jobs that are then treated like completely disposable commodities. Exactly! And don't even get me started on university fees! Remember when we were complaining about those back then? I could've bought a small house in Sunderland with what I paid for my Masters. It's mental. At least  you're  funded, with your PhD. That's a proper bonus, innit? Yeah, but that funding comes with strings attached. Constant pressure to publish, ridiculous grant applications… it's a different kind of anxiety, a different type of pressure. It’s all about output, output, output. No one really cares about the journey, or if you're actually  enjoying  the research. And they're starting to talk about raising postgraduate fees again… it’s just a constant cycle of debt and insecurity. Nae wonder nobody can afford a proper mortgage these days. It’s all a con, if you ask me. So, tell me, have you had any luck with that conference proposal? The Zurich one? Actually, yeah! Got it through. They liked my abstract on the impact of algorithmic bias on… …and they're offering a small travel grant, which is a massive help. It’s in November, so I’ll need to start planning.

Och, look at that wee bairn! A right proper dragon, isn't he? Much better than those modern ones, all sharp teeth and fire-breathing nonsense. This one looks… thoughtful. What's he thinking about, I wonder? He’s thinking about his family, Nana. That’s what the story’s about. It’s about Barnaby the dragon and how he learns about all his relatives. I’m trying to make it a bit like a family tree really, but for dragons. Think of it as a fun way to teach kids about genealogy. A family tree for a dragon? That’s mental, Mum. Dragons don’t  have  family trees, do they? They just… exist. Well, in this story they do, Leo! Every dragon has a history, a lineage. And Barnaby is struggling to understand it all. He knows he has a mum, of course, but then he hears about aunts and uncles who breathe different colours of flame, cousins who live in different volcanoes… it’s all a bit confusing. Aye, it reminds me of trying to explain our family to the wee ones. Half Inverness, half London, with a dash of… well, who knows what else! It can be tricky, you know. Especially when you’re trying to connect them to their granddad. He wasn't always easy to understand, was he? No, he wasn’t. It’s why I want Barnaby’s story to be inclusive, you know? To show that families come in all shapes and sizes. Even when things are complicated. Like… like with your step-sons, Leo. Yeah, I know. It's a bit weird sometimes, isn’t it? Ben and Finn… they don’t really talk about their dad much. Just that he… goes away a lot. It’s okay, darling. You don’t have to explain. It’s just… families aren’t always neat and tidy, are they? This book... it's about showing kids that. Even Barnaby’s grandma is a bit eccentric. Keeps hoarding shiny pebbles and has a habit of accidentally setting things on fire with her sneezes. Och, I love a good eccentric! My own sister, Morag, she’s a whirlwind! Always dashing about, causing mayhem wherever she goes. You wouldn’t believe the stories she has about her children. They’re a right handful! Much like my own boys when they were wee. Exactly! And it's those real-life quirks that make a story relatable, don’t you think, Nana?

Honestly, this placement at the bakery is killin’ me. Like, my feet are aching somethin’ fierce and Mrs. Higgins is forever breathin’ down my neck. She keeps tellin’ me to “fluff the scones more vigorously.” Vigorously! Like they're fightin' back, they are. Mrs. Higgins sounds… charming. At least you're earning some cash. My library placement is mostly alphabetizing historical pamphlets about Victorian button collecting. Thrilling, right? I felt like I was going slowly mad by Thursday. Victorian buttons? Now that’s a special kind of dull. At least I get the smell of fresh bread. Though, to be fair, yesterday someone dropped a whole tray of Eccles cakes. Sticky mess everywhere. I spent half an hour scrubbin’ the floor. Proper grim. Oh, that's awful. But at least you got Eccles cakes? Free food is a win, even if it requires a deep clean afterwards. Listen, speaking of…personal upkeep…have you been dealing with  that  again? You mean… under me arms? Aye, it’s a state. It’s always a state, isn't it? I tried that new razor you got, the one with the pivoting head, but it still gave me a right red rash. Barely got rid of anything proper, either. Just a few prickly bits. I’m thinkin’ of just givin’ in and rockin’ a natural look. A natural look? Truly? Don’t do that! You’d look amazing! But, yeah, the pivoting head one  was  a bit rubbish, I’ll admit. I found a brilliant cream – proper soothing. I’ll bring it round for you tomorrow. It’s called ‘Calming Cloud’ or somethin’ ridiculous. Honestly, it's a lifesaver. Calming Cloud? That does sound a bit posh, doesn’t it? I'm more of a ‘cheap and cheerful’ sort of girl, generally. Mum uses something that smells like lavender and old ladies. Gets the job done, but…well. Lavender and old ladies isn't exactly conducive to feeling confident, is it? Look, seriously, try the cream. Honestly, it's made a huge difference to me. I used to get such horrific ingrown hairs. It’s demi-exfoliating, apparently. Don't worry, it’s not like some mystical potion. Just helps the hairs grow outwards instead of…well, you know. Yeah, I know. The worst. I was thinkin’ of maybe getting one of them electric shavers. Mum's got one, she swears by it. Says it’s quicker and less likely to cause irritation.

…so then he genuinely asked me, clear as day, "Does ‘Q’ stand for ‘Queen’?" Like, I was mid-sentence explaining the alphabet to my little niece, Maisie, and he chimes in with that. Honestly, I nearly choked on me cider! You'd think, being a grown man, he'd know his ABCs, wouldn't ya? Right, that’s… something alright. Sounds like Uncle Barry being Uncle Barry. He’s always been a bit… adrift, hasn’t he? Remember that time he tried to build a birdhouse out of biscuit boxes? Don't remind me! The bluebirds looked terrified. Anyway, it got me thinking, doesn’t it? How easily people can fall back on these ridiculously basic assumptions, especially when they're a bit pickled. Makes you wonder what else they're not quite clued up on, eh? Possibly a lot, knowing Barry. Though, to be fair, sometimes it’s just a case of lacking any kind of real… curiosity. He's set in his ways. Different kettle of fish entirely to trying to navigate the research landscape, I’ll tell you that. Proper brain-bending stuff, this. Spending all day wrestling with statistical models… it’s enough to make a bloke reach for something stronger than bitter. Aye, I get that. Research management’s no walk in the park, is it? Got to keep everyone on the straight and narrow, chasing grants, deadlines… Speaking of ‘straight and narrow’ though, did you ever properly get into boxing as a kid like you used to talk about? Tried, yeah. Did a few amateur bouts, back in Brum. It’s… brutal. Exhilarating, but brutal. Learned a lot about myself, though. Discipline, respect... and how quickly a nose can bleed. Didn't stick with it, though. PhD got in the way. Too much time spent inside, staring at a screen. Needed sunshine, not a black eye. Although, watching Fury… he's something else, isn't he? Utterly captivating. He is, isn't he? Proper warrior. Though I hate how some of the comments online are, after his fights. So much awful stuff, especially when it’s race-related. Saw some right nasty stuff aimed at him the other night. Proper shameful, it is. It is. And not just in boxing. Football, too. The online vitriol is just… staggering. It’s a symptom of something bigger, innit? Years and years of ingrained prejudices just bubbling to the surface.

…and honestly, Penelope, the sheer volume of paperwork for the grant application is staggering. It's not just about documenting the restoration, it's about proving every single decision is historically defensible, demonstrating long-term sustainability… it’s exhausting. I've been wrestling with the ‘impact assessment’ for days. How does one quantify the impact of preserving a 17th-century tithe barn on, well,  anything  beyond the local pigeons? Oh, darling, you’re preaching to the choir. Impact assessment. It’s become the bane of my existence too. Remember the St. Giles’ Church project in Henley? The parish council were positively apoplectic that I couldn't put a precise figure on the 'community spirit' increase. Ridiculous, wasn’t it? I ended up writing something about bolstering the sense of local heritage and providing a valuable community resource for future generations. Very flowery, I admit. Flowery is good! Sometimes, you have to sidestep the numbers and appeal to the, shall we say,  sentiment  of the funding body. This barn, though… it's out in the sticks, completely isolated. There’s very little community attached to it currently. It was used for storage for decades, then simply… abandoned. That’s the trick, isn't it? Show them the potential. Don’t focus on what it  was , focus on what it  could  be. Think about a small rural crafts centre, maybe? Or a local produce market on weekends? Something that draws people in and gives the community a reason to engage. Even a space for educational workshops – traditional thatching, perhaps? It's all about demonstrating a viable future for the building. I’ve considered the crafts centre idea. But the access is a nightmare. The lane leading to it is barely wide enough for a tractor, let alone a coachload of tourists. And parking? Forget about it. That's part of the reason I’m leaning towards the workshops. Lower overheads, less foot traffic to contend with. What about bidding with a consortium? Has that ever worked for you? Bidding with a consortium? Absolutely! I partnered with a local stonemason and a heritage carpenter on the Old Mill restoration in Amersham. Shared the risk, shared the expertise. Significantly boosted our chances. The key is finding people with complementary skills and a shared ambition. And importantly, a good reputation. We vetted them thoroughly, of course. Due diligence, you know. Due diligence. More paperwork. It's relentless.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of data we're getting on regional pronunciation shifts is just… overwhelming. It's brilliant, don’t get me wrong, but it's also terrifying. I mean, we've got people from all over the Northeast submitting recordings, and you see these tiny, unexpected deviations. Like, a softening of the ‘a’ in ‘bath’ in South Shields that's completely fallen out of favour everywhere else. Did you know? That's fascinating, isn’t it? Though, I suppose it shouldn’t be a surprise. Language is always in flux. It’s the natural order of things. My supervisor, he’s obsessed with the Great Vowel Shift – still trying to prove the exact mechanisms that drove it. Bit of a rabbit hole, that. Aye, a right one! Though, the scale is different now, isn’t it? Back then, it was these gradual, centuries-long drifts. Now, you’ve got social media, migration… things are moving ten times faster. It's not just vowels shifting either. We’re tracking lexical changes too – words disappearing, new slang popping up. I swear, half the things kids are saying these days, I need a decoder ring. True, true. Trying to pin down the influence of online communities is tricky though, isn’t it? Is it genuine linguistic innovation, or just performative adoption? It's hard to tell. Are you finding it’s predominantly younger people leading these shifts? Mostly, yeah. Though, we're seeing older generations adopting some slang too. It’s often adapted, mind. They’ll take a word, but twist it slightly – a sort of linguistic hedging, you know? To show they’re ‘in the know’ without feeling completely… overwhelmed by the youth. It’s funny, really. Right, tea’s up. Milk and sugar for you? Always a proper cuppa here, I’m glad to see. You wouldn't believe some of the instant coffee some people drink. Sacrilege! Please, please. Milk, no sugar. And you? You’re getting ever so fond of your oat milk, aren't you? Can't believe you used to be a straight-up dairy man. Don't remind me. The ethical arguments got to me eventually. Anyway, back to your research. So, are you seeing any regional dialects particularly vulnerable to homogenization? Anywhere where you think we might see a significant loss of distinctiveness? That’s the worrying bit. The more rural areas, definitely.

“…and honestly, the sheer volume of pasta they serve is just ridiculous. I know they're trying to feed them, but two portions of fusilli with a watery tomato sauce? It's just not appealing, is it? Especially when you know Granny's roast chicken is waiting for the weekend.” Roast chicken  is  best, Miss Emily. Much better than… than squiggly pasta. It definitely is, sweetheart. Absolutely. Don’t you think, Leo? Chicken and pud! Pudding’s good. Pudding is  always  good. Right. So, the school dinners… I’m thinking maybe we need to look into packing lunches more often. At least a few times a week. What do you both think about that? Can I have cheese sandwiches? With cucumber? Of course, darling. Cheese and cucumber as much as you like. Leo, what about you? Still a ham and cheese situation? Ham. And apple. Ham and apple. Perfect. Right, okay. That’s a good start. It’s just… the cost, you know? It all adds up. I need to have a proper look at the budget and see where we can maybe cut back a bit. Honestly, between tennis lessons and school trips, it’s a constant juggle. Tennis is fun! I got a birdie today! You did! Fantastic! You were smashing it, weren't you? That tournament next week… are you feeling nervous about it? A little bit. But Sophie said she’s nervous too. Right, well, that's good to know you're not alone. Remember what we talked about – focus on having fun, playing your best, and celebrating even a little win. No pressure, okay? Can we have clowns at the tournament? Clowns at the tennis tournament? Where did that idea come from? I saw a man with a big red nose! He was waving! Like the circus! Ooh! A circus! Can we go to the circus? We went to the circus last year, remember? It was brilliant. Balloons and juggling and… Actually, you know what? Clowns are a bit scary sometimes, aren’t they? A little bit scary. The ones with the big shoes. They throw things! They do throw things, don't they! Maybe not the best idea for a tennis tournament. Let's stick with enjoying the tennis, okay? We’ll think about the circus another time. We need to save some pennies, after all, for those packed lunches and those tennis rackets. And Granny's amazing Sunday roasts!

Honestly, I’m still reeling from that film. “The Banshees of Inisherin” – devastating, wasn’t it? Such a simple premise, but the weight of it… Aye, it was good. Very good. Though a bit bleak for a Sunday evening, wouldn't you say? A bit like life, I suppose. All that cutting off without a word… reminds me of my cousin Bernard. He just stopped writing. Poof. Gone. Family tried everything. Never knew why. You always draw parallels, Dad. Bernard and the Irish island! Though fair point, it  was  emotionally draining. And the cinematography was just stunning, wasn’t it? The wind, the sea… incredible. What did you think, Sarah? I was pinging my Twitter feed with thoughts about the film’s commentary on masculinity and legacy. You and your Twitter, David. It’s too much for me sometimes. But yes, the visuals were breathtaking. I was mostly thinking about the teaching implications, actually. The way they portrayed history – this cyclical violence, inherited trauma… it speaks volumes about the importance of nuanced historical understanding. Which, of course, is exactly what we're failing to deliver in schools. Failing? Now, now, Sarah. When I were at school... we had history. All those kings and battles. Not much nuance, mind you. Just dates and names. But we learned something! It's not about dismissing your experience, Dad. But the curriculum now is so… prescriptive. It’s designed to tick boxes, to prepare for these awful exams, rather than to genuinely engage students with the complexities of the past. We're just regurgitating facts. And frankly, the current obsession with ‘British Values’ is just suffocating any real debate. I agree with Sarah on that, actually. I was at that Cambridge debate last week – the one on teaching history in the 21st century. The sheer frustration radiating from some of the teachers was palpable. One woman said she felt like she was teaching to a spreadsheet. Spreadsheet? What nonsense. In my day, we had slates and chalk! See? Simplistic. Which isn't inherently bad, but... David, you’re in advertising. You have to be adaptable, think on your feet. Shouldn't we be preparing students for that kind of thinking, rather than rote memorisation? Absolutely. And it’s got to be linked to industry, hasn't it? My company does a lot with universities, trying to bridge that gap between academia and the realities of the working world.

Missing! Gone, vanished clean away! A perfectly good, solid oak armchair. Solid, I tells ya. My Gran’s. Been in the family nigh on a hundred years. Wouldn’t let nobody touch it, I didn't. Now it’s just…gone. Honestly, Arthur. An armchair. You couldn’t leave it alone, could you? You were rearrangin' things again, weren't you? Rearrangin'? I was tryin' to get a bit o' sun, Doreen! The light was just right on that corner. Moved it a foot, that's all. A foot, Doreen! And now it's flown the coop. Well, Arthur, you know how you are. Sometimes things just…disappear around you. Perhaps you just put it somewhere and forgot? It’s happened before, hasn't it? Remember the garden gnome? The gnome was different, Bernard! That was a prank. Young Geoffrey, that scoundrel. This…this is serious. It's sentimental, see? My Gran, Elsie, she used to sit in that chair and knit. Knitted the best socks you ever did see, she did. Thick wool, kept your toes warmer than a summer's day. Elsie, you say? Was she one of those Eastern Counties knitters, Arthur? Fierce reputation for producing quality woollens, apparently. My mum used to tell me stories about Norfolk wool being the best. Fierce is right, Stephen! Elsie was a force o' nature. Wouldn't take no nonsense. Could chase you across a field with a broomstick, she could. Strong woman. Worked down at the sugar beet factory, she did, before she married. Terrible work, that. Dusty and cold. Makes you appreciate a good armchair, doesn't it? When you've earned it. We all have our memories tied to things, Arthur. That’s understandable. But a police report for a missing chair? That's a bit much, even for you. Remember that time you reported the magpie stealing your biscuits? That magpie was a menace! Snatching biscuits right off the windowsill. Bold as brass, he was. It was an affront to decency! An' besides, the police should be lookin' out for the little folk, shouldn’t they? Just like they were in the war. Ah, the war. You’ve told us stories about the war so many times, Arthur. What was it like being so close to Norwich during the bombing raids? Terrible, Bernard. Absolutely terrible. The sirens wailin', the ground shakin'…my father used to take us to the Anderson shelter in the garden.

…and honestly, Dad, I just feel a bit weird about it all. Selling the house. It's been Mum’s home for…well, for as long as I can remember. Feels like I'm signing off on a whole chunk of my childhood. I know, son. It's a big thing. Believe me, I do. But you know she wouldn't want us dwelling on it. She’d want us moving forward. And besides, it’s the right thing to do, isn’t it? Safer for her, closer to you and Sarah. And that…that Yorkshire pudding situation last week? Nearly had a heart attack watching her try to get it out of the tin. Yeah, that was…a sight. She did attempt to wrestle with it, didn't she? I offered to help, but she just waved me away, muttering something about ‘men not knowing how to cook a proper pudding’. Classic Mum. Still, it's just...it feels final, you know? All those Christmases, all those family Sundays… Final’s a strong word, Liam. It's a change. A big one, granted. But memories stay with you, don’t they? You’ll still remember the Christmases, the Sundays. You'll still remember the pudding battles. They’re imprinted, lad. Speaking of imprinted, have you had a chance to look at that leak report from the surveyor on the new place? Briefly. It flagged the bathroom needs some work, and the roof’s showing its age. Nothing catastrophic, fortunately, but it'll add to the mortgage, won't it? It's already stretching us. Are you sure you’re alright with taking on that extra bit? Don't you worry your head about that. I’ve been building up some savings, you know. Been careful. And anyway, it's for your family. It’s an investment, isn’t it? Better than leaving it sitting in a bank account, collecting dust and 0.01% interest. Remember when I saved up for that Ford Sierra back in '88? Practically starved myself for a year. Worth it though, eh? That car could handle anything. You and that Sierra. You practically lived in it. Do you remember when you drove it through Mr. Henderson’s prize-winning roses while trying to show off to Tracey from down the street? Oh, don't remind me! Henderson didn’t speak to me for a month! Tracey wasn’t impressed either, if I recall correctly.

Right, so, salmon or cod for Mum's main course? I’m leaning towards the salmon, it feels a bit more celebratory, doesn’t it? But she  did  mention the other day she was craving fish and chips… Salmon’s safer, innit? Cod can be a bit… unpredictable. You know how she is with flaky fish. Doesn’t want to end up with a forkful of bones. And fish and chips are a bit much for a sit-down dinner, even if she does love ‘em. You’re right, you’re right. It was just a fleeting thought. Okay, salmon it is. Now, the asparagus... I was thinking steamed, with a hollandaise sauce. Perhaps a little lemon zest? Ooh, hollandaise sounds fancy! Mum'll love that. Proper posh. But are you sure you’ve got enough lemons? Remember last time we made that lemon drizzle cake, you practically scraped the insides of the lemons bare. Yes, well, I've bought a whole bag this time! Lessons learned. Right, table plan… this is proving trickier than I thought. Auntie Margaret  absolutely  refuses to sit next to Uncle Barry, you know. Something about his jokes. Honestly, they’re like two toddlers. Barry doesn’t even  notice  she’s not laughing. Should just put them on opposite ends of the table. Saves the drama. Nan could go on the end next to Barry, she'll shut him up if he gets too silly. That’s potentially true, but then Cousin Sophie gets all upset if Nan isn’t near her. It's a minefield, truly. And I'm still trying to subtly move the heavier cupboards – the ones with all the old photo albums in - further away from the hallway. It’s a real tripping hazard, and with her memory playing up… Yeah, I noticed that when I was rummaging for photos earlier. It’s a bit dodgy. Maybe just put some of the albums on the shelves in the living room instead? That way they’re still accessible, but less likely to cause a fall. Speaking of photos… look at this one! Nan with Dad when they first met. She looks amazing! Oh, that's lovely. They were so young. It's heartbreaking, really, to see how much she’s forgotten. Sometimes it’s just little things, like forgetting where she put her glasses. Other times… it’s bigger. Last week she asked me who Dad was.

Right, so, they’re saying two more teeth? Two more wisdom teeth to get whittled away? It’s madness, innit? I mean, honestly, they're brewin' a right state of bother, these things. My mum’s gone on about it for a week, kept sayin’ “You’ll be lookin’ like a chipmunk, lass!” Which, you know, not exactly confidence boostin' before headin' back to uni. Two? Oh, Yorkshire grit, that’s rough. Mine were a breeze, honestly. Just a little numb and a week of looking like a pufferfish. Don’t listen to your mum about the chipmunk thing, that’s classic parental exaggeration. You look lovely. Besides, you'll be back at uni soon, who needs to look their best for lectures? Easy for you to say, miss Cambridge. You’ve always been proper picture-perfect. My face looks like a right map at the moment, especially 'round the back. Like, where my gums are gettin' all weird. The dentist poked around and declared it was "pre-extraction cavities". Pre! Like they’re planning ahead. It’s unsettling. He also said somethin' about “possible infection.” Lovely. Right, that  is  a bit grim. Infection isn't ideal. But hey, at least you're getting it sorted. My dad keeps going on about how having everything pulled out in your twenties is like tempting fate. Says he kept his until he was sixty and "dodged a bullet." Honestly, that man and his questionable life choices… Oh, your dad's a classic. My dad just keeps saying, “At least you'll have a good excuse for not smilin’ in your graduation photos.” He's got that dry Yorkshire humor, you know? Anyway, are you all sorted for moving back? You said somethin' about potential problems with the lease. Yeah, it’s a bit of a nightmare. The landlord’s being…well, he’s being a bit of a prat, to be honest. He's suddenly upping the rent mid-year. Says he found some obscure clause in the contract. I have to go back and have a proper look. Mum’s having a go at me – “you should have read the fine print!” As if I have time to read through twenty pages of legal jargon when I’m juggling essays and trying to stop my pasta sauce from boiling over. Tell me about it. Uni life is relentless. It's gonna be a rush, isn't it?

…and honestly, the lactose-free chocolate chip cookies are better than the regular ones now. I’ve perfected the recipe. Little tweaks here and there. It’s all about the brown butter, you know? Gives it a real depth of flavour. Can I have another one, Mummy? Please? Of course, sweetheart. But just one more, okay? We need to save some for Grandma. Are you listening, Leo? Grandma wants cookies! Mmm-hmm. Grandma likes… things. That's right, darling. And speaking of things… remember how we were talking about ways to be kind? We need to make a list. A proper list, like we do for Christmas. Ooh, can we do the kind thing where we give a flower to a grown-up? I gave Miss Davies a daffodil last week. She looked really happy! You did! That was lovely. Absolutely brilliant. We'll definitely put that on the list. Leo, any ideas? You’ve been awfully quiet playing with your games. Can we use these for money? Use chess pieces for money? What on earth gave you that idea? Uncle Ben said when he was little, he and his brother used to use draughts pieces to buy sweets. They’d trade them with their friends. Oh, he did, did he? Typical Ben. Well, I don’t think anyone would accept a knight for a packet of crisps these days, love. But it’s a brilliant story! See? Kindness isn’t always about big things. It's about imaginative play and sharing. We could put ‘making up games’ on our kindness list. Can we make a game where we give people little drawings? Like, pictures of happy animals? That’s a fantastic idea, darling! Absolutely. We’ll add that. Right, so we've got flowers, drawings… Let’s think about Chinese New Year. It's coming up soon, isn't it? I want to do something a little special this year. Maybe bake some red bean buns? Will there be fireworks? Possibly! If your Dad manages to convince the neighbours. Though mostly we’ll tell stories about the animals and eat lots of yummy food. And we can decorate the house red and gold! What colour would you like your hair, Leo? I was thinking maybe a little streak of red. Red like a dragon! Exactly! Or maybe blue, like the sea. Or even purple, like… well, like a really sparkly plum!

Honestly, Mum, Mr. Davies is  killing  me with Shakespeare. Like, why do we need to know so much about iambic pentameter? I mean, it's just…words. It’s beautiful words, love. And it helps you understand storytelling. Though I agree, sometimes it can feel a bit much. Did you finish your reading for English? Almost. I started  Alice in Wonderland  again. It’s still so weird, isn't it? All the nonsense. I keep thinking about that Cheshire Cat. It’s creepy but brilliant. It is! Remember when you were little and you insisted on having a cat costume for World Book Day? The one with the massive grin painted on it? You scared the life out of poor Mrs. Higgins! Oh my god, I totally forgot about that! Dad had to carry me everywhere because everyone was running away. That was embarrassing. What did you dress up as? I went as the Mad Hatter, actually. I made the hat myself, completely covered in felt flowers and feathers. It was a disaster, honestly. Kept falling apart. But we had fun. Speaking of fun… how’s the theatre club going? Rehearsals for  Midsummer Night's Dream  still on track? Yeah, it’s going well! I'm Titania. It’s a lot of lines but it's a really good part. I’m a bit nervous about the stage, to be honest. It's massive! You'll be brilliant, darling. You’ve always been a natural. Remember when you fell off your bike last summer? That nasty scrape on your knee? You were brave as anything. Yeah, that was awful. I still get a little twinge sometimes when it rains. It reminds me of those seagulls swooping down trying to steal my ice cream! Hastings seagulls are the worst, you know. They're like tiny feathered terrorists. They are a menace. I saw one try to nick a sandwich from a pensioner the other day. Absolutely brazen. Listen, I wanted to tell you about that article I read online… it was about the link between music and memory. Apparently, listening to songs from your childhood can trigger really vivid memories. Really? Like what? Well, it talked about how certain melodies can recall specific events, even forgotten ones. Made me think about that Spice Girls tape you used to play non-stop when you were seven. Remember how obsessed you were with Posh Spice?

…and so, I told them, really emphasized the importance of clear, documented evidence. Not just feelings, you know - "it’ll ruin the view!" – which, I understand perfectly, but it won’t hold up against a professional assessment. They were so focused on the aesthetic, bless them. Solar panels are, in their own way, quite unsightly too, aren't they? But the arguments are different. Absolutely. It’s the  justification  that matters. Last night's lot were relying heavily on anecdotal evidence about wildlife impact. Necessary to raise the issue, of course, but they need hard data. Something the council can't just dismiss. We went through the precedent of the Lower Marsh appeal, remember? The bat migration routes? That's what won it for us there. Precedent is key. And a good understanding of the planning regulations themselves, of course. These developers - the energy companies, really - they’re extraordinarily good at working the system. They know the loopholes, the grey areas. They even influence the local planners, don’t you think? Subtly, of course. Not blatant bribery, but…favours. Meetings over lunch. Strategic donations. It's insidious. It is. Honestly, I've been involved with these committees for years. You see these patterns emerge. They’ll bring in that "expert" witness who conveniently comes to the same conclusion as their projections. The Friends of the Village Trust, the clever ones, they've started commissioning their own assessments. Independent ones. It’s expensive, mind you. Expensive, yes. But vital. And often the council, or more accurately, the Development Control Committee, are just overwhelmed. They’re swamped with applications. They  want  to be seen to be supporting green energy, right? It’s politically advantageous. Advantageous for  them , perhaps. Not necessarily for the countryside. It’s a balancing act, isn’t it? One that’s increasingly skewed towards profit. It’s the subsidies, you see. Utterly disproportionate. They’re throwing money at wind and solar, massive amounts, yet the research into viable energy storage is chronically underfunded. Imagine if they invested just a  fraction  of that subsidy money into developing, say, vastly improved battery technology, or some form of kinetic energy storage…we'd be much further ahead. Exactly! And that’s what I kept trying to explain last night. It's not about  being against  renewable energy, it's about finding the  right  solutions. Turbines in areas with significant bird migrations? Solar farms on prime agricultural land?

…and honestly, Dad, the parallel parking was just terrifying. I nearly clipped that poor little Fiat. I could feel Mrs. Higgins watching from her window! She always gives me the stink eye, you know. Stink eye, eh? Happens to the best of 'em, love. Parallel parking's a right bugger, isn’t it? Always were. Even when I was learning, back in '62. Had a Morris Minor, I did. Bright red. Could barely squeeze it into a space the size of a postage stamp. Still, you get the hang of it, you know. Practice makes perfect. Don't get disheartened now. Don't listen to him, Annie. He’s still complaining about the reversing on the A38 back when he was 20. Honestly, a disaster in a Morris Minor! But he is right about practice. And have you looked at the insurance quotes yet? That’s a proper hurdle, isn't it? That’s what I was just about to ask. They’re… eye-watering. Like, seriously eye-watering. I got a quote from ComparetheMarket – you know, the meerkat? – and it was nearly a grand a year! A grand! For a little hatchback. I feel like I'm being penalised for being... me. Thirty-four and a language teacher doesn't scream 'high-risk driver’ does it? Well, that's insurance for you. Bottom line is, the more you're under, or over, a certain age, the more they charge. And new drivers... well, they see you as a blank slate ripe for an accident. You could try adding me as a named driver, love. Slightly less, perhaps. Though don't expect me to spend my days pottering about in a hatchback. My back won’t stand for it. He’d complain about the lumbar support, wouldn’t he? Seriously though, Annie, shop around. Go with a local broker. Sometimes they can get better deals than online. Remember Mrs. Davies down the road? She gets all our insurance. Worth a try. I will, Mum. Thanks. It's just… I really want to get this sorted. Imagine, driving myself to Cornwall! No more relying on taxis and buses. It would be wonderful. We haven’t been to Cornwall in ages, have we? Cornwall’s lovely. Been there a few times. St Ives, particularly. Lovely little harbour. Reckon we should all go next summer. Proper holiday. Spend a week down there. No rush.

Honestly, Dad, parking in Brighton is a nightmare. Absolutely mental. I spent twenty minutes circling just to find a space the other day. Twenty minutes! And then it was, like, £4.50 for an hour. Ridiculous. Brighton’s always been pricey, love. Never got the draw of it, to be honest. Too much…faff. Remember when you were little and we’d go down to Margate? That was a proper seaside holiday. Simple. Chips, sticks of rock, donkey rides… None of this artisan coffee and vintage clothes nonsense. It’s different now, isn’t it? Everything’s changed. Still, I like it. The energy, you know? It's good for me, keeps me buzzing. Plus, the job at the uni is brilliant, even if it is just admin at the moment. Good for you, pet. A job’s a job. Speaking of buzzing, did you see that horse, Golden Gale, at Ascot? Should have backed him. Told you he had it in him. Such a shame. Dad, you’re already planning your next bet. Honestly! It's costing you a fortune. Remember what the social worker said? Social worker’s don’t know anything about proper racing. It’s instinct, love. It’s in the blood! Your grandad used to say the same thing. Still, the council are sticking their noses in, aren't they? Harping on about my ‘financial contributions.’ As if I haven't lived a hard enough life! I know, it’s awful. But you’ve got to try and keep things… organised. Speaking of organised, I need to go through my notifications later. Facebook’s gone mental again. Constant pings, people tagging me in things. Drives me crazy. Do you know you can turn them off? Turn them  off ? What’s the point of having it then? Back in my day, if you wanted to talk to someone, you called them. Simple. Like I did with your Mum. . We had a little telephone in the kitchen. Remember that? The dial-up kind. Felt like a privilege to use it. I remember. And Mum made the best bread. Honestly, she could whip up a loaf in fifteen minutes that tasted better than anything you buy in a shop today. I'm trying to get back into cooking properly, you know? All that ready-made stuff isn’t good for you. It's expensive too, mind. You see those prices at the supermarket?

…and then Professor Davies actually  looked  disappointed! Like, genuinely deflated. He said, "Mr. Ellis, your interpretation of Hamlet's soliloquy was...creative." Creative! That's code for 'utterly bonkers' isn't it? I was arguing Hamlet was a secretly brilliant golfer, using the skull to practice putting. You did  what ? Honestly, you’re a menace, Ellis. A brilliant, entertaining menace, but a menace nonetheless. I still can’t believe you got away with that. Davies is usually so fiercely traditional. He probably spends his weekends re-enacting the Globe Theatre in his garden. I think he was just too stunned to properly reprimand me. Plus, the way I delivered it - all earnest and full of passion about the subconscious influence of putting on existential dread – it threw him completely. He looked like he was trying to calculate the optimal angle to deflect a rogue pigeon. Right. You’d have done better just saying, “To be or not to be…that’s the question, mate. Should I slice this shot or not?” See, that would have been more fitting. Speaking of skill learning, I've been trying to get my golf game in order. Bloody awful, it is. Keeps saying my backswing’s all wrong. Proper frustrating, isn't it? It’s like learning a new language, but instead of conjugating verbs, you’re trying to avoid hooking the ball into the lake. Have you considered taking lessons? My uncle, Desmond - you remember him, Aunt Moira’s brother? – he's a pro. Desmond “Deacon” Davies, everyone called him. A dreadful nickname, really. Deacon Davies? Vaguely rings a bell. Always seemed a bit… intense. Why "Deacon"? Apparently, when he started playing, he'd wear these ridiculously prim, old-fashioned blazers and a peaked cap. He looked like a particularly serious church elder on the green. The nickname stuck. He absolutely  hated  it, though. He'd fume whenever someone used it. Made him even more intense. So, yeah, he could give you a few pointers, though be prepared for some serious no-nonsense instruction. He’s less about encouragement and more about brutal honesty. Sounds delightful. Less encouragement is exactly what I need. I’m basically cheering myself on while completely flinging the ball into the rough. What have you been up to besides baffling professors with Shakespearean golf analogies? Still working at that… vintage record store? Yeah, ‘Grooves & Echoes’. It’s alright. The owner, old Mr. Pemberton, is a complete eccentric.

…and honestly, the caterers were a nightmare. They’d promised these artisanal mini-quiches, all flaky pastry and smoked salmon, yeah? And they delivered these... these things that looked like they'd been molded out of Play-Doh and tasted faintly of old socks. I had to stage an intervention during the drinks reception, practically wrestling the head chef away from the buffet table. It was mortifying! Play-Doh quiches? Blimey. Sounds like you had your hands full, then. Typical, innit? People promising the world and delivering… well, Play-Doh. You get like that at the building site sometimes, you know? "Oh, we’ll have it finished by Friday," and it's still half-built on Monday. You work on building sites now, Leo? I thought you were just, you know, doing odd jobs. Yeah, well, this is a bigger gig. A new sustainable housing development. It’s alright, actually. The lads are decent, and the weather hasn’t been too bad lately. Better than stacking shelves at Morrison’s, that's for sure. What about you, Chloe? Still managing to wrangle stressed-out CEOs and rogue caterers? Trying to! It's all a bit relentless, though, isn’t it? The expectation is just…constant. And because it’s events, it’s  always  on. Even when I’m supposed to be relaxing at the weekend, I'm usually checking emails, proofreading menus, making sure the flowers haven't died. I’m thinking seriously about a digital detox. I hear you. Production control is surprisingly demanding, too. Everyone wants everything  yesterday , and if there’s a slight hiccup in the supply chain, suddenly it's my fault the entire factory grinds to a halt. I've been trying this new intermittent fasting thing. Apparently, it’s meant to reduce stress levels and boost energy. Fasting? Nah, that’s not for me, love. I'd just end up feeling miserable and thinking about cake. I did try that juice cleanse thing last year. Don’t bother. Tasted like grass clippings and made me even more stressed than usual trying to hide from everyone while I suffered. Yorkshire pudding’s a much better stress reliever, I reckon. Hear, hear! Yorkshire pudding's the answer to pretty much everything. Speaking of food… are you two still living with your parents then? Sadly, yes. Still saving for a flat in London. Rent is just ridiculous, isn’t it?

Right then, Doris, can you hear me alright? Bit blurry this picture, innit? Like looking through a fogged-up window. Perfectly fine, Arthur. Just my eyes, you know. Getting on a bit, these old peepers. Lovely to see you, though, love. Lovely. Showing off that nice garden you got there too, aren't you? Oh, hello you two! Yes, Arthur’s garden’s looking absolutely splendid. Everything’s just bursting into life. And Arthur, don’t be moaning about the Skype, you’re the one who insisted on showing us those enormous dahlias! Well, you said you wanted to see 'em! You always were partial to a good dahlia, weren’t you, Doris? Remember Mrs. Higgins' prize-winners, back in Costessey? They were something else. Speaking of something else, did you folks catch the eclipse yesterday? Blimey, it was proper eerie, wasn’t it? Aye, it were. A bit spooky, to be honest. Reminded me of those wartime air raid drills. Went all dark in the middle of the day. Felt like the end of the world a bit. Don't be dramatic, Doris! It was magnificent! Such a rare thing, you know. Makes you think about… well, about the cosmos, doesn't it? Black holes, and all that. Do you think it's possible to travel to other galaxies, Arthur? You were always good at that sort of thing, being an engineer and all. Well, theoretically, yes. Einstein's theories, you see - relativity, general relativity... it’s proper mind-boggling stuff, really. Space-time, bending light, black holes… a consequence of extremely massive objects, collapsing in on themselves. Pretty powerful stuff. Makes you wonder about the beginning, doesn’t it? How it all started. All this talk of spaceporting… makes me weary. I’d rather be watching Bargain Hunt. They want me to pay for the telly licence again, you know. Feels a bit of a cheek, really, when we're not exactly rolling in it. Don’t get started, Doris. It's the law. And we need to eat well, too. Have you been getting enough fruit and vegetables? I was thinking of making you a nice lentil soup this week. Speaking of well, look at these bamboo shoots! They’re coming up a treat this year. Much quicker than those petunias you planted, Margaret. They’re a bit slow, those petunias. They’ll get there. And the neighbours have finally finished their fencing.

Honestly, this roundabout is giving me the willies. Three lanes! Three! Back home, a roundabout was lucky to have two and you just hoped for the best. It’s a bit more sophisticated than Sunderland roundabouts, isn’t it? You’re getting used to proper infrastructure. Relax, I've navigated worse. Remember that one in Cambridge with the mini-island in the middle?  That  was mental. Aye well, Cambridge is a fancy place. I’m still trying to wrap my head around the sheer number of posh restaurants here. Like, ‘The Gilded Spoon’? What’s even  in  a gilded spoon? Is it edible? Should I be expecting gold leaf on my chips? You’ll be fine. There's decent stuff if you look beyond the pretension. There's a really good Indian place down near St. Paul's, 'Spice Route'. I've been meaning to take you. Proper curry, not the watered-down stuff you get everywhere else. St. Pauls, eh? Right, that’s the big cathedral, isn't it? We drove past it earlier. It’s… immense. Makes Durham Cathedral look like a doll’s house, to be honest. Though, Durham's got that lovely Norman feel about it, you know? More… cosy. Yeah, St. Paul’s is something else. And it’s not just the scale, it's the history. Built over centuries. It's a proper landmark. Speaking of landmarks, have you found your way around on the buses yet? They’re a lot more organised than the ones back home, but still confusing. Don't even start me on the buses. I tried to get to Borough Market the other day. Ended up three stops past, near some block of flats that looked like a concrete jungle. Seriously, they need better signage. At least back in Sunderland, the numbers were big enough to see! Borough Market's a bit of a trek from where you're staying. Probably easier to grab an Uber. You thinking about looking at those properties we were browsing online earlier? The one in Notting Hill? Aye, I had a look. It's a cute little place, mind, but the garden is tiny. I'd need room for Maisie to roam about. She’d be miserable stuck in a postage stamp of a garden. Plus, the windows are all…facing brick walls. Proper gloomy. True. It's a trade-off, isn't it?

…and then he just said, "Well, you should really floss more, shouldn't you?" Like I hadn't been diligently flossing for twenty years! Honestly, these dentists these days. No bedside manner, not one bit. It's like they’re robots trained to deliver bad news. Oh, they can be, can't they? My Bernard was the same. Just drilled right in and told you exactly what was wrong, no sugar-coating. Though, I must say, he did have remarkably clean teeth himself. Perhaps that was his motivation. Doubtless. And speaking of noisy things, did you hear that blackbird this morning? The volume! Honestly, it’s enough to wake the dead. Almost more annoying than my alarm clock, which, by the way, I’m considering replacing. It’s that dreadful electronic bleep, isn't it? Just a jarring, unnatural sound. Wish I could wake up to a cockerel, like they did back in the day. Wouldn't that be lovely? So peaceful. Though, I suppose the neighbours might disagree! You know, this morning I was putting out the seed, and I heard something else, a little trill. I couldn't quite place it. Could have been a willow warbler, I think. Are you good at identifying birdsong, Margaret? You’re always at it in your garden. Oh, a bit! I've spent hours listening, I have. Willow warbler's a tricky one. A bit like a chiffchaff, but the chiffchaff’s a bit clearer, you see. It’s just 'chiff-chiff'. Keep an ear out for that. You've got a lovely garden yourself, Christine. Are you thinking of doing any more planting this year? Oh, I am. Roses, mostly. Though my knees aren’t what they used to be, bending down is a real effort. It’s funny, isn't it? You spend your whole life wanting a garden, and then when you finally have one… it’s just another set of aches and pains. I read something the other day about elderly women and gardening. Apparently, it’s the perfect way to stay active and stave off... well, you know. Stave off what? Oh, nothing. Just… all the things that come with age. My sister, Gladys, she's been battling… throat cancer, you know. Horrible business. Keeps me thinking. Oh, Christine, I’m so sorry. Gladys was always such a vibrant woman. Dreadful, just awful. She sends her love, does she?

…and honestly, Sarah, the judgement. It's relentless. You share a picture – a perfectly innocuous picture of a pumpkin carving with Leo - and someone comments, "Shouldn't you be working?" Like I'm failing him somehow because I took ten minutes to snap a photo. It's exhausting, isn't it? This constant, performative parenting on social media. Absolutely. It’s a curated reality, isn’t it? Everyone showing off the perfectly matched outfits, the organic quinoa bowls, the educational trips to the Louvre. It makes you feel like you're not doing enough. I see it with the families I work with too. The pressure they feel, the comparison… it’s genuinely damaging. It's a totally different landscape from when we were kids. Remember just… existing? Without documenting every single moment for strangers? Precisely! When Leo was tiny, I resisted entirely. I thought, 'This is  his  life, not a public exhibition.' But then there’s that pull, I suppose. To connect with other mums, to find some shared experience. And then you realise you’re just contributing to the madness. It’s a tricky balance. I’m trying to be more mindful myself. Less posting, more living. It's been easier since I started yoga, actually. It's completely shifted my perspective. The grounding, the mindfulness... I used to be a bundle of anxiety, constantly worrying about the next thing, the next deadline. Now… I feel calmer. More present. Oh, you should definitely get Leo along to a children's class! He'd adore it. I’ve noticed a huge difference in him since he started. He’s less… spiky, somehow. More regulated. And my back! Don’t even get me started. Years of leaning over children’s desks and lugging around marked essays have taken their toll. I’ve been meaning to, honestly. It sounds wonderful. But my energy levels… well, IVF really took it out of me. The whole process was just… brutal. And then the disappointment… I'm still working through it, I think. I’m so glad you’re doing so well with Leo. He's a gorgeous little boy. He is! And he's such a chatterbox now. Talking about wanting to write a book, actually. A dinosaur book. It's completely bonkers, but adorable. It's inspired me, to be honest. I've been idly jotting down some notes about… well, my own experiences, really.

Aye, it’s a bleedin’ shame, innit? Used to be, you could leave your door unlocked. Not now, though, is it? Not like that. My brother’s got a security system installed at his place in Solihull. Cost him a packet, it did. But he says he sleeps better. Elsie's only five, really. She just wants to chase butterflies and clamber on the climbing frame. It feels wrong to keep her cooped up inside because of what  might  happen. I mean, the local police seem stretched thin already. Stretched thinner than butter on toast, love. I know. Talked to a young constable the other day. Says they're responding to like, triple the calls they used to. All understaffed and overloaded. Used to be proper community policing, you know, getting to know the folk. Now it’s just… reactive. Exactly! And it feels like everyone's just… resigned. Like it's inevitable. Do you think things were better when you were teaching? Better? In some ways, yeah. Discipline was... stricter, let's put it that way. Though I wouldn’t want to go back to  that  entirely, of course. The kids these days, they’ve got so much information at their fingertips. It's a different world. You must find it fascinating as a language teacher. What are you teaching at the moment? French, mostly. A little Spanish for the older kids. It’s lovely, truly. Seeing them grasp a new language, a new culture... it's rewarding. Though trying to get them to conjugate verbs past the present tense is sometimes like pulling teeth! My little sister’s just started French too, at primary school. Smart lass. Languages are important. I always regretted not sticking at it myself. Tried to learn German back in the seventies. Gave it up after a month. Couldn't get my tongue around all those guttural sounds. I completely understand. It's a challenge. My parents have always encouraged us to learn. My dad's a history teacher – quite the stickler for detail, he is. Always correcting my pronunciation! Aye, teachers. A persistent bunch, aren't they? My own kids, they gave me enough grief. One's in London, working in finance. The other's a nurse up in Leeds. They’re alright, though. Ring up every now and then. My wife, bless her soul, she passed away a few years ago. Makes things a bit lonely, to be honest.

Anomaly, eh? Sounds right exciting, la. What sort of anomaly? Sounds like somethin' outta Doctor Who, that does. It's honestly quite difficult to explain without the diagrams, Ben. It was a fluctuating energy signature, localized to the experimental array. Nothing matches the predicted outputs, and the spectral analysis… well, it’s baffling. It’s part of why I'm glad I’m not stuck in the lab all weekend. This prosecco is much more reliable. She’s not kidding. It  is  complicated, even for me, and I've been looking at increasingly weird data for my thesis on soil stability influence on reinforcement piles. Prosecco does sound like a better option though. Anyone else? Absolutely. I’ll grab another. This cheese board is brilliant, Anon, seriously. Where did you find that aged cheddar? It’s outstanding. Bit of a change from the usual supermarket fare. Found it at a farm shop just outside Cambridge. Worth the detour, isn't it? Right, so, back to the anomaly… Think about it, Ben, it wasn't a sudden burst; it was a fluctuation over several minutes. It  felt … intentional. Intentional? By who, then? Aliens trying to signal us? Don't tell me you've got little green men poking about your lab, lass. Don’t be daft, Ben! It’s probably a malfunction. But the readings…they’re just so consistent with a patterned fluctuation. It’s like someone was…testing something. Testing what? And why would they test it specifically on your array? It's relatively small-scale. That's what I'm trying to figure out! It’s potentially related to the new quantum entanglement protocols we're running… it’s just a  massive  coincidence if it isn’t. Speaking of coincidences, did anyone see the new Oppenheimer film? Saw it last week. Quite heavy going, but brilliantly acted. Cillian Murphy was phenomenal. I’m still trying to wrap my head around the moral implications of his decisions. The visuals were incredible, though. Absolutely stunning. Oppenheimer? Nah, not my cup o' tea, that. Too much thinkin'. I did see "Barbie," though. Now  that  was somethin'. Didn’t expect it to be so clever, actually. Made me think a bit, too, in a completely different way. Oh, you and Barbie! Ben, you’re the least likely person I expected to enjoy that film. Hey! Don't knock it till you've tried it!

Proper, innit? I get you. My gym membership’s been gathering dust for, like, six months. It’s massively convenient being so close to the city centre, but the classes are all rammed. And the personal trainers… eye-watering prices. Yeah, tell me about it. I tried that new one down by the river, ‘Apex Fitness’. Loads of trendy equipment, all chrome and lights, but every machine was occupied. Plus, the monthly fee is, like, a mortgage payment. I’m tempted to just stick to running, but the weather's been atrocious lately. Seriously! It's been pouring since, like, Tuesday. I was hoping for a good summer. Remember last year? That heatwave? I do. Took a week off and drove down to Cornwall. Best week of the year, honestly. Found this little beach, completely deserted… just waves and pasties. Bliss. Cornwall's always been on my list. My Nan practically lives there. Always sending me postcards with seagulls on. Need to actually, you know,  go  and see her sometime. I'm trying to plan something for August. Thinking maybe a road trip through Scotland. Need to get out of Cambridge for a bit, see something other than brick and sandstone. Scotland! That sounds amazing. Dramatic scenery, castles… Bagpipes. Bagpipes are optional. There's some seriously good whisky up there, though. Just saying. Daniel, always plugging the drinks! Seriously though, Scotland’s brilliant. Remember that documentary we watched about the Outer Hebrides? The landscapes were stunning. What kind of music are you listening to, Liam? Need something to go with the road trip vibe. I've been getting into a bit of… well, it's a bit embarrassing actually. 80s synth-pop. Depeche Mode, New Order… that kind of stuff. Proper nostalgic. No shame in that! It’s brilliant music. So catchy. Honestly, Sarah, you need to expand your taste. It's got more depth than you think. Alright, alright, stop converting me! I'm more of a chilled indie kind of girl. Phoebe Bridgers, Bon Iver... stuff like that. Perfect for rainy days, you know. I've been on a bit of a classic rock kick lately. Led Zeppelin, Queen… just rediscoverinig all the greats. Essential road trip music. Speaking of rediscovering things, have you guys heard anything about that kids’ camp for little Finn? Auntie Carol was saying she might send him. The one in Norfolk? I think I saw a flyer for it.

Honestly, did you  see  that tackle, Mark? Absolutely blatant! Ref’s having a right blind day, he is. Typical. Blatant is a strong word, love. It was a bit clumsy, certainly, but not a foul. He got the ball, didn’t he? Just a bit high. "A bit high"? He’s practically taken his legs out from under him! It was a dangerous challenge! They get away with murder these lads, don’t they? Newcastle would never have let that slide. They'd be fair crunchin'. Newcastle's crunching is often bordering on illegal, remember? Besides, it’s early days. Plenty of time for the ref to, shall we say, find his eyesight. This City team's just riding their luck at the minute. Aye, well, luck only gets you so far. They need to start showin’ some grit. Speaking of luck… did your mum remember to get the chocolate eggs? I was expectin’ them this mornin’. She did! A veritable mountain of them. She said she went a bit over the top this year. Apparently, you're getting the special dark chocolate ones, since you complained about having everything milk chocolate last year. Dead on! You tell her thanks. I’ve got a nose for a good dark chocolate egg, I have. Much better than that sickly sweet stuff. So, are you watching this for the football, or are you thinking about your thesis? You look proper pensive. A bit of both, to be honest. The data analysis is proving trickier than I anticipated. I was just trying to clear my head, you know? The game's a good distraction. Actually, it reminded me of a paper I read… it uses a similar dynamic modelling approach to analyse team performance… Oh, here we go. Just let me watch the game, love. Don’t start givin’ me lectures on dynamic modelling now. We’ll talk thesis later. Besides, there’s a penalty shout happening now... see? I knew they'd get somethin'! Alright, alright. Your football, your kingdom. But seriously, if you’re interested, I could briefly explain the relevance of— Mark! Look! He’s going down! Oh, brilliant! Penalty! See, ref finally woke up! Now, will he actually be bothered to award it, or will he pretend he didn’t see anything? You’re incorrigible. Always a drama queen when it comes to football. You know, we haven't watched a proper film in ages.

Ah, look at 'im now, Liam. Tiny wee thing, wasn’t 'e? Barely bigger than a football. Remember when 'e used to chase the pigeons in the park, so determined. He'd be screamin' after 'em, little arms flailin'. Oh, he was a whirlwind, wasn’t he? All energy. It's lovely to see this, honestly. Things have been…well, you know. It’s nice to remember the good times, the happy times. He looks so pleased in this one, dressed up as a little soldier for his birthday. Aye, a fierce little soldier. He wanted to be just like his Daddy, marching around the house. Speaking of which, Liam was sayin' 'e’s off to London next month. London? Oh really? What for? The marathon. He signed up, can you believe it? A full marathon! I'm terrified for 'im, to be honest. Thirty-two miles…it’s madness. But proud too, obviously. He’s always been a determined lad, like his grandfather. A marathon, you say? That’s quite something! A good bit different than a wee run round the park at primary school. I always encouraged my class to get moving, you know. Even just a quick burst of jumping jacks could work wonders. Got them all fitter than the PE teachers thought they'd be! It is impressive, Nana. Liam's been training hard. I bet he'll do really well. Did you see the pictures I sent you of Iceland? It was absolutely breathtaking. We went for a few days after the tour. I did, love. Beautiful, it was. Reminded me a bit of the Glens, but…bigger, more dramatic, somehow. That blue ice… unreal. Liam's considering going back next year. Says he wants to try some glacier hiking. He's always lookin' for the next adventure. He certainly is. Daniel’s not bad either, though. Got quite into that new superhero film at the cinema. Daniel? He’s a wee rascal, that one. Always got his nose buried in a comic, or buildin' his Lego creations. Remember that horrific fairground trip we had a few years back? He wouldn't go on anything! Said it was "too scary for a master builder." He was a wee drama king, wasn’t he? Totally terrified of the bouncy castle. And you trying to persuade him! Aye, well, grandads try their best, don't they?

…and honestly, the interface on the Kindle is just so clunky sometimes. Trying to highlight passages for work is a nightmare compared to a physical book. I mean, I love the convenience – having fifty books on one device is brilliant for travel – but the reading experience itself… it’s not quite the same, is it? Aye, it isn't. You’re right about that. All this technology, innit? Doesn’t always make things better, does it? Remember when we used to get excited about a brand new Walkman? That really  was  something special. No streaming, no downloads, just popping a cassette in and knowing you had your tunes for the whole afternoon. Walkman? Goodness me. You youngsters and your… Walkmans. We had a wireless set. Big, wooden thing it was. Took up half the living room. And you’d have to fiddle with the aerial to get a decent signal! Still, there were some lovely singalongs on the radio. Maisie Gray, remember her? Of course, Gran! Maisie Gray! My mum used to sing “Touch the Earth” all the time. It’s funny the things you remember, isn’t it? I was just thinking about marbles the other day. Proper glass marbles. Not these plastic things they have now. Used to spend hours on the pavement with the lads, playing chutes and ladders. Remember that, Carol? Oh, aye! Hours we spent! Me and Shirley, down on the Green, swapping marbles. I had a real beauty, a fiery dragon one. I was convinced it was magic. Lost it at the fair, though. Nearly cried my eyes out. And Chutes and Ladders! My little brother, Darren, he always cheated. He’d sneakily move his piece further along the ladders! Ladders! We played jacks. Tiny little metal things. You had to pick them up with one hand, flipping them in the air. Wonderful game. Kept you busy, they did. Didn't have much else to do back then. No televisions every five minutes! You're right about that, Gran. We were constantly entertained with far less. Do you remember those little wooden dolls, Carol? The peg dolls, with the button eyes and yarn hair? They’d be your friends for weeks. Building little houses out of cushions and blankets. Peg dolls! Absolutely! My Nan made me a whole family of ‘em. There was Mabel, my mum, and Geoff, my dad, and little Kevin - Darren's namesake!

Lovely bread, Arthur. Really lovely. You've been practising your crustless skills, 'aven't you? Well, 'ave to, don’t I, Doris? Can’t be havin' bits o' crust gettin' stuck in me dentures. Makes a right racket, it does. You’d think I were gnawin’ on a tree branch. You do make a racket sometimes, you know. But it's a comforting racket. Like a familiar rumble. So, I was thinking about that letter from Susan… the one about her wanting us to visit. Susan? Oh aye, Susan. S’been rabbitin’ on about come and seein’ her and the grandkids for weeks now. Expensive business, that sort o’ thing. Train fares… and lodgin’. Likely be stuck in some bleedin' modern box of a 'otel. Not like the old days, not like stayin' at Aunt Millie’s. Don't be such a grump, Arthur. The grandkids are growin' up so fast. Little Thomas is apparently halfway to bein' taller than me now! And Emily’s got a little dance recital. Susan said she’d be chuffed if we could make it. Proper chuffed, she said. Chuffed, eh? Fancy words, them. Always were a bit poncey, Susan's husband. City folk, they are. Never properly learned to appreciate a bit o' peace and quiet. Give me Norfolk any day. Used to spend me days down by the River Wensum, watchin’ the barges go by... peaceful as you like. You’ve told me about the River Wensum a thousand times, Arthur. You realize I’ve heard every barge story there is to hear? Still, it was a good life, wasn’t it? Simple. Simple it were. Not much fuss. Just… bein’. Mind you, bein' unemployed for all these years… that weren’t so simple, was it? Not easy lookin’ at folks workin’ and havin’ a purpose. Don’t start feelin' sorry for yourself again, darling. You 'ad a purpose. You were a master of the crossword. A legend, really. Remember the time you finished that fiendishly difficult one in the  Eastern Daily Press  in fifteen minutes flat? Mrs. Higgins from next door was truly amazed. Mrs. Higgins. Always pokin’ 'er nose in, that one. "Seen you doin’ yer crossword, Arthur," she’d say. "You’re a clever one, you are." Cleverer than a lot of folks, I reckon. Just… not clever enough to get a right proper job. Not clever enough for this modern world, I suppose.

Five years old, you say? That's a right cheek, innit? My nan’s Vauxhall is older than that and still trundling along perfectly fine. Honestly, makes you wonder what they actually  do  during an MOT. Well, it’s supposed to ensure it’s roadworthy, isn't it? Sounds like someone’s taken advantage, though. Did they give you a breakdown of the costs? They did. And that’s the worst bit. Over a grand! A  grand ! I’m thinking I might as well just scrap it and get something else reliable. But then, everything is so expensive these days. A grand! Blimey. That’s a proper chunk. What sort of car were you looking at getting, then? Something sensible, I reckon, after that experience? I was eyeing up a little Toyota Yaris, actually. They’re supposed to be pretty dependable. But even those are creeping up in price. I’ve been saving for a holiday, you know? Oh, a holiday! Where were you thinking of going? Somewhere sunny, I hope! This London weather is doing my head in. Oh, tell me about it! I swear, you can go from sunshine to drizzle in the space of ten minutes. I'm hoping to get to Cornwall for a proper beach break in the summer. The kids are desperate. Cornwall! Lovely. The beaches are gorgeous. I'm thinking maybe Greece, just somewhere I can properly relax. Maybe Santorini – proper cliché, I know! Santorini is beautiful, though! You deserve a cliché. Although, speaking of clichés, have you seen Sarah's Instagram lately? She's just posted about her weekend in the Cotswolds - all cream teas and thatched cottages. It's peak influencer stuff. Oh, Sarah! She’s always been a bit…extra. Remember that posh Christmas do she threw last year? The canapés were practically works of art! Don’t even remind me! I ended up spending half the evening trying to decipher what a ‘deconstructed fig and prosciutto tartlet’ even  was . My mum would have just served sausage rolls. Absolutely! My nan would have served a mountain of mince pies and called it a day. She's a gem, my nan. She’s been knitting hats for all the little ones at school. They look like something out of a Beatrix Potter book. So adorable. That’s so sweet! My little brother just got a hamster. It’s chaos, apparently. He's named it Winston.

Aye, L8 is notorious for the damp. My Auntie Maureen lived just around the corner, on Granby Street, and she battled with it for years. Never managed to conquer it, poor lass. She ended up moving to Aintree, bit of a sterile place, but at least the walls didn’t breathe on you. This house, though, it’s got character, hasn’t it? You’ve really done it up lovely, Anon.      Character and…moisture, yes. It’s a Victorian terrace, you see. Solid, but with all the inherent issues that come with solid Victorian architecture. I was reading about the construction techniques the other day, fascinating, really. Lime mortar, naturally breathable, but prone to… well, the conditions we get here. . Anyway, it's a project. A constant project.      It  is  beautiful, Anon. I love the stained-glass in the hallway. It reminds me of Hogwarts! You know, in  Harry Potter ? The colours and everything.      Ah, yes, a kindred spirit! My daughter, Elara, is a devoted Potterhead, as you probably guessed. She’s completely obsessed with Luna Lovegood. It’s amazing how those books capture the imagination, isn’t it? Much better than the dreary screen-based distractions kids have these days.      My lad, Jack, he was all about Quidditch for a while. Wanted a broomstick for his birthday, can you imagine? . He’s more interested in footie now, proper grown-up stuff. He's doing alright at school, you know? He’s got potential. He even mentioned wanting to go to uni… crazy, innit?      It’s wonderful to hear. Education is everything. Though… …it worries me sometimes, the state of the world. Everything that’s going on… ISIS and the like… it’s frightening. Feels like we’re teetering on the edge of something.      Don’t I know it. It’s all on the telly, innit? Gives you nightmares. My niece, she's trying to convince everyone it's all doom and gloom. Always going on about climate change and food shortages.      My mum's really worried about the news, too. She works at the school – she’s a Site Assistant – and she says the younger kids are asking about it, about whether they’ll be safe. It’s awful.      It's right that they are worried. It's important to acknowledge those concerns without… well, without instilling panic. I try to talk to Elara about it, honestly and truthfully, but in a way that’s age-appropriate.

Oh, don't fret, Penelope! It'll be a grand adventure. Remember that trip to Morocco we took back in '78? You were terrified of the camels then, but you absolutely  loved  it. Nepal will be no different. And altitude sickness? Just take it slow, drink plenty of water, and don’t try and climb Everest on your first day! I've been going to the Alps for years, and you learn to listen to your body. Morocco  was  lovely, actually. And the tagine… absolutely divine. But Nepal… it's a different level of… everything. Though, I must say, I do fancy a good cup of coffee while I'm there. Better than that instant stuff from the Village Shop, that’s for sure. Mrs. Higgins has really let the quality slip. The Village Shop  is  going downhill. Honestly, it’s all pre-packaged this and processed that now. Thank goodness for the Farm Shop just outside of town. Their sausages are phenomenal. Pork and apple, particularly. I got some yesterday for a barbeque. Though, between you and me, my Harold thinks I spend too much on them. Harold always did have an eye on the pennies! Speaking of food, how’s little Leo getting on? You’re the auntie, Penelope, are you getting bombarded with requests for advice about weaning? Oh, don't even. His mother is wonderfully capable, really. But she keeps asking my opinion on everything. Gluten-free this, allergy-aware that... it’s a minefield these days! When I had my children, we just gave them baby food and hoped for the best. No fuss, no fussiness. It  is  different now. My granddaughter, Beatrice, is allergic to everything it seems! They’re feeding her some concoction of rice flour and avocado. I feel quite sorry for the poor thing's parents. It reminds me of rationing, to be honest. Not quite the same, but the scarcity of certain ingredients… My mother-in-law, Elsie, she went through unbelievable hardship during the war. Fleeing Siberia, then overland through Turkey and eventually ending up in Tanganyika. She used to tell stories of eating anything and everything just to survive. Potato peels, nettle soup… unimaginable. Elsie’s story is incredible. So resilient. My own mother had it tough, too. She worked at the munitions factory during the war, you know. All that powdered egg and bully beef... it wasn’t exactly haute cuisine!

Aye, tell me about it! I know exactly what you mean. It's worse at the conference centre, mind. Hundreds of attendees, speakers, catering…every single little thing needs an email confirmation. It’s like being a glorified email robot, innit? Though, I was saying to Sarah the other day, at least it’s a predictable chaos. Unlike… well, unlike some things. Predictable chaos definitely sums up my admin job, too. Mrs. Featherstonehaugh – can you  believe  that name? – is utterly reliant on me to manage her diary. It's filled with things like 'water the ferns' and 'discuss the merits of various rose bush pruning techniques.' I'm a postgraduate, people! I have a Masters in History! I'm not a gardener's assistant. Oh my god, Mrs. Featherstonehaugh sounds  amazing . A proper eccentric. My job at the factory is… well, it’s just soul-crushing in a different way. It’s all spreadsheets and KPIs and making sure everything streams through exactly according to the Gantt chart. Zero room for, you know,  thinking . I’m a production controller, basically telling people where to stand and what to do. It’s amazing how much someone can pay you to feel completely useless. Useful?
