I spent half an hour this morning trying to track down a packet of Yorkshire Tea. Apparently, the Head of Marketing is  highly  particular about his tea. Head of Marketing! Over a packet of biscuits. I nearly went mental. It's brilliant though, proper laughing stuff when you look back. See, that’s what I need, a bit of chaos like that. At least it's  interesting . Mrs. Featherstonehaugh criticised the slant of the floral arrangement this morning. The  slant ! I nearly told her to do it herself. You should! Tell her you’ve got a Masters in History and you’re far too important to be concerned with floral slant. Though I suspect she'd have a very specific, historically accurate, reason as to why the angle is crucial. Aye, some folk are just built differently, aren't they? So, anyway… back to the chaos. I'm trying to organise a team-building event for the conference centre. Anyone got any bright ideas? Something that doesn't involve trust falls or corporate murder mysteries, please. What about something practical? Like a volunteering day? At a local animal shelter, perhaps? That’s always good for team morale, plus it’s actually… worthwhile.

…and honestly, David, the consultation was a farce. A single evening, on a Tuesday! Who's going to be able to make that with work and childcare? It’s clear they’ve already made up their minds. Demolish it, build flats. Standard procedure. I know, love. I had a look at the Borough Council minutes online. They’ve been circling this for months. 'Exploring options for optimising assets', they call it. Optimising assets. That’s a lovely euphemism for gutting our community. Exactly! And the library isn't just books, is it? It's the kids' reading groups, Mrs. Davies’ computer classes for the elderly, the space for the local history society… It's a lifeline for a lot of people. We  have  to do something. This petition feels like a drop in the ocean, but it’s better than nothing. It's a start. I’ve been drafting some of the wording, you know. Tried to keep it concise, impactful. Hard when you're fuming, though. I spent half an hour trying to remember the mnemonic for remembering the order of operations! BODMAS, it was. Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. Why can’t I just  remember  these things? Age, darling. It's the curse of approaching fifty. My brain’s a sieve these days. I’ve been trying those Lumosity brain-training games. No idea if they actually work, but it's something to do while I'm transcribing those impenetrable insurance forms. They’re all jargon and clauses. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I'm deciphering ancient hieroglyphs. Insurance forms. Don’t even get me started. My shifts this week have been brutal. The new system rollout is a disaster. Everything’s slower, more complicated. The IT department promised it would streamline things… it's done the opposite. I spent three hours yesterday just trying to track down a missing document. Oh, that’s awful! Are they offering any extra support? Because if not, you need to flag it to HR. You can’t be expected to work under those conditions. You looked exhausted last night. Flagged it already. Standard response: 'Training sessions available, please book in'. Honestly, it's like talking to a brick wall. They don't seem to grasp the sheer volume of disruption this is causing. And they're already talking about cutting back on administrative staff. So, you’re worried about redundancies? It’s a concern.

Honestly, Arthur, it's a nightmare! Last summer, we drove round for nearly an hour trying to find somewhere. Ended up miles out and had to walk. My knees weren't thanking me, I can tell you. Did you hear about Ms. Higgins getting a ticket? Aye, I did. Right outside the lifeboat station, poor woman. Said she was only popping in for an ice cream. They're just greedy, aren't they? Lining their pockets. Reminds you a bit of those taxes, doesn't it? Stealing from the working man. Though I suppose 'working' is a relative term for me now. Working? You were a civil engineer, Arthur! Designed bridges, didn’t ya? A proper profession. I just helped my mum at the greengrocer's. Didn’t earn much, mind you. Never needed to. But these taxes... they keep going up, don't they? Makes a fella wonder where it’s all going. It's awful, isn't it? They tell you it's for the NHS, and schools, and all that, but... I don't see it. And what about that leaflet the Witnesses left today? About the impending doom and the rule of the Earth? Honestly, it makes your head spin. Those Jehovah's Witnesses…always peddling their prophecies. They were round here last week as well. Very persistent, some of them. Though, you can't fault their dedication, I suppose. A bit rigid in their thinking, though. Never room for a bit of reasoned argument, have they? Rigid is putting it mildly. Remember old Mr. Gable down the lane? Trying to convert him for years. Wouldn't have it. He’d just shut the door. Though, I always thought he was a bit eccentric anyway, what with all those pigeons he kept. Oh, the pigeons! Honestly, they were a menace. Cooing and flapping everywhere. My Doris used to say they were a sign of bad luck. Still, lovely birds, if you don't mind the mess. We’ve got a robin come to the bird feeder, a lovely little fellow. Much more polite than those pigeons. Aye, robins are alright. Reminds you of your childhood, doesn't it? Catching minnows down the river Wensum back in Norwich. Simpler times. Speaking of simpler times…remember when we used to go to the King's Head for a Sunday roast? Proper roast, it was. Not like this pre-packaged nonsense they try to pass off now.

Absolutely, dear. A far cry from the damp kindles they used to sell. It’s amazing what a difference good wood makes. Though, I do think we’re being a bit extravagant. Hugh, are you sure we can afford to be lighting the log burner  every  evening? Now, Margaret, don’t start. We discussed this. And besides, the weather's turned. A little comfort is all we’re asking for. ANON’s been working terribly hard lately – outsourcing all those medical transcripts to India, a right mess, if you ask me. India, eh? Used to have a chap from Delhi at the school, years ago. Brilliant Latin scholar. Though his cricket… well, lacking, to be frank. Still, a gentleman. Outsourcing...a necessary evil, I suppose, in this modern age. Keeps the coffers afloat. It’s not  all  outsourcing, Dad. I'm supplementing with some hand transcription; it's less prone to errors. But yes, the medical work... it’s a beast. And exhausting. Did I tell you about the new restaurant that opened next door? "Spice Route," they call it. Indian, naturally. They're doing a cracking business. Mrs. Henderson keeps complaining about the smells, though. "Like a curry house in my pot plants," she declared this morning. Honestly! Oh, the neighbours! Always something, aren't there? We had the Millers next door in Edinburgh. Constant complaining about the noise from my piano practice. Though, I daresay they were just jealous. Speaking of Edinburgh, did you ever get round to looking at that antique shop I mentioned? The one with the lovely Scottish pottery? We did, actually. Didn't find anything we particularly needed, though. Spent a small fortune on fudge, though. Honestly, ANON, you were clearing the shelves! It was exceptionally good fudge, darling! Sea salt caramel. It’s a weakness. We need to be sensible about the budget, though, you’re right. These log burner expenses are piling up. And the cats are demanding even more premium salmon lately. Cats and dogs… a constant battle for dominance, aren’t they? We always had a terrier at the school, Bartholomew. A rough little chap, but good for keeping the grounds tidy. Though, the girls found him rather intimidating. They used to refer to him as "The Terror of Torrington." Arthur, really! You’re dwelling on school anecdotes again. We’re here to relax and enjoy ourselves. What about your trip from Tokyo, ANON?

Well, Arthur, it’s a fair point. Used to be a proper pride in keepin’ things tidy, you know? A bit of elbow grease, a sweep o’ the pavement. Now it’s all about offsettin' your carbon footprint. Doesn't seem to fix much, does it? All this recycling… they wheel out the bins, we put our stuff in, and then where does it  go ? Probably China, probably. China! That’s right. They’re makin’ a fortune off our rubbish, they are. Remember old Mrs. Higgins down the road? Always scoffin’ at me for burnin' my garden waste. 'Environmentally irresponsible,' she’d say. Now look at her, takin’ three bins to the kerb every Wednesday. Three! And she complains about the price of fuel. Oh, you two are terrible. It’s not all about complaining. Recycling  does  make a difference. A small one, admittedly, but still. My daughter, bless her, practically lives by the recycling guidelines. She’s always on at me to rinse out my yoghurt pots. Though I do find it rather exhausting, to be honest. Exhausting? Good heavens, Penelope, you’re talkin’ like it’s hard labour! I spent fifteen years designin’ bridges, Penelope.  That  was exhausting. This…rinsing yoghurt pots... is hardly comparable. Bridges! That’s impressive, Ronald. You ever work on the A47 bypass? Terrible state it was, back then. Full of potholes you could lose a small car in. I did indeed. Part of the Foot and Mouth outbreak. Difficult times. Though, you know, the mindset’s changed. Back then, if you said you were layin' off people to save money, you'd get a right earful. Now, it’s just…accepted. These big corporations, they just shuffle numbers around and bleed the country dry. It's awful, really. And the taxes! Don’t even get me started on the taxes. They took a chunk out of my pension this year. A chunk! Where’s it all going? More leaf blowers for the council, probably. Pensions…another disaster. Promised us a fortune, didn't they? And what do we get? Enough to buy a packet of biscuits and a tin of beans. At least when I was a lad, a penny meant somethin'! You know, I was lookin’ at property prices the other day. Absolutely scandalous. My grandson wants to buy a house near Cambridge. A  terraced  house, mind you, not even a semi. Wants a mortgage of nearly three hundred thousand!

Jaysus, Liam, you wouldn't believe the state of it. Little Finnian here decided it was a good idea to use his crayons on the keyboard. Bright orange all over the keys. Absolutely savage work. Crayons? Seriously? My little brother once tried to feed my PS4 a biscuit. A  biscuit , Dad! See? They’re all the same. Wild little critters. Anyway, it’s not just the crayons. The whole thing’s running sluggish now, taking an age to boot up. I think there's somethin' serious going on under the hood. So, can you fix it, then, love? Finnian needs to do his homework tonight. He's been moaning like a banshee about it. I'll give it a go, Sarah. It’s probably just a right mess of temporary files and who knows what else. But I’m starting to think it might need a proper clean install of the operating system. That’s a trek, mind you. Takes a fair bit of time. Could you back it up first? In case you… you know… break it more? Very sensible, young man. Appreciate the concern. I'll definitely back it up first. Wouldn't want to lose all their pictures and whatnot. Speaking of pictures, did you send those rugby photos to your sister yet? The ones from last weekend? She was asking. Ah, not yet. Been a bit bogged down with this computer nonsense. I'll do it tonight, sure. Don’t want her fumin’. She loved seein’ little Cillian – Finnian's cousin – try to tackle a grown man. He nearly took out half the pitch. See? Even  he  thinks it was funny. Right, now, about the evening... Sarah, any plans for tonight besides wrangling a toddler and overseeing homework? Not really. I was thinking maybe we could order in some fajitas. But we’re out of that fajita sauce you like, the one with the smoked paprika. Jaysus, don't remind me. That stuff is crucial. Reckon we could manage with some chili powder and a bit of lime juice? My mum makes a really good one with mango! She puts diced mango in it! Mango? In fajita sauce? That's... brave, son. Very brave. He's got a point, love. It’s actually quite nice. Though, maybe not for you. Rest assured, I’ll stick with the more traditional approach. Though, I'll add mango to the notes for the next shop.

Right, so, two slices each, yeah? That’s four slices gone already. Honestly, these are enormous. Leo, darling, chew properly, you’re going to choke! But I want more! Pizza good! You'll get more, sweetie, but swallow first. Maisie, are you even eating yours? You're just staring at it. It’s...orangey. It’s cheesy, love. Cheese  is  orangey sometimes. It’s delicious, trust me. You know, I was thinking about that workshop I went on last week – communication in families – all a bit much, wasn't it? They kept saying, "Active listening, reflective language…" Honestly, sometimes a simple, "Eat your pizza" is just more effective. Mummy says 'active listing' means you have to look at people when they're talking. That’s… partially right, sweetheart. It’s a bit more complicated than that. It’s about really  understanding  what someone’s trying to say. Like, Maisie doesn’t  just  think the pizza is orangey, she's probably worried it doesn’t taste right. Right, love? Maybe. See? That’s active listening, trying to figure out what's behind the words. Anyway, back to pizza. You know, if we were creating the perfect family menu, I'd definitely include garlic bread. And maybe a proper salad, not just lettuce. And…what about you two? What’s your ideal menu? Chocolate cake! With lots of sprinkles! And dinosaurs! Dinosaurs? You want dinosaur-shaped… anything? Dinosaurs for dinner! Like, plates with dinosaurs on, and chicken shaped like dinosaurs! Fairy bread! And sparkly juice! Fairy bread and sparkly juice! Right, that’s a sophisticated menu. We’ll work on that. You know, I was reading about Loch Ness the other day… apparently, there's new sonar evidence suggesting… well, some quite intriguing things. The Loch Ness Monster?! Is it real?! That’s what they’re saying! Some scientists think there's something very large living in the loch. Maybe it likes pizza too! Maybe it’s got sparkly juice! Maybe it does! Leo, can you do a handstand? You were showing off yesterday. I can! Watch! Whoops! Well done, darling! Not quite perfect, but impressive! Maisie, you should try it. Don't worry, I'll spot you. No! I want to wear my party dress! The sparkly one! We need to make a fairy garden too! With glitter and stones and…and tiny houses! A fairy garden, brilliant! We can definitely do that this weekend.

Now, Chloe, don't knock it. Food technology's important. Understanding where your food comes from, how it's made… it's good knowledge. Besides, that Mr. Henderson’s a cracking teacher, even if he does have a bit of a quirky side. Remember that year he brought in a live badger for biology? It was a taxidermied badger, Mum. Not a live one. And he did a really good presentation on it. Well, near enough! The point is, he's engaging. And this fermenting thing… it’s apparently all the rage. Apparently there’s some sort of revival. Honestly, the fads people latch onto. Remember the quinoa phase? All this obsession with 'artisanal' everything? It’s just clever marketing, most of it. Though I must admit, this local olive oil is remarkably good. Far superior to anything you get in London. Aye, it is good. This bread is proper good too. Better than anything from Greggs, that's for sure! This Croatian food is smashing. I'm proper liking it, I are. It's just... Mr. Henderson showing us how to make kimchi? It felt bizarre. And then he went on about food preservation techniques from the Middle Ages. It was interesting, actually. He showed us about canning, and how they used to seal jars with wax. See? Liam gets it. And speaking of interesting, this Croatian sunshine is a welcome change from that dreary weather back home. Remember last October? Spent the whole month in waterproofs. Utterly miserable. Although, I do appreciate a good drizzle. Keeps the streets clean. It’s the relentless humidity I can’t stand. Makes my hair… unruly. My hair's fine. It's just a bit wavy. You're always moaning about your hair, Dad! Speaking of travel, you reckon we'll ever get to see Italy? You were talking about going to Rome last year. We will, love. Patience. Rome’s definitely on the list. What about you two? Where would you like to go? Besides, you know, another all-inclusive in Benidorm. Liam, where do you fancy? Japan, maybe. I've been looking at some photography stuff online. The cherry blossoms would be brilliant. And the architecture. Japan! Excellent choice. A fascinating country. Though the immigration officers there can be… thorough. I remember a colleague who had his suitcase practically dismantled once. Something about a rogue teaspoon. Seriously? A teaspoon? They’re proper strict then, aren’t they?

Right, I’ve just been reading this article... about PPI claims, actually. Apparently, there’s this last-minute rush on, because the deadline's looming.      PPI, eh? Blimey. All that fuss. Spent near enough a month going through paperwork for that, I did. Didn't get much back, mind. Not worth the bother, really. Costessey used to be a nicer place for botherin’ about finances, that’s for sure. Easier times.      Arthur, dear, stop worrying about Costessey like that. It was a long time ago. This article…is it helpful, David? Should we be looking into it again? I’m still a bit hazy on the details.      Not really, Brenda. Seems too late now, most likely. They’re really trying to squeeze everything out of people before the deadline. More of a warning, really. Speaking of squeezing... I’ve got those tickets for the party at Eleanor’s booked. Saturday, remember?      Yes, I remember. Eleanor’s parties are… lively. Too lively, perhaps, for a man of my age. My knees aren’t what they used to be. Trying to navigate a throng of people is a challenge. I ran rather a successful business, you know. Had proper staff, didn’t have to jostle for space.      Lively? That’s a polite way of putting it, Charles. Last time I was there, young Penelope started singing – proper belting it out! – and nearly knocked over the potted fern.      Oh, Arthur, you exaggerate. It was a charming rendition of “Amazing Grace.” You were singing along, weren't you?      Well, I might have hummed a bit. Lovely singing it is in the Abbey, though. That echo… marvelous. Remember when we went to Ely Cathedral? That acoustics, you could hear a pin drop. I used to enjoy choir practice... simpler times.      It’s good you’re in decent shape for the party. Eleanor’s getting a pianist in this year, apparently. Proper classical stuff. Though, knowing Eleanor, she’ll sneak in a bit of Abba at some point.      Abba? Good heavens. I prefer something a little more…refined. I read a fascinating article in  The Economist  the other day, about the impact of automated seed sorting on agricultural yields. Quite complex, really.      Seeds? You and your seeds, Charles. I've got these sweet peas to sow. Got a proper bargain at the garden centre. Best value you'll find this side of Norwich, I reckon. Always been good with a bit o’ gardening, y'know.

Honestly, Margaret, another day, another deluge of petty theft and public order offences. You wouldn't believe the excuses some of them come up with. It’s exhausting explaining the legalities to them, even more so when they genuinely seem surprised by the consequences. Aye, well, I’ve seen it all in my time, love. Thirty years I’ve been ushering in and out of these courts. You get used to the parade of faces. Though, I’ll admit, it's gotten busier, hasn’t it? Seems like there’s more pressure on the system than there used to be. Absolutely. They're cutting budgets everywhere, aren't they? Which, naturally, impacts everything from court staff to the probation service. Makes rehabilitation almost impossible. I was just thinking about one young lad today – clearly struggling with addiction. Sentenced to a community order, but where's the support to actually  help  him? Exactly! That’s what I’ve been saying for years. Punishment’s one thing, but sorting out the root of the problem, that’s what’s lacking. Back home in Aberdeenshire, we didn’t have this level of… well, chaos. People looked out for each other. It's changed, hasn't it? Not just the justice system, but everything. This climate, for starters. Ridiculous weather we’re having. Flooding everywhere. Tell me about it! I spent the weekend rescuing my neighbour's cat from a flooded garden. It’s frightening, isn’t it? All the scientists are saying… and it doesn’t seem to be registering with everyone. My nephew, he’s at university in Bristol, studying environmental science. He’s seriously worried. Good for him. Knowledge is power, isn’t it? Though, it worries me for his future, to be honest. Everything feels a bit… precarious, doesn’t it? Especially with the way prices are going up. Heating bills alone! I’m on a fixed income, you know. These pension increases are a joke. I know exactly what you mean. It's getting tight for everyone, isn’t it? My husband’s a primary school teacher, and they’re struggling with the cost of materials and energy in the classroom. We were talking about maybe cutting back on our holiday this year. We usually go to Cornwall. Cornwall is lovely! I went there with my late husband, David, years ago. Beautiful beaches. Shame you have to think twice about it.

Tell me about it, love. I’m sure you’re brilliant though. Florence Nightingale, eh? Bit serious for a Tuesday evening. Florence Nightingale helped people who were poorly! She had lots of lamps! That’s right, sweetheart. A very important lady. And what are you doing, my little engineer? Building a super-fast racetrack? It’s a motorway, Mummy. And it goes to a castle. A  really  big castle with gold! Gold, you say? Ooh, fancy! That sounds like a very happy motorway indeed. Eliza, do you know what makes people happy? Kittens! And chocolate! And sparkly things! Excellent choices, my darling. Proper happiness-makers. Leo, what makes  you  happy? Besides gold, of course. Cars that go  vroom ! And… and rhymes! Rhymes! You like rhymes? That’s brilliant! Let’s do a rhyme! “I saw a cat, sitting on a…?” …mat! Brilliant! You’re a rhyme master! Now, let's think. What if we had lots and lots of money? Like, enough to fill this whole house with bouncy castles? Really? A bouncy castle  in  the living room?! Could I have a pink one? With glitter? Absolutely, darling. A giant pink, glittery bouncy castle. And Leo could have a whole fleet of toy cars, no matter how many motorways he builds! Could I buy a real car? A red one! With a horn that goes  beep beep ? Well, maybe when you're a bit bigger, little one. But with lots of money, you could do pretty much anything you wanted. Travel to space! Learn to fly! Have a pet unicorn! Mummy, but will the unicorn like sparkly things too? I think any unicorn would adore sparkly things, sweetheart. But you know what? Having all that money... it wouldn’t  make  us happy, would it? Not really. No… It would be fun for a little while, I suppose. But the best things are free. Like cuddling on the sofa, making up rhymes, and… …having you two.  That's  what makes me truly happy. I make you happy? You absolutely do, my love. You both do. It’s the very best feeling in the world. Now, about that Florence Nightingale paragraph… even a bouncy castle queen needs to do her homework. But maybe we can reward ourselves with a biscuit afterwards? A chocolate biscuit, for extra happiness. Chocolate biscuits! And can I build another motorway to the castle? A  longer  one?

…and honestly, the whole “global leader” thing with China just feels a bit… scary, doesn't it? Like, they're investing everywhere, buying up everything. It's not just about phones and cheap electronics anymore. They're getting into infrastructure, technology, even football clubs! Yeah, it’s mad, isn’t it? Mr. Davies was going on about it in Geography. He said it's a calculated move – build influence, control resources. It’s a bit like the British Empire, but, you know, reverse. Except, unlike the Empire, they’re not exactly proclaiming a load of lofty ideals about spreading civilization. It’s more about economic dominance. Exactly! It's all so transactional. Makes you wonder, doesn’t it, what it means for us? For Britain? Will we just become a branch office for some massive Chinese corporation in fifty years? Don't be dramatic! Though, I can see where you're coming from. Dad was saying something similar the other day, actually. He’s been reading up on Chinese investment in Africa – mining rights, building railways… they've got a huge footprint already. He reckons we need to be smarter about how we interact with them, more strategic. Easier said than done, isn't it? Speaking of strategy... I’ve been thinking about patents, actually. Remember old Mr. Henderson, the design teacher? He was going on about how vital intellectual property is. Vaguely. He was always trying to get us to design ridiculously complicated folding chairs. Yeah, but he made a good point, though! Like, if you have an idea, a genuinely good one, you need to protect it. Imagine inventing something that revolutionises energy, or something... and then some Chinese company just copies it wholesale. Right! Like that drone company? DJI. They’re proper big now, but used to be a smaller thing, supposedly nicking tech from American companies. Mr. Davies was talking about that too – intellectual property theft is a huge issue. Precisely. It got me thinking. I've been messing around with coding, you know, little apps and stuff. Nothing serious… but what if I stumbled onto something useful? Something someone would want to pay for. You're always on that computer. You could build some kind of AI assistant for students, maybe? We’re constantly complaining about having to manage all our different logins and deadlines. Something that organises it all for you. Hmmm, not a bad idea.

Honestly, Sarah, I'm still a bit miffed about that blue run we attempted yesterday. I know you were saying it was "perfectly fine," but my knees were absolutely screaming afterward. I felt like I'd aged ten years! Oh, come on, Claire! Don't be so dramatic. It was a little steeper than the green, yes, but ‘screaming’? You’re being a bit over the top. Besides, you were going far too fast! I told you to ease up a bit near the bottom. Easing up is easier said than done when you’re trying not to end up in a snowdrift! And you were practically floating down it. Must be all those years you spent on the slopes. I'm a bit rusty, you know. Haven’t properly skied since… well, since the kids were tiny and we dragged them to Lapland. That was a horrifying experience, wasn't it? Little Leo nearly lost a ski. Anyway, look, today we’ll stick to the easier slopes. Promise. And maybe we can grab a hot chocolate afterwards, really nurse those knees of yours. That’s more like it. A proper hot chocolate, with whipped cream and marshmallows. Not that watery stuff they were serving up at the bottom of the ‘perfectly fine’ blue run. Speaking of the kids... have you heard from Emily? She hasn’t replied to my texts. I sent her a picture of the view from the hotel balcony. She’d have loved it. No, I haven't. She’s probably just buried in revision, poor love. Finals are looming, as you know. She mentioned something about a particularly nasty essay on Victorian Literature. Sounds dreadful. I sent her a postcard - a snowy mountain scene. Might cheer her up. How’s Tom doing? Still obsessing over that new video game? You know Tom. Perpetually obsessed. He's actually trying to learn coding now, apparently. Says it'll be useful for game design. Says he’ll build his own game one day. Ambition at fourteen… it’s both impressive and terrifying! Have you spoken to Mum recently? Not since Sunday. She seemed alright then, a little bit tired, but alright. She keeps saying she's "keeping busy" which, knowing Mum, probably involves reorganising the cutlery drawer for the fifth time this week. Should I call her tonight? Just to check in? Yes, please do. I’ve been meaning to, but things have been a bit hectic here.

Honestly, David, I'm just flummoxed by this string business. They keep snapping! It's the bane of my existence. We’ve repaired so many rackets, haven't we, and they're all lasting barely a week. A week, precisely. I’ve been charting it. It’s most frustrating. It’s not the tension, I’m certain. We're consistently stringing them to the spec recommended by the manufacturers. It’s just… the strings themselves. Inferior quality, I suspect. That’s what I thought! But sourcing a decent string that's affordable... that’s the challenge. We can't charge a fortune to repair a school racket, can we? Especially not for the primary schools. They're on such a tight budget. Precisely. That's why I was thinking about these cable ties. Thick, nylon ones. Secure as anything. We could use them to reinforce the string, running them parallel to the existing strands, particularly where they seem to be breaking most often. Cable ties… hmm. Clever! But wouldn’t they be visible? And wouldn’t that look rather… unprofessional? Especially for the secondary schools. They’d want something more discreet. Not necessarily. We'd use thin ones, black nylon. Position them carefully - barely discernible. And the positioning is key, isn’t it? Rather than simply running them along the entire length, we focus on the high-stress points, the inside edges of the frame, where the string tends to fray. Weight distribution is important too, wouldn’t want to add too much. Perhaps even just a few, strategically placed. Yes, that makes sense. Roughly how much do a packet of those thick ties cost? I looked online. A pack of fifty decent ones is about eight pounds. So, roughly fifteen pence a tie. Not bad. And they'll last. Unlike these flimsy strings! Though, honestly, the thought of advertising them… “Reinforced with Cable Ties!” Doesn't quite have the same ring to it, does it? Not quite. More like "String Stability System" perhaps? Sounds a bit more... impressive. You know, speaking of impressive, I saw a programme on the telly,  Dragons’ Den . We could pitch to them! Imagine! Dragging  that  idea in front of those ruthless dragons? They’d tear it to shreds. "Cable ties on badminton rackets? Preposterous!" They'd say. But what if we presented it well? Focused on the problem – string fragility – and our solution? A cost-effective, reliable repair that lasts longer?

Speaker_1 stirred his tea vigorously, a slight tremor causing a ripple effect in the floral china. Speaker_3 smiled patiently. "Yes, Grandad, I understand. It's about the physicality of the work. I was reading about Van Gogh's sunflowers, and how the way he applied the paint – almost swirling it – conveys such a sense of movement and energy." "Van Gogh! Now there was a fella," Arthur chuckled, a little wheeze accompanying the sound. “Right proper artist, he were. Didn’t have much else goin’ for ‘im, did he? But he could put a bit o' sunshine on a canvas, that’s for sure. Much better than that modern rubbish they try to flog you nowadays. All splodges and no sense, that is.” Speaker_2 tsked gently from the sofa. "Arthur, darling, don't be like that. Not  all  modern art is rubbish. Some of it is quite thought-provoking. Remember that exhibition we saw in London a few years ago? With the… the sculptures made of felt?" Arthur shuddered. “Felt! Looks like me grandmother’s old sewing box exploded. Give me a nice Constable any day. Flat Norfolk fields, you know - somethin' proper.” He took a long sip of his tea. Speaker_4 , who’d been silently observing, chimed in, “There's a lot to be said for tradition, Grandad. Landscapes, portraits, that kind of thing. But modern art isn’t necessarily about  representing  something, it’s about exploring ideas, pushing boundaries...” "Boundaries, is it? Pushin' boundaries is just an excuse for not bein' able to paint a proper picture, if you ask me," Arthur grumbled good-naturedly. "Eleanor, you're a smart girl. You got all them degrees and whatnot. What do you make of all this ‘pushin’ of boundaries’?" Eleanor paused, considering. “Well, I think it’s a reaction, really. After centuries of artists trying to accurately depict the world, they started questioning what art  should  be. It’s about prompting questions, challenging perceptions.” She looked at James. “Think about Rothko’s colour fields. They’re not ‘pictures’ in the traditional sense, but they evoke a powerful emotional response. It's less about  what  you're seeing and more about  how  you feel.” James nodded. "Exactly. And the conceptual art movement – artists like Duchamp – really questioned the definition of art itself. Was it the skill of the artist, the object itself, or the ideas behind it?" “Duchamp?” Arthur squinted. “Sounds French.

…and honestly, the way she was explaining the cognitive behavioural techniques? It was like she was reading from a textbook but hadn’t actually  absorbed  any of it. She kept saying things like, "Patients should strive for positive reframing," with this totally blank stare. Like, yeah, okay, brilliant, but you need to explain  how  they do that! It's frustrating, you know? You’re trying to help people, and you’re having to correct the training. Right? It’s the performative stuff, isn't it? Like they just learned the buzzwords and think they’ve cracked the code. Honestly, my project manager this week tried to use the term "synergy" approximately seventeen times in a single email. Synergy! It’s just… unnecessary. Synergy! Oh god, don't even get me started. It’s one of those words that sounds clever when you say it, but actually means absolutely nothing. Why can't people just say, "working together effectively?" Exactly! It’s like they’re trying to sound important. It's exhausting. Speaking of exhausting...have you done any cleaning this week? Because this kitchen is a disaster area. I swear, I cleaned it on Tuesday and it already looks like a bomb went off. Tuesday? You’re being generous. I think ‘bomb’ is an appropriate analogy, actually. No, I haven’t. I've been swamped. That training was six hours a day, four days this week. Brain fried. Plus, I’ve been trying to finish that report on the adolescent mental health initiative. Ugh, reports. The bane of my existence. My project's going sideways already. Apparently, Brenda in accounts has “misfiled” a crucial invoice, and now we’re facing a potential delay. Brenda. Of all people. Brenda sounds like a character from a sitcom. “Brenda from accounts, destroyer of projects.” Seriously though, try not to stress. Invoices get lost. It’s just…Brenda. It’s  always  Brenda. Actually, I was thinking… maybe we should just order a takeaway tonight? Cleaning can wait. I'm in serious procrastination mode. Absolutely. Chinese? Or are you feeling something more exotic? I craved Thai food all week. Thai’s good. Pad See Ew? And, like, actual spring rolls, not those sad, tiny ones you get sometimes? Definitely actual spring rolls. Look, I’m ordering. What about drinks? Wine? Yeah, a bottle of that Pinot Grigio we got last week would be amazing. You know, maybe after dinner, we could actually try to tackle the worst of the kitchen?

Right, well, that’s… classic Mark. You know he's got this, this fixed way of seeing things. He's not malicious, is he? Just… stubbornly unhelpful. No, not malicious, just… infuriating. I mean, I had to bite my tongue so hard during the board meeting last week when he kept interrupting Sarah with his "helpful" suggestions. It’s not about inherent logic, it’s about opportunity, education, the way we’re all socialized! It's infuriating that people still fall for that nonsense. Look, I get it. You’re bright, you’re capable. You're doing a cracking job keeping Mr. Henderson’s life from falling apart. He’d be lost without you, honestly. But Mark, he's rooted in his generation, isn't he? Some things you just can't shift. But  shouldn't  we be trying? Isn't that what progress is about? It’s not even about proving him wrong, it’s about... well, it’s about dismantling these outdated frameworks. I was reading something fascinating the other day about how women in some Nordic countries are given paternity leave  longer  than maternity leave. Can you imagine the shift that would cause? It’d be a bit of a shocker around here, wouldn't it? Dad taking six months off while Mum gets back to work. The blokes would be having palpitations. But I agree, it's a good point. It’s about rebalancing things, isn’t it? Though, knowing Mark, he’d probably say men aren't wired for childcare. Exactly! Which is another thing. People confuse common sense with intelligence. He thinks knowing how to fix a leaky tap means you're inherently cleverer than someone who understands quantum physics. There's a difference, yeah. Common sense is handy, though. You can't argue with knowing when to wear a coat, or how to avoid getting rained on. I mean, look at me. Didn’t even think to bring a bloody umbrella today. See? Common sense isn't world-changing brilliance. It's not the same thing. It’s reactive, survival-based. Intelligence is… proactive, creative. And it's certainly not gender-specific. True, true. Speaking of reactive, fancy a glass of something to take the edge off? All this feminist discourse must be tiring. I probably shouldn’t. I'm trying to cut back. Honestly, I think I'm relying on it a bit much these days.

“…and honestly, the tractor ride was the highlight for them both, wasn’t it? Little Leo kept shouting “Faster! Faster!” the whole time. It was adorable, really. Though, I was slightly worried he was going to launch himself off the trailer." “Tractor! Vroom vroom!” "Straw... itchy." "Yes, darling, the straw  was  a bit itchy wasn’t it? That’s why I got you that jumper. See, all covered up. Right, let’s clear this away. Did you two eat properly at the farm? There was that lovely picnic area…” “Sandwiches! Ham!” “No carrots. Carrots yucky.” “Okay, okay. No carrots. You’re a fussy one, aren’t you? Much like your father when he was little, I remember. Right, so school. Mrs. Davies called me this morning, actually. About Leo." “Leo?” “Yes, sweetie. Nothing terrible, don't worry. But apparently, he was disrupting story time again. Said he was ‘helping’ by making aeroplane noises.” “Aeroplane! Whee!” "Exactly! Apparently, the other children were struggling to hear. I explained to Mrs. Davies that he’s just bursting with energy, you know? It’s a tricky balance, isn't it? Trying to contain all that enthusiasm." "Teacher sad?" "Well, she was a bit frustrated. But she understands. We talked about finding something for him to do during story time, perhaps some quiet colouring or something. And you, sweetheart - how was your day?" “Painted! Blue! Like the sky!” “Wonderful! Blue like the sky. That’s lovely. Mrs. Peterson said you were really focused today, which is brilliant. It’s just… sometimes, you get a bit distracted, doesn’t it? Little wanderings around the classroom.” “Wander! See dinosaurs!” “Dinosaurs, yes. That’s right. Well, we’ll work on it. It’s all part of learning to concentrate. So, DVDs for tonight then? Fancy something with animals? We could re-watch ‘Babe’, you both loved that.” "Babe! Piggy!" "No piggy! Tractor!" “Alright, alright. We'll compromise. We  could  watch a bit of ‘Babe’ and then find something with tractors involved. Maybe that farm machinery documentary I downloaded? It’s a bit grown-up, but…” “Dinosaur! Then pig?” "Hmm, that  is  a good negotiation tactic... Dinosaurs  then  piggy it is. Though, I'm honestly starting to think I need a degree in child diplomacy. Honestly, navigating a simple evening’s entertainment is more complicated than teaching a Year 5 class some times. Right, let's get these dishes cleared so we can start the dinosaur hunt.”

…and honestly, the colour blocking on her jumper was  criminal . Like, who lets someone leave the house looking like a rejected Halloween costume? It were all neon pink and electric blue. Could’ve blinded someone, it could. Right, right. You're talking about Millie, from that…reality show documentary? The one about the influencers? Aye, Millie. The one trying to convince everyone she's an "artist" because she sticks glitter on fruit. Glitter. On fruit. I’m still reeling from it, to be fair. And the jumper! I’d have had words, I would. I’m just saying, if you're gonna knit, at least make it look like you put a bit o' effort in, eh? Like your mum’s Fair Isle, that's proper work. Your mum makes stunning things. It’s a different level entirely. Millie just...seems to be going for sheer volume, not quality. Speaking of knitting, did you finally finish that scarf for your gran? The one you were muttering about needing a week’s worth of yarn for? Nearly! Just the fringe to go. I’m procrastinating on the fringe. It's fiddly, isn’t it? I keep thinking about going back to the garter stitch. Solid, dependable, no fringe involved. It’s proving ironically distracting, thinking about how comforting that plain stitch is while I’m trying to execute a cascade fringe! There you go. Rooibos, as requested. It’ll clear your head. So, have you been following the Olympics at all? The artistic gymnastics have been incredible, haven't they? Aye, they have. Simone Biles being back is...well, it's more than just sport, isn't it? It's a real statement. Proper brave lass. Makes you think, doesn't it? About all the pressure they’re put under. My cousin's daughter's on a competitive dance team; it's intense. It is. And it’s a far cry from the casual crochet circles I ended up in at university. Remember that weird group of performance art students who thought making doilies was a political act? Using "domestic crafts to subvert patriarchal structures" – that was their slogan, I swear. Oh, God, you're not kidding! I vaguely recall something about that. Did they ever actually  sell  any of their doilies? Not that I'm aware of. They mostly just exhibited them on plinths in the student union. With very serious explanations, of course.

Cor, that Northern Line was a right nightmare, weren’t it, Arthur? Packed tighter than sardines in a tin! Honestly, you could barely breathe. And the heat... I felt like I was melting. Should’ve worn me lighter shawl. Well, I’ve seen worse, Margaret. Used to queue for buses in Hitchin worse than that. Back when I was a lad, you know. Not quite the same as the Underground, of course. All that rumbling… it’s a bit unnerving, isn’t it? Makes you wonder about the tunnels. Tunnels! Don't get me started, Arthur. Dark, dingy… I’m alright with a bit of grit, mind, grew up near the docks, you know. But this was just… grim. Anyway, the Science Museum was brilliant! Absolutely brilliant! Did you see that exhibit on robotics? Right clever stuff, that. Made me think about the future, it did. Robots, eh? Never been much of a science man myself. Numbers, scales, depths – that was my thing, as a quantity surveyor. But I did enjoy the railway exhibit. All those gleaming engines! Reminded me of my grandfather. He used to work on the railways, you know, down in Bedfordshire. Oh, grandads are good, aren't they? Mine was a docker. Strong as an ox, he was. More muscle than brain, but a good man. Right, so, the IMAX… what did you think? All that 3D, the dinosaurs looming over you… a bit much, weren’t it? I found it a bit dizzying to be honest. Dizzying, you say? Aye, a bit. Bit much for an old bloke like me. All that flashing and shaking… I felt a bit like I was on a fairground ride! Though, I have to admit, the sheer scale of those creatures… impressive. How they managed to create that… it’s quite something, isn't it? Scientific marvel. It were, Arthur. It were. But I prefer paintings, to be honest. Something a bit calmer, a bit more… still. Remember that Turner exhibition we saw a few years back? Now  that  was something special. Proper art. Aye, Turner. Lovely. Though, I always preferred Constable, myself. Those landscapes, so peaceful. Reminded me of Hertfordshire countryside. Fields and hedges… much more relaxing than dodging crowds on the Northern Line. Speaking of which, getting back was even worse! Absolutely rammed. Tell me about it! I swear a few people were clinging to me. Should've got the bus, really.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of decorations they put up in the expat area is just… relentless. It’s like a competition for ‘Most Tacky Christmas Village.’ I swear, I saw someone with inflatable snowmen on their balcony. In Guangzhou! It’s a bit much, isn't it? Aye, sounds about right. Folks gettin' carried away, do they? It's worse than Christmas market in Manchester, that’s for sure. Though, to be fair, they’re probably just missing home something fierce. Being so far away at this time of year…it must hit you hard. It does, a little. More the atmosphere, the smells, the traditions. Here, it’s… interesting. The Chinese New Year decorations are already creeping in, you know? Little red lanterns alongside the tinsel. It's a cultural collision. I was thinking, though, to try and make it a bit more "normal" for the kids. They miss the proper Christmas feel, I think. Good thinking. It's tough on the little ones, adapting like that. So, about this Christmas dinner then… So far as I can tell, we're the only ones doing a full-blown roast. Everyone else is opting for fancy restaurant bookings or celebrating in their own way. Exactly. And I was thinking, let's really go for it. Full works. Turkey, roast potatoes, Brussels sprouts, the lot. Though sourcing a decent turkey here is…a challenge. Did you manage to track down one of those supposedly superior ones from that import place near the French concession? Aye, I did! Got the last one. Bit of a price hike, mind. Nearly took my breath away. But it’s supposed to be properly free-range, not some farmed thing. Worth it for the kids, eh? And to keep the memory of a proper Christmas dinner alive. Should be more than enough for both our families, and anyone else who fancies popping over, right? Absolutely. Let’s put the word out. I’ll send a WeChat message. Though, be warned, I’ll have to warn them about the sheer volume of gravy I’m planning on making. My grandmother’s recipe. It's… intense. Intense gravy? Sounds dangerous! My Nan used to do a bread sauce that could knock you sideways. It tasted like… well, like bread and milk, basically, but it was an  experience . Speaking of experiences, have you seen anything good lately? Netflix is looking bleak.

…and honestly, the sheer vitriol some people unleash online is just baffling, innit? Like, one lukewarm cup of tea and suddenly you're getting a three-star review with a ten-paragraph rant about the condensation on the sugar bowl. Tell me about it. My bakery’s been getting some weird ones lately. Someone actually gave me a one-star because “the croissants were too buttery.” Too buttery! What were they expecting, cardboard? Oh my god, that’s ridiculous. You're a  bakery , Chloe! Butter is kinda key. Mine got one the other day that said my tables were "too wobbly." Like, I'm running a café, not an engineering firm! I’m trying to keep costs down, you know? New chairs are a  massive  expense. Seriously! People have zero perspective. I saw a thread on Twitter earlier, someone’s moaning about a restaurant because the water wasn’t sparkling enough. Sparkling! It's water! You want a bubbly beverage, order a lemonade. It's the entitlement, isn’t it? Like they're paying you to be their personal butler. And the anonymous cowardice! You’d never say that to someone’s face. Absolutely. I'm considering having a sign up: “Please be kind. We’re just trying to serve you coffee and cake.” Probably wouldn’t work, though. People are just…determined to be miserable sometimes. It’s amazing how one bad review can just linger, though, right? Like, it affects the whole algorithm. Proper, yeah. It's like, that one scathing review gets pushed to the top and drowns out all the positive ones. Makes you question your whole existence. Especially when you put your heart into something. I was looking at some cafe design stuff earlier. Found this Japanese place, super minimalist, loads of natural light… utterly gorgeous. Maybe I should get into interior design after uni. You'd be amazing at it, Jamie! You have an eye. But you'd be dealing with clients who complain about the  colour  of the napkins. Don’t joke! That’s precisely what I'm dreading when I finally open the second branch. I found this perfect spot in Margate, down by the beach. Really cute little building, needs a bit of work, but the location is unbeatable. Margate? That’s cool! I haven't been in ages. Is it still mad? It’s…evolving. Still got that seaside charm, loads of artists moving there, the Turner Contemporary is brilliant, but it needs a bit of a  lift , you know?

Honestly, this is lovely, isn't it? Just a simple shepherd's pie, but feels like a real treat after marking those history essays. Honestly, some of them… poor dears. They've clearly been cramming for weeks. Mmm! More, please! Of course, love. You’re a growing girl. Oisin, try a bit of the peas, alright? They’re good for you. Strong like a gerbil! Remember we talked about the gerbils at school? Gerbils are weird. Why are we always talking about gerbils? And vegetables are boring. Liam, don’t be like that. Vegetables are important. They give you energy for biking! Remember when you were showing me your new bike the other day? You were zooming about! Exactly! You need fuel, darling. It's like a car. You wouldn't run a car on raspberry jam, would you? Though, speaking of raspberries… I managed to pick a whole bowl this morning. They’re absolutely bursting with flavour. I’m already planning a crumble for tomorrow. Raspberries! Can I have some now? Please? Not right now, precious. They’re for dessert, alongside maybe a little… …chocolate ice cream? Chocolate! Yes! Can we go for a walk after dinner to get ice cream? I promise I’ll try to eat my vegetables. That sounds lovely, Liam. We could walk along the river, see if we can spot any birds. Remember last week, we saw those robin’s eggs, tucked away in the bush? So tiny! Oh, I do! It was beautiful. Brings back memories of my childhood, rambling around Middlesex. My Gran used to grow the most amazing roses. We’d pick them and put them in jam jars. Simple pleasures. These exams… they’re so high stakes, aren't they? I worry for my students. All that pressure. They are, love. But you're doing a wonderful job supporting them. They’re lucky to have you. It reminds me, when Thomas was little, he wouldn’t eat  anything  green. Honestly, it was a battle every single mealtime. I used to hide spinach in his mashed potato. He never knew! That’s cheating! A little bit, maybe! But a mum’s gotta do what a mum’s gotta do. At least you're trying, Liam. That's the important thing. Honestly, it’s just about finding something they enjoy. Like, you love biking, so you need energy for that. And raspberries are delicious and good for you.

…and honestly, the organic broccoli was practically glowing. You wouldn’t believe the prices though! It's extortionate these days. I'm starting to think I need to grow my own. Do you think you could clear a bit of space in the garden? Grow your own? Right, love. You and green fingers. Remember that basil plant you bought last summer? Looked like a tumbleweed within a week. No, leave the gardening to the professionals, eh? Me, I got a sale on bleach at the Co-op. Can’t complain, can ya? Mrs. Higgins’ bathroom needed a good scrubbing. Bless her, she’s a dear, but she lets things slide a bit. Oh, Mrs. Higgins! Always forgetting where she put her teeth. Had to help her find ‘em again just yesterday. Poor thing. Though, you know, she did make a lovely rhubarb crumble once. Best I ever tasted. Used to be proper rhubarb, not that watery stuff you get these days. Rhubarb crumble  does  sound lovely. We should definitely organise a meal out. Somewhere nice. Maybe that Italian place in town? They do a fantastic tiramisu. I was thinking Saturday week? Saturday’s good for me. Though I might have to pop over to Doreen's. Her cat's been lookin' a bit poorly. Keeps coughin’ up little hairballs. Awful sight, it is. You wouldn't happen to have any of that fancy salmon oil you buy, would you? Might do the poor thing good. I do indeed. I’ll bring some over. Doreen’s cat needs all the help it can get, doesn't it? Speaking of looking after people, have you heard from Margaret lately? She sounded a bit down on the phone last week. Not recently, no. She’s always a bit down, innit? Got a face like a slapped fish, that one. But she got that new bloke, doesn't she? Says he's a builder. Hopefully, he keeps her entertained. Although, I'd prefer she’d come round for a cuppa now and then. It gets lonely here. Lonely, you say? It's the world, love. Always changing. Remember when this street used to be full of children playing? Now, it’s just cars and empty houses. Still, a good cuppa and a biscuit does wonders for the soul. Absolutely. Right, back to practicalities. My eyebrows are a disaster. I need to book in with Chloe.

Aye, that’s lovely, love. It’s good to 'ear you’re gettin’ a grip of things. Teaching's not easy, is it? Especially with a room full of little whirlwinds. Leo’s observant, innit? He's been watching you chattering away. Progress, I reckon.   Chloe:   He is. He’s starting to try and babble more. Makes these little noises, like he’s trying to copy me. It's adorable. Are you still finding weaning a bit of a… challenge? I read that some babies really take to it, and others… don't. Little Leo seems to be in the ‘doesn’t’ camp.      Don’t I know it. He’s a right fusser, that one. Today, it was the sweet potato. Absolutely refused. Made the most dramatic face you ever saw. All scrunched up like he'd swallowed a lemon. I tried hiding it in the apple puree, but he still spat it out. It's exhausting, isn't it? I feel like I'm constantly experimenting. I’ve got that butternut squash recipe from Auntie Maureen - should I try that next?   Chloe:   Definitely try the butternut squash! Auntie Maureen’s stuff always goes down a treat. She’s got a knack with food, that woman. Speaking of family… Mum mentioned she and Dad were thinking of popping over on Saturday for tea. Are you up for it?      Saturday's a bit tight, love. I've got that doctor's appointment in the morning, remember? And frankly, I'll be knackered by then. Maybe Sunday afternoon could work better? I can whip up a shepherd's pie, you know how everyone loves a good shepherd's pie.   Chloe:   Sunday sounds perfect! I'll let Mum know. Oh, and Ben asked if he could bring Sarah over on Friday evening to watch that film, “The Banshees of Inisherin.” Have you heard good things about it?      Ben and Sarah, eh? Alright. Good thing they’re keepin' themselves busy. Aye, I’ve  heard  it's good – lots of critics been raving. As long as it’s not too depressing! I need something a bit...lighthearted at the moment. Everything feels rather heavy with this weaning business.   Chloe:   Fair enough! I'll tell him to keep it cheerful then. Right... Sign language. I spoke to that tutor again today, booked us in for the introductory session next Tuesday. 7 PM at the community centre.      Tuesday, eh?

Honestly, it's just…breathtaking, isn’t it? I mean, London's lovely, don’t get me wrong, but you just don't get  this . This quiet. This...greenness. It really is. Takes you right out of the academic goldfish bowl, doesn’t it? Though, even the hills here aren’t exactly the Himalayas, are they? A bit more…gentle. Gentle's the word. They’re rolling, really. Not like those dramatic peaks you see in the Lake District. This is…Norfolk. Flat-ish, but with these surprising little rises. Locals call them “hecks,” you know. Hecks? Seriously? That’s brilliant. What's the derivation? Some kind of ancient Norse term for a small hillock? Apparently! Something along those lines. Local folklore, anyway. Apparently there’s a whole history around ‘heck-running’ – kids used to race up and down them for fun back in the day. It's all in the village history book I picked up. They're not majestic in the same way as, say, the Chilterns, but they’ve got a charm all their own. See, that’s what I love about places like this. There’s a depth to them, even if it’s not immediately obvious. The Chilterns shout ‘landscape!’ Norfolk whispers it. And everything’s so…contained. These villages, for example. Each one feels like it’s nestled right into the landscape. Exactly. Look at Little Snoring over there . Seriously, Little Snoring! Perfect village name. And the way the houses cluster around the church, always. It’s almost quaint, isn't it? But it’s more than just quaint. It’s a sense of community, a feeling of history. Generations have lived and died in those houses. It’s the sense of continuity, I think. London’s constantly reinventing itself. Demolishing, rebuilding…it feels ephemeral sometimes. Here, it feels…permanent. Rooted. Do you think that translates to the people? Do they feel more connected to the land here? I think so. It's subtle. You don't just  feel  it, you see it in the way they talk about the weather, about the seasons. It's interwoven into everything. They're not fiercely patriotic, not in a flag-waving way, but there's a real pride in their local identity. I interviewed a farmer last week for a bit of background research, and he talked about the soil as if it were a living thing.

Honestly, Liam, you wouldn’t  believe  what Bethany was saying about her new job. Apparently, they're making her micro-manage the biscuit selection in the office. The  biscuit selection ! Like it’s rocket science. She’s a marketing analyst, for crying out loud! Well, that's… specific. Sounds dreadfully boring though. Marketing used to sound so glamorous. All those campaigns and creative strategies… now it's about digestive versus shortbread. Aye, exactly! She was fuming, proper riled up. Said she feels like she’s wasting her degree. And the worst part is, the office manager, Brenda, is obsessed with Jaffa Cakes being  either  cake  or  biscuit. Can’t have both, apparently. Absolute madness. Right. Brenda sounds like a character. You know, I dealt with a bit of a similar situation just the other day at a site visit. One of the subcontractors insisted on using a specific shade of grey for the steel beams, claiming it was “better for structural integrity.” Completely unfounded, of course. Just… stubborn. See? Bosses everywhere are the same, whether they're dealing with structural integrity or biscuits! Did you ever see that film, ‘Local Hero’? That Inverness guy, he just wants to build a chemical plant, and these weird Scots just keep fobbing him off with…lime green paint and bagpipes. Oh yeah, ‘Local Hero’! Fantastic film, clever writing. Peter Capaldi, wasn't it? Very understated. I actually saw that at the Everyman cinema with my dad a few years ago. They always have really comfortable chairs there, you know? So much better than the Odeon. Odeon’s a nightmare, especially when kids are running amok. Speaking of things causing trouble… did you nearly get taken out by a cyclist earlier? I swear, one nearly clipped my handbag! They’re getting bolder, aren’t they? Riding on pavements and weaving through traffic like they own the place. Tell me about it. I was cycling myself this morning, actually. Nearly had a heart attack when a van pulled out right in front of me. People just aren't paying attention. You'd think with all the cycle lanes they’re putting in – ostensibly to  improve  safety – things would be better. Aye, but they're just badly designed, aren’t they? Put in the worst possible place, right alongside parked cars and delivery lorries. It's like they’re trying to  encourage  accidents! Remember that article I sent you about the Groningen approach?

Honestly, look at those cornflowers. Absolutely bursting. Reminds me of my Gran’s garden, back in Norwich - she’d always have a patch just for them. She said they brought good luck. Though, I suspect she was secretly hoping they’d deter the aphids from the roses. Your Gran was a wise woman. Though, I doubt even she could predict the current state of the agricultural market. Did you see that report on the rising cost of fertiliser? It's knocking the stuffing out of arable farmers, isn’t it? Particularly with the push for more cash crops. Dreadful, isn't it? It's the ripple effect, really. Everything’s interconnected. Higher input costs for farmers, higher food prices for consumers... It all feeds back into inflation. Which, of course, makes the Bank of England have to make those tricky decisions about interest rates. It's fascinating, in a slightly terrifying way. My research just keeps circling back to the fundamentals of supply chain resilience. You and your resilience. It's admirable, truly. I get bogged down in the behavioural economics of it all. Trying to understand  why  people react the way they do to price fluctuations. It’s baffling. People will stubbornly cling to brands, even when a cheaper, perfectly adequate alternative exists. They’re emotionally attached to a tin of beans, for crying out loud. Exactly! Irrationality reigns supreme! And it’s not just food, is it? We saw it with petrol last year. People would queue for miles rather than switch to a different petrol station, even if the price difference was significant. It’s bizarre. Do you remember that anecdote Sarah told us at the conference – about how people often perceive a loss more acutely than an equivalent gain? Explains a lot, doesn't it? Absolutely. Loss aversion. Classic. It's why framing is so important in economic messaging. You could present the same information in two ways and get completely different reactions. Speaking of different ways… I’m trying to get my head around the phonology of Basque. It's utterly bonkers. A language isolate! No related languages anywhere. Basque? Wow. You're really delving deep, aren’t you? I dabbled with a bit of German at Uni, but nothing quite that challenging. The grammar alone sounds... imposing. Still, fascinating. It's amazing how languages evolve, isn’t it? Little windows into different cultures and ways of thinking.

…and honestly, the parking around Canary Wharf is a nightmare. Absolute nightmare. I spent fifteen minutes circling just to find a space – and it was extortionate! £6 for half an hour! You wouldn’t believe it. Aye, tell me about it. London parking, it’s robbin’ yer blind. Proper daylight robbery, innit? So, about Saturday, then? You’re still up for comin’ up to Sunderland? Absolutely. Wouldn't miss it. Been too long since I've seen the Angel. I’m really looking forward to that, actually. Remember when we tried to recreate that photo from childhood, standing under it? The one Mum has framed? Oh, god, aye! You tripped over your own feet and nearly ended up in the river Wear! Honestly, you were a right clown that day. I still get a laugh thinkin' about it. Proper, laughin' ‘til me ribs hurt. Well, you were equally clumsy trying to navigate those steps after too much Irn-Bru. Anyway, so, Saturday. What's the plan? We need to sort out somewhere to eat. Anywhere decent you’d recommend? There’s that new Italian place on High Street, 'Bella Luna'. I’ve heard good things. Proper hearty portions, they say. Or we could go back to Fat Buddha, you know you love the Thai food there. Bella Luna sounds good. Less…sticky than Fat Buddha. Remember last time? Felt like I was having dinner with a family of flies. Aye, it were a bit much. Right, Bella Luna it is. And I’ve been havin’ a look at flats, actually. Online, you know, just browsin’. There’s a couple in the city centre lookin’ alright – proper modern. Oh? Really? Still thinking about moving closer to the centre? That’s a big step. How’s the flat situation at work? Are they still dithering about the new office space? They are. It’s a right mess, to be honest. Apparently, the head honcho changed his mind about the location three times already. Makes me wonder if I should move further afield, closer to where you are! Less hassle, more…well, sunshine, I suppose. Though I’d miss the Angel somethin’ fierce. Don’t get ahead of yourself. Sunderland's got its charm. Although, you’re right, the sunshine… I did see a particularly nice one-bedroom just off Regent’s Canal. Good transport links, close to a tennis club, which you know I’m obsessed with at the moment.

…and honestly, the whole Depp vs. Heard thing has been utterly draining, hasn’t it? I mean, the level of detail… it’s just relentless. I’ve been trying to avoid it, but it's everywhere. Aye, it is a bit much, innit? All that washing-up liquid documentary evidence. Never thought I’d see the day. Bit mad, really. Though, I did find myself watching bits and pieces. You can’t help but, can you? Everyone’s talking about it. Exactly! It’s hard to ignore completely. Though I keep thinking about the impact on their children. It has to be dreadful for them. Poor little things. Must be a right circus. Still, you'd think they'd have enough money to keep it all private, wouldn't you? Well, that's the irony, isn’t it? Money doesn’t buy discretion, apparently. Speaking of things you can’t ignore, have you seen the geese lately? They’re absolutely enormous this year. Oh, you bet. They're right greedy, them geese. Been gobbling up all the dropped bread down at the park. Got proper territorial, too. Last week, I nearly got nipped trying to walk past. They’re getting bolder, I tell you. I’ve noticed! They're practically strutting. It’s fascinating, though. I was reading a bit about their migration patterns. Did you know that a lot of the geese we see here actually breed in Iceland and Greenland? Iceland? Greenland? Blimey! I wouldn't have thought so. Just thought they were local geese, you know? They’re incredible long-distance travellers. They fly thousands of miles. It’s remarkable, really – birds navigating across vast stretches of water, all instinct and something called magnetic alignment, apparently. Used to see ‘em flyin’ over, years ago. Before all this… this building happened. Used to be fields, you know. Proper fields. Full of birds. Not like now. You did, Mum? That's lovely. What sort of birds did you see besides the geese? Oh, everything. Skylarks. Plenty of skylarks. You don't hear them much now. Fieldfares and redwings, in the winter. And lapwings. Beautiful birds, lapwings were. Used to nest in the fields. You don’t see hardly any now, do you? They were a proper sign of spring, they were. I saw a lapwing once, down by the river. A flash of brown with those funny spikey bits on its head.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of applications! I mean, you’d think there were no language teacher jobs going anywhere else in the country. It's overwhelming, isn’t it? I’ve tailored my CV three different ways already for this one, highlighting different skills apparently. Do they  really  think we’re all robots, just slotting different skills in depending on what they ask for? Tell me about it! It’s the same with the primary stuff. My school's got a vacant Year 3 post and it’s got about a hundred applications. A hundred! For Year 3! You'd think headteachers were made of gold or something. It’s definitely a teacher's market, isn’t it? Though, I suppose, lots of people are looking for a change, especially after the last few years. Definitely. Though a change  to  something else, apparently. Everyone's desperate to escape the chalk face. Did you hear about Mrs. Davies from my old school? She’s applying to be a florist. A florist! After twenty years teaching French. No! Seriously? A florist? That's brilliant! Good for her, though. Brave. I remember her always having these beautiful little posies on her desk. Maybe it's a natural progression. Listen, speaking of changes... how’s the new flat coming along? You said you were still sorting through boxes. Don’t even ask. It's a disaster zone. I found a teacup from my Gran buried under a pile of textbooks. A  really  precious teacup! I nearly cried. I’m trying to be organised, I really am, but living in a constant state of unpacking is exhausting. At least the kitchen's usable, though. Right, more of this couscous. This is lovely, by the way, Anon. Really fresh. Glad you like it! It's that lemon and herb one from M&S, can’t go wrong. Seriously though, unpacking can be a killer. I remember when I moved into this place, I spent a good month just sorting through shoes. It's ridiculous, isn't it? So… how are you feeling about the interviews? Are you nervous? Terrified, to be perfectly honest. It’s not just the interviews themselves, it’s the prep. All the ‘behaviour management strategies’ and ‘differentiated learning’ jargon you have to trot out. It feels so performative. Last time, they asked me about scaffolding. Scaffolding! I felt like I needed scaffolding to  answer  the question!

Honestly, Chloe, I'm just…stuck. Proper stuck. Everyone else seems to have a plan. Liam's off to Amsterdam for that software development gig, Sarah's already looking at Masters programs in Edinburgh… and I’m here, coordinating widget deliveries in Cambridge. Widget deliveries? Seriously, Amelia? That sounds… intense. Don’t be so hard on yourself, though. It’s a good job, you said it’s well-paid, and you’re actually  good  at it. My admin work is mostly just organising spreadsheets and fending off Gareth from accounts trying to flirt. Thrilling, right? Paid’s alright, yeah, but it's not  it , you know? It’s not… fulfilling. It’s just…existing. I did that postgrad in Sustainable Logistics, like,  because  I wanted to make a difference. Fewer carbon emissions, ethical sourcing, proper supply chain transparency... Instead, I'm making sure the factory in Hull has enough screws by Tuesday. I get it. The gap between the ideal and the reality. My mum keeps saying I should become a PA to a celebrity. "Think of the travel, Chloe!" she chirps. Like I care about free tickets to the theatre when I’m just perpetually stressed about someone's dry cleaning schedule. Exactly! It’s the whole… trajectory thing. Did you ever think about a career change? Something completely different? I’ve been browsing online courses, mostly on environmental consultancies. But the competition is insane. I did have a brief, terrifying phase where I considered becoming a florist. Just ditch everything and create beautiful flower arrangements. My dad nearly had a heart attack. He’s very “stable income” oriented. What kind of consultancy were you thinking? Mostly, like, advising businesses on their environmental impact. Helping them streamline processes, reduce waste… things like that. There’s a company in Bristol, ‘Green Pathways,’ that seem to be doing really well. They’re advertising a junior analyst role. It'd mean moving, obviously. Bristol’s lovely. Good food scene. And it’s not  that  far. You'd only be a train ride away. You should apply! Honestly, what have you got to lose? Another six months in widget delivery? Don't let those screws hold you hostage. You’re right. It’s just… scary, isn’t it? Applying for something completely different. What if I’m not good enough? What if I fail? Amelia, darling, you’re the most organised, detail-oriented person I know.

Honestly, Liam. You’re makin’ a mountain outta a molehill, lass. Every lad looks at girls. It's what they do. Aye, Chloe's right. You're overthinkin' it, Bethany. It's probably nothin'. He probably just likes yer hair, that new cut suits thee. It’s the context that matters, isn’t it? Were you talking to him? Was there a reason he'd be focusing his attention on you specifically? Liam, what were you two actually doing? We were just talkin' about the train, see? I asked if he knew if it were on time, cos I'm proper late gettin' back to the Airbnb. And then  bam . The look. The whole staredown thing. It sent shivers down me spine, it did! Shivers down yer spine! Bethany, you’re dramatic. It’s France, not a horror film! Still, I get it a bit, though. It's annoying when lads are like that, actin' like they're better than everyone else. Remember Mark, back in Sixthform? Always sneerin’ at me. Mark. Right. The one who thought wearing a leather jacket and perpetually looking disgusted made him edgy. Charming. I remember him. He wouldn’t have lasted five minutes in Cambridge. Too...uncultured. See! Everyone understands! It weren’t about the train, was it? It were about somethin’ else. He were tryin’ to wind me up, I reckon. Maybe he fancies Emily. That miserable git. Emily? But she's all about vegan cheese and poetry readings! Liam wouldn't be caught dead near her. He's more of a…football and pizza kinda lad. Maybe he’s tryin’ to make her jealous. It’s a classic, innit? I just… I hate feelin' like I gotta watch me back. We’ve only been seein’ each other a few weeks. Look, it's early days. And you’re right to be aware, not blind. But don't let one awkward look ruin it. Does Liam normally act like this? Has he been giving you any other reason to be suspicious? Not really, no. He's usually alright, dead friendly even. He brought me flowers, proper fancy lilies, last week. Makes you wonder, don't it? Maybe he’s playin’ a game. Flowers  and  the smug look? That's a confusing combo. Maybe he’s just… inept at flirting? Like, he thinks being a bit of a git is charming. Some lads are just like that.

Alright, alright, settle down, Gareth. It's just a hockey match. Though, you  were  particularly vocal tonight. You practically vibrated off the sofa! I’ve never seen you so invested in a Sunday league game. Well, it’s a bit more than Sunday league, isn’t it, Dave? It’s Jamie’s team! And they were really playing well, up until that ridiculous call. Poor lad looked completely deflated. He needs cheering up, I think. Jamie was good, yeah. He made some  amazing  saves. Better than last week. See? Even Leo agrees! You were watching, Leo? Were you paying attention? Yeah, a bit. I was mostly watching the goalie, actually. He was really quick. Speaking of cheering people up, has anyone heard from Ben and Chloe? They were supposed to be calling tonight, weren't they? To tell us about the holiday booking? No, nothing. I’ve already sent a quick text, just a little ‘ping’ to say we were thinking of them. Urgent matters, I'm sure, with those two. Probably arguing over whether to go to Majorca or Tenerife. Tenerife's got volcanoes! Majorca just has beaches. Exactly. Good point, Alex. They'll sort it out, don’t worry. Anyway, back to Jamie. What are you thinking, Sarah? Should we pop over tomorrow and take him out for a pizza or something? Lift his spirits a bit. That’s a lovely idea, Dave. I was thinking the same thing. Maybe Liam too? He’s been a bit quiet lately. He always listens to Gareth’s hockey rants, doesn’t he? Gives him a good ear. Liam’s got cricket training tomorrow, though. I think. He was complaining about it yesterday. Something about needing a new bat. Oh, right. Typical. Always something. Well, pizza for Gareth and Jamie then. We can get Leo something nice as well. He deserves it for putting up with all your hockey commentary. Can I have pepperoni? Lots of pepperoni? Of course, darling. Anything you want. Though, you’ll be bouncing off the walls afterwards. Right, serious question then. Now the holiday thing  might  be sorted... are we still on for that weekend trip to the Lake District next month? I’ve been looking at some cottages online. Absolutely! I've been checking out some walking routes too. There’s this one that goes up to Derwentwater, it’s supposed to be stunning. We should pack proper waterproofs though, just in case.

Honestly, isn't this just  incredible ? I mean, you really don’t get a sense of scale until you’re actually  in  them. Pictures just don't do it justice. It's like…stepping into a cathedral, but made of living, breathing things. It is, actually. It's... overwhelming. Bit claustrophobic, a tiny bit, but definitely overwhelming in a good way. I mean, I knew they were big, obviously, but…wowzers. Did you see that one? The one with the weird sort of…knot in the middle? It looked like a giant’s hand gripping the trunk. You have a good eye! That's a burl. Apparently, they're quite common on redwoods. It’s a growth anomaly, caused by fungi or insects. They call them 'fairy castles' sometimes. Makes you wonder what’s going on  inside , doesn't it? Anyway, about what you were saying earlier… about Sarah and Mark’s wedding… Oh, right! Sorry, got distracted by the trees. It was…a lot. Honestly. All that fuss. And Mark’s mum, Patricia... don't even get me started. She kept hovering, offering everyone miniature quiches and telling everyone how perfectly everything was ‘according to plan.’ Even when it wasn't! Remember when the band’s drummer’s foot got stepped on? She just tutted and said, "Well, a slight deviation, but we mustn’t let it derail the schedule." Patricia! Of course. "A slight deviation." She’s a force of nature, isn’t she? I tried to discreetly steer her away from the cake table before she started rearranging the flowers. Poor Sarah looked utterly drained by the end of it. Did she seem okay? She did, surprisingly. She and Mark looked genuinely happy, despite Patricia’s best efforts. Though she did tell me later, after a few glasses of champagne, that she'd spent most of the day biting her tongue. She's terrified of upsetting her mother-in-law. I felt a bit bad for her, actually. You know, I wonder if Mum ever ended up sending that hand-knitted table runner she was trying to finish? Oh, goodness. I completely forgot to ask! She was so stressed about it. Apparently, the pattern was ridiculously complicated. Said it involved some sort of…intricate Celtic knot design. I'll have to call her when we get back. She’ll be mortified if she missed the deadline. She’ll be rehearsing apologies for a week!

Jaysus, this is grand. Proper grand. Better than that frozen muck we had last week, wouldn’t you say, Liam? Yeah, it’s… it’s good. Much better than Mum’s, actually. Oi! Don’t you be saying that, young man! My Chicken Kievs aren't  that  bad. And at least I bother making them from scratch. This is probably one of those shop-bought things, isn’t it, Conor? Now, now, Sarah. Let the lad have his say. It  is  shop-bought, alright, but a good brand. Don't be going all tetchy over a bit of poultry. Were you watching the rugby at all this afternoon? Ireland were magnificent! I saw a bit. Mostly just the highlights. Finn Russell was acting the wallie again, wasn’t he? Just messing around, throwing mad passes. Aye, a right divil he is. But entertaining, mind you. Ireland playing like that… it’s a pleasure to watch. Should’ve put more points on the board though. Honestly, the rugby's just noise. My head throbs after watching five minutes. And all those men shouting and falling over. Give me a nice cup of tea and a biscuit any day. Oi, Mum! I wanted one! You always get the first one. Don’t backchat me, Liam. Show some respect. And don’t grab! You’ll choke. So, are we still going to see Granny next weekend? I need to sort out some photos for her. Aye, Granny’s expecting us. I’ll ring her tomorrow, confirm everything. Maybe I’ll send her a couple of pictures beforehand. Speaking of pictures, I was thinking about cleaning up some of the old family ones.
