But honestly, the research methods are giving me a headache. Qualitative vs. quantitative… it’s a nightmare. What about you? What's gripping you about Maths? For me, it's definitely the problem-solving. The feeling you get when you crack a particularly difficult equation? It's like… everything clicks. I'm leaning towards a theoretical focus, potentially something in applied statistics. Thinking about modelling financial markets. Dad thinks it's genius. He’s always going on about algorithms. Right, your dad. He’s got a point about algorithms, though. Everyone’s talking about AI. Still, modelling financial markets sounds… stressful. I need less stress, not more. I'm already stressed about these UCAS deadlines. Have you started your personal statement properly? Nearly. Got the core experiences down, the ‘why I want to study Maths’ waffle… just need to polish it. I’m trying to hook them with a story about solving a complex problem in a coding competition last year. You should write about that time you organised the charity bake sale for rugby. It wasn’t  that  organised. Honestly, Sarah ended up doing most of the actual baking. I mostly just… supervised. And tried not to eat all the brownies. You supervised admirably! And the brownies were  delicious . It shows you can take initiative, work with a team… all those buzzwords they want to hear. Speaking of rugby, are you still going to training on Tuesdays? Yeah, trying to. It’s a good release, you know? All this thinking about the future… it's exhausting. Need to channel that energy somewhere. How's your shoulder? Still feeling it from that tackle last month?

…and honestly, Dad, I just don’t  get  it. They keep changing things. Like, Universal Credit – it feels like a constant shifting of the goalposts. One month you’re just breaking even, the next you’re facing a shortfall. It’s incredibly stressful for families, you know? Especially with inflation the way it is. Aye, it is. It really is. And don’t you worry yourself about it too much, love. Government policy...well, it’s a right muddle, it is. Always has been, always will be. Remember Callaghan's 'Winter of Discontent'? Things were nigh on as bad then. Not the same  kind  of bad, mind you, but a bad feeling all the same. This Universal Credit thing… it's all trying to simplify things, see. They wanted one system, instead of all these different benefits. Good in theory, dreadful in practice, as often is the case. But simplify  for whom , Dad? It feels like it’s making life harder for the people who need the support the most. And the clawback with earnings... it feels so punitive. You work a few extra hours to try and get ahead, and suddenly you're losing benefits. It actively discourages working! I’ll grant you that, lass. The taper rate is a tricky customer, that is. They say it's designed to encourage work, and it does to a degree, but you’re right, that sudden drop-off… it's a disincentive. See, the idea is, the government provides a safety net, but they don't want to make people entirely dependent. It’s a balancing act, a rather clumsy one as it happens. Back in my day, with the old National Assistance, things were simpler, if not always better. Just a more consistent system. Different times, of course. And what about the inheritance tax? Aunt Carol was saying she's considering giving away a load of her assets just to avoid it. Seems rather silly, doesn’t it? All that paperwork and potential complications. Aye, Carol’s always been…creative with her finances. Tax planning, they call it. Perfectly legal, no doubt. But you're right, it can be a faff. I always thought it was a bit unfair myself, this inheritance tax. A bit like taxing someone twice, isn’t it? They’ve paid income tax on the money during their lifetime, then you're taxing their family when they pass it on.

…and honestly, the whole thing just felt so rushed. They wanted the presentation delivered by Friday, but the data wasn’t fully validated until Wednesday afternoon! It was a nightmare trying to pull it all together. I practically lived on coffee and adrenaline. Cor, that does sound a bit of a kerfuffle, doesn’t it? Friday, eh? A bit tight, that. Reminds me of when young Timmy had that school project on the Tudors, due in on Monday. He’d left it till Sunday evening, bless ‘im. Was a right shambles, kept dropping bits of paper and muttering about Henry VIII’s wives. You get like that, don't ya, when the pressure's on? Absolutely! I was muttering about KPIs and stakeholder alignment all day Wednesday. My brain felt like scrambled eggs. And the worst part is, Mrs. Davies – the project sponsor – kept wanting to change things  after  I’d already started building the slides. Like, seriously? Mrs. Davies, is it? Sounds like a bit of a bossyboots, that one. We had a Mrs. Higgins at the school, similar sort. Always wanting to tweak things, never happy with things as they were. You just had to roll with it, didn't you? Learned that early on. Though it can grate, can’t it? Sometimes you just need to tell ‘em, gently, “Look, this is what I’ve got, and it's the best I can do with the timeframe." I  wanted  to say that! Trust me, the thought crossed my mind. But I’m still relatively new to the company, so...playing it safe. Anyway, did you hear from Emily? I haven't seen a text from her in ages. Emily? Just this morning, actually. She’s proper busy with the new puppy, you know. Little scamp, apparently. Chewing everything in sight. She sent a picture, all wriggling paws and big eyes. Adorable, really. She says she’s exhausted, but hasn’t slept a full night in weeks. Parenthood, eh? Oh, that’s lovely! I’m so pleased for her. I keep thinking about getting a dog, but the responsibility… It feels a bit much with the job at the moment. It is a commitment, definitely. But the love you get in return? Worth every sleepless night, every chewed slipper. Reminds me of Buster, your dad's Labrador when you were little. You were inseparable. Remember that time you dressed him up in your doll’s clothes?

Aye, Sarah. Fancy that. Always were a bit flighty, weren't she? Proper wild child, even back then. What's she say, specifically? Just offering a hello, or...? No, she said she was needing a break, a bit of fresh air. Said she misses the sea, claims London’s got her down. And she asked if we were having any of that fancy Italian stuff for dinner on Saturday. You know, the lasagne you made last time? She practically inhaled it. Sounds like a decent reason to visit. London  can  be draining. Though, hoping for your lasagne is a very specific expression of affection, Liam! Don't be getting any ideas, lad. It's a simple dish, that is. Few layers, bit o' mince, proper cheese. Not rocket science. Still, good to hear from Sarah. Reminds me of the old days, doesn't it? Remember that time she tried to dye her hair blue with beetroot juice? Ended up looking like a parrot. Oh, God, yes! Mam was furious. She spent hours trying to get the stains out of the bathroom. And the smell… horrible! I’ve only heard these stories, obviously. It sounds…colourful. So, what are we doing about the Saturday dinner? Lasagne is definitely on, right? I’m happy to bring a bottle of something decent to go with it. I’ve got a Rioja that's been waiting for the right occasion. Rioja’s always welcome, young man. Always welcome. Right, let’s get this sorted. Sarah’s proper bugging me about needing a room. You’d think I ran a blooming hotel. Still, we’ll manage. Got that spare room all ready, cleaned it proper last week, got the old iPod dock working. She'll like that, she always did love her tunes. Actually, speaking of iPods, I’ve started converting all your old vinyl to digital. You know, for preservation and ease of listening. Got ages of stuff on there now. I can load some onto her phone too, if she wants. You did, did you? Lass, you’re a marvel, you are. Proper treasurer, that's what you are. Getting those old records safe. Never thought anyone'd bother with 'em. Spendin' all me time lookin' at me telly, I have. Shame, really. Used to lose meself for hours in those records. It's a brilliant project, Elodie. Preserving history! It’s what I’m doing with my engineering reports, archiving everything properly.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of acronyms they threw at us during that workshop on blended learning was just  bonkers . I scribbled down a load, but I'm fairly sure half of them were made up on the spot. I think "FLIPPED" was one, for Flipped Learning... but then they started talking about "SAMR" and “TPACK” and I just stared blankly. It's like they're deliberately trying to make us feel inadequate! Oh, I know exactly what you mean! Conferences are brilliant for networking and picking up new ideas, but sometimes they prioritise jargon over actual, practical takeaways. SAMR, right? Substitute, Augment, Modify, Redefine. It's the tech integration model, remember? I actually quite like the idea behind it, but the way they presented it was... overwhelming. Felt like they expected everyone in the room to be coding their own apps. Exactly! And you know me, I’m happy to embrace new tech, but I'm still trying to get half my students to remember to bring their textbooks! Coding apps is a  bit  beyond the scope, innit? Speaking of students, how are things at Brixham College? Still battling the phones under desks? Don’t even get me started. It's a constant battle, Sarah. They're glued to those things. I’ve tried everything - taking them, negotiating phone-free zones, ironically using their phones for quizzes... absolutely nothing seems to stick. Mrs. Henderson in Year 11 practically had a breakdown last week when she caught three of them TikTok-ing during a Shakespeare lesson. Oh, bless her! I can imagine. At least my lot are mostly still grappling with basic sentence structure. Korean teenagers are often more focused on learning verbs than scrolling through Instagram, thankfully. Though, their pronunciation of "th" is something else. It’s a linguistic nightmare for a Torquay girl, let me tell you. Sounds like a frog gargling sometimes. You're terrible! I bet you have a secret fondness for the challenges. It's rewarding, isn't it, watching them progress? Even if it’s just one tiny step forward. That’s why I went to the conference, really. Feeling a bit…stuck. Like I'm just repeating the same lessons year after year. That session on differentiated instruction was actually really useful; it gave me a few ideas for tackling those disengaged Year 10s. That's brilliant. Glad you found something worthwhile. I'm not sure I did.

…and honestly, the sat nav’s being a right pain. Keeps insisting we turn down roads that are barely wide enough for a bicycle, let alone this beast! I swear, it's got a vendetta against campervans. Are you sure Tarnow was the right route? It felt a bit… circuitous. Well, dear, it  was  the scenic route. I wanted to see a bit more of the countryside. All those motorways are so… depressing. Just grey and concrete. This was lovely, wasn't it? All those little villages. Though I do apologise if it’s added an extra hour to the journey. I’m terribly bad with directions, as you know. I’m relying entirely on that thing, aren’t I? . Don't worry about it. It's a grand adventure, isn't it? Though, adventure often involves getting lost, I suppose. So, speaking of feeling good… you seem a bit perkier than you did last week. Still sticking with those little walking circuits around the campsite then? Oh, yes. Tidying up my walking routine has done wonders, really. Just half an hour each morning. Helps with the digestion, you see. And I bought new trainers! They’re practically leaping me along. I feel… lighter, somehow. You, on the other hand, you look absolutely knackered. All that marking, I presume? You have no idea. End-of-term essays are brutal. And then Year 9s are a special kind of challenge. Anyway, I’ve been trying to get to the gym, but life keeps getting in the way. I've been reading about these HIIT workouts... do you think they'd be any good? I need something quick and effective. HIIT? Sounds rather… intense. I'd always thought a gentle walk was much preferable. Less strain on the joints, more conducive to contemplation. Speaking of reading, I’ve just finished 'The Cazalet Chronicles'. Delightful! Proper escapism. You should try it. Much better than whatever academic tomes you're usually burdened with. Actually, I'm reading some Brene Brown at the moment. About vulnerability and resilience. Properly nerdy, I know, but fascinating. It's helping with dealing with a… a bit of a tricky situation at work. Oh, darling. Do tell me. You know you can always talk. Though, if it's about that chap from the English department, I’m going to say what I think. He strikes me as utterly pretentious. It's not him, thankfully!

…and honestly, the whole thing just feels a bit… overwhelming. Finn’s speech is still so delayed, you know? The waiting list for another assessment is ridiculous, and I just feel like I’m constantly battling. It’s not just the therapy, it's advocating for him, explaining to people… it’s exhausting. Aye, I hear ya, love. It’s a tough hand to be dealt. It’s easy to get bogged down, isn’t it? But you’re doin’ brilliant. Truly brilliant. Finn’s a lucky lad to have someone like you fightin' his corner. Reminds me a bit of…well, thinkin' back, the Viking chieftains – all about protectin' their families, their clan. Stoic, you know, but underneath it all, fiercely protective. That's a lovely comparison, actually. Though I don't feel very chieftain-like most days. I tend to feel more like a slightly exasperated, perpetually tired mum. Anyway, you were saying something about… telomeres? It completely went over my head. Right, right. Sorry about that, driftin' off into historical tangents again. Telomeres, yeah. It’s fascinating, really. They’re these protective caps on the ends of your chromosomes, like the plastic tips on shoelaces. Each time a cell divides, these telomeres get a bit shorter. Eventually, they get too short, and the cell stops dividin’, or it starts to malfunction. That’s linked to ageing, of course. There's this whole field of gerontology lookin’ at how to slow down that process. They're even lookin' at things like boosting telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres, potentially lengthening lifespan. It's all very early days, mind. So, immortality then? Is that what everyone's chasing? Not quite immortality, though some folks get carried away. More like…extending healthspan. Livin' longer  and  live a longer time in good health. It's about delayin' the onset of age-related diseases - the heart trouble, the Alzheimers… all that. It's not about magically livin' forever, but about adding quality years. Think about the pyramids... impressive engineering, but if the builders hadn't had a good understanding of tectonics, they'd have crumbled a long time ago. Same principle, really – understand the underlying mechanics, and you can influence the outcome. That’s a really good analogy. So, what about global warming then? Isn’t that impacting life expectancy, regardless of how well we maintain our telomeres? Absolutely. It's a huge factor.

Right, so, about that voucher for Casa Roma. Mum said we could use it, but it expires next week, doesn't it? And it's only valid on weekdays. Yes, next Thursday. We could make a go of it. It’s been ages since we’ve been out for Italian. It's getting a bit manic here with the little 'un, isn't it? Aye, manic’s a good word for it. Little Liam’s a whirlwind. Speaking of whirlwinds, has anyone seen my sunglasses? I'm fair blind in this glare. They were on the windowsill earlier, Grandad. Liam was trying to chew on one of the arms. Oh, dear. Maybe he'll leave your sunglasses alone then. He did just spit out a petal from one of those lilies you bought, didn't he, darling? He does love a good flower taste test. Anyway, Casa Roma. Is Thursday good for everyone? I’ve got that essay to finish for History, but I could get a good chunk done after. Thursday’s grand. Gives me a chance to escape Liam's… enthusiasm, for a few hours. Although, I reckon those chickens are giving me more trouble these days. They’ve dug up half the flowerbeds! Honestly, Cyril, the chickens are your own fault. You let them free range! Remember we were talking about building that proper chicken coop? We still need to get prices. Actually, speaking of prices, did you see that new baby chair at Mothercare? The one with the reclining function? It’s £180! Honestly, it's daylight robbery. 180 quid? For a chair? When I were a lad, you got a normal chair and you were lucky. These prices… It’s all this European thing, innit? Everything's gone up since the… well, you know. Cyril, let's not go there again. It's a complicated issue. Remember how much cheaper the fruit trees were last year when we could get them direct from that nursery in Poland? That’s gone now, hasn't it? Though, to be fair, the plums we got were blooming fantastic. Totally. Massive plums. But honestly, this chair… I’m searching eBay. I bet I can find something a bit more reasonable. We don’t need all the bells and whistles. eBay’s a good shout. Always a bargain to be had. What about our Sarah? Still considering that solicitor? She is.

Oh, love, you always did pick the strangest clients. Remember when you were doing that campaign for… what was it? Those novelty garden gnomes? Don’t remind me! Mr. Higgins and his "Gnome-tastic Gardens." It was soul-crushing, but paid the bills. Still, cheese feels… insulting. Like I’m selling something I actively enjoy. Well, think of it as appreciating the craftsmanship. At least it’s not selling something awful, like those inflatable dinosaurs you nearly landed last year. Speaking of which, have you seen Mrs. Henderson’s tree? Absolutely massive this year. Nearly blocked out the entire street view, it did. No! Seriously? She always goes all out. It’s slightly terrifying, to be honest. Mine’s… minimalist. I got a little artificial one from Home Bargains. Felt a bit too early to spend a fortune, you know? Plus, Leo keeps trying to chew the tinsel. He’s a handful, isn't he? Proper little terror when he wants to be. Though he did give me a rather nice head-butt this morning. Practically a Christmas cuddle! How's your boyfriend, Tom? Still talking about moving to Berlin? Yeah, he is. He’s been researching like mad, mostly German history and culture. Apparently, Berlin has a surprisingly vibrant underground cabaret scene. He’s obsessed. Says it’s like stepping back in time, but with a really cool, modern edge. Berlin, eh? Bit of a long way to go, innit? Though I suppose it's good for him to be interested in something. He always did have a head for history, like his grandfather. Did you know your great-uncle fought in the war and… Mum! Let’s not bring up Great-Uncle Reginald just yet. I'm trying to picture myself there, you know? Cold, grey, lots of sausage. It’s…different. My birthday’s so close after, too. Imagine celebrating in Berlin! Wouldn't that be something! We’d have to come visit, of course. We'd need to learn a few phrases. "Where's the loo?" should be top of the list. And “more tea, please!” You know, I saw a lovely nail varnish at Boots yesterday, a sort of berry red. Thought of you. My nails are a complete mess, mind you. All that cleaning and handwashing. Ooh, berry red sounds perfect! Thanks, Mum. Seriously. I’ve been neglecting my nails, work’s just been so demanding.

…and honestly, the estate agent made it sound like the internet was already set up. "High-speed broadband," he said, all breezy. Turns out, it's just…not. I’ve been on the phone to Virgin for two hours already, trying to schedule an engineer. They can’t come until Wednesday. Wednesday! Wednesday? Seriously? You’ve been on the phone for two hours? Are you even allowed a break? My phone bill alone is terrifying. They offered me a voucher for a pizza. Honestly, the cheek. I said no. I need the internet more than I need a pizza, believe me. How are we supposed to function without it? No Netflix, no online banking… utter chaos. Right? And I was looking forward to streaming that new documentary tonight. Okay, Wednesday it is. Can you check if we have a router? Or did we even think about that? Good point. I… I think I packed it, somewhere in this mountain of cardboard. I'll dig it out. Right, while I'm doing that, about food. We need to hit the shops tomorrow. Want to make a proper meal? I was thinking butternut squash risotto – it’s in season, you know. Ooh, risotto sounds lovely. Much better than surviving on instant noodles and adrenaline. Did you see the recycling bins down there? Are we allowed to put everything in them, or is it like some weird Sussex system? I peered over the fence. Looks pretty standard. Glass, plastic, paper. No food waste bins, though. Which means we'll have to compost if we want to be proper eco-warriors. I’ve ordered one of those tumbling composters online, should be here next week. Good thinking. Right, let’s talk about something less practical… is there anything around here? Pubs, cafes, anything interesting? I’m already feeling slightly isolated. There's a little pub about ten minutes' walk, "The Red Lion," I think. Seemed fairly lively when I walked past earlier. And there’s a café just down the road – "The Bean Scene," apparently makes a decent latte. We could explore more properly this weekend. Okay, that's promising! I’m craving a proper coffee. Speaking of craving things… are you planning on smoking out here? Honestly? I probably will, a few. Been trying to cut down, you know, but moving always triggers it. I was hoping to use the balcony, but I don't want to annoy the neighbours.

Oh, that sounds awful! Peterborough traffic isn't great either, I’ve noticed when I've come to visit Mum. But moving? That's a big decision. You’ve got your routine down there, haven’t you? So, you’re still coordinating that big charity gala, right? How’s that going? Yeah, still battling that beast! It's...intense. Loads of moving parts, dealing with a million different personalities, but actually, it's really rewarding when everything comes together. We've got a comedian booked – Aiden Grimshaw, have you heard of him? Aiden Grimshaw! Yes! He's hilarious. Mum loves him. Proper observational stuff. Good choice! Better than that disastrous magician you had last year, remember? Don't remind me! He kept accidentally sawing his assistant's hair off. It was a nightmare. This year, we’re going for a foolproof option. How are things with you? Still in that placement at the marketing agency? Sort of. It’s…okay. The agency's really small, like, ten people small. It’s good experience, obviously, but I'm not sure it's what I envisioned when I finished uni. Mostly just making teas and coffees and scheduling client meetings. Although, I did get to help brainstorm for a campaign last week – for a local bakery, can you believe? ‘Dough-lightful Treats!’ was their slogan. Seriously. Dough-lightful! Oh dear. That's brilliant though, isn’t it? Getting any practical experience, even if it’s for a bakery. Better than analysing Shakespeare all day, eh? Remember those seminars? Professor Davies was terrifying. Don't even  mention  Professor Davies. I still have nightmares about his essay marking. He'd just stare at you across the table, silent, then give you a single, cryptic comment. "Lacks…resonance." What does that even  mean ? I think I need a holiday. We all do! I’ve been looking at Greece – Santorini, maybe? I’ve always wanted to go. It looks incredible in the pictures. Though bearing in mind my budget, it’ll probably end up being a campsite in Skegness. Skegness! Classic. Santorini is beautiful, though. My Auntie Shila went last year and sent loads of photos. Have you thought about Portugal? It’s a bit more affordable, I think, and the Algarve is gorgeous. My grandparents used to go every year. We’d build ridiculous sandcastles – Mum kept one that lasted, like, three days! Wow, three days is impressive!

…So, then Mr. Henderson, bless his cotton socks, says, ‘Lass, are you sure you’ve got the right data? It’s lookin’ a bit… optimistic, isn't it?’ Like I’d fudged a report for Cambridge University! Honestly, the man! Optimistic how? Was there something statistically improbable happening in your research? Aye, but not in a bad way! It showed a significant rise in engagement with the online resources, particularly amongst students from… well, not exactly privileged backgrounds, shall we say? And instead of saying, "That's brilliant, we’re reaching a wider audience!" he focuses on the  how  it's happening. Like it's some kind of trick. Proper Sunderland way, that, always lookin’ for a catch. Right. Classic. Academia can be… protective of its established narratives, can't it? My supervisor’s the same, sometimes. Always wanting to poke holes in things, even when they’re promising. What’s the focus of your research, anyway? You haven’t really told me much beyond the Henderson debacle. It’s about accessibility and digital inclusion in higher education. Basically, lookin’ at how universities are adapting to meet the needs of a more diverse student body. It’s fascinating, actually. And exhausting. But proper good to see some positive results, even if they do give folk a right proper conniption. How’s the PhD goin’, then? Still knee-deep in 18th-century agricultural practices? You have no idea. It’s worse than ever. The latest chapter is on the impact of turnip rotation on… well, turnips. Riveting stuff. I swear, sometimes I think I'm going to sprout roots myself. Fancy a refill? My treat. Aye, please. And tell me, are you still rockin’ that corduroy suit? It's… a choice. Hey, it’s vintage! Sustainable fashion! Besides, it keeps me warm. It's freezing here, even in a pub. Though, I admit, I saw some cracking coats in the window of that shop on Mill Road. Proper long, padded things, like something you’d see someone wearin’ up north. You’d look amazing in one. You think so? I’m more of a Barbour jacket kinda gal, myself. Classic. Always reliable. Reminds me of me mam, she had a green one, worn to bits. Remember The Futureheads? They’re playing a gig in Newcastle next month. Fancy a weekend away? Proper proper rave. The Futureheads! Brilliant band. Haven’t seen them live in ages.

Right, so, like, this whole Rwanda thing, Grandma, it's a right mess, innit? Everyone’s shoutin’ at everyone else. My History teacher, Mr. Davies, he was proper red in the face tryin’ to explain it. A mess is right, lad. A right proper pickle. All this talk of planes and people… reminds me a bit of the Empire, doesn’t it? Though that’s a whole different kettle of fish, o' course. Used to be, folks thought sending folk off 'round the world was just the done thing. But it's not fair, is it? Sending people to another country 'cause they needed help? Seems a bit… harsh. Mr. Davies said it's about stopping people comin' 'ere illegally, but… where's the compassion? Compassion’s a rare thing these days, isn’t it? Used to be, people helped each other out. My own father, bless his soul, he helped a family who'd lost their farm in the floods. Didn't ask for nothin' in return. Just… did it. Course, that was before all this paperwork and lawyers and committees. Everything's got so complicated. Yeah, it is. And the politicians, they’re just arguing, aren't they? Like, Rishi Sunak, he’s sayin’ it's gonna work, but everyone else shouts him down. And Labour, they’re sayin' it's barbaric, but they don't have a plan either, do they? It's just… noise. Politicians, eh? Always havin’ a good ding-dong. I remember back in ‘64 when Harold Wilson was Prime Minister. My Da used to say he could talk the birds off the trees. He was a clever one, Wilson. But even he couldn't solve everything. Seems like the more things change, the more they stay the same. This immigration thing... it’s been goin’ on for centuries, hasn't it? People always seekin’ a better life. True, but it feels different now, doesn't it? Like, the world's so much more connected. You see everything on the news, on social media… you can’t ignore it. Back in your day, Grandma, did you know what was happenin' in other countries as much? No, not at all. We had the wireless, of course, and the newspapers. But it was different. Things felt... further away. You didn’t see the faces of the people involved. Didn’t feel it as much. Wars were reported, of course, but it was all a bit distant.

Now, now, Moira. Leave the boy be. He's fair tired after FitzGerald's Park. Running around with the wee ones, chasing pigeons… buildin’ empires out of bread crumbs, the lot. It’s a fair effort, really.      He’s right, Moira. Don't fuss. Charlie's had a good day out. Though, I do agree, a little more consideration for the plate wouldn't go amiss. It's lovely to have Granny here, you know, she appreciates a well-set table.      Oh, I appreciate good food and good company, that's for sure. And a neat table is always a comfort. Reminds me of the school dinners, actually. Not that they were always neat, mind you! But the teachers always insisted. Builds character, didn’t it?      Sorry, Granny. Just... really hungry. The pond was awesome, though. We saw a heron! And Dad nearly dropped Finn in the lake.      He did indeed, didn't he? A close shave for the wee fella! See, Charlie? That's why you need to keep your wits about you. Not just devourin’ your dinner.      He's right. And honestly, darling, a little less talk with your mouth full would be lovely. You'll choke. Liam, did you see that article about the Blood Moon? Apparently, it’s going to be visible tonight.      Aye, I did. Thought about dragging everyone out for a look, but the Midleton road’s still a mess after that flooding last week. Wouldn’t fancy it in the dark with the kids.      A Blood Moon! Goodness me. I remember them from when I was a girl. They always had such a… a feeling about them. Eerie, but beautiful. Reminded you the world was a big place, full of secrets.      Is it, like, a bad omen? Like in Harry Potter?      Charlie! It’s not a bad omen. It’s just science. The moon passes through Earth's shadow. It's something to marvel at, not to be scared of.      Exactly. Though, my grandmother used to say it meant fairies were dancing, and best to keep the doors bolted. Old wives' tales, of course.      Your grandmother was a wise woman, Liam. There's always a bit of truth in the old tales. Don't dismiss them so quickly. They're full of history and connection. We've lost a lot of that, haven’t we? Just rushing about, heads down.      Well, Granny, I think we're trying to connect.

…and honestly, the whole thing just feels rather precarious, doesn’t it? This referendum business. I mean, you’ve got these young people, bless ‘em, caught up in ideals and promises, and then you've got the older generation recalling, rightly or wrongly, what independence meant back in the day. It’s a whirlwind. Whirlwind's a good word for it, Charles. A right dust-up. Though I reckon a spot of independence might do them good, shake things up a bit. Been too much reliance on Westminster for too long, hasn’t there? Down here in Sussex, we feel it too, you know. A bit remote, a bit… forgotten. Forgotten, yes. Aye, it does. It's a right tight squeeze, this one. I’m tryin’ to be careful, Grandad. Don't want to scuff up your good coat, do I? You've got a lovely tie on, by the way. Right, we’re just approaching Puddlebrook Farm. According to the GPS, we should turn left in about 200 yards. Are you sure about this route, Anya? It looks… rural. Very rural. Relax, Liam. Everything's automated, eh? No character. It's more about efficiency, Grandad. And sustainability. We’re trying to minimize impact. Speaking of impact, Anya, you’re getting awfully close to that hedge… Sorry, sorry! It’s narrower than it looks. Right, there's the turn. Sharp left. You never appreciate the simple things, do ya, young man? I appreciate data-driven agricultural solutions, thank you very much. Systems optimization… predictive analysis… Right then, quiet, both of you. I’m tryin’ to concentrate.

…and honestly, Mum, the choir’s really lifted my spirits this week. We're working on a really lovely arrangement of 'Scarborough Fair'. My knees are protesting louder than a politician facing a tough question. Seriously though, the fells are beautiful this time of year. Saw a buzzard circling over Derwentwater yesterday. Proper majestic. Your mother here's been pushing me to join the local walking group. Pushing might be a strong word, Michael. Encouraging. And honestly, it’s good for you. A bit of company, a bit of gentle exercise. You can't just sit in that recliner all day, you know. It's not good for the circulation, and you get muddled. Muddled? I'm not muddled! They  are  an affront! Honestly, someone should write to the government about this. No one forced us to eat those vile things when I was at school! You’re incorrigible. Remember Mrs. Henderson, Dad? She had a way of making you feel utterly inadequate. But she also made you  think . That was the key. I always admired her dedication. She even used to donate her free time to tutoring struggling students. Now  that  was philanthropy. Not like some of these celebrities doing photo ops. Teachers! All right! They were a different breed back then. Proper disciplinarians. Gets you somewhere. Nowadays, they’re worried about someone’s feelings more than teaching them Pythagoras’ theorem. You’re going to start a whole debate there, Dad. I'm not sure I have the energy after trying to explain the intricacies of transcription software to Aunt Maureen on Sunday. She thinks a "cloud" is a fluffy white thing in the sky.

“…and Mrs. Davies said, honestly, I was a bit taken aback. She said Leo's really struggling with fractions. Fractions! He's eight, not tackling astrophysics! It's just… frustrating, isn’t it? I’ve been trying to help him after school, but he just clams up.” Clams up? Like a shell, Mummy?  makes clawing motion with hand  Yes, exactly like a shell, darling. Very clever. It means he stops talking and doesn't want to do it. Right, Leo? Stop clamming up! I don’t  want  to do fractions! They’re pointy! They’re not pointy, sweetheart. They’re just… numbers broken into smaller pieces. Think of your pizza last Saturday. Remember? We cut it into slices, and each slice was a fraction of the whole pizza. Pizza! Can we have pizza tomorrow?  nods vigorously  Maybe, love. Let's focus on fractions first. Leo, did Mrs. Davies explain  why  she thinks you're struggling? She said I get confused with the top and bottom numbers. Right. Okay. Well, that’s something we can work on. World Book Day is next week, isn’t it? Are you excited about dressing up? I'm being a fairy princess! With sparkly wings!  twirls excitedly  I'm being Bilbo Baggins. From  The Hobbit . Excellent choices! I love Bilbo. What’s your favourite part, Leo? When he finds the ring! And the riddles with Gollum. Ah, yes! Gollum. A very sly character, that one. You know, Mrs. Davies did say you were engaging in class discussions about characters and their motivations. That’s really good! It just needs to translate into the Maths. Gollum’s tummy rumbled! Did he eat… um… people? That’s… a complicated story, sweetheart. Let’s just say Gollum didn't have very good table manners. It’s probably best not to think too much about what he might have eaten. It was a very, very long time ago, in a story. Imagine it smells like burnt toast and… and old socks. Definitely wouldn't be a nice smell. Yuck! Burnt toast and socks! Precisely. Now, after school on Tuesday, I was thinking of getting you both to the circus? The one at the showground? Circus! With clowns and elephants!  jumps up and down  They have trapeze artists! And lions! Yes, all those things. I’ve booked two tickets. But you need to promise me you’ll try and do at least fifteen minutes of fraction practice with me before we go, understand?

Ah, that was grand, Mary. Proper feed. Oisin clearin' out the curtain shop, is he? Never thought he’d take to that. Good lad, mind you, pickin' up a trade. Beats bein' idle. He’s actually really enjoying it, Liam. Mrs. O’Malley at the shop is wonderful with him, teaching him all sorts of things. It's good for his confidence, you know? He was gettin' a bit... listless last few months. Boooo! He certainly has a spirit, that wee lad. Reminds me of my grandson, Jock, at that age. Always gettin' into mischief. Though, Oisin… he speaks differently, doesn't he? A bit of a mixed bag, his English. Aye, he does. That’s somethin’ alright. He’ll be sayin' 'Right, pet', and then throw in a bit of Cork slang outta nowhere. It's a pure delight, really. Keeps ya on yer toes. Think he picked it up off YouTube, God love him. He certainly did! Trying to imitate those American YouTubers. It’s hilarious. Right, so about the party... I was thinking bouncy castle? Bouncy castle’s a bit ambitious, isn’t it darlin’? For ten kids in the garden? We’ll end up with a pile of scraped knees and tears. How about just a few of the wee ones from school. Keep it simple. But he really wants a bouncy castle, Liam. You'll be brilliant at it though. You’re so good with figures. It is, alright. Keeps me busy. And the tax on these rented houses… it's killin’ ya. I’m practically subsidising someone else’s lifestyle. Tell me about it! I’m getting those charity calls constantly. It’s just relentless. I try to ignore them, but… It’s a difficult one, dear. You want to help, but it’s so hard when your own finances are tight.

Right, so you’re telling me “flummoxed” is a legit word to use? Seriously? It sounds like something me mam would say when she’s trying to confuse you. I mean, honestly, it's so… roundabout. It absolutely is. It's Victorian, actually. Came into common usage in the mid-1800s. Means bewildered, perplexed, utterly confounded. Quite a useful word, really, when you need to convey a sense of well, flummoxation. See, anon here’s a word nerd. Doesn't surprise me, does it? He probably dreams in etymology. It's a useful skill! Knowing where words come from gives you a deeper understanding of them. And it's good for my job, actually. Being able to analyse language patterns... Aye, well, that’s fancy. My job's all about making sure the computer understands what people are saying. Tidying up language, you know? So, “flummoxed” – you’d never use that in a chatbot, would ya? It’s too theatrical. I think you'd be surprised, Beth. Modern chatbots are getting pretty sophisticated. They can pick up on nuance, sarcasm… and probably even a well-placed "flummoxed." Maybe. Still sounds a bit bonkers, though. What about this one? You were showing me that one earlier, the… "susurrus." What on  earth  is that? I’m struggling that one. Ah, yes! "Susurrus." It's a beautiful word, actually. It’s Latin in origin –  susurrus  – and it means a whispering or rustling sound. The gentle sound of leaves in the wind, or water flowing over stones… Whispering… rustling… Right. So, like when you’re at the coast and the waves are coming in soft, not crashing? Exactly! Spot on, Beth. That’s precisely the sort of sound it describes. I used it in my thesis, actually. Describing the auditory landscape of a peat bog. A peat bog? Cor! What was that all about, then? Digging for buried treasure? Not quite. I was analysing the impact of micro-habitats on vegetation growth. The sounds – the susurrus of the water, the rustling reeds – provide valuable data points. You lads are something else. So, this "susurrus" – is it commonly used? Or is it one of those words you only hear in posh books? It’s relatively uncommon, yes. More literary than conversational. But that's part of its charm. It adds a certain… elegance, shall we say? Aye, alright. "Elegant." I'll stick to "windy," thanks very much.

…and then Liam just tripped, right into Mr. Henderson’s prize-winning begonias! Honestly, I nearly died! Poor Mr. Henderson, bless ‘im, he just stood there with his mouth open. Liam, eh? You're bringing that out? Annie, look at my hair! It looks like a badger’s nest! And you’re wearing that awful blue dress! Don't you dare mock the blue dress! It was the height of fashion then! And your hair  did  look like a badger's nest! You looked like a scarecrow! I looked perfectly respectable! You were the one trying to recreate Britney Spears… badly.

Right, so, they’ve asked for specific justification for the extension. Not just ‘it’ll improve the property’, but  how  it will improve it. And the precedent thing. Honestly, Ben, that’s what worries me most. Precedent? You're stressing about precedent? We're talking about a single-story extension at the back of a detached house, not demolishing the town hall to build a supermarket. Easy for you to say, you're not the one who has to articulate why a slightly larger kitchen doesn’t set a dangerous precedent for the entire conservation area! They’re waiting for the gotcha moment, aren't they? Someone looking for an excuse to deny it. Cynical as ever, love. Look, the planning officer, Sarah, she seemed genuinely receptive when we spoke last week. She said the initial assessment was favourable, just that they needed a little more detail about the impact on neighbouring properties and, yes, the precedent. Receptive doesn’t equal approved. I've been down this road before. Remember the garden shed debacle? "Perfectly reasonable request," they said. Then six months and a heated debate about impact on dormice later, and we were back to square one. Okay, okay, deep breaths. We've got this. Let's break it down. Impact on neighbours – minimal. They're both retired, mostly inside, and their gardens don't directly overlook ours. That's fairly watertight. Precedent... that’s the tricky one. What if we frame it as sympathetic extension  consistent  with existing additions in the area? There’s that cottage a few doors down with the conservatory; we can draw parallels. That's… a thought. Need to find photos of that conservatory. And we need to stress the design. It’s not some sprawling glass box, it’s a continuation of the existing style, using the same materials… subtle, almost invisible from the street. Exactly. And we emphasize no increase in overshadowing, minimal impact on drainage, and that it genuinely enhances the enjoyment of our home, which in turn, ensures we’re likely to maintain the property to a high standard – benefit to the neighbourhood, right? We're selling the idea of responsible homeowners. Selling. That's exactly what it is, isn't it? Selling them on the idea that we’re good citizens who deserve a slightly bigger kitchen. Alright, let’s structure this properly. I’ll draft a detailed addendum addressing their concerns specifically.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork is insane. I swear, half my job is just filling out forms. You’d think with all the technology we have, it’d be easier, wouldn’t you? But no. Just a lot of people arguing about things that don't actually matter. Sounds grim. At least you're almost done with that project, right? Think you'll get a decent bonus? Hopefully. I'm banking on it. Need to use it for that weekend in Brighton we were talking about. Remember? The Lanes, proper fish and chips... Salt and vinegar, naturally. Oh my god, yes! I completely forgot about Brighton! It’s just… Sarah from accounting keeps going on about her engagement. Like, I'm genuinely happy for her, I am, but hearing about diamonds and floral arrangements  constantly  is a bit much. No, no, nothing like that. Apparently, she's convinced the new fella you were seeing, Liam, is a… a ‘charter’ she said. Like, a dodgy one. Something about him having a van and doing “odd jobs”. Remember that time he wore a full leather outfit to the pub? Don’t remind me. It was like something out of a dodgy 80s music video.

Honestly, Liam, look at this. “Lose 10 pounds in a week!” It’s just…ridiculous. The way they target people's insecurities, makes you wonder about the ethics of advertising, doesn't it? Aye, tell me about it. They’re all at it, innit? Bombarding ya with stuff. Remember that car boot sale we went to last summer? Found a right bargain, didn’t we? This old record player, practically new. Couldn't get that online. That was brilliant, yeah! Though, admit it, half the fun was rummaging. I'm thinking of going again this weekend. Need to clear out some old clothes. Got loads I never wear. Fancy coming? Potentially, love. Depends what the week looks like. I’ve got that extra lesson on Tuesday, remember? Bit of a nightmare, trying to squeeze everything in. All this prepping… sometimes I wish I’d just stuck to bar work. Don't be daft! You’re brilliant with those kids. You really connect with them. Especially the one, what's his name… Michael? He’s got dyslexia, doesn't he? You’ve been amazing with him. He is a clever lad, proper determined, the little fella. I've been using some NLP techniques, just basic stuff really, to help him focus. Visualisation stuff. Makes a difference, doesn’t it? He’s actually started enjoying reading. It’s chuffed to bits me, seeing that. It's wonderful! You should write something about it, actually. For a teaching journal or something. You could showcase those NLP strategies. It's genuinely valuable work. You think so? I'd rather not. Journalism’s not exactly me. I'd rather be having a brew and watching the telly. Speaking of which, this program's mental. Although, on the subject of news, have you heard about that spate of burglaries down on Prenton Road? Makes you think, doesn’t it? Considering we left the back window slightly ajar earlier… Aye, you're right. Gotta be more careful. I don’t like the idea of someone poking about. We should get one of them motion sensor lights fitted. Definitely. Right, I’m starving. Fancy a takeaway? I was thinking Thai. Been meaning to try that new place on Hoyle Road. Thai sounds spot on, love. Proper lush.

Oh no! That's dreadful. All that effort! Did you follow a recipe? I know, I know, sourdough's supposed to be intuitive, but even I cheat a bit with online resources. Proper dedication, Sarah! You're talking my language. I tried making focaccia last week – monumental disaster. Ended up looking like it’d been run over by a lorry. What flour are you using? That can make a difference, apparently. You know, I’ve been reading about this new app, BreadBot. Sounds ridiculous, but basically, it controls the entire baking process remotely. Temperature, humidity, even lets you know when it needs feeding. Apparently, it makes  amazing  sourdough. BreadBot? Seriously? That just sounds dystopian, David. Like, outsourcing the joy of baking to an algorithm. What's next, robot-written novels? Robot novels! Now there’s a thought. Though, you’ve got a point, Chloe. Everything's becoming so… automated. Still, Sarah, if you’re desperate, maybe it’s worth a look? I’m struggling to see the appeal myself, though. I’m not sure I  want  to outsource the baking, Emily! It's the process I enjoy. Though, I'm feeling pretty defeated right now. I was hoping to wow everyone at Christmas with homemade crusty bread. Christmas is ages away, Sarah. Plenty of time to redeem yourself. Speaking of wowing people, have any of you seen that new documentary on BBC Two about the resurgence of vinyl records? Absolutely brilliant. Really got me thinking about the whole media landscape. I did! It was good. Though slightly predictable, you know? The whole 'analog warmth' versus digital crispness argument. It's been done. I’m more interested in the impact of streaming on artists' royalties. That’s properly depressing. Depressing is putting it mildly. It's daylight robbery. We need a proper overhaul of copyright law, surely? That’s why I've been chucking a bit extra into my ethical streaming service subscriptions recently. Feel like I'm doing  something  at least. That’s a good shout, David. I’ve done the same. It's a wee drop in the ocean, but it's something. I’ve been working on a piece for radio about independent record shops – the ones that are still clinging on. Proper characters, they are. Stories for days. That sounds fascinating, Emily. You always uncover the most interesting things. Honestly, all this talk about media is making me want to bury my head in a good book.

…and honestly, finding anywhere decent to rent back then was a nightmare. Absolute chaos. Everything was damp, or needed rewiring, or had some frankly bizarre previous occupant. Do you remember anything like that, John? Damp? My dear Margaret, you're describing my first flat perfectly. It was in South London, just off Brixton Road. The wallpaper was peeling, the floorboards sloped alarmingly, and there was a persistent smell of… well, I still can’t quite place it. Let's just say it wasn’t potpourri. But it was affordable, and that’s all that mattered when I was fresh out of university, interviewing for a teaching post at the grammar school. The interview itself was a shambles, too. I tripped over the Headmaster's foot as I entered the room! Oh, good heavens. You, John? Clumsy? Never would have pegged you. My early days here in [Town Name] were just as fraught, though in a slightly different way. Trying to find somewhere to live when I got my lecturer post at the university – everyone was already settled. Student digs were…rustic, let's say. Ended up in a converted attic room above a bakery. The smell of fresh bread was lovely in the morning, less so when the bakers started cleaning the equipment at six o’clock! A bakery, you say? At least it was a pleasant aroma. My initial foray into this area was considerably less charming. I came down from Birmingham to interview for a position at the local practice. Imagine, driving down in my little Morris Minor, feeling utterly terrified. The interview went surprisingly well, I must admit, though I did drop my pen into the dentist’s model of a jaw! He just looked at me, completely deadpan, and said, “Well, that’s certainly one way to make an impression.” Oh, you always were a charmer, David. Speaking of interviews and housing… I remember arriving here with Peter, fresh from teacher training. We’d both managed to secure jobs almost simultaneously. Absolute panic setting in about where we were going to live! Everything seemed either miles outside of town or ridiculously expensive. It was a different world then, wasn't it? Buying was almost unheard of for young teachers. Renting was the norm, and you were lucky to find anything that hadn’t been through numerous incarnations. I recall seeing one place that was advertised as "charming Victorian cottage" – turned out to be a glorified shed with a leaky roof.

Oh, dear me, isn't it though? Arthritis. I’ve got a touch of it myself, mostly in me fingers. Makes picking up a brush quite a bit of a bother now. Still, I can potter about, can’t I? Run the gallery, mostly. Though even  that  can be a bit of a strain sometimes, shifting these old chaps around. It's such a pity. You have a real talent, Marion. I remember seeing your landscapes down at the Taunton Art Trail a few years ago. Absolutely stunning. Reminded me a bit of… well, just the hills of home, really. Of the Blue Mountains, around Sydney. Before they concreted over half of them, of course. Oh, you did? You saw me then? That’s lovely to hear. I’d nearly forgotten about that trail. It’s been a while. Australia... well, I always fancied a bit of travel. Never got round to it, though. Being a Somerset girl, you see. Roots, you know? Stuck firm in the clay. My grandmama used to say everything good came from the West Country. Bit romantic, perhaps, but she meant it. What brought you to England, then? My husband, David. He was a botanist, studying the native flora. Wonderful man. We came over in the seventies. Initially to Cambridge, then settled here in Taunton. He loved the quiet, the cider orchards… less Australian sun, he said, better for his studies. He passed away, oh, fifteen years ago now. Time slips away, doesn't it? Indeed it does. Terribly sorry to hear that, dear. Fifteen years… that’s a long time. Did you… did you work, then, with him? I was a speech and language therapist, actually. Initially with children, then adolescents. A rewarding, if sometimes heartbreaking, profession. Helping those who struggled to find their voice, to communicate… it's humbling. Though, goodness, the paperwork! Hospitals were such a bureaucratic nightmare. It kept me busy, though. Gave me purpose. What about you, Marion? Did you always paint? Always, dearie, always! Since I were a little girl. Doodles in the margins of my schoolbooks, filling notebooks with wildflowers and ponies… Me father, he was a farmer, you see. Not a man of many words, but he always let me wander, took me on long walks across the fields. That’s where I learned to  see , I reckon. The way the light caught the barley, the colours of the heather… They’re all in me paintings, those memories.

…Honestly, I’m still kicking myself about not getting that hummingbird on my forearm. Mum went mental, obviously. Said it was “permanently frivolous.” Like studying astrophysics isn’t frivolous! Your mum will freak about anything remotely artistic, Liam. Remember the hair blue phase? She nearly had a heart attack. A hummingbird's better than turquoise hair, wouldn't you say? Besides, you've got that whole sleeve already. One little bird isn’t gonna make or break your aesthetic. Yeah, but…it would have been  the  bird. The perfect little detail. Nah, never mind. So, what are we doing for the main course tonight? Lamb? I’m starving. Lamb’s a bit much for a Tuesday, innit? I was thinking roast chicken. Simple, lets me concentrate on the Christmas pudding – I’m trying a new recipe this year. Brandy-soaked cherries…it’s going to be mental. Brandy-soaked cherries sounds  amazing . Seriously, you outdo yourself every year. Better than your nan’s even, and that’s saying something. Remember that time she tried to recreate a Black Forest gateau she saw on a travel show? Oh god, don’t remind me! The whipped cream was like concrete. And the chocolate…it tasted like sawdust. Anyway, chicken it is. You thinking about ordering those fairy lights for the café, Chloe? It's looking a bit…sparse. Chloe's mentioned it, yeah. She's been swamped with the pre-Christmas rush. Apparently, everyone’s going mad for her gingerbread lattes. Insane levels of demand. She was saying she needs to check stock levels on the candy canes too - she’s thinking of getting those massive swirly ones. Chloe: Right, I’m here! Smells good in here. Chicken, I hope? I need serious comfort food after the day I've had. Chicken it is! Come on, grab a seat. Everything alright at the café? Liam was just telling me you’re selling out of everything. Chloe: You have no idea. It's chaotic! People are already talking about Christmas decorations - asking when they’ll have the full range in. Honestly, it's like Christmas started in October this year. I was thinking… maybe getting in a couple of those frosted pinecone garlands? They looked really pretty at Mitchell's the other day. Mitchell's, eh? Bit pricey, aren't they? Chloe: Yeah, but they’re good quality. Unlike some of the plastic rubbish you find elsewhere.

Honestly, Mum, I'm still reeling from it all. Getting offered a place at Oxford, I mean. It feels…surreal. Like a really elaborate prank. It's not a prank, love. You earned it. Your thesis on Woolf was brilliant, genuinely. Professor Davies practically gushed about it. You should be proud of yourself. I  am  proud, yeah. Just… Oxford. It feels different to Cambridge. Smaller, somehow. More intense. I’m really not sure if I can handle it. Cambridge felt like home, you know? The cobbled streets, the punting… It  was  a good fit. And I’m glad you had those years there. But you’ve always been ambitious, darling. Remember when you were ten and insisted on building that ridiculously complex Lego castle, even though you needed help with every other brick? You thrive on a challenge. Yeah, well, that castle collapsed spectacularly. Still, the point stands. It's a big shift. And what about… you know… the flat? What are we going to do with it? We’ll figure it out. Don’t worry about that right now. Let’s focus on your Oxford adventure. As for the flat… I’ve been talking to some estate agents. It’s on the market, but quietly. No rush. I'm trying to get a decent price. Thinking maybe a couple close to the Southbank? Somewhere with a balcony would be lovely, somewhere I can grow a few geraniums. Geraniums, right. Classic Mum. Are you… are you going to be alright here on your own? It’s a big flat for one person. Don’t you start worrying about me! I’ll be perfectly fine. I’ve lived on my own before, remember? And honestly, it’ll be nice to have a bit of… breathing space. Besides, I’m thinking of doing that pottery class I mentioned. The one at the community centre. Always wanted to try it. That’s brilliant, Mum. You’d be great. You always were good at crafting, remember those hideous Christmas decorations you’d make when I was little? Hideous! That’s a generous description. But they were made with love. So, Oxford. Have you looked at the accommodation yet? Are they offering you college rooms or are you looking at private halls? They’ve offered me rooms in St. Hilda’s. It looks… ancient. All dark wood and portraits. A little intimidating, to be honest. I'm leaning towards private halls though.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork involved in just  getting  permission to excavate felt disproportionate to the potential historical significance. It's a frustrating balance, isn’t it? Weighing the bureaucratic hurdles against the possibility of uncovering something truly remarkable. Absolutely. I can completely sympathise. We run projects looking at language shift and evolution across different communities, and navigating heritage permissions, especially when it involves potentially impacting active linguistic practices, is a nightmare. It’s meant to be protective, of course, but sometimes it feels like it stifles discovery. Are you working on a specific site currently? Well, my dear, I'm retired, nominally. Though I still pop in to the university to give a few lectures, you see. Archaeology's in my blood. I spent most of my career excavating small, deserted villages across Shropshire and Cheshire – the kind that just… faded away. Really remarkable stuff. Tiny clusters of homes, sometimes just the outline of foundations, but teeming with stories if you know where to look. We found a remarkably well-preserved Roman coin hoard near Ludlow once - quite the surprise. Reminded me of the challenges you mentioned – getting the landowner to fully grasp why we needed to painstakingly sift through his field for three weeks! A Roman coin hoard! Incredible! What a find. Were you ever involved in anything internationally? We’re starting to consider scoping out a potential dig site in Jordan, focusing on early Arab settlements around the trade routes. It's preliminary, but we're hoping to link their language and trade patterns. Jordan! Oh, that's fascinating! I actually did some initial data collection in Xi’an a few years ago. Part of a larger project comparing the phonetic development of Mandarin dialects across different regions. It was my first real overseas fieldwork. The sheer scale of the Terracotta Army is breathtaking, of course, but what really struck me was the cultural richness – the food, the calligraphy, the ancestral reverence... completely different to anything I’d experienced before. Did you ever consider working with the languages of the nomadic tribes of the steppes? Their connections to early Silk Road traders are often overlooked. Ah, the steppes! Wonderful suggestion. I've always been rather captivated by the linguistics of those regions. It's remarkable how much linguistic evidence we have of cultural exchange. My colleague, Professor Davies, actually dedicated a good portion of his career to tracing the influence of Turkic languages on Old English.

…No, seriously, I’m telling you, the algorithm just  loves  cats playing the piano. It’s mad. I saw one the other day, a ginger tabby absolutely hammering out something vaguely resembling Chopin. Millions of views! Meanwhile, my dissertation on post-structuralist literary theory gets, what, twenty-seven? Mostly from my mum. Twenty-seven’s better than zero, Liam. At least she cares. And speaking of algorithms... honestly, the whole creator economy thing feels a bit dystopian, doesn’t it? Like we’re all scrambling for fifteen minutes of fame based on whether a cat looks particularly expressive. Tell me about it! I’ve been trying to boost my café’s Instagram – honestly, it’s a  nightmare . Everyone wants aesthetically pleasing lattes and staged photos of sourdough. I’m just trying to sell a decent cuppa and a slice of cake to locals, innit? It's exhausting trying to keep up with all the trends. Plus, the competition is mental. Literally three new coffee shops have opened in the area  this  year. It's the same in the film world, in a way. Everyone’s chasing viral clips, short-form content. It’s bled into proper production, you know? Clients want something instantly shareable, even if it compromises the quality. It's tough maintaining artistic integrity. Exactly! And it feels like that pressure particularly hits young people. Everyone's constantly comparing themselves, posting their "highlight reel." My cousin, Jamie, he dropped out of uni because he felt like he was "failing" compared to everyone’s seemingly perfect Instagram lives. That’s awful. Education, though…it’s such a weird system, isn’t it? I mean, I did a degree in English Lit, loved it, used it to get into marketing for a bit, then realised I hated corporate life. Now I bake, which is significantly less lucrative, but infinitely more fulfilling. But Jamie dropping out…that makes you wonder what's the point of all the tuition fees, really? True. I left sixth form. Didn't fancy uni at all. Honestly, I was probably a bit too overwhelmed by everything anyway. My mum always says I'd have been better off with more support... didn't get diagnosed with dyslexia until I was almost fifteen. It explains a  lot , doesn’t it? Trying to keep up with readings and essays… it was just a constant struggle. I regret not getting that support earlier, but wishing won't change it.

Honestly, David, I'm just… stressed. Absolutely riddled with it. This new cohort, they just don't seem to  want  to learn. It’s not about the material, it’s about engagement. They’re all glued to their phones, passively absorbing, and when I try to instigate discussion, it’s like talking to a wall. The digital natives, eh? My experience in the History department is similar. They expect information to spoon-fed. I tried a really interactive seminar on the Dissolution of the Monasteries last week, incorporated primary source analysis, everything. Crickets. Absolute crickets. Exactly! And the marking… oh, the marking. Half of them submit work riddled with plagiarism. Not blatant, you know, copy-paste from Wikipedia. But just… vaguely worded summaries of online sources. It's demoralising, really. I spent hours correcting a student’s essay last night just to point out that their 'analysis' was lifted verbatim from a JSTOR article! The university needs to crack down harder on Turnitin, I reckon. They're too worried about being seen as punitive. What about this new policy they’re proposing about performance-based pay? Ridiculous. Don’t even get me started on that! It's completely skewed. It rewards those who teach the biggest classes, not necessarily those who are doing the most innovative research or providing the best student support. I’m worried it'll just incentivise teaching under-grad modules and churning out students, rather than fostering genuine scholarship. It's rather short-sighted, isn't it? Massively. And the timing’s terrible, with everything else going on. The latest polling numbers are bleak. Labour’s got a real momentum. Don’t get me wrong, I’m not necessarily saying the Tories should win, but this constant instability… it’s unsettling. It is. And the cost of living crisis just keeps getting worse. Did you see the latest energy price predictions? We might need to seriously re-evaluate our… savings. We were thinking about that holiday to Italy next year, weren't we? We were. Look, let’s not panic. We’re comfortable. We’re not going to have to choose between heating and eating, unlike a lot of people. But you're right to be mindful. Maybe we dial it back a bit. We could do a long weekend somewhere closer to home, explore more of Norfolk. Cromer's lovely this time of year. That’s not a bad idea actually.

It’s quite fascinating really, Gran. Think of it like… two coins flipped at the same time, but inextricably linked. If you know one is heads, you instantly know the other is tails, even if they’re miles apart. Miles apart? Doesn’t that defeat the point? If they’re miles apart, well, surely it’s just a coincidence then, isn’t it? Just… chance. Like finding two ducks in the park both facing the same direction. Now, now, Elsie. Don't go dismissing quantum physics like that. It’s more complicated than two ducks. Remember that documentary we watched on black holes? That was a bit mind-bending, even for me. Black holes! All that stuff just feels… made up. Like something from a particularly preposterous science fiction novel. Remember ‘Forbidden Planet’? Now  that  was science fiction. Walter Pidgeon, giving a proper performance, not this… this digital frippery they have these days. It's not frippery, Gran. Science is building on what we know. And the ‘digital’ bit is just how we process and understand the data. Look, there's a brilliant animation explaining it – I’ll send you the link later. It’s animated, so it’s less… verbose. Sending me links! Honestly, you young people and your ‘links.’ I used to have a perfectly good encyclopaedia set, you know. Bound in leather. One could actually  feel  the knowledge in your hands. It’s not the same as staring at a screen. And the glare! Dreadful for the eyes. Elsie’s right about the animation, love. Sometimes a visual helps. Remember when you were trying to understand how a combustion engine worked? That little model I built you, with the pistons moving? That  was  rather clever, Arthur. Though it did take you three entire weekends. And you nearly glued your fingers together. Speaking of weekends, have you two decided where you want to go for the Jubilee celebrations? Aunt Fiona’s suggested a barbecue, but with the weather, it'll be a washout. Fiona's barbecues are always a washout. She insists on using that dreadful charcoal that tastes like chemicals. No, I think we should stick with a nice afternoon tea at the Tea Rooms. Do you recall, Arthur, back when Mrs. Hathaway ran the Tea Rooms? Her Victoria sponge was something else. Aye, Elsie, it were magnificent. Proper clotted cream, not that whipped stuff they sell now.

Right now, right now, love. Ye’re lettin' off steam about Minecraft again, are ye? We're all tryin' to have a bit o' dinner here. Liam, did ye hear that? Your cousin, Finn, was nearly gettin’ the Ender Dragon. It’s not just “a bit o’ Minecraft,” Dad! It took me ages to build the portal! And the dragon’s AI is messed up, it just bugged out. It's frustrating! I was  this  close to beating it. Honestly, Liam, sometimes a game just… ends. Things happen. It doesn't mean the whole world is ending, does it? Finn, darling, are you alright? Did you want a piece of carrot? Baa! Baa! Cah-rot! See? Even Finn knows carrots are important. Less dragon-slaying, more carrot-eating, I say. So, you were sayin’ about the emeralds? What level are ye at now, anyhow? Level 68. And it's not about  just  emeralds, Dad. It's about the whole progression! I’ve been working on this seed for like, three weeks! It's a perfect jungle biome. He’s putting his heart into it, isn’t he? It’s lovely to see a passion for something. You know, when I was a girl, all I was passionate about was collecting stamps. Mum would go mad when I traded away my Queen Elizabeth II sheet for a half-penny George VI. Stamps, is it? Now that’s a bit o’ alright. A world of adventure built on sticky paper. Finn, maybe ye’d like to build a little stamp collection… once ye’ve finished conquerin' the Minecraft universe. Very funny, Dad. You wouldn’t understand. It's about resource management, crafting, strategic combat… it’s like a digital version of… well, it’s complicated. It sounds complicated, sweetie. But you're clever. You’ll figure it out. Liam, is Finn still getting enough fresh air? He spends so much time indoors with those screens. He needs a good walk, doesn’t he? It’s supposed to be a nice day tomorrow. Aye, a walk would do him good. Might even tire him out properly for bed. We could take Finn too. He loves the park near the community centre. He'll be chasin' pigeons and rollin' around in the grass. Paaark! I guess a walk wouldn’t be the  worst  thing. But I was hoping to finish building the Nether Fortress tomorrow. The Nether Fortress, is it?

A ferret, you say? Blimey, now that’s a sight, innit? Never seen one o’ them loose in a pub. Costessey pub, was it? The King’s Head? No, no, up in Harrow. The Red Lion. Much smaller, mind you. Not like your King’s Head. More… well, more intimate. Though probably not at the time for the poor gentleman with the ferret on ‘is nose. Anyway, it reminded me of that little joke you told us last Christmas, Arthur, about the badger in the beetroot patch. Ah, yes! "Why did the badger cross the beetroot patch? To get to the other side!" Still gets a giggle out o’ me, that does. Though young Elsie here she just rolls 'er eyes. Gran, seriously? That's so old. Young people today, no appreciation for a proper joke. Not like when I was a lad… used to be a laugh a minute down the market! Arthur, be nice to Elsie. It’s Christmas. Besides, I’m sure she’s got better things to occupy her mind than badger jokes. Is everything alright with Liam, Elsie? You seemed a bit quiet earlier. He's… complicated. He said he might not be able to come for Christmas dinner. No way! Why not? Did you argue? He’s got… rehearsals for something. Some band thing. He says it’s really important. Oh, love. That’s a tricky one, innit? Follow your heart, dear. Though Christmas dinner  is  rather special. Especially with ANON’s roast potatoes. Best potatoes this side o’ the Broads, I’ll tell you that. An' you’ve gone to a lot o' trouble with the decorations this year, ANON. Proper sparkly! Makes a change from just the fairy lights, doesn’t it? Yes, it does look lovely. Though all that tinsel does give me a bit of a headache. I'm already wishing I'd remembered to take some antihistamines. Speaking of travelling, how was the drive over, Arthur? You looked a bit strained earlier. Didn’t half! That old Ford’s playin’ up again. Started makin’ a funny clatter just past Wymondham. Thought I was gonna be stranded. Need to get it seen to, I do. Found a fella in Attleborough, says he might be able to have a look at it next week. Costs a bomb, mind you… these car fellas. All takin' you for a ride, they are. You should take it to old Dennis down the road from you, Arthur.

Tell me about it, love. It sounds brutal. Did you manage to grab anything for your tea? I'm making a quick risotto, nothing fancy. Just a bit of toast, really. Been buried in Ms. Davies’ report on the new training protocols. Honestly, the things they want us to implement… It’s a minefield. They’re suggesting mandatory mindfulness sessions during breaks! Mindfulness! When I’m trying to catch up on emails and find out who's gone off sick, they want me zen! Mindfulness? Seriously, Dad? That’s brilliant. You trying to meditate away the departmental chaos? Exactly! Typical. Bureaucracy gone mad, I tell you. Though, I suppose a bit of calm wouldn't go amiss... just not in a scheduled session, thank you very much. What about you, Chloe? Still drowning in words for that new campaign? Pretty much! The brief is so vague this time. "Evoke a feeling of aspirational comfort." What  is  aspirational comfort? Is it a cashmere blanket? A sunny morning? A perfectly brewed cup of tea? Honestly, I'm pulling my hair out. Sounds like a right struggle, darling. Remember that ad for the car? The one with the couple driving through the countryside? That felt pretty aspirational, didn’t it? Maybe something like that, but with…what are they selling? Cleaning products. Aspirational cleaning. The horror. But you’re right, the visual direction helps. It’s getting there. Right, speaking of aspirational – did you ever find a proper birthday present for Auntie Sheila? Her birthday’s next week, you know. I had a look, darling. Nothing sprung out. She's got everything she needs and wants. Sentimental, though. That's the key. Remember that little porcelain robin she used to have as a child? Oh, yes! Lost it during the move, poor thing. That was heartbreaking for her. Perhaps we could try and find a similar one? There are some lovely antique shops in Sevenoaks. We could make a day of it. That's a really good idea, Mum! A little trip to Sevenoaks, vintage hunting. Sounds lovely. Better than another scented candle, anyway. Auntie Sheila wouldn't know what to do with  another  scented candle. Absolutely. Although a good smell  does  lift the spirits, doesn't it? Reminds me of your Gran’s lavender sachets. Heaven! Speaking of which, did you ever get around to clearing out the attic? It’s like a time capsule up there.

'Ere, Doris, did you 'ear from young Michael? Promised 'e'd pop 'round with a few candles, didn’t 'e? Feels like a proper gloom in this 'ouse, it does. Like a damp cellar. Michael called earlier, Arthur. He’s stuck in traffic on the M25. Said he’d be here as soon as he can. Honestly, that motorway...it's the bane of everyone's life. At least we’ve got the Aga going, though. Keeps the place marginally warmer than a refrigerator. You know, remember when we had central heating? Proper proper heating, like. Indeed. Though I question the wisdom of relying on an Aga in this climate. Inefficient, really. My firm installed a geothermal system at the new offices. Substantially more eco-friendly and, frankly, far more effective at maintaining a consistent temperature. Though, I suppose, this situation is rather...different. How are you managing with the lack of power, Arthur? Really, it's quite shocking, isn't it? The council should be doing more. Don't start railing against the council, David. They’re doing what they can. It was a massive storm, wasn’t it? Blew the whole lot out. I heard on the radio – though the reception’s dreadful – they’re working to get it back on. Remember that terrible blackout in '74? Now  that  was a proper nightmare. We were without power for three days! '74, eh? I was sweepin' the streets then. Took longer to sweep them, mind you, with no streetlights. Fell over more than once. Foot caught in a drain. Blisters somethin' dreadful. Ah, memories... Speaking of memories… Remember Brenda from the Women’s Institute? Apparently, she’s been telling  everyone  about that little affair her husband had with Mrs. Higgins’ niece! She's being so dramatic. Apparently, they’re both at the church fete today. Can you imagine? Brenda, eh? Always was a gossip. Serves Mrs. Higgins right, I say. Though, I do feel for the poor woman’s children. Awful for them, really. You wouldn’t believe the parents I've had to deal with over the years, John, in my Quality Reviewing role. The levels of dysfunction...it’s astounding. Honestly, human nature is quite fascinating, isn’t it? Complicated, messy… reminds me of a particularly challenging merger I oversaw a few years back. So many competing interests… so much emotional baggage. Required a very delicate hand, let me tell you.

…and then, right proper rudeness, innit? My Auntie Brenda, she just  stared . Like I’d grown a second head or summat. Just, “Doncaster? Really, Elodie? Still?” As if there’s summat wrong with Doncaster! I mean, it’s got the Robin Hood statue, hasn’t it? And Meadowhall, obviously. Proper shops! Not just this, like, organic vegan cafe nonsense you lot have down south. Oh, come on, it’s not  all  organic vegan nonsense. Though, I’ll admit, Cambridge does lean that way sometimes. But Auntie Brenda’s just… Auntie Brenda. She’s always been a bit… parochial, hasn't she? Remember when she refused to try Indian food because it was “too spicy for a proper English person”? Aye, she’s a brick. A lovely brick, mind, but a proper brick. She thinks anything north of Watford is wilderness. Honestly, I was trying to tell her about the new tram line. Progress! She looked at me like I'd announced I was joining the circus. A tram line! That  is  progress. London's still clinging to the Tube like it's the 1950s. I’m perpetually jammed in there. Speaking of films, did you manage to download that documentary I told you about? The one on female filmmakers in the 70s? Nah, I haven’t had a chance yet. Been flat out with the conference at the hotel. We've got a vegan cheese tasting next week. Can you imagine? A  vegan cheese tasting . Honestly, it's making my teeth ache just thinking about it. It’s all saffron this and truffle that. I told them it’d be better with a proper cheese board - Wensleydale, cheddar, maybe a bit of Lancashire. Actual cheese! You're practically vibrating with indignation. I completely understand! That documentary’s brilliant though. Really sheds light on how women had to fight tooth and nail to get their voices heard. It's made me think a lot about the industry, actually. Production control can be... well, it's not openly sexist, but you definitely feel a lack of representation sometimes. Aye, don’t I know it. The event industry’s full of lads in suits, all talking about profit margins and ‘synergy’. They wouldn’t know a good buffet from a compost heap. My mum keeps saying I should go into teaching, but… then I’d be dealing with kids and homework. No thanks. True, dealing with kids is a whole other level of stress.

…and that’s why I think the younger ones are gettin’ it wrong, Jamie. Absolutely gettin' it wrong. All this ‘Scotland for Scotland’ talk. It's not as simple as that, is it, love? Not after all these years, all the sharing and the building… But Gran, they say they feel ignored down south. Like their voices aren't heard. And the oil money… they feel entitled to more of it, don't they? Entitled? Och, Jamie, everyone feels entitled to somethin’ these days! But it ain’t about oil money, not really. It's about… identity, I suppose. A yearning for somethin’ independent. I get that, a bit, mind you. North Ferriby's changed so much over the years, a lot of it’s not the same place I grew up in. Folks callin' for 'traditional' ways, even though ‘traditional’ changes with every generation. But ripping ourselves apart... it just feels… drastic. My history teacher, Mr. Davies, he was saying it's about more than just oil. He talked about historical grievances, the Clearances, things like that. Makes you think, doesn't it? Aye, the Clearances were a terrible time. Terrible. Don’t you be forgettin' that, love. But dwellin' on events centuries past doesn’t solve the present, does it? It stirs up bitterness. And bitterness never built anything good. My own grandad, eh, he came down from County Durham, workin' in the mines. Had a terrible accent that nosey Mrs. Hargreaves used to take the mickey out of.
