Right, so, Davies  had  to go offside there, didn't he? Absolutely blatant. Honestly, the ref’s having a shocker. Typical Saturday afternoon, innit? Aye, it were a dodgy one. But, Ben, could you keep it down a bit? I’m trying to sort this regression analysis. It's proving a nightmare, the outliers are absolutely skewing everything. Sorry, love. Just… venting about the atrocious officiating. Can’t a bloke have a bit of a grumble while watching the footie? It's practically a national pastime. You get that back home, don’t ya? All the lads moaning about the ref down the pub. Aye, back home it’s practically a religion. But I’m trying to be a serious research manager here, not reminiscing about sticky floors and lukewarm pints. It’s about statistical significance, Ben, not “dodgy decisions”. Right, right. Being all brainy for me. Look, what are you even researching anyway? Still that thing about consumer habits and… what was it? Ethical sourcing? Something like that. I'm looking at the correlation between consumer awareness of environmental impact and their purchasing behaviour. It’s boring, I know. But important, apparently. And yes, I’m being brainy. You're currently offering me a critique of a Premier League referee’s performance as a valid contribution to intellectual discourse. Fair point. So, no interest in a cheeky kebab after this then? I'm starvin'. There's that new place down the road, "Kebabs R Us," apparently they do a decent one. I saw a review online – 4.8 stars! Kebabs? Ben, you know I’m trying to be… responsible. All that mayonnaise and questionable meat. Responsible? We just watched a game where grown men chased a ball for 90 minutes. A kebab is  responsible  compared to that? Come on, Anya. Little treat. Reckon we deserve it. And besides, they’ve got proper donner meat, not that pre-packaged stuff. You can tell the difference, you know. Proper donner? How do you know it's proper? Experience, pet. Years of research. . You can smell it, y’know? Proper donner has that…tang. It’s got a bit of...char. That supermarket stuff just tastes…flat. Like sadness, basically. You’re ridiculous. And you're winding me up. There's no such thing as 'proper donner'. It's all greasy meat on a rotating spit. Don't be daft. Quality varies, just like everything else.

Right then, that’s a bit strong, Grandma. You didn’t add enough milk again, did ya? Never you mind, lad. Strong tea keeps you awake. You look like you need it, always rushing about, you do. What’s all this talk about projects, anyway? Sounds like a right load of bother. It is a bit, love. He’s managing the new stadium development down in Liverpool. Massive project, apparently. All the delays have been keeping him on edge. Aye, Mum's right. It's been a nightmare. The contractors, the planning permissions, the weather… honestly, it feels like I’m battling everything all the time. Keeps me up at night, it does. Reminds me of trying to get my dissertation finished at Uni – the sheer bloody weight of it. Dissertation? What was that then, something to do with horses? You were always obsessed with horses, weren’t you? Going on about the Derby every year. Remember that chestnut mare, 'Sweet Sally'? Won by a nose! Grandma, seriously? That was when I was seven! My dissertation was on post-industrial urban regeneration. Not exactly Sweet Sally and the Derby. He was a very serious young man, our Liam. Always head in a book. Remember when he used to build those elaborate Lego castles, Liam? He wouldn't let anyone touch them! They were fortifications, Mum! Strategically important! I was planning my own kingdom, right there in the living room. It wasn't just Lego, it was... resource management! I guess that's what got me into project management, in a way. Thinking about logistics and scale. Resources… that's what it was like back then, wasn’t it? Getting anything. Ration books and all. Remember when we saved up for that Morris Minor? Your grandfather, bless him, practically spent every spare shilling on it. That car was our pride and joy. Red, it was. A proper beauty. I've seen old photos, Grandma. It  was  a beauty. Wish I could find a decent classic these days, something I could restore. The price of them is ridiculous! Everyone's obsessed with them. Honestly, Liam, you’d spend all your money on a car instead of putting it towards a house deposit. Your father would have a fit. I know, I know. But a nice classic… it’d be relaxing, you know? A proper hobby. Something to take your mind off spreadsheets and Gantt charts.

Honestly, the assembly this morning was a bit… much. Mrs. Davies went on about Shrove Tuesday and Lent for twenty minutes. Twenty minutes! I felt for the little ones, especially Thomas – he was practically drooping. Did you manage to sneak him a bit of pancake when I wasn't looking, Liam? Mmmhmm! Big one! That’s my girl. Good thing you had yours, then, Poppy. Seems like some of the children in my class are going home with barely a crumb. It’s heartbreaking, really. I had little Maisie asking if she could have the leftover syrup. Mine's cold. Can I have more syrup? Just a tiny bit, darling. You've already got loads. And Poppy, eat your banana, sweetheart, please! We need to make sure you're getting enough fruit. It's just… seeing that disparity, you know? So many of them are clearly struggling, and then you've got others who barely touch their food. It’s hard to know how best to address it, isn't it? I mentioned it to Mr. Henderson, but he just said ‘within the school's remit, we provide nutritious lunches.’ Doesn’t fix the problem, does it? I like pancakes best! Not bananas. I know, love. But sometimes we have to eat things we don’t  really  like to get strong. Remember when we read  Green Knowe  and Old Knowe was all about being resourceful? It’s a bit like that, isn’t it? Making the most of what you’ve got. Was Old Knowe a wizard? Not a wizard, darling. A very old, wise sort of person. He knew how to grow things, and fix things, and tell amazing stories. Like about finding secrets hidden in the attic! I think we should read it again next weekend. Can we go to the Science Museum then? Pleeeease? The Science Museum... that’s a good shout. We could make a weekend of it, couldn’t we? Maybe Saturday, the museum, and Sunday… hmm. The Festival Hall has that new orchestral show, the one with the space-themed music? I was thinking of booking tickets. Space music? Cool! But I want to go to the beach! Well, we can’t do the beach in March, can we? But we’ll definitely get to the beach soon. Perhaps with some of your school friends? We could pack a picnic. You know, remember when you were tiny, Poppy, and thought the bubbles were fairies?

Absolutely. It was… a lot. I mean, the sheer volume of people! And did you see what Uncle Barry was wearing? That tweed suit? It looked like he'd raided a particularly dodgy charity shop. Classic Barry. He probably thought it was funeral-appropriate. Though, to be fair, the vicar did well. Kept things moving, didn't he? A good eulogy, brief but touching. Better than that rambling disaster at Great Aunt Mildred's, anyway. Oh god,  that  was excruciating. I still have nightmares about Aunt Mildred’s performance of “Amazing Grace” on the recorder. This was… significantly less traumatic. Although, I’m starving, and this Chinese is incredible. Seriously, best we’ve had in ages. Did you order extra spring rolls, Liam? Yeah, felt like it was needed. Didn’t want a repeat of last week’s spring roll shortage debacle. Remember Finn’s face? He nearly had a meltdown. He does have a dramatic flair, that one. Though, seriously, the news is bleak, isn’t it? This heatwave… the crops are suffering terribly. Even with all my mitigation strategies, the yields are likely to be down significantly. It’s a nightmare for farmers. It is awful. Did you see they are predicting record temperatures for next week? And Boris Johnson's announced he’s going on holiday to the Caribbean  while  the country’s on fire. Talk about tone-deaf. Ugh, don’t even get me started. It's galling. I was reading an article – probably from The Guardian, so take it with a pinch of salt – about how the government’s effectively ignoring climate change warnings. Blame game. Always the blame game. You know what would cheer me up right now? Bob the Builder. Proper comfort viewing. Anyone else feel like a nostalgic binge? Oh, Liam, you’re ridiculous. Bob the Builder? You're nearly thirty! Hey, some things are timeless! Can we at least watch  one  episode? We could have a themed night, builder's snacks and everything. I appreciate the sentiment, Liam, but I've got to finish reviewing these soil samples. They’re looking rather… unhappy. So, Bob the Builder will have to wait. Perhaps something a bit more…mature? Ooh, what about  Everything Everywhere All At Once ? I’ve heard amazing things, and it’s supposed to be hilarious and heartbreaking all at once. That sounds brilliant, actually. I’ve been meaning to see that for ages.

…and honestly, Auntie Maureen was always the drama queen. Remember when she tried to convince everyone Mr. Henderson next door was a spy? Because he had a satellite dish? It was utterly ridiculous. A spy! Goodness me. Maureen always did have a vivid imagination, your Auntie. Though, to be fair, Mr. Henderson  did  spend an awful lot of time fiddling with that dish. Thought he was getting signals from Mars, he did. People back then, you know, they didn't understand technology. Nowadays, with those driverless cars everyone’s on about… that's a different kettle of fish entirely. I don’t trust those things, not one little bit. You’re worried about the safety, Dad? It  is  a bit disconcerting, isn't it? Though, statistically, they're supposed to be much safer than human drivers. Less prone to error, no drink driving... Statistics! Pah! Statistics don’t matter when you’re hurtling along at sixty miles an hour and a computer decides you're an obstacle. I'd rather have a human being behind the wheel, even if they're a bit slow sometimes. At least you know  why  they’re slowing down. Now, speaking of hurtling, did you ever fly, Sarah? Back when it was a proper adventure, not just a way to get somewhere. Of course, I’ve flown, Uncle Arthur! Several times. Though, I must say, I still get a bit jittery during turbulence. It reminds me of when Auntie Agnes tried to make rice krispy cakes for my birthday. The whole kitchen was covered in melted butter and marshmallow! A disaster. Oh, I remember those! Agnes’s attempts at baking were legendary. She followed the recipe to the letter, but always got the quantities wrong somehow. Always ending up a sticky mess. It’s funny how things change, isn’t it? Even supermarkets now. That 'Scan As You Go' thing… I tried it the other week. Complete chaos! Nearly knocked over a display of avocados. Scan as you go? Fancy that. We used to go to the grocers, you know, a proper little shop. Mr. Partridge knew everyone by name. He’d order you in your favourite jam if he had to. Now look at them, all these giant supermarkets, scanning everything... It’s lost all the personal touch, hasn't it? And the insurance! Don’t even get me started on the insurance. When we built the house in Wolverhampton, it was a pittance.

“…and then Mr. Davies said it was absolutely brilliant! He said it was the best dragon anyone in Year 3 had ever drawn. Honestly, Maisie, you just  nailed  the scales. Remember how we talked about overlapping them like tiles on a roof?” “Yeah! Like on Grandma’s house! It was sparkly, Mummy! Lots of glitter!” “Mine was… pointy.” "Pointy is good, Leo! Sharp dragons are very impressive indeed. Did you use really dark blue crayon for the horns? That was a smart choice, making them stand out." "Mm-hm. And a bit of red. For fire." "Exactly! Very observant. Now, what do you think we should eat for Chinese New Year dinner? I was thinking sweet and sour chicken, and maybe some noodles?” “Egg fried rice! Please, Mummy! And those little spring rolls with the sweet dip!” "Can we have fortune cookies?" "Of course, we can have fortune cookies! Always fortune cookies. Right, while we’re talking about China, let's remember what this year’s animal is, shall we? What comes after the Rat?" “The Dragon! Like my drawing!” She holds up the drawing proudly. "That's right! The Year of the Dragon. Did you know that in China, they have these amazing fireworks displays to celebrate? Huge, colourful ones that light up the whole sky." "Like fireworks for my birthday?" "Similar, but bigger! Much bigger. And sometimes they even shape the fireworks into dragons flying in the sky!" "Wow!" “It's a bit like building with LEGOs, but with fire! Speaking of building, Leo, did you manage to finish your solar system model at school today? You were telling me about Saturn's rings…" "Yeah. Miss Jones said I remembered all the planets in the right order. Even Pluto! She said it was super good." "See? You’re a little space expert! It's fantastic you're learning about that. Though, do you remember I said Pluto's technically not a planet anymore? Gets a bit complicated, doesn't it?" "Complicated like my piano practice?" She makes a dramatic face. "Definitely complicated! But you’re getting really good at 'Für Elise,' Maisie. Mrs. Hopkins said you have such a lovely musical ear." "I'm getting good at drums! I can do the… the… what’s the noise called?" He struggles for the word. "The beat? The rhythm?" "Yeah! The rhythm! Mr. Bell says I’m really getting the hang of it."

Yeah? What was wrong with it? I had a proper nightmare with one in Barcelona a few years back. Damp everywhere, and the wifi… forget it. Well, the pictures showed a charming little balcony overlooking a courtyard. Turns out the ‘courtyard’ was a back alley overflowing with bins and the balcony… it was barely big enough for a potted plant. And the kitchen! Oh, the kitchen. Tiny, chipped tiles, ancient appliances… I felt a bit sorry for the previous tenants, to be honest. Right, stories like that! My cousin booked a place near the Pantheon last year. Claimed it had a roof terrace, panoramic views. Ended up being a tiny window looking out onto a brick wall. She nearly went mental. Still, you're  in Rome , innit? Can’t complain  too  much. Tell you what, mate, Rome’s a cracker! Bloody love it here. Best coffee I’ve had outside of Melbourne, and the people are alright. Proper relaxed vibe, you know? Where are you lot staying exactly? Maybe I can point you towards a decent little gelato place nearby. We’re just off the Piazza Navona. Lovely area, a bit touristy, yeah, but can’t be bad. Trying to avoid the total mayhem. Thinking about heading to Trastevere for dinner tonight. Any recommendations, Elsie? Trastevere’s always a good shout. There's this little place, Da Enzo al 29, supposedly amazing pasta. But you  need  to book – it's tiny. I tried to go a few years ago, had to wait hours. Oh, Da Enzo! Proper institution. I’ve been there twice. Book  weeks  ahead, trust me. Or just go and queue – it’s an experience in itself. I was thinking we could try Armando al Pantheon tonight. Slightly more… structured. Less chaos. Structured? That’s not exactly the Roman way, is it? But Armando's alright, yeah. Good, solid food. Keeps the tourists happy. You blokes still struggling with the Italian, then? I tried to pick up a few phrases before I came, but my pronunciation’s a disaster. Mine's appalling. I can order a beer and ask where the bathroom is, and that’s about it. My mum tried to teach me some basic phrases when I was a kid, but it never stuck. I mostly just nod and smile and hope for the best. I’m a bit better, I think. I managed to compliment a shopkeeper on her shoes the other day without completely butchering the grammar.

Absolutely, El. I feel that. Remember last year, trying to plan Sarah's? Ended up being a complete nightmare with the villa falling through and the weather being atrocious. A relaxed weekend with close friends seems far smarter. What were you thinking? I was toying with the idea of renting a huge cottage in the Cotswolds. Think roaring fireplace, baking competitions, craft afternoons… loads of blankets and comfy sofas. Total hygge vibes. Hygge is brilliant! I'm in. We could even do a crafting theme – embroidery, maybe? I bought a starter kit ages ago and it's just been sitting in my cupboard. A crafting theme is  genius . Seriously. I could probably source some really lovely materials too, you know, bulk discounts and interesting suppliers. It aligns beautifully with the relaxed vibe. But baking competitions… that’s dangerous. You two are ruthless bakers. Guilty as charged! I’m still slightly traumatised by the Great Christmas Bake-Off of 2018. My gingerbread house looked like it had been through a demolition derby. It did! It was… creatively collapsed. But that's the point, isn't it? It's  us . It doesn’t have to be perfect. Which brings me back to the cottage. I’ve found a few, but one looks a bit… dated. Think floral wallpaper explosion. Floral wallpaper explosion is acceptable! Embrace the kitsch! We'll bring fairy lights and cushions. We can make it cosy. As long as they have a decent kitchen. I need space to, you know, critique the baking. Seriously though, Chloe here has a comprehensive understanding of spaces, and how to efficiently utilise them. We're bringing her in as a consultant. You are no fun, Chloe. Although, you're probably right. A functional kitchen is essential. And enough bathrooms... can't stress that enough. Remember Beth’s hen do and the single bathroom situation? Never again. Right, bathrooms noted! Okay, I'll filter the cottages based on kitchen size and bathroom count. Rosie, can you look into some embroidery kits? Different levels of difficulty, just in case some of the guests are total beginners. Absolutely! I’ll send you links tonight. I’ve been dying to try some shibori dyeing too. We could do a little workshop. Ooh, shibori! That’s gorgeous. I can research some good dye suppliers for that, too. What dates are we thinking? I’ve got a few tricky events in October, but beyond that, I’m pretty flexible.

Right, this gravy’s being a nightmare, innit? Keeps splitting. I swear, Mum’s gravy always worked a treat, but I can’t seem to get the hang of it. Feels like I’m wrestling a greased pig. You're probably rushing it, Liam. Low and slow is the key. And did you use cold stock? That's the number one culprit for split gravy, you know. Cold stock? Didn’t… I just chucked some hot water in. Didn’t think it mattered, to be honest. Everything feels like a secret, doesn’t it? Cooking, car maintenance, apparently now gravy. It’s chemistry, really. Hot stock messes with the roux. Listen, let me show you next time. We’ve got ages before your family gets here. You look peaky, by the way. Still feeling rough after that bug you had? Yeah, still a bit knackered, to be fair. Head’s a bit fuzzy. Just glad it’s not the flu. Remember last year? I was laid out for two weeks. Ruined Boxing Day. Speaking of ruined... I’m eyeing up that TripAdvisor review of the hotel in Prague. Honestly, ‘functional’ is the nicest thing anyone said about the bathroom. Functional? That's brutal. Where were you looking at? The one near the Old Town Square? I thought that seemed reasonably priced. Yeah, that one. I was thinking of surprising Chloe with a short trip in February. A bit of a city break, you know? But if the hotels are all going to be like glorified storage cupboards, I’m reconsidering. Maybe we just book a long weekend in Brighton. Less hassle. Prague's amazing, though. You should fight for it. Maybe look at a different hotel? There are cheaper options a bit further out. Transport’s easy. And think of the dumplings! Seriously, go for the dumplings. Brighton's nice, don't get me wrong, but… Prague. Still a bit grainy… You reckon a bit more flour would help? Or is that just a disaster waiting to happen? God, I wish I’d asked Mum for the recipe properly. She just kind of, you know,  does  it. It's like it's in her blood. A tiny bit, maybe. But really gently. Just a teaspoon at a time. And whisk like your life depends on it. Right, I’ll grab a potato peeler. Need to get the roast potatoes going. You’re focusing too much on the gravy.

…and honestly, Doreen, I’m just baffled by these birthday cards. They want ages  and  dates. Who needs to know I’ll be sixty-three on the 17th of October? It's just…overkill. Makes you feel ancient, doesn't it? Oh, don't be silly, Margaret. It’s just a bit of fun. A little spark of personalisation, they reckon. Though I agree, it does feel a bit much. Still, got to tick those boxes. Right, well, let's get this shopping list sorted. Are we getting those calendar fobs as well? The ones with the little knitted animals? The little knitted penguins! Of course! Mrs. Higgins at the WI makes them. Such a lovely woman, bless her. And yes, the calendar fobs. They’re always popular. We'll need a good stock. I was thinking, a couple of each, at least, for the church bazaar. And fabric markers, definitely. People love personalising them. Good thinking. I’ll put them on the list. Remember when we had to do art and craft at St. Mary’s? Mrs. Pemberton always smelt faintly of glue and sawdust. And she made us cut out paper snowflakes every December. Dreadful! Oh, goodness, yes! And the clay modelling. Remember trying to make pinch pots? Mine always looked like lumpy potatoes. Yours were actually quite respectable, though. You always  did  have a knack. Did you ever have those awful leather hockey boots back then? The ones that smelled like wet dog? Don't remind me. I had to wear those for a year. My feet were agony! Honestly, they should have been a biohazard. But you know, I was surprised at how much I enjoyed history in primary school. Mrs. Davies – proper stern woman she was – she made it so fascinating. She did. I was more into the drawing, really. Though I did enjoy listening to her read. Remember the stories she used to tell about the Vikings? Used to keep us captivated. What about you then – what did you end up studying at university? I can’t quite recall. I did English Literature, of course. Always loved reading. You went with sound recording, didn’t you? Such a clever choice. Remember how primitive computers were back then? It’s barely recognisable now, is it? It's astonishing, really. I was working with reel-to-reel tape recorders back in the seventies! And now…well, you wouldn’t believe the processing power in a smartphone.

…so, the Henderson’s, next door. Lovely couple, they are. Real busybodies, mind you, but in a harmless sort of way. Brought us a victoria sponge on moving day, they did. Bit dry, if I’m honest, but the gesture was appreciated. Proper Devon cream, though, you have to give them that. That's sweet, Dad. Are they the ones with the prize-winning roses? I saw them from the drive, they were spectacular. Aye, that’s ‘em. Apparently, they spend half their lives tending to those roses. Nearly as much time as Brenda does fussing over her dahlias, the woman next door up the lane. Speaking of which, Brenda’s a bit of a character. Keeps herself to herself mostly, but she did wave when we pulled up. Oh, Brenda. Don’t get me started on Brenda! Remember when Mrs. Davies’ cat got stuck in her apple tree? Brenda was the one who rescued it, using this complicated system of ladders and blankets. Quite a sight, it was! No! I missed that! This place is full of stories already. It’s so much quieter here than back in London, though. Remember the noise? Sirens, buses... constant. Quiet is an understatement. The biggest drama we've had is a rogue badger getting into Farmer Giles’ allotment. Caused quite a kerfuffle, it did. The trains, though... that’s what I was worried about. Thought I’d be hearing them all night. They’re not as bad as you thought, are they, dear? They’ve rerouted a good few of them since the new line was built. It’s still noticeable, of course, but it's not intrusive. Besides, you’re right in the middle of all this beautiful countryside. You can hear the birds singing! It  is  stunning. Though, honestly, I’m a bit overwhelmed with all the… gardening. It needs a lot of work. That’s where I come in. I’ve always fancied myself a bit of a green-fingered chap, you know. Bought myself a rotavator – a bit extravagant, perhaps – but it’ll make short work of that overgrown patch at the back. Mind you, I’ll need your help. My old bones aren’t what they used to be. Your "old bones" managed to navigate a boardroom for thirty years. I think you can handle a few weeds. Anyway, what did you think of the village fete last Saturday?

…Nah, still no joy. Sent off another application this mornin’. Just… feels like throwin’ yer hopes in a bin, reet? Another one for a warehouse job down in Workington. Gotta be somethin’, surely? Mmm, I’m sorry, Liam. It’s gotta turn around eventually. Did you tailor your CV this time? Like, specifically to the job description? Aye, well, as much as I can. I’ve been messin’ with that template you showed me, the one with the fancy headings. Just… everythin’ asks for experience, doesn't it? And what experience have  I  got, eh? Graduated, full stop. Ain’t exactly a gold star on me record now, is it? Don’t talk like that. You volunteered at the community centre for ages. Put that on there! And you helped your Gran with the gardening, that shows responsibility. Think about it, Liam. Gran's prize-winning marrows don't exactly scream "motivated warehouse worker," do they? . What are you studyin’ anyway? Still obsessed with that Psychology thing? Seems a bit… fancy, doesn’t it? It's fascinating! And it's a proper career, unlike… well, unlike what you keep sayin’ you want. Look, I ordered a new phone case for you online yesterday. It’s supposed to be comin’ later. It'll at least protect that screen of yours. You’re always droppin’ it. Oh, you did, did ya? Cheers, love. Right bargain, was it? Online shoppin’s gone proper mental, hasn’t it? I was lookin’ at a pair of trainers yesterday - jumped up a fiver just while I was on the page! That’s price gouging. It’s awful. They know people are desperate for a bit of retail therapy. Speaking of which, did you see that new series on Channel 4? "Northern Lights"? It’s cracking. Proper gritty, set up in Newcastle, you know. Nah, missed it. Been too busy sendin' off emails into the void. Mum keeps on about watchin’ Ant & Dec, but that’s just… noise, isn’t it? Just fillin' the hours. Reckon I could get into that Newcastle thing though. Something real, you know? Not some manufactured talent show nonsense. It's proper tense. Loads of twists and turns. It’s not like that rubbish they show on the telly these days. You should try and record it, see if it’s any good. I’ve been meaning to upgrade the aerial anyway.

…and honestly, the radiators are just  awful . They clang when they turn on, and they're freezing cold in this corner here. It's like living in a draughty Victorian mansion, isn't it? You said you were looking at those combi-boilers, Dad? Aye, I am, love. Been browsing online. Problem is, everyone's charging an arm and a leg for the installation. And the warranties… don’t even get me started on the warranties. Used to handle that sort of thing, you know. Procurement, contracts… but now… now I'm just trying to figure out how to keep my toes warm. You wouldn’t believe the prices now. Back in my day, a decent boiler was a reasonable investment. Now, it's like buying a small car. Well, a small car  would  probably last longer than some of the boilers they’re selling these days! Remember that Morris Minor your dad had, Arthur? That thing went on forever! We used to go camping in it every summer. It was rattling and wheezing by the end, but it kept going. Such a shame when they stopped making them. The Morris Minor… good times. Proper engineering, that was. Solid. Unlike these new things. Everything's built to fall apart, isn’t it? Planned obsolescence, they call it. Makes you wonder what it’s all about. Right then, lunch. Sarah, you’ve been quiet. What are we having? I was thinking a simple Ploughman’s, Dad. Cheese, crusty bread, pickles, salad. Easy peasy. We could do it on the patio if the sun comes out. Sounds lovely, dear. I’ll get the chutney. I’ve made a batch of my plum and apple chutney, it’s just perfect with cheddar. And we can get some proper cider, can’t we? Not that fizzy stuff, but the proper stuff. Cider it is! You always know how to put a spread together, Margaret. Right, so, after lunch… you’re still up for the walk, Sarah? I was thinking along the coast path. Just a gentle amble, nothing strenuous. Definitely, Dad. We could go down to the Clovelly area. I heard there's a really nice little cafe there with amazing Cornish pasties. Though, I do need to get some new walking boots. Mine are falling apart. Speaking of falling apart, have you looked at that chest of drawers yet, Arthur? The one we found at the auction.

…and honestly, the whole thing just felt a bit performative, didn’t it? Professor Davies kept going on about his “groundbreaking” methodology, but it was just a slightly tweaked version of something Hernandez published five years ago. I bit my tongue, obviously, couldn’t exactly air that in the presentation, but... ugh. It’s these conferences, isn't it? All about the networking, the name-dropping, rarely anything genuinely useful. Tell me about it. Academia’s got a veneer of intellectual rigour, but underneath, it’s just… competitive posturing. Sounds exhausting. At least our lunch was good though, that salmon was lovely. It was! Comfort food after a day of inflated egos. How was your day, by the way? Did you manage to wrangle those SEN assessment deadlines a bit? They looked positively terrifying when I glanced at your calendar this morning. Surprisingly, yes! Mrs. Henderson finally submitted all the required documentation for young Liam – took a  lot  of gentle persuasion, I can tell you. She’s clearly got her own anxieties about the process, which makes it even harder to navigate. But we got there. Liam’s going to get the support he needs, which is the important thing. It’s days like that where I feel like I'm actually making a difference, you know? More tangible than… well, than debating the subtle nuances of cognitive appraisal scales. Absolutely. That's brilliant, honestly. It sounds much more rewarding than what I was doing. It’s just… sometimes I wonder if all my research, the clever statistical analyses, the sophisticated models… do they actually  matter  in the real world? Or am I just contributing to the academic bubble? Don't talk like that, Liam. Of course they matter. Understanding anxiety, depression, coping mechanisms... it’s fundamental. Your work  informs  practice, even if you don’t see the immediate impact. Think about all the therapists using evidence-based practices now - yours could be contributing to that. You’re laying the groundwork, creating a better understanding. I try to remind myself of that. It's just… it’s hard sometimes, being so removed from the people directly affected. It feels… detached. Do you ever feel that with your work? Like you're just processing paperwork rather than truly connecting with the children and their families? Definitely. Especially when you're dealing with a backlog of assessments and the system feels like it's designed to obstruct rather than facilitate.

Oh, come on, Dad! They're not  that  mushy. And they’re good for you, you know, healthy fats and all that. Besides, this guacamole is proper good. Sarah made it, didn't you love it, love? It was brilliant, honestly. Way better than anything I could whip up. And I’m addicted to avocados now. I put them on everything! Toast, salads… even in smoothies, apparently. Smoothies? Avocados in smoothies? Blimey. You young 'uns are somethin’ else. Back in my day, avocados were somethin' you put on a cracker with a bit of smoked salmon. Simple pleasures. Your dad’s just being a grumpy old man, love. He’ll come around. Remember when he refused to eat anything spicy for years? Now he's practically demanding chillies on his chips. He does! Took a while, though. It’s funny though, isn’t it? How tastes change. I used to hate mushrooms, practically gag on them. Now I put ‘em in everything. It’s all to do with exposure, isn’t it? The more you try something, the more you might come to like it. Me, I never liked olives. Still don’t. It's like learning a language, really. At first, it’s all just a jumble of sounds, makes no sense. But then, gradually, patterns start to emerge, you pick up the grammar, and suddenly you can understand it. I’m trying to learn Spanish, you know. Getting there, slowly but surely. That’s brilliant, love! Proper impressive. I wish I'd kept up with my French. Mrs. Peterson at school was a stickler, she really pushed us. Do you remember her, Mum? The one with the perm and the terrifying stare? Oh, Mrs. Peterson! I do indeed. She was fierce, that one. But she knew her stuff. She made us conjugate verbs until we were blue in the face. Taught us a good foundation, though. Wish they did that now. Kids don't learn languages like they used to. Languages? Waste of time, most of 'em. Unless you're gonna be a diplomat or somethin'. I’ve got by just fine with English and the occasional yell. Works a treat in the decorating business, believe me. Though, I did have a bloke from Lithuania the other week. That was tricky. Lots of pointing and gesturing. You’re just saying that, John. You’re secretly brilliant at miming.

Aye, pigeons. Always were bold, weren't they? Back in Timperley, we used to have flocks of 'em pickin' at the chips outside the chippy. Lovely smell, chippy grease. Don't get that sort of smell anymore. Everything's sanitised these days. Doesn’t smell of nothin’. Honestly, Grandad, it felt like a scene from a film! I was just makin’ a cuppa, and there’s this pigeon, seemingly judging my tea-makin’ abilities. I’m Anya, by the way, for Ben’s benefit. Pleased to meet you, Anya. Ben told me a bit about you, actually. He said you’re a… a Corpus Administrator? That sounds fascinating. I'm Ben, by the way. My work is a bit less… linguistic. I'm a consultant engineer. Mostly bridges and railways, you know. Solid, reliable things. Unlike pigeons, apparently. Bridges and railways? Now that’s work! Real work. Used to work for BT meself, you know. Before… before things changed. Long time ago. Lines and exchanges, that was me. Connecting people, that's what I did. Different world then. Folks relied on the phone, you know. Didn’t have all this… internet contraption. It's wild, innit? How much has changed. I spend all day working with language data, massive collections of text and conversation. Trying to understand how language is used, how it changes. It’s surprisingly complex. It sounds incredibly interesting, Anya. A modern-day linguist, in effect. I’m always amazed by the nuances of language, how meaning can be subtly conveyed. Have you ever looked at how regional dialects evolve? Loads! That's a huge part of my job, actually. My dialect, for example – proper North-East it is - is fascinating for researchers. Things like vowel shifts, phrases that no one outside the region understands... it's a living thing! I try to preserve some of it, really. Aye, the dialect. Losing it, isn’t it? All these youngsters speakin’ like they’re readin’ from a script. They don't use the proper words anymore. Remember “quine”? Used to mean a small boy, a scamp. Don't hear that now, do you? I confess, I’ve never heard "quine." I grew up in Harpenden, Hertfordshire. Very… well, quite refined language. Pretty standard, RP really. Though my grandmother did have a few quaint phrases, mainly from her Lincolnshire roots. “Gettin’ yer ducks in a row,” that kind of thing.

Right, so, the seminar on post-structuralism – I’m still wrestling with how to make it engaging for them. They’re just…not clicking with Foucault the way I thought they would. It's like they're treating it as a checklist, 'mention the Panopticon, done.' Yeah, I understand. It’s the theory equivalent of explaining quantum physics with a PowerPoint. Dry. Have you considered, instead of just presenting the concepts, using a really specific, contemporary case study? Something they can  relate  to. I’ve been trying to think of one. The usual suspects – social media surveillance – feels a bit…obvious, doesn't it? A bit predictable. It almost feels like they anticipate you going there, and then they shut down. True. Maybe something a little less headline-grabbing. Remember that article we read about the algorithmic bias in dating apps? How they subtly reinforce existing social hierarchies? It’s Foucauldian power structures in action, just packaged in a shiny, millennial interface. That’s brilliant, actually! Much more nuanced. We could break down the architecture of the algorithms, how they collect and utilize data... It’s practically a visual representation of the Panopticon. They’re perpetually being observed, and the observation shapes their behaviour, even if they don't realise it. Exactly. It also allows for a discussion about agency – do they really have a choice, or are they being subtly guided? It's far more interesting than just lecturing about Bentham's prison design. And it’ll keep them focused. They’re easily distracted here, aren't they? Massively. It's the cafe culture, I swear. They need constant stimulation. Right, okay, algorithmic bias it is. I’ll rework the slides tonight. What about your class? Still struggling with getting them to critically engage with the Zheng He voyages? A bit. They're so caught up in the sheer scale of it – the number of ships, the distances covered – they forget to actually question  why  it ended. They see it as a shame, a missed opportunity. I'm trying to steer them away from that simplistic narrative of ‘China could have conquered the world.’ It's a historical trap, isn’t it? Always projecting current geopolitical anxieties onto the past. They need to consider the internal political dynamics at the time. The Confucian bureaucracy’s aversion to overseas trade… Precisely. And the cost - the sheer logistical, financial cost. It must have crippled the country.

Honestly, this coffee machine is a nightmare. It's leaking  again . I swear, I'm going to take a hammer to it. Ah, the Whirlwind Deluxe. Always was a bit temperamental, wasn't it? Your Dad insisted on it, you know, said it made the 'perfect crema'. Though I rarely saw any crema, just a puddle. The perfect crema! He was obsessed. Spent a fortune on those fancy beans too. Wasted, absolutely wasted. Should have just stuck to Yorkshire Tea. Now, about those storage units… I got another quote today. Nearly choked. Don't even start me on that. They're robbing us blind! £150 a month for a 20ft unit? Just for boxes full of… well, mostly your Dad's old vinyl records and duplicated planning documents, isn't it? They're  historical  documents, darling! And your father had a discerning ear. Those records… some of them are first editions. He built up a very significant collection. Significant to  him . Nobody else is going to pay a penny for them, are they? Look, we need to scale it back. We're going to be paying more for storage than we are for the cottage itself. Exactly. I’ve been looking at self-storage options further afield, smaller units, you know, moving some things into friends’ garages temporarily… but the removal costs are insane. They charged me like a queen for the garden furniture. It's just… everything feels so overwhelming. Moving after all these years… it’s more than just boxes, isn't it? It's leaving a life behind. This home… this place held so many memories. I know, love. I know. It's a big change. But we've got to be practical. We can't afford sentimentality when it comes to the bills. Besides, Hunsonby is lovely. It'll be a new chapter. Speaking of chapters… did you see Keir Starmer's speech yesterday? It was… underwhelming, to say the least. Underwhelming? That's putting it mildly. All talk, no substance. Where's the fire? Where’s the passion? It’s like he’s deliberately sanitizing his politics to offend nobody. He’s trying to broaden the appeal, Maureen. Trying to win back the Red Wall. It’s all about electoral strategy. Strategy! We need  ideals , Derek! We need somebody who believes in something! Somebody who isn’t afraid to stand up for what’s right, even if it’s unpopular.

River? Yeah, that's not bad at all, Chloe. Bit poetic, innit? Better than "Basil" like you were suggesting last week. Right, that was a moment. You massively changed your mind. I know, I know! Basil was a terrible idea. My cousin’s got a ferret called Basil. It just screamed ferret, not…me. River felt more… versatile. It could work for, like, anything. Plus, I’m obsessed with the Thames at the moment, spending every Sunday walking along it. Real connection, see? Speaking of rivers, did you lot see that thing about those canal boats they're doing up in Little Venice? Absolutely gorgeous. Tiny little houses on water. I reckon I should buy one. Next big venture after the café, maybe. A canal boat, Priya? You'd be permanently damp! Bit different from running a cafe, eh? Speaking of things a bit out of left field though... why River? Isn’t it a bit…bloke-y, Chloe? Not necessarily! It's got a softness to it. Look, you wouldn't understand. You’re all about that harsh, direct Aussie thing. I’m going for something…fluid. Besides, I think my mum will hate it, and that's worth it alone. Right, hate. My mum would probably suggest something like… Deirdre. Just to wind you up, you know? She’s got a real thing for old-fashioned names. Anyway, proper lunch this though, Priya? This pasta’s banging. Was this place empty when you came? It was! Got a deal with the owner. Said he needed to clear out the staff meal leftovers - a bit dodgy but tasted alright. He's desperate, poor bloke. So, River it is then? Actually, thinking out loud… could you technically get away with a cosmetic business called River? Like, skincare? Feels right! See! Versatile! And speaking of kosher... I was thinking while I was kneading dough this morning - have you ever thought about how strict the rules are? Like, you can't even heat up dairy with meat in the same microwave. Crazy! I tried to explain it to Ben, my flatmate, he just stared at me with his mouth open. Seriously? Microwaves? Didn’t realise it was that nuanced. You learn something every day, don’t ya? You’ve always been obsessed with this, Chloe. Like, you'll be quoting the Torah next week. Right then, so we’re talking about microwaves, let's talk about grills.

Aye, right? Proper cheek, that is. Did you tell 'im you knew exactly where 'e was? I nearly did! But I just said, “Yeah, it’s a small world, isn’t it?” Then I blocked him. Sorted. Honestly, lads, Tinder’s a minefield. You think you’re meeting someone decent, and then…bam! Exes crawling out of the woodwork. I've had a few weird ones too. One bloke sent me a picture of… well, let's just say it wasn't a scenic landscape. Immediately unmatched. Though, I kind of feel sorry for the lads who don’t get any matches. Must be a bit depressing. Depressing for them, maybe. Saves me the bother, doesn't it? I'm not spending my evenings deciphering cryptic messages and judging blurry selfies. Remember Liam from the rugby club? Sent me a message saying he liked my ‘vibe.’ A vibe! What’s a vibe, then? Is that code for something? Oh, God, Liam! He was proper weird. My cousin dated him for like, a week. Said he spent the entire time talking about crystals and aligning his chakras. No, ta, thanks. I'll stick to lads who can at least kick a ball without injuring themselves. Exactly! Speaking of lads… how's things with Mark? You were seeing ‘im a bit, weren't you, Liv? It’s complicated. He’s a sweet lad, really. But he lives for his gaming. Like,  lives  for it. Last night I was trying to watch Bake Off, and he was shouting at his screen about guilds and loot. Didn't even look up! I felt like I was dating a console. Oh, that’s rough. You need someone who can balance their hobbies with… well, with you. It's about compromise, innit? Compromise is a good word. Our housemates are all about compromise. Or, more accurately, constantly bickering about who gets the last of the biscuits. Ben ate the entire packet of digestives yesterday. The  entire  packet. No way! Those were my emergency biscuits! I was saving them for a bad day. Ben’s a biscuit monster, I swear. And then there's Chloe, leaving her hair all over the bathroom floor... it's like living in a shared zoo sometimes. Sounds familiar. Mine’s just permanently leaving mugs of tea everywhere. Everywhere! You can't swing a cat without hitting a discarded teacup. We had a clearing operation this morning.

Honestly, Arthur, you’d think they'd have learned by now. It's just kicking the can down the road. The Tories, bless their hearts, are just… hopeless. They never seem to understand how people really  live , do they? All spreadsheets and theory and nothin' about puttin' food on the table. Cor blimey, you've hit the nail on the head, Margaret. It’s not just the bills, is it? It's the Universal Credit, too. They’re makin’ it near impossible to get by. I had a right palaver with them last week, tryin' to sort out a discrepancy. They kept askin' me questions about… well, about nothin' really! Like I was tryin’ to pull a fast one! After all I've contributed to this country, mind you. Decades in civil engineering, I was! Bridges, roads, the lot. And now…now I’m bein' interrogated like some sort of criminal. Remember that bridge they built over the River Tas, Arthur? The one they closed down after three years? ‘Engineered’ it wasn't, more like… a bit dodgy, wasn't it? Now, Harold, that wasn’t  my  design. It was young Derek from Ipswich, the clever clogs. I flagged it up, I did! Told 'em the foundations weren’t right. But did they listen? No. “Derek’s got a degree, Arthur,” they said. “Trust the experts.” Ended up costin' ‘em a fortune, though, didn’t it? When it collapsed. Honestly, men and their bridges. It’s always been the same. Anyway, what about that dreadful newsreader on the telly last night? The one with the permanently furrowed brow? Breheny, you mean? Dreadful chap. No warmth whatsoever. Reads the news like he's reciting the telephone directory. Give me Trevor McDonald any day. Now  he  knew how to deliver a proper news report. They’re all awful now. No charm. Remember when they had those presenters who actually looked… respectable? They had voices you could listen to. Not this blatherin’ on they call news these days. It's the programmes themselves too, Harold. It's all reality TV and talent shows. Nothing with substance anymore. I tried to watch that documentary about the bees last week. Couldn't concentrate. Too many adverts. They cram more adverts in than actual content. That’s right, Margaret. It's the same with everything. Just a constant stream of sellin’ somethin’. Even the adverts are depressing.

Honestly, David, this pie is lovely, really it is. But I’m just… tired. Bone-achingly tired. Long day then, love? You’ve been quiet all through dinner. More quiet than usual. Anything in particular? Did that grant application fall through? Not exactly fallen through, no. They’ve…delayed it. Said they need further clarification on the impact assessment. Impact assessment! Honestly, it's like they haven't read the bloody thing. I laid out exactly how it helps the community, the volunteer hours involved, the number of families benefitting… it's all there! Bureaucracy, eh? The bane of everyone's existence. You know how it is. You poured your heart into it, showed them exactly what you're doing, and they still find a way to throw a spanner in the works. Happens to me all the time with the charity, believe me. They want endless reports on how many paperclips we’ve used and who stared at them. So true. It’s just… frustrating. We really need that funding, David. The youth centre is relying on it to keep the after-school programmes running. If they cut back... well, you know what that means for those kids. I do, love, I do. Don’t you worry. You'll sort it. You always do. Just… take a breath. Have a bit of pudding. That crumble looks good, doesn't it? Granny’s recipe, can’t go wrong with that. Tempting. Though I feel guilty eating anything more. I walked Millie for ages this afternoon, you know. Rain absolutely lashed down. Poor thing was soaked through when we got back. She loved it though, chasing those pigeons. Millie’s got a good life, doesn't she? Lucky dog. Speaking of… did you remember to book her the vet appointment? That lump she's got, needs checking. Oh, blast it all! I completely forgot. I’m so scatterbrained tonight. Can you do it, love? Please? I’ll feel terrible if she's in any discomfort and it's down to me forgetting. Just… ring them tomorrow, would you? Don't you fret, love. Sorted. I'll give them a ring first thing. Anything else I can do? Fancy a cup of tea? That would be lovely, actually. Strong, please. And maybe just a tiny bit of that crumble after all. It does smell rather wonderful. Did you hear they’re doing that old Doctor Who series again?

Aye, tell me about it. Bury’s been grey too, though not as relentlessly as you sound. My mum sent me a picture of it this morning - proper pea-souper. Feels like everywhere's drowning at the moment. I'm so sorry about your Uncle George, though. It’s awful timing with this weather, and flying over… you must be knackered. Knackered barely covers it, love. It’s been… a blur. And trying to navigate the airport, navigate the bureaucracy… it all just felt overwhelming. It's just a relief to be back here, even with the damp. At least I know where all the shops are, you know? Feels… solid. How's your mum holding up, by the way? She’s taking it bravely, I think. Trying to be strong for everyone. It’s tough, though. She was closer to him than anyone. Listen, are you alright? You look a bit peaky. Did you catch something on the flight? I think I might have. My throat’s terribly scratchy. I’ve got a bit of a cough brewing, too. Probably the stress, really. Honestly, I'm surprised my immune system hasn’t completely given up on me. It’s been under constant attack for… well, for years, hasn’t it? Remember when I was convinced I had that tropical disease after the trip to Barbados with your Aunt Penelope? How could I forget? You were convinced you’d brought something back that would wipe out the entire village! And Penelope just rolled her eyes. Still, it’s good you're laughing about it. You should really see someone about that persistent tiredness, though. I keep telling you to give therapy another go. You did seem to find it helpful for a while. It’s just… difficult, isn't it? Opening yourself up like that. And it's expensive. Honestly, I’d rather just… avoid thinking about it. It’s silly, really. Given my history, you’d think I’d be a pro at introspection by now. It's not silly, it's human. Plus, you’re paying for TEFL lessons, which is good, but you could prioritize a bit more. Maybe just a few sessions? It’s about looking after yourself, isn’t it? What about those online ones? Fewer travel costs. Hmmm, maybe you're right. We’ll see. It’s just… what’s the point, really? I keep looking at these pictures on Facebook, everyone’s off to Thailand, climbing Kilimanjaro… and here I am, stuck in Tarnow, marking essays on the present perfect tense.

…and honestly, the client just  doesn’t  get it. They want a campaign for dog food targeting millennials, and they’re insisting on using Comic Sans. Comic Sans! For a premium, organic dog food! I swear, sometimes I think I’m dealing with a time traveller who's stuck in 1998. Oh, bless. That sounds… stressful. It's like, you can lay out the reasoning, the branding guidelines, the whole nine yards, and they still just want what  they  think looks nice. My Gran used to do that with my university essays – red pen everywhere, insisting on certain fonts that were, like, fundamentally wrong for the subject matter. Exactly! It’s the wilful ignorance that gets to me. I tried to politely explain the hierarchy of typography, the importance of readability… you know, the basics. They just said, “But it’s friendly!” Friendly doesn’t sell nutritional kibble, does it? My boss just keeps saying ‘manage expectations,’ but managing expectations means smiling while watching perfectly good content get butchered. Right? It’s draining. So, how's Liam doing? You said he’d been looking at that apprenticeship with the web design firm, wasn't it? Yeah, he had the interview last week. Apparently, it went really well. He’s giddy, completely giddy. Keeps showing me mock-ups of websites he's designing in his head. It’s proper cute, innit? Think he might actually be on to something this time. He needs it, though. Living on instant noodles and sheer enthusiasm doesn’t exactly pay the bills. That’s brilliant news! Seriously, that’s what he needs – something to focus on. I remember when I was dithering about postgraduate applications. Felt like I'd never make a decision. Speaking of decisions... have you been to that new supermarket, ‘Earthly Delights’? The one just off Brick Lane? Earthly Delights? No, haven't. Is it any good? I’m dreading the weekly shop at Tesco again. It’s just… a vibe killer, you know? Endless aisles of beige food and screaming toddlers. It's... something else. Very curated. Organic everything, locally sourced, predominantly vegan options. Bit pricey, mind you, but they have the  best  avocados. Seriously, the texture is incredible. They’re like, perfectly creamy every time. Perfectly creamy avocados? You’re selling me. I’m always battling rock-hard avocados. Is it, like, a massive trek to get there? Because I'm proper skint this month.

Honestly, you two! Four o'clock! It's far too early for a Saturday. My brain hasn't quite caught up with the day yet. But Mummy! We want to show you! Look! I can do it too! Watch! Woah there, little man! Easy does it. A handstand later, okay? First, let's all have a proper breakfast. Are you two hungry? I was thinking pancakes. Pancakes! With berries! Please! And syrup! Lots of syrup! Right you are. Lots of syrup. So, after pancakes, we were thinking… remember that Neon Moon event we saw advertised? The one with the projections and the music? Oooooh! The sparkly one! Is there food there, Mummy? There should be, darling. Some food stalls, I think. It’s in Cambridge, so we’d need to leave around… say, half past two? That gives us plenty of time for pancakes and, crucially, practice our circus skills. Can I practice my ribbon dancing? Absolutely! You were brilliant the other day, twirling that ribbon. And you, my little acrobat, can keep working on your… rather enthusiastic attempts at handstands. Though maybe not on the kitchen table! But I almost did it! Nearly! Nearly is good! Right, let’s get some breakfast going. While I’m doing that, I was reading about something interesting online last night. Apparently, a friend of a friend in Australia says "G'day" instead of "good morning". G'day! That's funny! G'day, Mummy! G'day! See? It is a bit silly, isn’t it? He also said they call shoes "sandshoes." Imagine calling trainers sandshoes! Can you picture it? Trainers are for running. Sandshoes are for… sand! Yes. Sand. Exactly. You’re both very clever. Now, before we go completely off on a tangent about Australian slang, how about I whip up some pancakes? I was thinking of adding a pinch of cinnamon… With the berries! Don’t forget the berries! And lots and lots of syrup! Please, Mummy, please! You’re relentless, you two! But that’s what makes Saturdays brilliant. Just promise me, no attempting any advanced circus maneuvers before we’ve eaten. Alright? Speaker_2 & 3: Alright! Good. Now, who wants to help me sprinkle the blueberries? It's going to be a good weekend; I have a feeling about it. Especially if we don't end up climbing the curtains! Can we go on the bouncy castle at Neon Moon? Perhaps! We’ll see if there is one, darling.

Now, now, Eleanor. Let’s not get ourselves worked up three hours into a drive. You know I appreciate a good political argument, but shouting at the dashboard isn’t exactly conducive to safe driving, is it? And defending it entirely? No, I wouldn't say I  defend  it. I'm simply suggesting there's a degree of pragmatism at play. Fifteen years of Conservative austerity hasn't exactly left the Labour Party a vast well of resources to wave around. Pragmatism? David, it’s a dereliction of duty! The NHS is the bedrock of this country. To suggest we need to look at ‘efficiencies’ and ‘streamlining’ – which is code for cuts, let's be honest – is an absolute betrayal of everything the party stands for. Remember Nye Bevan? He fought tooth and nail for this, and now they’re…nibbling around the edges. Grandad always used to say Nye Bevan was a saint. Remember that, Mum? He had a statue of him in his shed. He used to tell me stories about how he queued for hours when his little sister needed an operation. Oh, yes. Your grandfather did have strong opinions. He always did. He’d be furious, wouldn’t he? Absolutely incandescent. Though, goodness knows, he'd have even  stronger  opinions on the current state of Welsh rugby… Now there’s a conversation for another time. But your grandfather understood, Gareth, that political realities aren’t always ideal. Bevan operated within a very specific context – a post-war Britain with a different economic landscape. Things have changed. Starmer's trying to navigate a minefield. Navigating a minefield or just… abandoning ship? And don't even get me started on the Lib Dems. They've become utterly indistinguishable. It's all so disheartening. It feels like… like we’re just going through the motions. It's just… a bit depressing, isn't it? All the talk, and so little seems to actually  change . The climate crisis is getting worse, tuition fees are ridiculous, and everyone’s just… shouting at each other. That’s a fair observation, Gareth. It's not all doom and gloom, mind you. There’s still good in the world, you know? Look at the community projects springing up. The grassroots activism. It takes time, progress doesn't happen overnight. Your grandfather understood that too, you know. He wasn’t just a Bevan fan; he was involved in local politics, campaigning for better services, right here in Nantyglo.

Speaker_1, Amelia, finished, a playful glint in her eye as she looked at her daughter, Elsie. Speaker_2 : "Sparkly mud? Was it  really  sparkly, Mummy? Like, did it have glitter in it?" Elsie’s eyes widened, bouncing on the kitchen stool. "Definitely sparkly, love. Because Barnaby the badger had been rolling in pixie dust earlier. He was trying to disguise himself as a dandelion! Silly badger, wasn’t he?" Speaker_3 , who'd been quietly building a tower of cereal boxes in the corner, piped up. "Badgers don’t  look  like dandelions, Mummy. They're stripey." "True, Finn. Very true. That’s why he was a  very  silly badger, trying to trick the squirrels. They were having a picnic, you see, and Barnaby wanted to steal their acorns." She paused, taking a sip of her tea. "Right, what happens next? Elsie, you tell me. Barnaby’s muddy and the squirrels see him. What do they do?" "They chase him! And he runs into the river, and then he slides down the muddy bank!" Elsie declared, her voice bubbling with excitement. "Perfect! Excellent. Finn, do you want to add something? Maybe a talking frog that gives him advice?" "A frog? Nah. He bumps into old Mr. Hawthorne, the owl. Mr. Hawthorne knows all the secrets of the forest." Finn abandoned his cereal box tower and hurried over, leaning against the counter beside his sister. "Mr. Hawthorne! Brilliant! And what does Mr. Hawthorne say to Barnaby?" "He says, 'Barnaby, dear boy, stealing is never the answer. Share your finds and you’ll make true friends.' And then he blinks his big, wise eyes." Finn demonstrated the owl blink, exaggerating it for comedic effect. "He’s spot on! He's a very wise owl indeed. That’s a lovely bit in, Finn. That’s much better than a talking frog, I think. It's almost as good as a Helen Moss story!" "Helen Moss! Are we going to the Book Festival this year, Mummy? Remember last year? She read the one about the dancing hedgehogs!" Elsie's face lit up. "Yes, darling, we are! I booked the tickets ages ago. It’s next Saturday. I'm so excited! Do you remember how everyone was wearing hedgehog ears? We should make some this year." "I want to meet her! Maybe I could ask her about...about world-building. She makes her worlds so real." Finn blushed slightly, a rare show of shyness for the usually boisterous boy.

Honestly, I still feel a little guilty even making this. It’s lovely, don’t get me wrong, but knowing where some of these ingredients come from... like, the palm oil in the satay sauce. The deforestation… it's just depressing. It's a systemic problem, Liv. It's not just the ingredients  we  choose, it's the whole damn system. One of the reasons I've been reading up so much on cultured meat. Shmeat, effectively. Isn’t it incredible? They’re growing real meat from cells, without needing animals. Shmeat. Sounds a bit… dystopian, doesn't it? Like something out of  Black Mirror . Though, admit, the environmental impact is potentially huge. Less land needed, less methane... But is it  really  meat, Cal? Like, what  is  it, fundamentally? And won’t it just be controlled by massive corporations? Same story, different medium. That's a fair point. But research is happening everywhere, not just in corporate labs. Think about the potential to eliminate factory farming entirely. Imagine, veganism isn't about deprivation anymore, it's about...choice. And morally, if we can have real meat without the inherent cruelty, shouldn’t we? Cruelty is absolutely the key, isn’t it? I spent a shift at that assisted living place yesterday and one of the residents, Mrs. Hawthorne, was absolutely distraught after seeing a documentary about hunting. Just sobbing. I had to make her a pot of chamomile and watch  Curb Your Enthusiasm  with her to distract her. Larry David, surprisingly comforting. Always a win. Though, hunting versus abattoirs... it feels like we’re just shifting the obfuscation. People see the hunter’s trophy, the dramatic landscape. But they don’t see the systematic, horrific processing and conditions in an abattoir. It’s all the same end result, isn't it? Exactly! It’s the  disconnect  that’s the problem. We've become so divorced from where our food comes from. People wouldn't happily watch a hunter skin a deer on their kitchen table, but they’ll happily eat a burger without thinking about what that burger  really  represents. Have you both been taking those B12 tablets, by the way? Doctor’s nagging me about it again. I feel fine, but apparently, my levels are “slightly suboptimal.” Always the slightly suboptimal. I’ve been pretty consistent, yeah. It's annoying, though, isn’t it? All the supplements we need to compensate for not eating meat.

Honestly, this washing machine. It's driving me mad. Three years old, and already making a racket like a cement mixer. I swear, the neighbours must think we’re having a rave every Tuesday. Oh, don't start on that thing, love. You know I’m useless with anything mechanical. Tried to fix the tap once, flooded the downstairs. Best left to the professionals, isn't it? Though, at the price of these appliances, you’d think they’d last a decade, not three. It’s just the spin cycle, isn’t it, Mum? I’ve heard loads of people say their washing machines do that. It's basically a sign of the modern age, I suppose. Constant noise pollution. It's more than just a bit of a rattle, darling. It’s a full-blown, vibrating, shuddering... ordeal. Honestly, I'm half tempted to just throw the whole thing out. Though where would we put it? And then there’s the cost of a new one! Remember how gutted your Auntie Carol was when she had to replace hers? Ended up buying one second-hand that smelled faintly of wet dog for months. Carol and dodgy appliances. That's a classic combination. Speaking of throwing things away, I was clearing out some old boxes in the attic earlier… found your Year 7 school project, Sarah! Remember that dreadful papier-mâché volcano? Oh god, don’t remind me! It leaked red paint all over Mrs. Davies’ carpet. She was not impressed. The internet has completely changed research, though. We could’ve just Googled “volcano eruption types” back then. Exactly! Everything's so much easier now. Remember trying to find a decent recipe for trifle back in the day? Cookbooks, library trips... it was a mission. Now you just type ‘Christmas trifle’ and bam! Fifty different variations appear. Still think a proper trifle needs a proper jelly, mind you. Not that wobbly blancmange stuff some people try to pass off now. And speaking of Christmas, any plans for New Year's Eve? Still thinking of that quiet night in, Sarah? Yeah, probably. Honestly, the thought of battling crowds at a pub just doesn't appeal. I'd rather Netflix and order a takeaway. Maybe watch that new series everyone’s talking about on BBC iPlayer. Have you seen “The Crimson Bloom”? No, haven't. Sounds a bit gloomy. I'm more of a “Call the Midwife” gal, myself.

Honestly, I can’t believe you two are arguing about forks. Butterfly forks! Of all the things… It's supper, not a royal banquet. But Mum, I  need  the butterfly fork. The regular one just doesn't scoop the pasta properly. It all slides off! Yeah! I’m using the butterfly one too. You’re hogging them, Finn. Hogging? Really? There are plenty of forks, boys. It’s just…why the butterfly? Where did this obsession come from? They’re better! It’s a fact. They're ergonomically superior, Mum. I read about it online. Ergonomically superior? You're ten, Leo! Eleven! And I’m serious. It's about efficiency. Right. Efficiency. Look, let’s just try to be civil, shall we? We’re supposed to be observing the two minutes' silence for Remembrance Day in a few minutes. It hardly feels respectful arguing about cutlery. Two minutes? That's ages! It’s a very important two minutes, Sam. Think about it. Think about people who didn’t come home. They sacrificed a lot. I know, Mum. It's just… boring. Boring? Suffering and sacrifice are boring? No, I didn’t mean it like that. Just… quiet for that long. I was thinking about Poppy’s birthday next week actually. Should we get her that craft set she wanted? That's a lovely idea, Leo. And yes, we absolutely should. Perhaps we can get it after we’ve paid tribute. Speaking of birthdays, remember Aunt Carol’s party? She was going on and on about that trip to Russia she took. Russia? Was it cold? Apparently freezing. She spent most of the time complaining about the weather and the borscht. Though she did say St. Basil's Cathedral was absolutely breathtaking. She took a million photos. Said the architecture was incredible. Did she see any bears? No, thank goodness! Just a lot of grey buildings and very serious-looking people, apparently. She did try to learn a few phrases though. It didn't go well, from what I gather. Kept accidentally insulting people. Like what? Oh, something about wishing them a long life…and then unintentionally saying they looked a bit…pale. Apparently, it’s not a very polite thing to point out. That’s hilarious! It wasn’t particularly hilarious for Carol at the time, I suspect. Anyway, back to forks. Can we please just agree to share? There  are  enough.

“…and honestly, the tide pools were just  packed  with tiny crabs! Leo, remember you were trying to catch one with your bucket? Nearly tipped the whole thing over!" "I  did ! It pinched me, Mummy! Ouchy!" "Crabs are funny. They walk sideways." "They are, aren't they? Proper little sideways scuttlers. Right, so, Cornwall was brilliant. Really. But… well, it did remind me we need to properly plan something for next year, doesn’t it? Something a little less… sandy-everything." "I liked the sand! I built a big castle!" “You  did  build a magnificent castle, darling. But remember how grumpy you got when it got all washed away? This year, I was thinking… Adventure Island?” "Adventure Island! With the rollercoasters?!" "Yes! The little ones, for now, of course. We can start with the gentle ones, build up. Remember the books? The Adventure Island series we used to read before bed?” "Yeah! With the pirate and the princess!" "Exactly! It’s a bit kitsch, I know, but it could be different. And it's not  miles  away. Much easier to manage with the two of you. Plus, they’ve got that seal show, which you both love." "Seals! Can we feed them fish?" "I don't think you can feed  them  fish, love. But there's definitely a lot of watching! Now, Sarah, have you looked at any dates yet?" "Mummy's busy marking. She’s got loads of papers!" "That's right. The bane of my existence. Year 11 English Literature. Honestly, the interpretation of ‘The Great Gatsby’ this year is… questionable. Some of them seem to think Gatsby eloped with Daisy’s mother! I’m going to need a strong cup of tea after this. Anyway, no, I haven’t really looked at dates. Mid-June, maybe? After I've wrestled with Fitzgerald and his flappers?" "Can we have ice cream at Adventure Island? Lots and lots of ice cream?" "Of course, we can have ice cream. As much as you like! Although, we might need to be a bit careful with you, Leo. Remember how you felt after that gelato in Cornwall?" "My tummy hurt. Too much sugar!" "Exactly. We need to be mindful of that. Maybe some sorbet for you? Or even just a little cone? And for you, darling," "what flavour would you like? Pink bubblegum?" "Pink bubblegum!" "Right. So, Adventure Island, June, potential sorbet for Leo.

…and then Mr. Davies just  stopped  mid-lecture! Like, right in the middle of explaining the French Revolution. Just stopped, looked at Liam, and said, "Liam, are you drawing dinosaurs again?" Honestly, the whole class erupted. It was brilliant. Proper brilliant, yeah. Liam’s got no shame, does he? He was sketching a velociraptor wearing a tiny powdered wig, apparently. Mrs. Patel saw it this time, though. That’s why Mr. Davies lost it. She’s got zero tolerance for anything remotely artistic. Seriously! It’s always Mrs. Patel and her spreadsheets. She's marking us down for not using enough acronyms in our history essays. Acronyms! Who actually  talks  like that? It's mental. Remember last week? You nearly had a meltdown trying to force ‘GUI’ into a paragraph about the Magna Carta. Don’t remind me! I was panicking. I felt like I was going to fail. Still, at least we got a laugh from the dinosaur incident. Speaking of laughs, are you still biking to the party on Saturday? Yeah, man. My dad’s given me a proper check-up on my bike. New tyres and everything. Should be smooth sailing to Chloe’s. You coming on your scooter? Nah, mum's dropping me. I'm trying to be sensible. Plus, I'm still worried about what Anya will say about that… incident. Oh, you mean the food fiasco? Trust me, she'll forget. Remember what happened to me last year with the peanut butter incident at Ben’s birthday? Nobody talks about that anymore. True, true. But Anya’s allergic to nuts, remember? I just felt awful thinking I'd almost let someone bring a peanut butter sandwich to a party she’s attending. You were quick on your feet though, alerting Chloe’s mum. You saved the day. Speaking of Chloe, she's freaking out about the prefect selection. Apparently, Ethan's putting himself forward. Ethan? Seriously? He’s got the charisma of a damp tea towel. No offence to Ethan, of course. None taken, I'm sure. He’ll probably promise everyone free wifi and early lunch breaks. That's his whole strategy. The school prefects are a joke, honestly. Remember when Chalmers tried to implement a 'silent corridor' policy? Oh god, that  was  a disaster! Everyone just found creative ways to whisper louder. It was ridiculous. I’m glad I don’t want to be a prefect.

Honestly, this road's a nightmare. Proper pot-holed, isn’t it? Makes you bounce about like a bairn in a bouncy castle. You’d think they'd do summat about it. Sunderland Council, eh? Don’t hold your breath. It's not great, I'll grant you that. Hertfordshire roads aren’t exactly known for their impeccable condition either, but… well, this is a different level. Less… enthusiastic. So, were you saying something about bouncy castles? Aye, just giving it a bit o’ colour, weren’t I? You always gotta add a bit of Geordie flair, don’t ya? It's a bit grey otherwise, this whole journey. Speaking o' flair, did you see the lads did alright in the cricket yesterday? A little bit, yeah. Kept an eye on the scores. Looked reasonably comfortable, didn't they? Root's form is still a worry, though. You know, I was thinking, with the Ashes coming up, they really need to get him firing on all cylinders. Perhaps a slight adjustment to his stance... Now you’re proper getting nerdy, aren't you? You and your stances. Proper technical, like. I just like seein' them smack it for four, to be honest. Don’t need to be over-analysing every single step, you know? It’s meant to be a bit o’ fun. Anyway, I’ve been thinking about getting a new bike. Oh really? What for? Your old one seemed perfectly fine last time. Are you planning on doing more cycling? Aye, well, I’ve been getting back into it a bit more. Used to cycle all the time as a kid, all around Sunderland, but life just got in the way, didn’t it? And I’m fancying a bit o’ an upgrade. Something a bit lighter, maybe. Something I could actually take out on some proper routes, not just the coast road and back. That sounds good. What are you thinking of? Road bike? Mountain bike? Hybrid? There's a  lot  of choice, you know. It’s not just about the weight, though. You have to consider the geometry, the gears, the brakes... Don’t start with the engineering jargon! I haven't got a clue about all that. I was looking at some at Cycle Republic down near the stadium, but they were all a bit pricey. I’d love something carbon fibre, but, well… a girl’s gotta eat, don’t she?

Honestly, this menu is a nightmare. So many options! And half of them are things I’ve never heard of. "Mapo Tofu"? What even  is  that? Just order the sweet and sour chicken, Elara. You always get the sweet and sour chicken. It’s foolproof. That’s precisely why I don’t  want  the sweet and sour chicken, Liam! I want to branch out. I feel like I've been eating sweet and sour chicken for the last decade. I want…adventure! Culinary adventure! Adventure sounds good! I'm starving. What are we thinking? I've googled “popular Chinese dishes” and there's a whole world beyond the usual suspects. Apparently, Dan Dan Noodles are a thing. Dan Dan Noodles... that  does  sound intriguing. But is it spicy? I don’t want to be sweating buckets while trying to watch a film later. Everything’s spicy. That’s the Chinese food rule. You order something that doesn’t explicitly say "mild" and you’re in for a fiery experience. Remember last time, Elara? You were red-faced for an hour after that Kung Pao chicken. Don’t remind me! That was traumatic. I thought I was going to breathe fire. But I  do  like a little heat. Just… manageable heat. Is there anything with a bit of flavour but not nuclear-level spice? I'm seeing a lot of recommendations for "Shui Zhu Yu" – it’s steamed fish with ginger and soy sauce. That sounds fairly mild, right? And apparently, it’s really good. Steamed fish... Okay, that’s a contender. But it feels a bit... bland? I want something with a bit of punch. What about those dumplings you were raving about last week, Chloe? The ones from that TikTok? Oh! The Shanghai soup dumplings! Yes! Those are amazing. They’re called Xiaolongbao. But they take ages to cook, apparently, and they’re a bit fiddly to eat. You have to be really careful not to squirt hot soup all over yourself. Just order two portions of sweet and sour chicken then. Problem solved. Plus, you can use the empty boxes to build a fort. Liam! This is about expanding my palate, not regressing to childhood! Chloe, are these soup dumplings something we could actually manage? I’m willing to risk a bit of soup spillage for something delicious. Yeah, I think so. They come frozen, apparently, so it’s just a matter of steaming them.

Tell me about it, Karl. Six months is nothing. We're seeing patients with chronic pain referrals delayed for upwards of a year. A year! It’s heartbreaking, really. They’re just getting sicker and sicker while they wait. You read about the funding cuts, don’t you? It’s like they  want  it to crumble.      Crumble’s the right word. I mean, you see it impacting every level. My niece, Elsie, she’s in sixth form, applying to uni. Needed to see a specialist about her eyesight, right? Prescriptions weren’t working. They said at least another two months just to get an appointment. Two months! Her grades could be affected. It’s a nightmare. I keep thinking back to when my parents would get anything sorted in Germany – felt like a production line, efficient as you like.      Germany’s always been a bit more… organised, hasn’t it? We’re all stretched so thin. Look, I’m seeing more and more people self-diagnosing and buying medication online because they’re just giving up on waiting for the official channels. It's risky, obviously, but what else are they meant to do? It's creating a whole other set of problems.      Absolutely. And the morale amongst the staff... I’ve heard stories. Sarah, my student, her mum’s a nurse at the Royal. She comes home absolutely shattered, saying they’re constantly short-staffed, asked to do extra shifts, and then they're dealing with patients who are frustrated and angry. It's a vicious cycle, innit?      A proper vicious cycle. You know, speaking of neighbours, have you seen that new family move in next door to me? The Millers?      Can’t say I have. I haven't been over that way much lately.      They’re a bit... loud. Very lively. Lots of children, which is lovely, don’t get me wrong – love kids - but they have a habit of letting off fireworks at all hours. Last night, it was nearly midnight. Nearly scared the cat witless.      Fireworks? In L8? At midnight? That's a bit much, even for me, eh? I’ve had some interesting neighbours in my time, living in various places. Once had a bloke who collected vintage gas masks... and played the tuba. Every. Single. Evening.      Oh, good grief! A tuba player and gas masks? That’s a combination! Well, the Millers aren't quite that eccentric, but the noise... it’s testing the patience, I can tell you.

…so, the whole situation with that Universal Credit claim… it’s just baffling, isn’t it, Arthur? They've sent young Liam another letter, saying they need proof he's  actively  seeking work. Actively! The lad's dusting shelves at the local corner shop, five mornings a week. What more do they want? A signed declaration from the owner? Aye, lad. Bureaucracy, innit? Bleedin’ ridiculous. Remember back in my day, you were grateful for any work, anythin’ to put a bit of food on the table. Didn't need a form for that, did ya? Just  did  it. Precisely! It feels like they’re actively trying to trip people up. And the language they use! “Suitable employment opportunities.” As if there's a queue of employers banging down the door for someone with, well, limited qualifications. Limited qualifications? You’re being kind, Stefan. Liam's a lovely lad, don’t get me wrong, but school weren’t his scene. Never really took to it. My grandson’s the same, you know. Bright lad, could’ve done somethin' good.
