But he’s off, traveling ‘round Europe, ‘doing his own thing.’ Parents are proper worried. It's a worry, isn’t it? This whole idea that young people need a structured path, a university degree… It’s alienating so many, and those opportunities aren't equally distributed, are they? I was reading about the police presence increasing around here, too. Seems they’re cracking down on petty theft, but… Police, eh? Always around when you need ‘em, they ain't. Back in ‘68, there was trouble down by the docks, real trouble. Riots, smashing windows… the police were nowhere to be seen. Then, suddenly, they were everywhere after the worst of it was over, arrestin’ anyone who looked remotely shifty. That’s precisely my concern. It feels performative, a show of force. And then there's the talk about immigration… The rhetoric gets more and more heated, doesn't it? My colleague, Zara – she’s originally from Nigeria – she mentioned feeling increasingly unwelcome in lectures. Immigration… always somethin’, isn't there? My dad used to say, “Liverpool’s always been a city of immigrants, Stefan. Irish came over, then the Chinese, then the Caribbeans… what’s the bleedin’ fuss now?” But they all get blamed, don’t they? Taking our jobs, drainin’ our resources... Never mind that they're often doin’ the jobs nobody else wants to.

Aye, tell me about it. I saw a tweet the other day – someone said their cat was "literally flying" because it jumped on the sofa. Like, relax, pet, ya noot! It didnae achieve flight, did it? Exactly! It’s become this ironic intensifier. It used to mean… well, literally. Now it’s just… fluff. It’s a linguistic apocalypse, really. I’ve flagged several instances in the corpus referencing this semantic shift. It’s fascinating from a research perspective, albeit infuriating from a purist one. I think you’re overreacting a little, aren’t you, Eleanor? Language evolves. Think about "awesome." It originally meant inspiring awe and reverence. Now, people use it to describe a particularly good sandwich. It's just the way things go. I definitely agree with Amelia. And, from my perspective, having grown up with American English, I see this kind of semantic drift all the time. “Like,” for example. It’s practically a linguistic Swiss Army knife. It indicates emphasis, pauses, filler... It’s practically its own grammatical element. The ‘literally’ thing feels very similar, albeit currently more controversial. But see, it’s different, innit? "Awesome" and "like" evolved slowly, gradually. This is like...bam! It's changed massively in, what, five years? And it's being used to mean the  opposite  of what it actually means! It’s rude to the englishto, really. All the hard work my granda put inta learnin’ it. You're getting awfully worked up about this, Chloe. Remember that time we had that whole debate about "literally" versus "figuratively" with my flatmate, Raj? He was convinced “literally” was always the correct choice, regardless of context. It was a three-hour siege of arguments. Don’t remind me. He claimed it added depth and nuance. He's a philosophy student! Oh, Raj! He always had a unique interpretation of things. But Chloe’s got a point. The speed of the shift  is  unusual. And it does feel like it’s undermining precision. My worry is, where does it stop? Are we going to end up with a language where everything means absolutely nothing? That's a bit dramatic, Amelia! We’re not there yet. I think it’s more of a symptom of a broader trend – a casualization of language, an acceptance of ambiguity. Social media probably plays a big role. Short, snappy communication… nuance gets lost. Aye, social media. Restin’ yer hopes on that lot.

…Right, so the algorithm's  still  pushing me cat videos. I swear, I watched one once, purely out of morbid curiosity, and now my entire feed is filled with fluffballs. It’s ridiculous. You’d think having a PhD in linguistics would give me some edge against the digital overlords. Wouldn’t be the first time, would it? Remember when I tried to teach my nephew about the subjunctive mood? He just looked at me like I'd sprouted a second head. Said he’d rather watch a cat chase a laser pointer. The little tyke's got his priorities straight, I reckon. Absolutely. Teaching's a lost cause, isn't it? Or at least, getting genuine engagement. I'm giving that seminar on sociolinguistics next month, and I’m dreading it. The undergraduates will mostly be thinking about what Instagram filter to use. Tell me about it. I’m doing a guest lecture on Cornish language revival at Bristol next term. It’s fascinating stuff, properly. But trying to get a room full of twenty-year-olds to care about a language spoken by, what, a few hundred people? It’s a challenge, innit? Especially when they've got TikTok beckoning. Cornish! That's brilliant. I read somewhere that they’re quite clever with the storytelling aspect. Using myths and legends to bolster language learning. Works much better than dry grammar drills. That’s exactly what I’m planning to do. I’ve been digging up old Kernewek folk tales - smugglers, giants, the whole caboodle. Much more engaging than conjugating verbs, wouldn't you say? It’s a bit like teaching French, really. Need to inject some  joie de vivre . Precisely. It’s all about context, isn’t it? Makes it relatable. Have you seen that new Korean drama on Netflix,  Extraordinary Attorney Woo ? Can't say I 'ave. Not really my cup of tea, that sort of thing. My viewing tends to be a bit more… historical, I suppose. All that pomp and circumstance. You're missing out! It’s fantastic. Really insightful look into Korean culture, but also just a genuinely entertaining story about a brilliant lawyer with autism. The way they handle the cultural differences is really clever. Subtitles permitting, of course. You know, my sister’s been trying to get me to learn Spanish for years. Says I need to broaden my horizons. But it all feels a bit… daunting.

Aye, Liam gets a bit over-enthusiastic sometimes, doesn't he? Luckily, your Grandad Arthur, he kept his counsel. You know Arthur, always the calming presence. It's a good job really, ‘cause Elsie can get right riled up if anyone disagrees with her. Well, she  was  saying they were invented by the devil to confuse children! Honestly, Gran! I told her they’re used in engineering, building bridges and stuff. She just sniffed and said bridges were built with common sense, not numbers. Common sense is all a body needs, lad. Numbers, they’re fancy. Back in my day, we built things with our hands, not a calculator! Your Grandad, he used to be a dab hand at carpentry, he could build a shed from scratch with just a hammer and a saw. No need for all these equations! Aye, Elsie's right about that. Common sense, that’s what counts. Used to fix anything around the house, I did. Radios, washing machines… nobody needed fancy math for that. Just a bit of elbow grease and a good eye. See, Arthur? Liam's trying to educate the elders! Though, I suppose, in a way, common sense  does  stem from understanding patterns and problem-solving, doesn't it? Which is what maths is all about. Right, are you two alright for tea? I’m thinking a nice roast, Elsie’s favourite. Roast sounds lovely, dear. As long as there’s a proper Yorkshire pudding with it, not one of those little sad ones you get in restaurants. A proper one, filled with gravy. Sorted, Gran. I told Mum, full-size Yorkshire puddings are non-negotiable. She’s even got that special tin she uses to get them to rise properly. Aye, a good pudding's important. We used to have them for every Sunday lunch. Used to smell wonderful, it did. All the way down the street. Speaking of Sundays, I need to sort out church on Sunday. Do you both fancy going? It's a bit of a wander, but the organ music is lovely down at St. Michael's. I was thinkin’ Liam could give you a lift after. He's got that fancy car now, doesn't he? Doesn’t drive like his dad did, though. Always rushin' about. Yeah, I can drop you off after church, Gran and Grandad. Mum says she's going to see Auntie Carol after, could I give her a lift too?

Oh, look at this! Remember Sarah’s disastrous attempt at recreating that Korean street food stall at her leaving do? The tteokbokki looked more like… well, something you'd feed the pigeons. Vaguely. It was a bit of a spectacle, wasn't it? She swore she’d watched fifteen YouTube videos. Fifteen! And it still ended up a gloopy, neon-red mess. Poor thing. She was mortified. Mortified doesn't even cover it. She hid in the bathroom for a good half hour. We had to coax her out with Prosecco. I think that’s the key to a successful leaving do – copious Prosecco. Speaking of people we miss, have you heard anything from Liam lately? Liam? No, not really. I saw something on his Instagram – he's in Nepal, trekking. Looks incredibly picturesque. All snowy peaks and prayer flags. Very Liam. Living his best adventurer life. Makes me slightly jealous, to be honest. This Beijing air is hardly inspiring. It does make you think, doesn’t it? Everyone’s out there doing exciting things. Nepal, Mexico, Iceland… and we’re… here. Which isn’t to say it’s bad, you know. It's just… different. Different, definitely. But remember why we’re here, love. The research, the connections, the opportunity for Mei. It’s not a permanent thing. It’s a chapter. And a pretty crucial one, at that. Besides, we've got pictures! Look at this one from our trip to Yunnan last year. Remember that little tea plantation? Oh, goodness, yes! That was incredible. The air was so clean, and the tea… honestly, the best I’ve ever tasted. And the guy showing us around, with his ridiculously oversized straw hat! I’m so glad we took that trip. I felt like I was breathing for the first time in ages. See? We  do  have adventures. They just might not involve scaling Mount Everest. Though, maybe we should look into some proper hiking trails around here. Something a bit greener than this concrete jungle. That's a good idea. Maybe when the weather improves. I was looking at some holiday photos my mum sent – she and Dad are in Cornwall. Beaches, pasties, cream teas… it makes me miss Norwich dreadfully. Everything smells of the sea and freshly baked bread. Cornwall's always lovely. Although, I’m not sure my stomach could handle another Cornish pasty after that street food fiasco.

Honestly, last night was…a lot. Like, a  lot  a lot. I think I need a week to recover. My head's still buzzing. Tell me about it! I feel like I've run a marathon, and all I did was stand around shouting at people to buy me another VK. Your Insta story was wild, though. Dancing on a table? Really, Liv? Don’t judge! It was Lauren’s birthday, innit? And she was blasting that cheesy 90s stuff, and everyone was just…losing it. Plus, Mark bought me a round. You know I can't say no to a free drink. Mark, eh? He looked a bit…intense in your story. Bit too much staring. Nah, he’s alright. Just… enthusiastic. He kept asking about my degree. Like, interrogating me. "So, what's Linguistics, then? Is it, like, decoding alien messages?" Honestly! Does he think I'm some kind of spy? Oh, bless him. Typical bloke, trying to make conversation. My cousin, Jay, is the same. He asked my mum what I  do  at uni the other day, like I’m just hanging about. My mum just gave him this look… you know, the one that says "Don't you  dare  underappreciate my daughter’s education." Your mum is iconic. Speaking of families, my Nan's been on at me about getting a cat. Says I need some 'stability' in my life. A cat? Right. Like you'd have time to look after a cat, Liv. You barely manage to water your succulent. I know, I know! But she showed me this adorable kitten online… fluffy, grey, with one ear slightly folded. I nearly crumbled. Plus, it'd be good for my mental health, yeah? All that purring and cuddles. You and your cats. Remember when you were obsessed with that cartoon, Felicity? You wanted a ginger cat called Pipsqueak. Don't remind me! That was, like, ten years ago! I was a weird kid. Anyway, what about you? Did you manage to actually hit the gym this week? You were all fired up about it last Friday. Nearly. I went for a walk, which counts as exercise, right? I meant to go on Monday, but then I remembered I needed to do that essay on the Victorian novel. And the library was packed. Found myself just scrolling through TikTok instead. Same old story. Tell me about it. I’ve been doom-scrolling  hard  lately.

…and honestly, Mum, I don’t think it’s fair to lay all the blame on Gran. She’s eighty-seven! She gets confused, she forgets things - it’s natural. It was more Dad’s responsibility to make sure she remembered the details of the visit, wasn’t it? Especially after last Christmas, when she nearly booked a flight to Australia! Now, now, love. Don't you start pointing fingers. Your grandfather – bless him – had a lot on his plate. He was trying to organize everything, and she…well, she's always been a bit…spirited, hasn't she? A whirlwind, that woman. And she does like to embellish the truth a bit, doesn’t she? She told me last week she was practically a wartime spy, you know. A wartime spy? Nana? More likely she was hiding biscuits from your Grandad, Mary. That's her usual form of subterfuge. But, aye, your Dad was trying to juggle a lot. It's tough, managing an elderly parent, especially one with… a vibrant imagination. But he  knew  she was getting forgetful! He knew she’d get the dates wrong. And now we’ve got her booked to come up here for the  fifteenth  of June, when we booked the cottage for the eighth. It's a nightmare trying to rearrange everything. I had to cancel my online editing project! Well, these things happen. It’s not the end of the world. Think of it as an extra visit. And honestly, a bit of sunshine would do her good. Cumbrian air is bracing. Though, keep an eye on her with the hills. She always did have a fondness for a tumble. Right, but about that fifteenth? Should we ring her? Just a gentle prod? Might avoid another international incident involving passport applications. I still can’t believe she tried to go to Brazil last year. Said she was meeting a tango instructor. I was thinking the same thing. But how do you bring it up without sounding patronizing? "Gran, you’re booked for the wrong date, again"? It’s a no-win situation. Maybe Dad should do it. He's better at the 'sweet' approach. He’ll just end up arguing with her. You know he will. He gets so frustrated when she doesn’t listen. Someone needs to be firm but kind. Perhaps you should, love. You've got that way about you.

Honestly, Mum, I still can't believe it. Just… smashed. Like a toddler attacked it. How does a laptop  slide  off a table like that? Well, it looked like you were a bit preoccupied, love. You were going on about mineral water versus tap, remember? Honestly, you two were quite the show. It’s the minerals, you see. The subtle nuances. You’ve really got to appreciate the… the  crispness  of a good bottled water. None of that Thames muck. Thames muck! Honestly, Ronald, you say the most ridiculous things. It’s perfectly good water! You’ve always been a fussy one. Anyway, at least it was just a laptop, dear. Could have been worse. Remember when I dropped your Nan’s favourite porcelain cat? Yeah, and I was about six. I still feel bad about that. Right, so, new laptop. Any thoughts? I was thinking maybe a Chromebook this time, just something simpler. Less… smashable. A Chromebook is sensible, yeah. Less to go wrong. Listen, about that walk around Brighton tomorrow... Dad, are you feeling up to it? We could check out the Lanes. The Lanes? Packed full of tourists, likely. Too much hustle and bustle for an old fella. I prefer a quiet stroll along the seafront. Maybe we can watch the gulls? Fine by me, Ronald. And if the weather’s decent, we can get some chips. You always did like your chips. Remember that time you tried to build a bird feeder, Ronald? Using that ridiculous didgeridoo you bought in Australia? It looked like a collapsing Martian spaceship. Oh, God, I’d forgotten about that! You tried to explain the physics of airflow to him for a solid hour. Speaking of ridiculous things, I’m still wrestling with this old Blackberry. Voice recognition is utterly useless. "Call Mum" results in "Calculate plum." I’m seriously considering just smashing  that  too. You’d be doubling your expenses! Honestly, Liam, you need to have some patience. It's a retro phone, not a spaceship. Oh, speaking of retro, remember Sarah from school? She's got twins now! Twins! Little darlings, I’m sure. Unlike young David down the hall. Always blasting loud music. No consideration for his neighbours, that boy. And falling asleep with the TV on… you’d think  someone  would switch it off. Tell me about it! Happens at least twice a week. Then I’m trying to find my glasses in the dark, cursing the universe.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of verb conjugations they’re struggling with is just…exhausting. It’s the Perfekt tense, Sarah! It's not rocket science! They just keep getting the auxiliary verbs mixed up. I spent half the lesson today re-explaining  haben  versus  sein . Oh, dear. You’re right, it shouldn't be. Are they having trouble with the grammar tables? My lot used to fall flat on their faces with those. Cambridge Students, of course; they think everything should be spoon-fed. No, they get the  idea  of the tables. They just… freeze. It's the application. They understand the concept of auxiliary verbs, but when presented with a simple sentence, their brains seem to just… shut down. It's almost like exam nerves even though it’s just a formative assessment. Dreadful. Makes you feel a bit responsible, doesn't it? Like you haven't quite equipped them for the world. Is it just this group, or is it across the board? A bit of both, to be honest. Some are absolute stars, really absorbing everything. But a good chunk are… struggling. It’s making me feel a little overwhelmed, I’ll admit. Did you catch the Liverpool game yesterday? Urgent news, I know, but… Briefly. Just saw the score. Disappointing, wasn't it? Typical really. Always a drama. I do miss watching it properly, you know. Everything feels so… distant here. The whole atmosphere. It was a nail-biter. Honestly, I was on the edge of my seat. Speaking of distance, how are you feeling? Still getting those grey days? My mum keeps saying I need to come home for proper winter. Don’t remind me. It’s… subtle, but it’s there. The light just lacks something. The SAD's creeping back, I think. I’ve started taking those Vitamin D supplements again. Not sure they do much, but… anything’s worth a try. I did see a little robin outside this morning, though. A cheerful touch. That’s good! Little things. You need to latch onto those. I remember when I was working on that farm near Bury for a summer, the birdsong was incredible. Proper cacophony. You'd wake up and there'd be this absolute chorus. It felt like… a reset, you know? A reset. Yes, I quite understand. A connection to… well, to something  real , I suppose. I’m thinking of getting some proper walking boots, actually.

, Liam , and Maya are sprawled around the living room, plates in hand.)     Maya:   …and then the factory manager, honestly, he just looked at me, blinked, and said, "So, are you  sure  this is the correct order?" Like I’d messed up a shipment of teabags! It was vital components for a flight simulator, Liam! Vital!   Liam:   Blimey. Sounds stressful. Though, I reckon anything involving flight simulators must be a bit intense. My job’s pretty chill, y'know? Shifting pallets around, stacking bricks… Real honest work.   Zara:   Aye, Liam, honest alright. Me, I’m dealing with floral arrangements and seating plans for the National Association of Cheese Mongers. Cheese! It’s a lot less explosive than flight simulators, but still requires intense diplomacy. Mrs. Higgins, the chairwoman, is  fierce  about her cheddar.   Maya:   Oh god, you’re kidding! A cheese mongers’ conference? What's the dress code? Formal cheese attire?   Zara:   You'd laugh. Proper business attire, apparently. And muted colours. No bright yellows, because, apparently, it clashes with mature cheddar. Honestly, I'm thinking of suggesting a 'Best Cheese Outfit' award next year.   Liam:   Now  that’s  a conference idea I could get behind. Speaking of outfits, I saw Chloe last week… you know, from sixth form? She’s got a new haircut. Proper sharp.   Maya:   Oh yeah? What's she doing these days? Still at uni?   Liam:   Nah, she’s doing somethin' with social media, I think. Loads of influencers wearin' her clothes. Sounds alright, innit? Better than puttin' bricks about all day. Though, the pay’s… well. It’s somethin'.   Zara:   Don't knock it, Liam. It’s honest work, like you said. And social media's no easy ride either. It’s a right minefield of filters and fakeness. I've been scouting locations for this charity gala – they want a ‘raw and authentic’ aesthetic. Raw and authentic! In a five-star hotel! It’s ridiculous.   Maya:   That  is  ridiculous. Everything’s got to be performative now. So, Zara, how's the dating scene? Still swiping left on blokes who only post pictures of their protein shakes?   Zara:   Don’t even get me started. Honestly, the apps are brutal. It’s just endless pictures of gym selfies and blokes fishin'. I met one bloke last week who spent the whole evening explaining the proper technique for casting a line. Honestly, I threatened to chuck a breadcrumb in the canal.

…and honestly, the sheer scale of it all, you know? Chengdu Panda Base. It's not just a few pandas in a pen. It's an enormous operation, breeding program, research facilities, all geared around these adorable bears. Reminded me a bit of Whipsnade, but multiply it by, I don’t know, ten? Right, right. Sounds impressive. Though, given the scope of the country, I suppose it has to be. It's just...a lot to take in, isn’t it? I’m still trying to wrap my head around teaching TEFL out there. It’s a world away from Bath, innit? All those classrooms… Absolutely. And the expectations. They're  very  keen on pronunciation, you see. Almost obsessive. You can spend half an hour correcting one student’s “think” and they'll still say it wrong the next class. It's frustrating, but you learn to deal. Got a colleague, Matthew, proper Yorkshireman - you wouldn't believe the looks he gets trying to explain the offside rule. Oh, I can imagine! That’d be a right kerfuffle. Speaking of explanations, what’s it like driving in rural China? I’ve been thinking about going to Devon next summer, maybe explore Dartmoor. Always fancied that. Driving? Don’t. Seriously. Don’t even  think  about it. It’s…an experience. Let’s just say the rules are… suggestions. And everything’s in Chinese, obviously. I remember trying to get to the Isle of Wight last year, feeling similar panic. The sat-nav kept trying to direct me across the Solent! Good thing I had a paper map. You're having a laugh, surely? Similar to trying to navigate Exmoor with a dodgy map, then? I always get hopelessly turned around. Brings me back to that holiday we had, what was it, 2012? Ended up on a sheep farm… Ah, yes! And they tried to feed us salted cod. Everything's salted, isn’t it? It's a major flavour profile there. It's not something you adapt to easily. It’s not a bad thing, just...different. It reminds me, one of my Chinese friends, Li Wei, he was saying Chinese birthdays are completely different to ours. They don't do big parties like we do. Much more subtle. That’s fascinating. My supervisor, Professor Davies, he's got a Chinese student, Qiao, doing a fascinating piece on…well, it's a bit dense, actually, but it’s about landscape architecture and the philosophical underpinnings of Chinese gardens.

Honestly, Liam, I still can't believe you’re doing this. Just… leaving. For a whole year! It feels mental, it does. Mental for  you , maybe. For me, it's a pretty fantastic opportunity. You know that. Working on the A303 tunnel project? It's cutting-edge engineering, Eleanor. It's exactly what I need to properly kickstart my career. Aye, I know, I know. But that doesn’t make it any less… upsetting. A year is a long time, Liam. And you know I'm not great with long distances, let alone a whole year's worth of 'em. How often are you even coming back up North? I’ve already looked into it. I can realistically get back every six weeks, maybe, on weekends. flights are a pain, but doable. I’ve booked a few in advance now - just to lock them down. End of September, mid-October… I'll send you the confirmation details later. We can even look at AirBnBs closer to Sunderland while I'm down. Fancy a weekend away somewhere nice? An AirBnB? Proper cobbled arches and a tea room nearby, like? That does sound a bit nicer than crashing on your mum's sofa again. She’s lovely, mind, but… she’ll start filling me up with everything and then give me the lectures about looking after meself. Exactly! A proper escape. Look, I know it’s a lot, El. I’m not going to pretend it’s not. But I promise I’ll make the effort. We'll FaceTime every night, I’ll send you ridiculous pictures of the tunnels – which, trust me, are surprisingly photogenic – and I’ll bring you back loads of posh biscuits. Posh biscuits don't make up for you not being 'ere, Liam. They're a start though. Right, so flights… when do you need to be down in Salisbury then? I need to clear my schedule a bit. Mr. Henderson's got a new batch of tagged data coming in next week that’s gonna need sorting. They’re expecting me on Monday, the 14th. I’ll have to be at Heathrow Sunday evening. Can you drop me off? I'd really appreciate it. Saves me the hassle of navigating the airport alone. Aye, I can do that. Though you’ll be lugging around that massive engineering bag of yours, I expect. Don’t expect me to be carrying it though.

Right. Not ideal. Still got the dodgy tummy, then? You said you were feeling a bit better on Tuesday. Aye, a bit. For like, four hours. Four glorious hours where I could eat toast without wanting to fling it back up. But then the cramping started again. Dr. Patel just says it’s “a viral thing” and to rest. Rest? Like I've got time for rest, Liam! The Henderson account is breathing down my neck. They want a full proposal on the team-building day by Friday. That’s rough, Sarah. Seriously. You’re working yourself ragged. You need to delegate, seriously. You don’t need to do  everything . Delegate? To who? Gareth? Gareth couldn’t organise a raffle, love. He’d probably give the prize to himself before anyone even bought a ticket. Liam: Harsh, Sarah. But fair, probably. Look, you need to listen to your body. And honestly, that Henderson account… it's not worth a trip to A&E. Easy for you to say, you're building fences all day! Fresh air and physical exertion. It's practically a cure. My life's spent staring at spreadsheets and trying to prevent Brenda from accidentally booking a llama farm for a corporate away day. Chloe: Brenda is a menace. Seriously. Remember the time she tried to order three hundred miniature rubber chickens for the marketing launch? Don't remind me. I nearly had a breakdown then and there. Anyway, enough about Brenda. You two seem chipper. Everything alright with you two? You've been a bit quiet. Liam: Yeah, fine. Just... a bit complicated, you know? It’s been a bit of a week, hasn’t it, love? Complicated how? Spill. Yorkshire women are notoriously good listeners, apparently. Though I'm currently listening to my stomach rumble, so my bearing capacity may be hampered. Liam: It’s Maya. We…we had a row. A proper one. About… well, about her family. Chloe: Her parents again? Liam, you’ve told them you’re serious about her, haven’t you? Liam: I’ve  tried . They keep saying I'm not “stable enough” for her. Apparently, being a labourer isn’t the most impressive career choice for their daughter, who, you know,  works in finance.  Right. That’s… that’s rotten, isn’t it? Like, seriously awful. Don’t let them get to you, Liam. You're a good lad. You're hard-working and… and you actually  listen  to people.

Honestly, it was the presentation, wasn’t it? That’s what did it for me. Mr. Davies just… stared. Like I was offering him a plate of lukewarm gruel instead of a comprehensive recovery plan. Could you  feel  the disappointment radiating off him? Yeah, Davies is… Davies. I’ve seen him do that to loads of people. He just has this default expression of mild disapproval. Don’t let it get to you, Liv. You know the plan was solid. The patient advocates loved it. They did, which makes it even more frustrating! Sarah from the advocacy group practically burst into applause. But Davies… he just mumbled something about needing “more data.” More data! I’ve got growth charts, patient testimonials, everything! Data overload, more like. You know, I spent a solid two weeks poring over that presentation. Rehearsing it in the mirror, analyzing the colour scheme… You always go all-out. It's brilliant, honestly. That’s why it’s so rubbish that Davies acted like that. Still, one grumpy old man doesn't invalidate all your hard work. Want a biscuit? I got those ginger ones you like. Please. And thank you. It’s just… it’s a pattern, isn’t it? Like, I put in the effort, I create something good, and someone always finds a reason to shoot it down. Remember the handover report last month? The one that saved Mrs. Henderson from being discharged too early? He critiqued the font size! Seriously? Over the font size? Davies is impenetrable, that’s for sure. But look, you’re making a difference, Liv. You  really  are. I hear the patients talking about you, about how reassuring you are. That’s worth more than any presentation approval from Davies. It’s just… exhausting. I came into this job to help people, not to battle bureaucratic nightmares. And then there's Mark… Oh? What's Mark doing now? Developing a sudden allergy to your existence? You have no idea. He apparently decided I was "suffocating" him. Apparently needing to, you know, actually communicate and build a relationship is suffocating. Liv, that's ridiculous. Honestly. Did he even give you a proper explanation? Vague, as always. Something about needing his "space" and "rediscovering himself." Poet, apparently. He's off to a pottery class now. To "find himself" through clay. A pottery-induced existential crisis? That’s rich. You deserve so much better than someone who ghosts you with flowery metaphors.

…and that's why the Green Knight’s challenge seemed so mad, doesn't it? He rides in, demands to be beheaded, and insists someone then has to seek him out and finish the job a year later. It’s daft, really. But why did he do it, Miss Emily? Was he being naughty? Like a goblin? Well, Elara, he wasn't exactly  naughty , not in the way you'd call stealing biscuits naughty. He was testing Sir Gawain, testing his honour. Sometimes, the things seemingly most foolish are actually tests, you see? Like when you have to share your toys even when you  really  want to play with them all yourself. But goblins  do  steal biscuits! I saw one in my storybook. He had a big sack full. You're right, Finn. Goblins often do, don't they? But this was a different kind of creature. He was magical, connected to the land, and he wanted to see if this knight was brave and true, even if it meant risking his own head. Legends are full of tricky characters, aren't they? Like the Puck in  A Midsummer Night's Dream . He loved playing pranks! Did Sir Gawain get his head chopped off? No, sweetie. That’s the exciting bit! He had to go on a long journey to find the Green Knight, and it was perilous. He faced all sorts of dangers, and he had to make very difficult choices. It’s all about temptation and doing what’s right, even when it's hard. What kind of dangers? Were there dragons? Not dragons, Finn. But there were giants, and thick forests, and strange creatures who tried to trick him out of his honour. And he had to be kind to everyone he met, even if they didn't seem very nice. It's a bit like being a good friend, isn't it? Even when someone’s being a bit… challenging. Like when Thomas took my sparkly sticker? Exactly like that, darling. He was testing you, seeing if you’d get cross and snatch it back, or if you’d be kind and understanding. Now, about supper… I was thinking shepherd’s pie tonight. It's a proper comfort food. Shepherd’s pie! With cheesy mash? Yes, with cheesy mash. You both helped me choose the vegetables earlier, remember? Now, Finn, can you go and clear up those blocks, please?

Yeah, it is. Bit of a trek. But apparently, it’s a really good opportunity for them. Prospect Research’s connected with a few people in the industry, trying to get kids interested in documentary filmmaking. Good experience, innit? Absolutely. Practical experience is invaluable. Though, I do worry about her. Anon’s still a bit quiet, you know? I hope she’ll actually  enjoy  being filmed. She hates being the centre of attention. She'll be fine, love. It's a group thing. Loads of other kids there. She'll blend in. Besides, they're doing a documentary about the local wildlife. She loves the badgers down at the river. That'll keep her engaged. Badgers! Yes, sweetheart, badgers! They’re going to film the badgers! Can we see the badgers? Maybe, mate, maybe. They’ll be busy filming. Anyway, the weather's been alright, hasn't it? Surprisingly. Still a bit nippy at night though. Did you need an extra blanket last night? It was! I actually put the heating on for a bit. Thought I was going mad, expecting to need it in May! It’s just… unpredictable these days, isn't it? Remember back in Dartford, summers were reliably hot, properly hot. Not this wishy-washy stuff. Don’t remind me. I miss a good scorcher. Keeps the motivation for the gym up, you know? Been trying to get back into it. That running machine’s a killer though. Really pushes you. You’re doing well! I noticed you looked a bit more… toned. I’m dreading getting back myself after half term. I’ve promised myself I'll rejoin the tennis club, but… oh, Anon, you’re awfully quiet. Are you alright, darling? My leg hurts. Oh, sweetheart, where does it hurt? Let me have a look. Where did you bump it? Was it at school? What happened? On the playground. I fell over. Liam pushed me. Liam pushed you? Oh, that’s not very nice. Did you tell your teacher? No… We need to mention this to the school, don't we? Bullying isn’t alright. Don’t you worry, love, we’ll talk to your teacher. It’ll be alright. Does it hurt when I push gently? Don’t get too worked up, love. Probably just a little bruise. Kids fall over, don’t they? Remember when I used to climb the old oak tree back in Norwich… nearly broke my arm once.

…and honestly, the waiting list for the hip replacement is just ludicrous. Six months! Six months feeling like this. You’d think with all the fuss about the NHS, they'd be moving these things along a bit quicker. Aye, it’s a disgrace, that it is. Though, you know, they're stretched thin, aren't they? Heard on the radio this morning they're short staffed across the board. Doesn’t make it any easier for you, of course. How’s the pain today? Manageable, I suppose. Just… persistent. Like a dull throb that never quite leaves. It’s the getting up and down that's the worst. Walking the dog is becoming a real ordeal. Little Winston’s getting frustrated, poor thing. He wants his walks, you know. Winston’s a good lad. Remember when he chewed that one of young Emily’s shoes? Sent her into a right state. Goodness, that was... what, ten years ago now? Near enough. Time flies, doesn’t it? Anyway, I was reading about the Green Party's latest proposals... the one about re-wilding the seafront. Seems a bit… ambitious, don’t you think? Turning the beach into a natural habitat? Ambitious is one word for it. Ridiculous is another. Look, Brighton’s a tourist town. People come here for the beach, for the sun, a bit of a paddle. They don’t want to be dodging reeds and wading through marshland. Used to run a little souvenir shop down by the pier, you know. Saw a lot of tourists. They want what they expect. I see your point. Though, something  has  to be done about the coastal erosion. It’s getting worse every year. We need a long-term solution, not just another concrete wall. Maybe there's a middle ground. Middle ground, aye. Now you’re talking sense. Look, my nephew, Liam, he's been struggling to find decent work. Finished his apprenticeship in carpentry a year ago, and nothing. Full of enthusiasm, he is, but no one wants to give him a chance. The competition’s fierce. It is, isn't it? Remember how easy it was to find a teaching post back in the 80s? You could almost pick and choose! Now they’re practically begging for qualified teachers. They need to invest in young people, really. Training schemes, apprenticeships… Exactly! Speaking of investing, you wouldn’t believe the bargains I got at the boot sale on Sunday.

…and honestly, Liam, the whole thing just felt…performative. Like he thought waving that flag around was going to magically revitalise his approval ratings. I mean, come on. Even  I  know you can’t just trot out dusty nationalism and expect people to forget everything else. Yeah, it was pretty textbook Trump. Tried to distract from the, you know,  actual  problems. Though, I have to admit, the reaction it provoked was pretty predictable too. Seems like everyone’s just… exhausted, isn’t it? By the constant drama. Aye, drained. Absolutely drained. It's the relentless nature of it all. Like, I was reading this thing earlier about the link between constant political anxiety and actual physiological impacts. Blimey. Gives you a right headache just thinking about it. Speaking of headaches… did you ever manage to track down that Cornish pasty place you were telling me about? Nearly did. Found a place online, seemed promising, but apparently their pastry was… suspect. Apparently, it was more like a soggy biscuit than a proper crust. Major disappointment. I’m on a mission, though. A proper, flaky, buttery pasty is a fundamental human right, I reckon. You’re mental, you are. A fundamental human right! I love it. Still, I get it. A good pasty is vital for morale. Reminds me of home, a bit. Mind, having everything shipped up from Cornwall is a bit mad, isn't it? I saw this article about vertical farming, actually. Proper cutting-edge stuff. They’re growing strawberries in shipping containers, apparently. Strawberries in shipping containers? Seriously? That’s…wild. So, like, hydroponics and LED lighting? Aye, all that jazz. Apparently, it uses a fraction of the water and pesticides. It’s all about efficiency and sustainability. I'm doing a paper on urban food production at the moment, and it's just fascinating. It’s not just about growing food, it’s about rethinking entire supply chains and the impact on the environment. It could change everything, really. That’s amazing. Though, I do worry about the slightly sterile nature of it all. You lose that connection to the earth, don’t you? That feeling of… nurturing something. Plus, the initial investment is astronomical. Who's going to foot the bill for those shipping containers full of strawberries? That’s the rub, isn’t it? It'll need investment, definitely. And it'll need to be accessible. It can’t just be a fancy thing for rich city dwellers.

…and honestly, I think it’s the lack of engagement. They just sit there, all digital natives apparently, but they can't articulate a single considered opinion on anything. I set them an essay on Marina Abramović, you know, performance art, challenging societal expectations, engaging with the body… and half of them wrote about how uncomfortable they found her covered in snails. Like, yes, it's uncomfortable, that’s the point! Right, the snails. Dramatic. Sounds like a really frustrating lecture. It's the instant gratification thing, isn't it? They're expecting entertainment, not… intellectual wrestling. Exactly! And Mark – you remember Mark from my seminar last year? The one who kept asking if he could film everything for his YouTube channel? – he actually argued that Abramović was "exploiting her vulnerability" for views. I wanted to scream. Oh, good grief. Poor you. It’s a different world, isn't it? Remember when we were at uni, arguing passionately about Deleuze and Guattari over lukewarm coffee in the refectory? Seems a lifetime ago. It does. Though, to be fair, we were fuelled by cheap instant noodles and a misguided belief in the inherent coolness of post-structuralism. But there was a  passion , you know? Now, it’s all TikTok dances and influencers. Did you see that documentary about the orcas in the Pacific Northwest? The one about J35? The one grieving her calf? Yes, absolutely heartbreaking. Brilliant documentary though. The way they were able to track their movements, interpret their calls… it’s incredible. It makes you feel so… small, doesn't it? Against the vastness of the ocean and the sophistication of these creatures. It does. And it makes you incredibly angry about what we’re doing to them. All the pollution, the noise… It feels so utterly senseless. Speaking of senseless… did you catch that new series on Channel 4? The one with all the gruesome violence? “Crimson Tide”? Yeah, I switched off after twenty minutes. Too much. Honestly, I'm starting to think all action shows are just getting relentlessly bleak. It's almost performative nihilism at this point. Precisely! And the justification is always, “It’s just entertainment.” But it normalises… everything. It's the same reason I got into trouble recently. I was chatting with a group of students about gentrification and someone brought up squatting. They were genuinely shocked that it  was  still a thing! Shocked?

Aye, Costessey weren’t all fields and daffodils, you know. Folks think Norfolk’s just pretty villages and windmills, but there were some proper rough things there in me day. That abattoir… my poor mother used to line the windows with damp cloths tryin’ to block out the smell. It’s amazing, isn’t it, how places change? Harrow was mostly residential when I grew up. The closest we got to anything like that was the butcher’s – Mr. Peterson, lovely man he was. Always gave me a sausage for my little charges. Such a reliable chap. Though, you know, I remember my father used to say, “Always question where that meat comes from, Marjorie.” Smart man, my father. Worked himself to the bone in his hardware shop. Well, you were both lucky to have parents who worked hard. My mum and dad ran a small grocer’s shop in Handsworth. Didn't make a fortune, mind, but it was honest work. And the customer service was unlike anything you see today, wasn't it? Everyone knew each other. It’s just… different now. This hostel business, eh? It's amazing you've taken it on, Liam. Well, needed summat to do. Besides, it keeps me out of me own head, doesn't it? But bless me, it's a challenge! Some young uns are alright, proper chaps, eager to work. Others... well, let’s just say they need a bit more guidance than I’m used to givin’. We've got a lad from Ukraine now, brilliant with engineering, apparently. Says he used to help his grandfather fix tractors. Engineering, you say? Fascinating! Reminds me of that documentary I saw about the Dyson. Amazing bit of science, that. All those little parts, working together… makes you wonder, don’t it? It’s not just about the build, though. It's about problem-solving, isn't it? Something I tried to instil in my little ones when they were having a tantrum over biscuits. Absolutely. Critical thinking. I spent my entire career trying to foster that. You know, I had a student last year, brilliant kid, could write essays that would knock your socks off. But he couldn’t  think  for himself. Just regurgitating what the textbook said. It’s soul-destroying, really. You’ve got to understand the  why , not just the  what . Sounds right. My nephew did sums at school, never understood a word they were teachin’ him.

Honestly, David, I'm still reeling from this evaluation. Lecturer Davies' course… it was a bit of a disaster, wasn't it? The students’ written work was… concerning, to put it mildly. I mean, undergraduate level, and they’re struggling to construct a coherent argument? Yeah, I saw the samples. Pretty rough. I mean, you know tertiary education isn't meant to be a walk in the park, but there's a baseline expectation of academic literacy you’d hope for. What do you reckon the biggest issue was? Just a lack of foundational skills, or something in Davies' teaching approach? That’s what I’m wrestling with. Part of me thinks it’s just a systemic thing. Years of dumbing down in schools, pressure on grades over genuine understanding… But Davies! He's been lecturing for, what, fifteen years? You'd assume he’d have a handle on this. He seemed so exasperated, blaming the students for not "wanting to learn." It's not that simple, is it? Definitely not. Fifteen years and he's still pointing fingers at the students? Bit bog-standard, that. Look, I’ve only been doing this a few years, but I found breaking down the concept of academic argumentation really helpful. Honestly, just mapping out the logical structure, identifying supporting evidence… sometimes it's like they’ve never even  considered  it. Did he do anything like that? Not really. There was a brief mention of Toulmin’s model, but it was glossed over. And he seemed more interested in prescribing  what  they should write, rather than  how  to structure their thoughts. The feedback I read was… vague. “Needs more analysis.” Well,  yes , but why? What kind of analysis? How do they even  begin  to do that? Sounds familiar. You know, it’s funny. Before I started lecturing, I was in recruitment for five years back in Sydney. Sounds completely different, I know, but the skills are surprisingly transferable. One of the biggest parts of my job was essentially extracting information from people, identifying their key strengths and weaknesses, and discerning the  reason  behind their answers. You learn to look beyond the surface pretty quickly. Recruitment? Really? I never would’ve guessed. That’s fascinating, actually. How did that translate into teaching? Well, it taught me to really listen to what students are  trying  to say, even if it's buried under layers of grammatical errors or weak phrasing.

Aye, reet! That's champion! Poor Professor Davies, though. He’s a bit of a stickler, isn't he? I'm Maisie, by the way. Doing my Masters in Archaeology. A bit weird, I know.      Liam. Sales assistant at Sports Direct, down in the city centre. Not as weird as diggin’ up old pots and pans, eh? The pigeon thing was brilliant though. Happened during the accounting lecture. Absolute chaos.      It does sound like you've had a week! I'm Chloe. Studying Psychology. So, Liam, Sports Direct? Anything exciting to sell these days? Apart from, you know, trainers and protein shakes.      Nah, not really. Mostly just dealing with people wanting the latest Air Max. It’s… repetitive. Though I did have a bloke try to pay for a football with a coupon for dog food last week. Kept insisting it was a "fair trade."      That’s… unforgettable. I’m Priya. I'm studying English Literature, which, conversely, involves a lot of  reading , not unbelievable customer interactions. Dog food for a football? Honestly! What were the prices like?      Priya, that's a lovely name. Archaeology’s all about uncovering stories, in a way, just like literature. Though my stories involve things like Roman pottery shards, not Shakespeare! What kind of literature are you into?      Mostly contemporary - Arundhati Roy, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie... Things that explore identity and displacement, you know? My parents are from India, so there's a lot I want to understand about belonging and moving between cultures. It’s… complicated.      That sounds fascinating! I’m totally into the psychology of belonging too. It's a huge factor in mental wellbeing, isn't it? I’m doing a module on attachment theory at the moment, which is surprisingly relevant to a lot of things.      Attachment theory? Sounds a bit heavy, doesn’t it? I’m more of a simple pleasures kinda guy. Like… finding a decent deal on a football shirt. Or watching a particularly daft cat video.      Don't knock simple pleasures, Liam! They're important. I spent last weekend trying to unearth a whole Anglo-Saxon settlement in my back garden. Didn't find much, to be honest. Just a lot of worms and my dad's old gardening tools.      You were digging in your garden? Like, seriously? That’s brilliant! Were you allowed to do that? I bet your dad wasn't too thrilled about having his tools unearthed.

Aye, sounds a bit daft, that does. Like, what’s the point o’ makin’ someone pretend to rescue folk when they’re supposed to be, you know,  actually  rescuing folk? My grandad was in the army, he’d have a right go at 'em. Said it was all a load of fancy paperwork and pretend games these days. Exactly! It's bureaucracy gone mad. My dad’s always going on about how different it was “in his day.” He says they were actually  doing  things, not running around a mock village with ping pong balls representing hostages. Though, I can see the logic in training scenarios, just… this sounds unnecessarily elaborate. Did he say what the exercise involves? Nah, just that it's supposed to be incredibly realistic. Like, they’ve got actors playing civilians, and he’s got to make split-second decisions and all that. Ben reckons it’s more stressful than actual training exercises! He’s proper worried about messing it up. He’s always been a worrier, that one. Remember when he got into a flap about picking the right colour tie for his graduation? Oh god, yes! He did. Completely overwhelmed by the formality of it all. So, computers then? You were saying something about needing help with your work system? Aye, that’s right. The conference software they’ve got at work is awful! It’s proper clunky, you know? It's like something from the nineties. I’m trying to set up a virtual breakout room for this sustainability conference next month, and it’s a nightmare. Keeps crashing, the invites don’t work properly… it’s drivin' me up the wall! You’re much better with that sort of stuff, aren’t you? All that postgrad stuff must have given you some serious skills. A bit, yeah. Mostly I just use Excel and JIRA. But I’m happy to take a look. What system is it? We could hop on a video call tomorrow and have a delve. Honestly, if it’s as bad as you say, I’m surprised they haven't just upgraded. They're pouring money into fancy coffee machines, but can't fix the basic IT infrastructure? Tell me about it! It’s ridiculous. They’re all about appearances, aren't they? Shiny new branding, but running on ancient technology. Speaking of appearances, have you seen the new issue of 'Wallpaper '?

Honestly, Liam was just…  so . Saying he’s 'not really into commitment' is like saying the Sahara is ‘a bit warm’. It’s ridiculous. I mean, six months? That’s long enough to know if someone's going to stick around, isn't it? Six months? You’re being generous, Rach. Six weeks is pushing it for that kind of declaration. You deserve better, love. Proper well, you do. You're an architect, for crying out loud! You’re building the  future . He’s probably still living with his mum and collecting Pokemon cards. Don’t be horrible, Ben! He's just trying to look out for Rach. But he’s right, Rach. You're too clever to waste your time. Remember that bloke from uni? The one who kept trying to explain Bitcoin to you? Don't remind me! He once explained quantum physics to me using a pizza. It was aggressively awkward. And frankly, I’m starting to think dating is just a huge waste of energy. Especially when half the guys seem to be auditioning for a reality TV show. I saw a bloke the other day, practically flexing in the supermarket. Like, nobody cares about your biceps, mate. It's the same everywhere, isn't it? It's dead disappointing. You know, my cousin’s just moved down from Leeds to try his luck in London. All excited about the film scene and "meeting creative types". He’ll be back in three months, broken and disillusioned, I reckon. London, eh? Mum's going down next week for that antique fair. Says she’s proper excited. I told her to keep an eye out for a decent Art Deco lamp. You know she's been hunting for one for ages. Please tell me she’s not going to buy another porcelain cat. My flat is already overflowing with them. She thinks I  want  a ceramic Siamese staring at me while I’m trying to work on structural engineering plans. You know, I was watching that documentary about gentrification the other day. Proper depressing. All these areas being priced out of reach, people displaced… and it’s all connected to this ridiculous influx of, well, people like your mum going down to London and buying up quirky little shops and antiques. It creates this… artificial charm, you know? Pushes out the actual community. That's a bit harsh, Ben. Mum’s not trying to destroy communities.

Right, so, Dad, Mum, thanks again for coming down. Hope the train wasn't too awful. It can be a bit of a nightmare, especially on a Sunday. It was fine, dear. Bit crowded, but fine. You've got a nice little… flat. Bit small for my liking, mind you. But clean, which is the main thing. And smells of… is that curry? It  was  curry! I’m trying to get a bit more adventurous with the spices, you know? This turmeric is amazing. It’s supposed to be good for the joints. Turmeric’s alright, but don't go overboard. It can interfere with certain medications. Here you go, love. Shortbread. Gemma baked them. Thanks, Mum. Dad, have a biscuit. Gemma, want one? Thanks, yeah. This place  does  need a better spice rack though. It's all just piled in a drawer at the minute. Maybe one of those tiered ones? And a new tea towel… this one’s got a curry stain. Tea towels! That's always a battle, isn’t it? My Doris, bless her, used to hoard them. We'd find piles of them under the sofa cushions. Said they were "just in case." Sounds familiar! My mum was the same. Got so many plastic bags, it was ridiculous. I'm trying to make a conscious effort to reduce my plastic, you know. It’s just… easier sometimes. Tell me about it! I keep meaning to get some reusable shopping bags, but then I remember I've left them at work and I end up grabbing a plastic one anyway. It's a vicious cycle. Speaking of work, things are a bit mad at the language school. We’re trying to entice more students with promises of holidays… travel, you know. I keep telling them about Brighton, it’s only about half an hour away. You should go! We could have a cream tea. Properly. With scones. Scones! Now there's a debate. Cream first or jam first? Cream  first , obviously! That’s the Cornish way. Gemma! That's barbaric! Devon's jam first, dear. Always. It's much more sensible. See? Even scones cause arguments! You two are incorrigible. Mum, how's the window cleaning going? It’s been drizzly all week, I bet. It’s a nightmare, really. Drains you. And the price of everything's gone up, hasn’t it? Even window cleaner! I was looking at the utility bills the other day… terrifying.

Aye, tell me about it! It's bonkers, innit? Remember when a corpus was just, like, a collection of newspaper articles? Now, you’ve got to wrangle algorithms and deal with… well, I'm still not entirely sure  what  half the data  is . My boss keeps banging on about "sentiment analysis" and "entity recognition." Sounds like some sci-fi film to me. Sentiment analysis is actually pretty cool, once you get your head around it. Essentially, the computer tries to figure out if a piece of text is positive, negative, or neutral. It's used for all sorts of things - market research, political campaigns… even predicting outbreaks of flu! Flu prediction? Right. Typical. We’re spending millions of pounds processing tweets to see if someone's got the sniffles. Me mam would just say, "Drink a hot cuppa and wrap up warm, love." Simpler times. How's the structural modelling going, then? Still wrestling with that Cambridge housing crisis? Oh, believe me, it's a wrestle. Found a plot yesterday, looks perfect for a couple of terraced houses, but the ground conditions are… challenging. Massive clay layer, horrible for foundations. Means expensive piling. These house prices are insane though, aren't they? You’d need a mortgage the size of the Tyne Bridge just to get on the ladder. Aye, the Tyne Bridge wouldn't even cover it! I swear, Cambridge is like another planet. Back home, I could get a decent little semi for, what, fifty grand? Here, you’re looking at half a million for something that’s falling apart. It's no wonder young folk are all living with their parents. It’s ridiculous. And the politicians aren’t helping, are they? All this talk about 'levelling up' but nothing actually changing. It feels like they're just throwing a few crumbs at the North while they sit pretty down south. Exactly! It’s all mouth and no trousers, isn’t it? My uncle Brian, he's always going on about Brexit and how it’s ruined everything. Can’t have a sensible conversation with him about it, though. Gets proper heated. Brexit… don’t even get me started. My grandfather, he's German, so it's a particularly sensitive subject. He says he can barely recognise England anymore. Feels like we've shut ourselves off from the world. Well, the weather’s certainly reflective of that. Dreich and grey as usual.

Right, yeah, that's rough, Tracey. Absolutely rotten, really. You’ve got the kids to think about. Agencies, eh? They all say one thing and do another. I remember when I first started, back in the day at St. Michael’s, we had a proper rota system. Everything was predictable. Now…it's a free-for-all. It sounds incredibly frustrating. You'd think with the nursing shortage, they'd be  grateful  for reliable staff. My friend Chloe, she's a primary school teacher, says it's the same with supply agencies. Constant cancellations, last-minute changes... Tell me about it! I’m hearing the same thing down at Willowbrook. We’re short-staffed something awful. Mrs. Henderson's been complaining something fierce about it too, doesn’t seem to be getting the help she needs. They're squeezing us all tighter and tighter, expecting us to do the work of three. I’ve had days where I’ve been on my feet for twelve hours straight. Yeah, it's mad. I work with an older gentleman, Mr. Davies. Lovely man, but he needs constant support. And you can feel the pressure on the other carers – they're rushed and stressed. I try to take things slow and make sure he’s comfortable, but sometimes… You're doing a good job, love. Don’t beat yourself up about it. It's a difficult job, caring, whatever form it takes. Speaking of difficult, I had a right palaver with Dr. Peterson yesterday. He’s moving, you know. Footloose and fancy-free, off to Cornwall! No! Seriously? Dr. Peterson? He was brilliant. Always took the time to listen. Who are we going to get? That’s what I said! He just shrugged and said, "Retirement beckons." Retirement! The man’s only sixty! And he was the only one who knew how to deal with Mrs. Higginbottom’s dodgy knee. She'll be going round in circles trying to get an appointment now. Oh, that’s awful for Mrs. Higginbottom. She relies on him. Honestly, the NHS is a shambles, isn’t it? It’s just getting worse and worse. We need a proper overhaul. It feels like it. Sometimes I just want to pack up and move somewhere completely different. Somewhere quiet. Ireland, maybe? Ireland's lovely. Restful. I was thinking of doing a writing retreat there next year, if I can save up.
